Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

Surat an-Nahl (The Bee)
It is also called, as Ibn Abi Hatim narrated, Surat an-Ni'am (the Chapter of Blessings). Ibn al-Faras said: because Allah the Exalted enumerates in it the blessings He bestowed upon His servants. A group of scholars stated without qualification that it is Meccan, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn az-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them. An-Nahhas narrated through the route of Mujahid, from al-Habr (Ibn 'Abbas), that it was revealed in Mecca except for its last three verses, which were revealed between Mecca and Medina on the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ return from Uhud. In another narration from him, the whole of it is Meccan except for the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a small price﴾ up to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿with the best of what they used to do﴾. Umayya al-Azdi narrated
Page 90
from Jabir ibn Zayd that forty verses of it were revealed in Mecca and the rest in Medina, and its total is one hundred and twenty-eight verses. At-Tabarsi and others said: without any disagreement. What ad-Dani mentioned in the book Al-'Adad is that it is one hundred and twenty-three, and it was said four, and it was said five, in the rest of the codices. It contains abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one): it is said to comprise four verses by consensus and one verse on which there is disagreement. The truth of the matter in this will become clear to you, if Allah the Exalted wills. When the preceding surah mentioned at its end those who mocked and denied him ﷺ, this surah began, after the saying of Allah the Exalted, "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful," with the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾, which is fitting for this, as many have mentioned concerning its meaning and occasion of revelation.
In al-Bahr, in explaining the connection, it is said that when Allah the Exalted said ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾, this was an alert to their gathering on the Day of Resurrection and their being questioned about what they did in the world. Then it was said: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾, for the intended meaning of it, according to the view of the majority, is the Day of Resurrection. As-Suyuti mentioned that the end of al-Hijr is closely linked with the beginning of this, for the saying of Allah, glorified is He, ﴿And worship your Lord until certainty comes to you﴾, which is interpreted as death, has clear connection with His saying here, ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾. Consider how in the earlier verse the word ﴿comes to you﴾ is in the present tense, while in the later one it is in the past tense (atā), because the future is prior to the past, as established in its proper place. The word amr (command) is the singular of umur (affairs). Its interpretation as the Day of Resurrection is as stated in al-Bahr, and it has been interpreted as that which includes it and other things, namely the descent of the punishment promised to the disbelievers. It is narrated from Ibn Jurayj that it is interpreted only as the descent of punishment; he said: the intended meaning of "command" here is what Allah the Exalted promised His Prophet ﷺ of victory and triumph over the enemies, and of taking vengeance upon them by killing, taking captives, plundering wealth, and seizing their dwellings and homes. Ibn Jarir and others narrated from ad-Dahhak that the intended meaning is the rulings, the prescribed limits and the obligations. It seems he understood it as one of the commands, and in what he mentioned afterwards, since no one is reported to have hastened the obligations of Allah the Exalted and His limits, glorified is He. The expression of this as "the command of Allah" is for magnification and grandeur, and in it is an indication that its realization in itself and its coming are dependent upon His binding, effective judgment and His dominant decree. Its "coming" is an expression for its approach and drawing near, in the manner of composing the expected as if it were the occurred. It is also permissible that the intended meaning is the coming of its beginnings, so the past tense remains on its literal sense. Perhaps what Ibn Mardawayh narrated through ad-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he interpreted the "command" as the emergence of the Prophet ﷺ, supports what has been mentioned. Some scholars kept the verb on its literal meaning and claimed that the meaning is: "The command of Allah has come as a promise, so do not hasten it to occur," and this, as you see, is weak. The apparent practice of the majority indicates a preference that the past tense is used with the meaning of the present, by way of metaphor, likening the certainly realized future to the past in the certainty of occurrence. The indicator of this is His saying, glorified is He, "for if what was sought to be hastened had occurred..." This is what the heart inclines to. The pronoun object in ﴿do not seek to hasten it﴾, according to what is apparent, refers to "the command," because it is what is spoken about. It was said that it refers to Allah, glorified is He, meaning: do not seek to hasten Allah with the punishment or with the coming of the Day of Resurrection, like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment﴾. This goes against what is apparent, but it has been said that this is more suited to what follows. The address is to the disbelievers specifically, and this is indicated by the reading of Ibn Jubayr, "fa-la yasta'jilūhu" in the form of the prohibition of the third person absent. Their hastening, although it was by way of mockery, was taken in its literal sense, and they were prohibited in a kind of sarcasm, not together with the believers, whether by "the command of Allah" is meant what we have mentioned before, or the punishment promised specifically to the disbelievers. As for the first, it is because
Page 91
it is not conceivable from the believers that they would hasten the Hour, or what includes it of punishment, such that the prohibition would include them. As for the second, it is because hastening from the believers is literal and from the disbelievers is mockery, so one single form does not unite both, and resorting to intending a metaphorical meaning that embraces both together without there being some secret subtle point is a far-fetched interpretation not befitting the status of the revelation.
Some have claimed the generality of the address and used as evidence what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that when the saying of Allah the Exalted ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ was revealed, the disbelievers said among themselves: "This man claims that the Resurrection has drawn near, so refrain from some of your deeds until you see what is to occur." When it was delayed, they said: "We see nothing." Then ﴿The reckoning of people has drawn near for them﴾ was revealed, so they became apprehensive and awaited its nearness. When the days lengthened, they said: "O Muhammad, we see nothing of what you threaten us with." Then ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ was revealed, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ leapt up, and the people raised their heads. When ﴿So do not seek to hasten it﴾ was revealed, they were reassured. Then the Prophet ﷺ said: "I was sent, and the Hour is like these two," and he indicated with his two fingers, "they nearly outstrip me."
There is no indication in this for that, because the basis of their reassurance is only their understanding that the intended meaning of the "coming" is the figurative coming, not the literal one which necessitates the impossibility of hastening, which in turn entails the impossibility of prohibition against it, since prohibition against a thing implies its possibility in general. The basis of that understanding is only the prohibition against hastening, which implies its possibility, which in turn requires that the impossible has not yet occurred. This does not differ according to the one who hastens, whoever he may be. Rather, there is clear indication in it of the absence of generality, because the intended meaning of "the command of Allah" is the Hour, and the occurrence of its hastening from the believers is impossible. Yes, it is permissible to restrict the address to them on the assumption that the command of Allah the Exalted is the punishment promised to the disbelievers specifically, but what the inimitability of the revelation requires is that it is specific to the disbelievers. So said Abu as-Su'ud.
It has been criticized from several aspects. Firstly, what is not conceivable from the believers is hastening in the sense of seeking the occurrence quickly, not regarding it as near; and the context of what is narrated indicates the latter, for when they heard the opening of the speech they took it literally and became agitated, so it was said to them: ﴿so do not hasten it﴾, meaning do not consider it near. Moreover, the non-conceivability of the first meaning from them is also open to objection, since they may hasten it to soothe their hearts, relieve the rage of their hearts, mock them, and laugh at them. Secondly, the combining of the literal and the metaphorical is perhaps the view of that speaker. Thirdly, the claim that the reading in the form of the prohibition of the absent third person indicates that the address is specific to the disbelievers is disputed, and its basis is evident. Fourthly, the claim that what is narrated does not indicate generality of the address is not directed at the generality of the word "people," and fifthly, his saying: "Rather there is clear indication in it of the absence of generality, because the intended meaning of the command of Allah the Exalted is only the Hour..." is refuted by saying that there is no indication in it at all of absence of generality, let alone a clear one, and you have known what is in his saying "you have known." And sixthly, his restricting the intended meaning of the command to the Hour contradicts what he mentioned in explaining His saying, ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾, where he said: that is, the Hour, or what includes it and other punishments. After this explicit statement, how can he claim that restriction? In some of these discussions there is scrutiny. Some learned scholars said: It may be said that the intended meaning of "the people" in the report is the believers, because of another report that Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Habr, who said: "When ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ was revealed, the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ were alarmed until ﴿So do not seek to hasten it﴾ was revealed, and they became calm." This too, as it is said, does not necessitate that the address is to the believers, for it may be said: when they heard the beginning of the verse they were alarmed and agitated, thinking that it had occurred; then when they heard the address of the disbelievers
Page 92
in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿So do not seek to hasten it﴾, their hearts were reassured and they calmed down. It may also be objected to the claim that the occurrence of hastening the Hour from the believers is impossible that this is true only if their hastening was in the manner of the disbelievers' hastening of it, and that is not accepted, for it is permissible that by their hastening is meant their agitation and preparation for it, which is treated as literal hastening. It was cited as evidence that the address is to the disbelievers by His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Glorified is He and exalted above what they associate with Him﴾, for on that assumption its connection with what precedes becomes apparent, and that is by saying then:

Since their hastening (for the punishment) was among the results of their polytheism, which entails ascribing to God, exalted is He, what is unfitting for Him of incapacity and need of another, and their belief that someone could prevent Him from carrying out His threat or fulfilling His promise, this was said as a new sentence (*istinaf*, a resumptive clause that begins a new statement), meaning: He is exalted and holy beyond their polytheism, which leads to the emergence of such falsehoods from them, or beyond His having any partner who could repel what He intends for them in any way. Some of them were saying, according to some reports: "If that (the punishment) does come, then the idols will rescue us from it through their intercession for us." The use of the present tense (*al-mudari'*) indicates the renewal and continuity of their polytheism, and the shift to the third person (*iltifat*, a shift from address to reference) indicates that mentioning their vile deeds calls for turning away from them, casting them out of the rank of direct address, and relating their abominations to others. This does not work if the address is restricted to the believers.

It has been said, regarding the connection on that assumption: when He forbade them from hastening, He mentioned what implies that His warning and His information are for frightening and guidance, and that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The command of God has come﴾, is only for that purpose, so that everyone prepares for his return and, before the journey, makes ready his provision. Therefore He followed this with that without a conjunction. Some have indicated the connection in terms of what follows it, so that what was mentioned serves as an introduction and a preface to it. Also, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The command of God has come﴾ is an alert and an awakening to what follows of the proofs of monotheism, end quote. You know that the connection as first established is clearer than it on this formulation, so understand.

Then, *mā* (in ﴿ما يُشْرِكُونَ﴾ context, i.e., the *mā* in *ʿammā yushrikūn*) may be relative (*mawṣūliyyah*) or verbal-infinitive (*maṣdariyyah*), and the second possibility is clearer. The first possibility necessarily requires considering what we have pointed to, otherwise the exoneration from having a partner does not become evident.

Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿تُشْرِكُونَ﴾ with the *tā'* of address, in agreement with ﴿فَلا تَسْتَعْجِلُوهُ﴾. The rest of the seven readers, along with al-A'raj, Abū Ja'far, Abū Rajā' and al-Ḥasan, read it with the *yā'* of the third person. It has already been noted that in the speech there is then an *iltifāt*, and this is based on the premise that the preceding address is to the unbelievers. But if the address is to the believers, or to them and to the unbelievers, then the two pronouns do not share one referent, so there is no *iltifāt*. Nor is there an *iltifāt* on the reading ﴿تُشْرِكُونَ﴾ with the *tā'*, whether the first address was to the unbelievers or to them and to the believers. Yes, on the assumption that the address is general, there are two instances of *taghlīb* (prevailing of one group over another in grammatical gender or reference), as has been said: the first is the prevalence of the believers over others in the address, and the second is the prevalence of others over them in the attribution of polytheism. On the reading ﴿يَسْتَعْجِلُوهُ﴾ and ﴿وَيُشْرِكُونَ﴾ with the *yā'* in both, there is neither *iltifāt* nor *taghlīb*.

﴿He sends down the angels﴾: it has been said that this is an indication of the means by which the Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, knows of the coming of what he is threatened with and of its approach, as a removal of the improbability that this knowledge is specific to him, peace and blessings be upon him, in this matter. Al-Kashf says:

"The verification is that His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿The command of God has come﴾ is an alert and an awakening, so that what follows it may be conceivable in a present mind receptive to it, and it is a preparation for the proofs of monotheism that follow."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 2 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He sends down the angels﴾ and so on, is an elaboration of what was stated in summary in His words, glorified and exalted be He: He first awakened them, then rebuked them for the polytheism they were engaged in, then followed this with the proofs of revelation (sam') and of reason ('aql). He mentioned the proof from revelation first, because its holder is also the one who establishes and refines the rational proof. So the consideration is not directed at the proof from revelation itself, but at those among the angels and messengers, peace be upon them, who carry it, and they are the ones who establish both matters together. So understand this.

Sibawayh (Sibawayh, the grammarian) inferred from this that making ﴿yunazzilu﴾ (He sends down) a circumstantial clause (hal) of the pronoun in ﴿yushrikun﴾ (they associate partners) does not fit the context at all, end quote. What he mentioned about the circumstantial status is an allusion to an objection against his teacher, the scholar al-Tibi (al-Tibi, the commentator), since he made that one of two possibilities for the clause. The second is that it is a resumptive (mustanaffa) clause, which is the apparent reading. What he alluded to regarding the aspect of connection (rabt), which he claimed to be the verified view, is not free of what is contrary to what comes first to mind. The use of the imperfect form (sighat al-istiqbal) indicates that sending down is a continuous practice of His, exalted be He. According to the majority, the word "the angels" refers to Gabriel, peace be upon him, and a single being may be referred to with a plural noun when he is a chief, as al-Wahidi said. According to some, it refers to him and those with him from the custodians of revelation (hafaza al-wahy).

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited ﴿yunzilu﴾ with a single n, from inzal (causing to descend). Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, al-A'mash and Abu Bakr recited ﴿yunazzalu﴾ with a doubled z in the passive voice, with ﴿al-malaika﴾ in the nominative as the deputy of the subject. Al-Jahdari recited it likewise but with a single z. Abu al-'Aliya, al-A'raj and al-Mufaddal from 'Asim recited ﴿tanazzalu﴾ with a feminine t at the beginning, a doubled z, and in the active voice; one of the two t's has been dropped, and the original form is ﴿tatanazzalu﴾. Ibn Abi 'Abla recited ﴿nunazzilu﴾ with the first-person plural "we" (nun al-'azama) and doubled z. Qatada recited with n and a single z. In these two readings, as stated in al-Bahr, there is a shift of person (iltifat).

﴿with the spirit﴾, that is, with the revelation (wahy), as reported by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim from Ibn 'Abbas. This includes the Qur'an. It is also narrated from al-Dahhak and al-Rabi' ibn Anas that they restricted it to this. In any case, using "spirit" for that is by way of an explicit and established metaphor (isti'ara musarraha muhaqqaqa), the aspect of resemblance being that revelation gives life to dead hearts through the disease of ignorance and error, or that religion subsists through it just as the body subsists through the spirit. This entails an implicit metaphor (isti'ara makniyya) and an imaginative metaphor (takhyiliyya), which is the comparison of ignorance and error to death and their opposite to life, or the comparison of religion to a human being with a body and a spirit. This is like when you say: "I saw a sea from which people draw, and a sun by which they seek help." This includes the comparison of the praised person's knowledge to a great water and a shining light. But it came as an accidental attribute (min 'arad), so it is not, like the nails of the sickle, anything other than an explicit metaphor. The claim that this is, in al-Kashshaf, a metaphor by way of allusion (isti'ara bil-kinaya) is not correct.

The preposition ba' (with) is connected either to the preceding verb, or to what is a circumstance (hal) of its object, meaning: He sends down the angels, being associated with the spirit. His saying, glorified be He: ﴿from His command﴾ is an explanation of "the spirit," and what is meant by it is revelation. "Command" (amr) here means "matter" (sha'n), the singular of "affairs" (umur). This does not move the spirit out of metaphor into simile (tashbih), as was said regarding His words, exalted be He: ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread of dawn﴾, because they said that there is a great gap between them, since the dawn itself is the very thing being compared and is likened to a thread. Here the general sense of "command" in the sense mentioned above is not the thing compared. For this reason, the real spirit is explained by it in His words, exalted be He: ﴿Say: the spirit is from the command of my Lord﴾, just as the figurative sense is made clear by it. Had it been said: "He casts His command which is the spirit," it would not have moved out of metaphor. So the pattern of ﴿from His command﴾ is not the pattern of ﴿from the dawn﴾, and not every explanation prevents metaphor, as may be inferred from the words of the verifier (al-Muhaqqiq) in his commentary on al-Talkhis.

It is also permitted that the prepositional phrase be connected to an omitted verb that serves as a circumstance of "the spirit," meaning: being one who arises from His command and originates from Him; or that it is a relative qualifier (sifa) of it, according to the view of one who permits omitting the relative pronoun together with part of its clause, meaning: the spirit which is from His command. Or it is connected to ﴿yunazzilu﴾ (He sends down), and "min" (from) is causal or explanatory, meaning: He sends down the angels because of His command or for its sake. The word "command" in this case is the singular of "commands." On the earlier understanding, it has been said that there are two possibilities.

Some held that "the spirit" is Gabriel, peace be upon him, and supported this with His words, exalted be He: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾, and by making the preposition ba' mean "with." It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "the spirit" is a creation of Allah, exalted be He, like the forms of the sons of Adam, and that no angel descends from the heavens except with one of them accompanying him. This was reported from Ibn Jurayj, and some have taken the verse here to mean this.

Ibn 'Atiyya criticized this, saying that this is a weak view, for which no reliable chain (sanad) has come that one can rely upon. And weaker than it, indeed, is what is reported from Mujahid, which one would hardly prefer in the verse: that what is meant by "the spirit" is the spirits of creation, and that no angel descends except with a spirit from among those spirits. ﴿upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾, that is, to send it down upon them, not because they possess attributes that qualify them for this.

The verse is evidence that prophethood is a bestowal (ataiyya), which is the correct position. It is also used to refute some Sufis who claimed that there is no need for creation to have messengers sent to them, peace be upon them. They said: "The messengers are other than Allah, and everything other than Him, glorified be He, is a veil from Him, exalted is His majesty. So the messengers are a veil from Him, exalted be He, and whatever is a veil there is no need for creation to have. Therefore there is no need for the messengers." This is manifest ignorance, and by my life it is heresy (zandaqa) and atheism (ilhad). Its corruption is as clear as its being heresy. It suffices to refute it to deny the major premise, which says that everything other than Him, glorified be He, and so on. For the messengers are a means to Allah, exalted be He, and reaching Him, mighty and majestic be He, is not a veil. Would any rational person accept that the deputy of a ruler in his lands is a veil from him? Even supposing this speaker is able to reach Him, glorified be He, without intermediary through the strength of spiritual discipline (riyada), preparedness and capacity, what of the vast majority who are not able to do what he is able to do? How will they manage?

Among those who fall into the ranks of these heretics are the Brahmins (al-Barahima), for they too denied prophethood. But they argued that reason is sufficient for what the one who is responsible (mukallaf) ought to practice: he does good, avoids evil, and takes precaution regarding what is doubtful, whether by doing or by refraining. So the prophets, peace be upon them, either bring what agrees with reason, in which case there is no need for them, or bring what contradicts it, in which case no attention should be paid to them. The answer to this is that this argument is based on the view that good and evil are rational (al-husn wal-qubh al-'aqliyyan), and the pens have been lifted, the pages have dried, and the matter has been settled in refuting this. Even if we grant it, we do not grant that reason alone suffices for everything that ought to be done. Nor do we grant that if they bring what agrees with reason there is no need for them, because they may inform the responsible person of some matters hidden from him that he ought to know, or confirm his judgment with their own judgment, and two proofs are stronger than one. Nor do we grant that if they bring what contradicts reason, no attention should be paid to them, because they may contradict it in matters hidden from it. Moreover, that supposition is impossible, since people agree that the law does not come in contradiction to reason in reality, but brings what reason falls short of grasping by itself, such as the obligation of fasting on the last day of Ramadan and the prohibition of fasting on the first day of Shawwal. The full discussion of this is to be sought in its proper place.

﴿that warn﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the spirit," on the basis that "an" (that) is the one which by its nature governs the imperfect verb (the nasiba), and it is connected to the command, just as it is connected to it in the saying: "I wrote to him: 'that stand up' (bi-an qum)." There is no harm in this, as has been verified in its proper place. That is, He sends them down while engaged in asking them to warn. Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu al-Baqa' and the author of al-Ghaniyan permitted that "an" is explanatory (mufassira), so it has no place in grammatical parsing (i'rab). This is because in the sending down of the angels with revelation there is a sense of speech, as if it were said: He says through the angels to whomever He wills of His servants: "Warn." Al-Zamakhshari permitted this, and also that "an" is the lightened form of the heavy "anna," and that the substitution applies in a certain way. He said: "The estimate is: 'that He: warn,' that is, 'that the matter is: I say to you, warn.'"

Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that making it lightened, with the omission of its noun, which is the pronoun of the matter, and estimating a verb of saying so that the predicate becomes a declarative sentence, is an artificial construction for which there is no need, given the ease of making it the dual particle which by its nature governs the imperfect verb. There is some discussion in this. In al-Kashf it is said that the verification of connecting the command with this particle, whether governing or lightened, and the omission of the verb of saying, has already passed. The real question is about the preference for the lightened form here and in Yunus, and the governing form in Nuh, which is the original, because of its fewer estimates. This is because the context of emphasis requires preferring the lightened form, which is why it was made a substitute, and the thing substituted for is what is known in its matter. Likewise in Yunus, its meaning is: "They were amazed at this matter, which is established, namely that the matter is such." As for Nuh, it is an initial statement. Their claim that the purpose of the verb of saying is to prevent the command from being a predicate, out of narrowness of disposition, is not accepted in the case of the pronoun of the matter, because it is united with what follows it, and it is like when you say: "My speech: strike Zayd."

It is read ﴿li-yunzirū﴾ (that they may warn), and warning (inzar) means informing, as has been said, except that it is specifically restricted to informing about something to be feared. That is: "Know that ﴿there is no god but I﴾." Here the pronoun refers to the matter, and this goes against the apparent rule. The benefit of beginning the sentence with it is to announce from the outset the grandeur of its content, along with what that adds of establishing it in the mind. "An" and what follows it are in the position of the second object of "warn," without any preposition being estimated for it, and the first object is omitted. The intended sense is generality: inform the people that this momentous matter is such. The reason its content signifies something to be feared is not because of its own nature, but because of the attribution to the warners of what contradicts it, namely associating partners with Him. The actual existence of the thing feared is not a condition for the reality of warning, just as the attribution described does not need to be actually realized in order for the reality of warning to hold. If you insist on the condition, then the realization of the attribution in some individuals among the warners, especially the majority, is sufficient.

Al-Raghib said: "Warning is a report containing intimidation, just as giving good news is a report containing joy." This is close to what has preceded, and its essence in both expressions is intimidation. For this reason some permitted interpreting it that way, and they estimated the first object as specific, with "an" and what follows it in the position of the second object, with a preposition estimated: "Frighten the people of disbelief and disobedience that the momentous matter is this." This is similar to what was permitted in interpreting it as informing. In that case the first object is general, and no preposition is estimated for the second. It has been mentioned that this is the original sense of the word, and that restricting it to informing about something to be feared is a later development. If that original sense is intended, its connection to what follows is clear in the extreme. If another sense is intended, it requires justification. You have already understood this where the first object is general, and the matter is even clearer, beyond needing mention, where the first object is specific.

Some of the learned have mentioned that the established usage in the language is that *anzara bihi* (نَذَرَ بِالشَّيْءِ), like *fariha bihi*, means "he was warned of it," so that *hadhdharahu* and *andharahu* mean "he informed him of what he should beware of." The language does not use it to mean "to frighten." Its root meaning is informing together with frightening, and they used it with each of its two meanings, informing and frightening, as the two parts of its meaning. End of quotation. In this there is an oversight of what we have pointed out. It is probably for this reason that it was said: he has not produced anything worth considering. ﴿So fear Me﴾: Abu al-Su'ud took this as an address to those who were hastening (the punishment), by way of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person, a sudden turn from one mode of address to another). The *fa'* is *fasihah* (an elliptical particle that introduces a conditional sense), meaning: "If the matter is as it has been mentioned, namely that it is God's custom to send down the angels upon whomever He wills of His servants, and He has commanded those upon whom they are sent down to warn people that He, may He be exalted, has no partner in divinity, then fear Me in failing to uphold its content, in engaging in what contradicts it, and in its branches, of which hastening (the punishment) and mocking are among the parts." End of quotation.

It rests, as the apparent sense requires, on his inclination that the preceding address is specific to disbelievers. Some have taken this address as also a return to the address to Quraysh, but as a consequence of monotheism. The reason it follows from it is that when He, glorified and exalted, is One, it cannot be conceived that anyone could rescue another from His punishment if He wills it. It is not permissible to make it part of what is revealed, in the sense of: "Inform them that My word is that the matter is: there is no god but I, so fear Me," or: "Frighten them with this," on the grounds that if it were so it would be said *inna* with a kasra, not with a fatha.

This was objected to by denying the necessity, since *anna* does not follow a clear or implied verb of saying. They only mentioned this in explaining the meaning in order to depict it. It is chosen that if warning means frightening, then it is evident that this matter enters into what is warned of, because it is in reality what is warned of and is the intended object of mention. If it means informing, then what is intended by informing is the first sentence, and this follows from it by way of *iltifat*. This does not escape discussion, so consider it. What the heart inclines to is that the whole is within the scope of warning. It includes monotheism, which is the culmination of the perfection of the theoretical faculty, and the command to piety, which is the highest perfection of the practical faculty. The human souls have a relation to the world of the unseen, by which they are prepared to receive forms and to be adorned with knowledge and perceptions from that world. They also have a relation to the world of witnessing, by which they are prepared to act upon the bodies of this world. Their preparedness acquired through the first relation is called the theoretical faculty, and their preparedness through the second relation is called the practical faculty. The highest perfection of the theoretical faculty is knowing that there is no god but God, the Exalted, and the highest perfection of the practical faculty is performing righteous deeds that protect from the disgrace of the Day of Resurrection.

[p. 96]

The saying of the Exalted, ﴿There is no god but I﴾, is placed before His saying, glorified is He, ﴿so fear Me﴾, to indicate that what is based on the theoretical faculty is higher in perfection than what is based on the practical faculty. Human perfection in terms of these two faculties is called psychic perfection. It has other perfections, which are its bodily perfections and its animal faculties, and this has been explained in its proper place.

Then He, exalted is He, began to lay out the rational proofs that point to His Oneness, which is the greatest aim of sending the Messengers, peace be upon them. So He, mighty in speech, said: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾.

Some of the verifying scholars (muhaqqiqun) have mentioned that He, exalted is His majesty and great is His proof, has comprehensively set out the proofs of Oneness and the attributes of His noble Essence, with the qualities of majesty and generosity, in a wondrous style in which He combined the indication of the created thing upon the Creator and of blessing upon the Benefactor. He drew attention to the fact that each one of these is sufficient to turn the polytheists away from the polytheism they are engaged in. The whole noble surah revolves around this: whenever He gives them insight through some of the insights, He includes in it their rebuke and their ingratitude for the two blessings of providence (ri'aya) and guidance (hidaya). Look at its opening, and then at its closing, in His words, glorified is He: ﴿And be patient﴾ to the end of the surah; there is made clear to you some of the secrets of eloquence and the lights of inimitability that the noble Book contains.

By "the heavens and the earth" is meant either these known bodies and masses, or the directions of above and below; that is, He brought that into being connected with what is due to it according to the requirements of wisdom. This indicates a living, knowing, powerful, willing Creator, singular in divinity and lordship. Otherwise it would follow that mutual opposition (tamanu') is possible, which entails the possibility of the impossible, as is explained in the science of kalam (theology). For this reason He followed it with His words, exalted is He: ﴿Exalted is He above what they associate with Him﴾.

Al-A'mash read «fa-ta'ala» with a fa' (فَتَعالى). The ma (ما) in ﴿عَمّا يُشْرِكُونَ﴾ may be a verbal (masdariyya) particle, meaning: exalted and sanctified is He, in His Essence and His acts, above their association; and it may be a relative (mawsula) particle, meaning: exalted is He above the partnership of what they associate with Him of falsehood, which neither originates nor restores. The verse has been cited as evidence that He, exalted is He, is not of the kind of bodies and masses, as the anthropomorphists (mujassima) claim. The reasoning is that it indicates that bodies and masses need a Creator, glorified and exalted is He, who is not of their kind; otherwise He would need one Himself and would not be a Creator. When both meanings are intended, the indication of the verse becomes clearer. Al-Kisa'i read «tushrikun» with a ta' (تُشْرِكُونَ).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 4:**

﴿He created man﴾, meaning this species, other than its first individual. ﴿From a drop of semen﴾, whose origin is pure water, and by which the male fluid is expressed. That is, He brought him into existence from an inanimate substance that has no sensation or movement, a fluid that holds neither shape nor position. ﴿Then, behold﴾, after being created from that, ﴿he is a disputer﴾, an eloquent contender who argues on his own behalf and confronts opponents. *Khasim* is an intensive form (*sighat mubalaghah*, a form expressing emphasis). Al-Wahidi said it means *mukhasim* (one who disputes). The pattern *fa'il* in the sense of *mufa'il* is well known among them, as in *nasib* meaning *munasib* (related), *khalit* meaning *mukhalit* (mixing with), and *ashir* meaning *mu'ashir* (companion).

﴿Clear﴾, one who makes the proof manifest, which he was taught to present. It has also been said that the meaning is: He brought him into existence from that, and then he is a disputer against his Creator, glorified is He, denying His great power, saying: ﴿Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ The first meaning is more fitting to the context of blessing, by granting the capacity to deduce from this His power and His oneness, may His majesty be exalted. The Imam explained the manner of the inference, saying, after asserting that man, in nobility, comes after the spheres and the stars, and indicating that for this reason he followed the inference from the creation of those with the inference from the creation of man:

Know that man is composed of a soul and a body. The beginning of the verse is an indication of inferring from his body the existence of the Wise Creator, and its end is an indication of inferring from his states. The explanation of the first is as follows: the drop is either uniform in its parts or varied in them. If it is uniform, then it is impossible that the cause of the generation of this body from it be the nature inherent in its substance, because the influence of nature is essential and necessitating. Whenever nature acts upon a uniform substance, its action must be spherical in form. Since this is not the case in our matter, for it is evident that bodies are not spherical, we know that what produces them is the Wise, Choosing Agent. If it is varied, then we say: the analysis of its composition must end in parts, each of which is in itself a simple body. In that case, if the governing force of these were a natural power, then each of those simple bodies would have to be spherical in shape, and it would follow that man would be in the shape of spheres joined one to another. Since this is not so, we know that the cause is also the Choosing Agent, glorified is His majesty. Furthermore, the drop is moist and quickly changes, so it does not preserve its position. The part which is the matter of the brain could be located below, and the part which is the matter of the heart could be located above. Since man is always in this specific arrangement, while another arrangement is possible, we know that his coming to be in this arrangement is only by the direction of the Wise, Choosing Agent.

It is not valid to say that this is due to the influence of the stars and celestial configurations, because their influences are uniform. Moreover, it has been shown in its proper place that they do not influence in any other way. The explanation of the second is that human souls, at the first stage of nature, are less in understanding, intelligence, and perception than the souls of all other animals. For the chick, upon emerging from the eggshell, distinguishes between enemy and friend: it flees from the cat and seeks refuge with the mother, and it distinguishes between food that suits it and food that does not. As for the human child, upon separating from his mother's womb, he does not distinguish between enemy and friend, nor between harm and benefit. Then, after he grows older, his intellect strengthens, his understanding increases, and he becomes able to know God, the Exalted, and to know the kinds of created beings, the higher and the lower, and to become acquainted with many of their subtle states, and with disputes and discussions. So the transfer of his soul from that extreme dullness to this extreme shrewdness must be by the direction of a Choosing, Wise God, who moves it from its deficiency to its perfection, and from its ignorance to its knowledge, according to wisdom and choice.

The second [explanation] has been said to be more fitting to the context of enumerating the blunders of the unbelievers, for it includes an account of the audacity of him who disbelieves toward God, the Exalted, his lack of shame before Him, glorified is He, and his impudence in persisting in disbelief.

Some have mentioned that the second interpretation is supported by the words of the Exalted in Surah Ya-Sin, after mentioning a similar matter: ﴿He said, "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?"﴾ For it explicitly states what was mentioned, so the beginning of the verse is for inference and its end is for affirming the impudence. This was objected to, saying that it is not valid, because the context of what precedes it in that surah revolves around the mention of resurrection and their obstinacy regarding it, unlike this [surah]. Every context has its own discourse. As for the verse being intended to establish the impudence of man, there is no contradiction between inferring the oneness and power [of God] and establishing the impudence of the deniers. For this reason the closing phrase was placed to follow what precedes it: ﴿Exalted is He above what they associate.﴾ The absence of contradiction does not require the presence of a suitable connection. In my view, each has its own direction.

In *al-Kashshaf*, both meanings are appropriate to the context, except that the second contains an additional element that suits the words ﴿Exalted is He above what they associate﴾. Then the first meaning is incorporated into it.

Al-Wahidi narrated that Ubayy ibn Khalaf came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a decayed bone and said: "O Muhammad, do you think that God will give life to this after it has crumbled to dust?" So there was revealed a verse similar to what is at the end of Ya-Sin.

It is well known that this is the verse revealed concerning that incident. Then the reason for the sequence, and the use of *idha* (behold, suddenly) in the Exalted words ﴿then, behold﴾ and onward, is that his being a manifest disputer, in whatever sense is intended, does not directly follow his creation from a drop, since between them there are intermediate stages. It is an explanation of his stages up to the perfection of his intellect. So the sequence is considered in relation to the last of these stages. Therefore there is no basis for supposing intermediaries, nor for saying that it is an instance of expressing the state of a thing by what it ultimately becomes. Understand this.

**[Page 97]**

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 5:**

﴿And the livestock﴾. They are the eight pairs of camels, cattle, sheep and goats. Al-Raghib said: "The word *an'am* (livestock) is not applied unless camels are among them." Some scholars restricted it here to camels, but this is not correct. The accusative (*al-nasb*) is by way of the object of an implied verb, which is explained by His words, exalted be He: ﴿He created them﴾. This is more preferred than the nominative (*al-raf'*) in such a position, because of the priority of the verbal sentence. It has also been read this way in the irregular readings (*al-shawadhdh*, readings that are not among the widely transmitted canonical ones). Or it is by way of coordination with *al-insan* (mankind), and what follows, after the statement of the purpose for which they were created, is an elaboration of that.

[Page 98]

His words, glorified be He: ﴿for you﴾ may be connected to *khalaqaha* (He created them). His words, exalted be He: ﴿in them﴾ are a fronted predicate (*khabar muqaddam*), and His words, majestic and exalted be He: ﴿is warmth﴾ are a delayed subject (*mubtada' mu'akhkhar*), and the sentence is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the object. Or the first prepositional phrase is the predicate of the mentioned subject, and the second is connected to what is in it of the meaning of stability (*al-istiqrar*). It has been said that it is a circumstantial clause from the concealed pronoun in it, which refers back to the subject. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause from *dif'* (warmth), since if it were delayed it would be a qualifier (*sifah*). Abu al-Baqa' allowed that the second be the predicate and the first be in the position of a circumstantial clause from its subject. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that it is not permissible, because when the governing element of the circumstantial clause is a meaning, it is not permissible to place it before the whole sentence; so it is not permissible to say *qa'iman fi al-dar Zayd* (standing in the house is Zayd). If the circumstantial clause is placed after the sentence, it is permissible without any disagreement; if it is placed in the middle, al-Akhfash permits it while the majority prohibit it. Abu al-Baqa' also allowed that *dif'* be nominative by (*li-kum*) or by (*fiha*), and the whole sentence be a circumstantial clause from the concealed pronoun in the accusative. Abu Hayyan also objected to this, saying that this is not considered a sentence but rather a single word. He related that they allowed *lakum* to be connected to *khalaqaha*, and the sentence *fiha dif'* (in them is warmth) to be a resumptive new clause (*isti'naf*) mentioning the benefits of the livestock. He preferred that the sentence *lakum fiha dif'* be a resumptive clause. Then he said: "The resumptive clause in *fiha* is supported by the resumptive clause in its counterpart, namely His words, exalted be He: ﴿and for you in them is beauty﴾. Thus, glorified be He, He set the necessary benefit against the non-necessary benefit." The Qutb inclined to this view and preferred that the speech is complete at *khalaqaha* (He created them), because of this coordination. Sahib al-Kashf disagreed with him in this, saying: "His words, exalted be He: ﴿He created them for you﴾, according to al-Zamakhshari's interpretation of it with his statement, 'He did not create them except for you and for your interests, O mankind,' is a part of the completion of the second meaning in His words, glorified be He: ﴿then he is an open adversary﴾, because of what the shift (*al-iltifat*) referred to indicates of that. As for the restriction referred to by his words, 'He did not create them except for you,' it comes from the particle *lam* (for), which indicates exclusivity, especially since He varied the address with what indicates greater distinction and exclusivity. This is better than making *lakum fiha dif'* (for you in them is warmth) a counterpart to *lakum fiha jamal* (for you in them is beauty), because it conveys the second meaning and is more eloquent, and because *fiha dif'* is then an elaboration of the first. He repeated *lakum* in the second because of the distance of the reference and the increase in reproach." End of his words. The truth, in the claim of the priority of connecting *lakum* to what precedes it together with it, is clear.

*Dif'* (warmth) is the name of what one is warmed by, that is, what heats. The Arabs say: *daf'ia yawmuna fahuwa dafi'* (our day became warm) when there is heat in it, and *daf'ia al-rajulu daf'an wa difa'an* (the man became warm), with both the vowel *fatha* and *kasra*. A man is *daf'an* and a woman is *daf'a*. The plural of *dif'* is *adfa'*. What is meant by it includes clothing and the tent that is made from their hair and wool. Ibn Abbas interpreted it, as related from him by Ibn Jarir and others, as clothing.

Abd al-Razzaq and others related from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that it is the offspring of every animal. Al-Umawi transmitted this from the language of some of the Arabs. The apparent meaning is the first.

Al-Zuhri and Abu Ja'far read *dif'* (*dif-f*) with a *damma* on the *fa'*, with its doubling and with tanwin. Its explanation in al-Bahr is that he transferred the vowel from the *hamza* to the *fa'* and the *hamza* was deleted, then he doubled the *fa'*, treating the connected form as if it were the pause form, since it is permissible to double it in pause.

Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read *dif'* with transfer of the vowel and deletion, without doubling. In al-Lawami' it is said: al-Zuhri read *dif'* with a *damma* on the *fa'* without a *hamza*, and it is vowelled by its vowel. Some of them compensate for this *hamza* by doubling the *fa'*, and this is one of the two modes of Hamzah ibn Habib in pause. It was objected that doubling in pause is a distinct dialect even if there is no deletion from the word on which one pauses. It was answered that this is only the case when one pauses on the last letter of it; but if one pauses on the letter before the last, as in *qadin* (judge), then it is not.

*Wa-manafi'* (and benefits): they are its milk, its riding, ploughing with them, drawing water with them, and other things. It was expressed by *them* (not *from them*) to include all of this; and it is more fitting for the context of bestowing favours. He put warmth first in observance of the style of ascending to the higher. ﴿And from them you eat﴾, that is, you eat what is eaten from them of meats, fats and the like. So *min* (from) here is partitive. The eating is either in its apparent meaning, or in the sense of consuming in general, which includes drinking, so milk enters into the count. It was also permitted that *min* be for the starting point, or be partitive in a figurative sense, or causal, meaning that you eat what is obtained by means of them, for grains and fruits that are eaten are acquired through hiring out camels for example, and through the prices of their offspring and milk and hides. The first is more apparent and more inclusive, since what is obtained from hiring them is hiring, by means of which many benefits are achieved. As for changing the noble arrangement, it is said that it is to indicate that they do not remain when eaten, unlike in what precedes and what follows; for warmth, the benefits we mentioned, and beauty are obtained from them while they remain in their own state, and for this reason they were made to be the place of these things, unlike eating. Fronting the adverbial phrase (*zarf*) is for restriction, in the sense that eating from them is the customary and reliable means of livelihood among all other animals. Thus it does not refute eating chickens, ducks, game of land and sea, for that belongs to enjoyment. Likewise it does not refute eating horse meat according to those who permit it, because it is not customary and reliable either. The summary is that the restriction is relative (*idafi*), and by this it also does not refute eating bread, herbs and the like. Added to this view in fronting is observance of the rhyme (*fawasil*). Making it solely for this, as in al-Kashf, is deficient. Abu Hayyan denies that fronting is absolutely for restriction, so its justification here is restricted to the observance mentioned.

And for you in them ﴿ولَكم فِيها﴾ (is beauty), in addition to the essential benefits already mentioned, ﴿جَمالٌ﴾ (jamal, beauty): an adornment in the eyes of people, and greatness and honour in their sight. The term is commonly applied to abundant goodness. Its beauty lies in the form, in the harmony of its composition and the proportion of its limbs; in its character, through its possession of praiseworthy qualities; and in its actions, through their suitability to what is good, by warding off harm and bringing benefit. Originally it is a masdar (verbal noun) of جَمُلَ (jamula) with the vowel ḍamma on the mīm. It is said of a man: جَمِيلٌ (jamīl), وجَمالٌ (jamāl), and جَمالٌ (jammāl) by intensification. Of a woman it is said: جَمِيلَةٌ (jamīla), and according to al-Kisā'ī, جُمَلاءُ (jumalā'). He recited:

"She is jumalā', like a rising full moon,
she surpassed all creation in beauty."

Some scholars held that it is applied to tajammul (adornment), and so they thought it to be a masdar with the extra letters dropped. ﴿حِينَ تُرِيحُونَ﴾ (when you bring them back in the evening), that is, when you return them from pasture to their pen (marāḥ) at evening time. One says: أراحَ الماشِيَةَ (arāḥa al-māshiya), when he returned the livestock to the pen at that time. ﴿وحِينَ تَسْرَحُونَ﴾ (and when you send them out), that is, you bring them out in the morning from their enclosures and their resting places to their pastures and grazing grounds. One says: سَرَّحَها يُسَرِّحُها سَرَحًا وسُرُوحًا (sarraḥahā yusarriḥuhā saraḥan wa surūḥan), and سَرَحَتْ هي (sarahat hiya), which is transitive and intransitive. The first verb, and likewise the second, is transitive, and its object is omitted for the sake of the fawāṣil (the rhyming endings of the verses). The two times are specified because what gives beauty its effect, namely the adornment of the courtyards, and the calling and answering of their lowing and bleating, occurs only in the going out and coming back at those two times. As for when they are in the pastures, their sensory connection to their owners is cut off, and when they are in the enclosures no one sees them and no observer looks at them.

The mention of the bringing back (ītrāḥ) before the sending out (sarḥ), although the bringing back comes later in time, is because it is more evident than the sending out in producing the beauty mentioned, and more complete in attracting companionship and delight, for in it there is presence after absence and approach after withdrawal, in the best state, with bellies full and udders abundant. ʿIkrima, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Jaḥdarī recited حِينًا (ḥīnan) in both places with tanwīn and without the idāfa (genitive construction), so that both clauses are descriptions of ḥīnan before them, and the returning pronoun is omitted, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿واتَّقُوا يَوْمًا لا تَجْزِي نَفْسٌ عَنْ نَفْسٍ﴾ (And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul), meaning: a time in which you bring them back, and a time in which you send them out.

The governing element of حِينَ (ḥīn) is either the mubtadaʾ (subject), since it carries the meaning of tajammul (adornment), as has been said, or its khabar (predicate), because of the meaning of settledness it contains.

It is also permitted that it be attached to an omitted element which occurs as a description of جَمالٌ (jamāl).

[Page 100]

﴿and it carries your loads﴾: that is, your heavy burdens, plural of *thiql*. It has also been said that it means your bodies, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿and the earth brings forth its burdens﴾ (99:2), where *al-athqal* is interpreted as the bodies of the children of Adam.

﴿to a land﴾: It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it means Yemen, Syria and Egypt. It seems that he viewed these as the trading destinations of the people of Makkah, as indicated by what al-Khazin (d. 741 AH) reports from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "He means from Makkah to Yemen and to Syria." In another narration from him, and from al-Rabi' ibn Anas and 'Ikrimah, it is Makkah. It seems they viewed that their loads and burdens were greatest upon their return from their trade, and their need for beasts of burden was most pressing. The apparent meaning is that it is general to every distant land. This is the view taken by Abu Hayyan. He treated the specific identifications that were transmitted as examples, not as meaning that this particular place alone is intended to the exclusion of others. Likewise, what he transmitted from some of them, that it is the city of the Messenger (ﷺ), is treated as an illustration and not as meaning that this specific place alone is intended.

﴿you would not have been able to reach it﴾: that is, to arrive there by your own selves, stripped of the burdens of travel, let alone carrying your loads on your backs, if the cattle had not existed and had not been created ﴿except with great hardship to yourselves﴾. That is, with its difficulty and toil. It has also been said that the meaning is: you would not have been able to reach it by them except with what has been mentioned, and *bi-ha* ("by them") has been omitted because the traveller must have burdens. The purpose is to draw attention to the distance of the land, and that even with the aid of these beasts in carrying the loads, you cannot reach it except with hardship. There is no doubt that the first interpretation is more eloquent.

Mujahid, al-A'raj, Abu Ja'far, 'Amr ibn Mu'in and Ibn Arqam read *bi-shiqqi* with a fatha on the shin (*bi-shaqqi*). This is also reported from Nafi' and Abu 'Amr. Both are valid usages in the language, and the meaning is what has preceded. It has been said: *al-shaqq* with a fatha is the verbal noun, and with a kasra it is the noun, meaning hardship. With the kasra in this sense comes the line of verse:

*"And a man with camels who drives them on, / a brother to him of weariness from their hardship and constant toil."*

He means "from their hardship" (*mashaqqatihā*).

It is reported from al-Farra' that the fatha form is a verbal noun from *shaqqa al-amr 'alayhi shiqqan*, and its essential meaning returns to *al-shaqq*, which is the cleft. The kasra form means the half. One says: "I took the *shiqq* of the sheep," meaning half of it.

And there came in a hadith: "Guard yourselves against the Fire, even with half a date."

The meaning is: except with the loss of half of the selves, as if the selves melt away from weariness and exhaustion because of the hardship that reaches them, just as one says: "You cannot do such-and-such except by losing most of yourself or a piece of your liver." This is figurative language (*majaz*). Some have permitted that it be understood with an omitted modifier, meaning: except with the splitting of the powers of the selves. The exception is then "incomplete" (*mufarragh*), meaning: you would not have been able to reach it "by anything at all" except with the splitting of the selves. Abu al-Baqa' made the preposition and its object a circumstantial phrase (*hal*) referring to the raised pronoun in *balighihi*, meaning "afflicted upon you." The subject of *tahmilu* ("carries") is the cattle, but the carrying mentioned applies to some of their kinds, namely camels. Many examples of this exist. From this it becomes clear that the argument of some who used this construction to prove that by "the cattle" (*al-an'am*) previously mentioned only camels are meant is weak. The change of the preceding noble structure, which indicated that the cattle are the source of blessings, to a verbal sentence which implies occurrence, has been explained by some as follows: it may be to indicate that this blessing is not general either in its origin or in its object, and in its extension over times and its regular occurrence in the customary seasons, it is like the earlier blessings. For in its origin it is specific to camels, as you have heard, and in its object it concerns those who move about the earth for trade and other purposes, at times that are not constant. As for the rest of the blessings enumerated, they exist in all kinds and are general to all the addressees always and at all times. End of quotation.

Those who deny the miracles (*karamat*) of the saints (*awliya'*) argued with this verse, as the Imam said. It indicates that a human being cannot move from one land to another except with great hardship and by carrying loads on camels. Those who affirm the miracles say: the saints may move from one distant land to another in a short time, without fatigue or bearing hardship. That would then be contrary to the verse, and so it would be invalid. If it is invalid in this case, it is invalid in all cases, since no one distinguishes between them.

He answered that we restrict the generality of the verse by the proofs that establish the occurrence of miracles. End of quotation. Perhaps those who deny that the saints can "fold distance" (*tay al-masafah*) rely on this verse. But these people do not deny miracles absolutely, so the statement "since no one distinguishes between them" is not valid. Whoever is fair will know that using this verse to prove this matter is hardly worth consideration, on the basis that it is given in the context of enumerating favours. And the existence of this in most circumstances for most people is sufficient. So understand.

﴿Indeed your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾. For this reason He has bestowed upon you great favours and made easy for you the difficult and arduous affairs.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 8:**

﴿And horses﴾ is, as more than one scholar has said, a collective noun (ism jins) for the horse, with no singular form derived from its own root, like *al-ibil* (camels). Al-Raghib mentioned that it originally applies to mares (afras) and horsemen (fursan). It is coordinated with *al-an'am* (the grazing animals), meaning: and He created the horses. ﴿And mules﴾ is the plural of *baghl* (mule), a known animal. ﴿And donkeys﴾ is the plural of *himar* (donkey), likewise. In the paucity plural it takes the form *ahmirah*, and in the plural of multitude *humur*, which is the regular form. Ibn Abi Abla read *al-khayl* and what follows it in the nominative (*al-khaylu*). ﴿That you may ride them﴾ gives the reason (ta'lil) for the creation of the things mentioned. The discussion of God's purposes in His acts is extensively treated in its proper place. ﴿And as adornment﴾ is coordinated with the位置 (mahall) of ﴿that you may ride them﴾, so it is, like it, an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi). Its being stripped of the preposition *li-* while the other is not is because adornment is the act of the one who adorns, and that is the Creator, Exalted is He. Thus the agent of the two verbs, the one given as reason and the one given the reason, is one. This is unlike the agent of riding and the agent of the reason given. The condition for the accusative case, which those who stipulate it have stipulated, is therefore present in the coordinated element but not in the element it is coordinated with. This is what more than one scholar has said. Some of the careful scholars mentioned that the non-uniformity of the construction indicates that the primary intended purpose is the first one. Thus the particles set for this purpose were used, the address was continued, and the pronoun was repeated for the three in ﴿that you may ride them﴾. The second was introduced for completion and to indicate that, since it was among their aims, it was counted within the context of favour. Otherwise, adornment with a passing accident is not something that the people of God, who are the addressees of the address in its primary sense, intend. The above has been objected to: even if the unity of the agent is established, the conditions for the validity of the accusative are not fulfilled, because another condition is missing, namely contemporaneity in existence, since the creation precedes the adornment. It is answered that this is according to the intention of the intention of adornment, as it is said in "I beat Zayd as discipline," that the discipline is understood as the intention of it. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that *zinatan* be a verbal noun (masdar) of a deleted verb, meaning: and that you may adorn yourselves with them as adornment. Ibn Atiyyah said that it is a direct object of a deleted verb, meaning: and He made them an adornment. Qatadah related from Ibn Abbas that he read "that you may ride them as adornment" without the conjunction *wa*. The author of al-Lawami said that *zinatan* in that case is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿He created them﴾ or from the pronoun in ﴿that you may ride them﴾. He did not specify the pronoun, but Ibn Atiyyah specified it, saying it is the accusative one. More than one scholar said that the circumstantial reading is permitted from either of the two pronouns, meaning: that you may ride them while adorning yourselves, or while they are adorned with them. Al-Zamakhshari, after citing the reading, said: meaning He created them as adornment so that you may ride them. What he intended, as it has been said, is that the adornment is either the second object of *khalaqa* (created), treating it as *ja'ala* (made), or it is a circumstantial qualifier of the three objects collectively. He also permitted that it be an object of purpose for ﴿that you may ride them﴾, while it has the meaning of adorning, so the difference in the agents of the two verbs is not raised against it. It has been said: as for the necessity of restricting the required riding to being for the sake of adornment, and that the wisdom in creating them is that, and that this is the primary intended purpose for us, there is no harm in it, because adorning oneself with clothing and mounts is not prohibited by the Law, and this does not preclude that their creation has a more important ruling, such as jihad upon them and travel for acts of obedience. It was specified because of its suitability to the context of favour, although adornment, as al-Raghib said, is that which does not disgrace in this world or in the Hereafter. As for what adorns in one state but not in another, it is from one aspect a blemish. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

It has been cited from this verse as proof of the prohibition of eating the flesh of the animals mentioned, because the driving (of the animals) is in the context of argument from the creation of these blessings as a favour to this kind, as evidence of monotheism and of the evil conduct of whoever opposes this with polytheism. The Wise does not bestow favour with the lesser of two blessings while leaving the greater of them. How so, when it was mentioned first?

Ibn Jarir and others related the view that eating horseflesh is disliked, on the basis of this verse, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. It is related from Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, that he said: some scholars permitted the flesh of horses, but as for me, I do not like eating it. In another narration he said: I dislike it. The first points to disapproval in the sense of reprehensible-but-not-forbidden (makruh tanzihi), and the second indicates prohibition, based on what was related from Abu Yusuf: he asked him, "If you say about something, 'I dislike it,' what is your view of it?" He said, "Prohibition." It seems that for this reason the author of al-Hidayah said: the more correct view is that the disapproval of eating its flesh is prohibitive according to the Imam. In al-Imadiyyah it is stated that he, may Allah be pleased with him, retracted the view of disapproval three days before his death, and the legal opinion (fatwa) is based on it. His two companions and Imam al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with them all, said: there is no harm in eating horseflesh.

Some of the Shafi'is answered the argument from the verse by denying that what was mentioned is the lesser of the two blessings with respect to horses. He said: this is because the verse came as a favour to them in the manner they were accustomed to, and no one of understanding denies that the main purpose of horses is riding and adornment, not eating, unlike the grazing animals. Mentioning the more prominent of the two benefits and leaving out the lesser is no novelty; rather it is the custom of the Qur'an's concise expressions. Even if its mention in the first part does not serve as proof for us in being content with it, together with the indication that it is trivial in comparison, it does not become proof against us. Thus it became clear that there is no argument from it, neither from its explicit wording nor from its implication.

They (the permissive scholars) argued for permissibility by what is authentically transmitted from the hadith of Jabir: "The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the flesh of domestic donkeys and mules, and gave permission regarding the flesh of horses on the day of Khaybar." In it, according to them, is evidence that the verse does not indicate prohibition, since it shows that the prohibition of domestic donkeys' flesh occurred in the year of Khaybar, as is established according to most hadith scholars, and this surah is Meccan. So if prohibition had been known from it, it would have been established before that. It was objected that although the surah is Meccan, this verse may be Medinan. The reply is that such a claim requires a report, and mere possibility is not sufficient. The hadith of Jabir was opposed by what Abu Ubayd, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Khalid ibn al-Walid, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade eating every animal with fangs from the beasts of prey, and the flesh of horses, mules and donkeys."

The preponderant view, as al-Hidayah said, is for the prohibition. But you know that this report weakens the argument, since Khalid embraced Islam in Medina, and the verse is Meccan. So if the prohibition had been known from it, the prohibition that he heard would have had little benefit. In sum, the argument from the verse for the prohibition of horseflesh is not free from error, so one must return to the reports on this matter. The ruling when they conflict is not hidden from those of insight. What I incline to is permissibility, and God knows best.

﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾, that is, He creates other than what He has detailed for you, Glorified is He. The expression of it with what was mentioned is because their totality is not known and hardly can be known. So the statement is a general one covering what is other than the animals, which mostly are needed, either by necessary need or by non-necessary need. The shift to the form of the future tense indicates continuity and renewal, or to bring the image to mind. It is also possible that it is an informing from Him, Exalted is He, that He has creatures of which we have no knowledge, so "what you do not know" is in its literal sense.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: Among what Allah, Exalted is He, has created is a white pearl the distance of a thousand years, upon which is a mountain of red ruby, surrounding which, on that earth, is an angel who has filled its east and its west. He has six hundred heads; on each head six hundred faces; on each face six hundred thousand and sixty thousand mouths; in each mouth sixty thousand tongues, praising Allah, Exalted is He, sanctifying Him, declaring His oneness, and magnifying Him with every tongue six hundred thousand and sixty thousand times. When the Day of Resurrection comes, he will look at the greatness of Allah, Exalted is He, and say: 'By Your might, I have not worshipped You as You deserve to be worshipped.' That is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾." In another narration from him: that to the right of the Throne is a river of light, like the seven heavens, the seven earths and the seven seas. Gabriel, peace be upon him, enters it every dawn and bathes, and so he increases in beauty upon his beauty and in greatness upon his greatness. Then he shakes himself, and Allah, Exalted is He, creates from every drop that falls from his feathers so many thousands of angels. Of them, every day, seventy thousand angels enter the Bayt al-Ma'mur, and seventy thousand angels enter the Ka'bah, and they do not return until the Day of Resurrection.

This was also related from al-Dahhak, Muqatil and Ata'. Among things we do not know is the land of Simsimah, about which al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may God sanctify his secret, mentioned what he mentioned, and Jabarsa and Jabalqa, as more than one scholar has mentioned. Even if some consider such things to be fables, like what was mentioned by our contemporary, the head of the group who named themselves "Kashfiyyah" (the unveilers), whom their enemies among the Imamiyyah called "Kashfiyyah" in most of his books, which would make one laugh by the life of your bereaved father, and which the scholar, on hearing it, would wish, out of his great modesty before the ignorant, to descend into the lower earth. So be content with what has come in the reports, and do not let the resemblance to the philosophers deter you from it, if its chain is sound, for they are like a mirage in a valley. What I think is that none of the unbelievers, let alone the believers, doubts that God, Exalted is He, has creatures we do not know, such that one would need to cite proofs for that.

It is also possible that what is meant by this creation is the creation in Paradise, that is, and He creates in Paradise, beyond the worldly blessings mentioned, what you do not know, that is, what it is not within your capacity to know. This is what is pointed to by his saying (ﷺ), relating from Allah, Exalted is He: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and it has not occurred to the heart of any human."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 9:**

﴿And upon God is the direction of the path.﴾ *Al-qaṣd* (direction, straightness) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used in the sense of the active participle. One says *sabīl qaṣd* and *sabīl qāṣid*, meaning a straight path, as if it is heading toward the way that the traveller intends and from which he does not deviate. It is like *nahr jār* (a flowing river) and *ṭarīq sā'ir* (a travelled road). *ʿAlā* (upon) here denotes obligation, metaphorically, and the sentence is elliptical with a omitted noun, meaning: it is incumbent upon Him, exalted is He, and determined for Him, like an obligatory command, because the promise preceded the explanation. It has also been said: the guidance to the straight path, which leads whoever travels it to the truth, is the tawhid (oneness of God), by the establishment of proofs, the sending of messengers (peace be upon them), and the revelation of books to call people to it. Or it is a maṣdar in the sense of *iqāma* (establishing) and *taʿdīl* (making upright). *ʿAlā* remains as it was previously, except that there is no need to posit an omitted noun: it is upon Him, glorified is He, to set the path straight and make it upright, that is, to make it such that whoever travels it reaches the truth, in the manner of "the smallness of the gnat and the largeness of the elephant." Its reality returns to what was mentioned: the establishment of proofs, the sending of messengers (peace be upon them), and the revelation of books.

It is also permitted that *al-qaṣd* means *al-qāṣid*, that is, the straight one, as in the first explanation, and *ʿalā* is not for obligation or necessity. The meaning is that the direction to the path, and its straightness, leads to God, exalted is He, and passes by Him, exalted is He. In this there is a comparison of what points to God, mighty and majestic is He, with a straight road whose nature is that. Ibn ʿAṭiyya mentioned something similar, and it is, as you see, [weak]. The *al-* in *al-sabīl* is, according to many, for the genus (*lil-jins*), so it includes both the straight and other than the straight. The idafa of *al-qaṣd* in the sense of "the straight" to *al-sabīl* is an idafa of the general to the specific, and the idafa of an adjective to its noun is contrary to the apparent, according to what has been said. It has also been said that *al* is for specificity (*lil-ʿahd*), and the intended meaning is the path of the Law (*sabīl al-sharʿ*).

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and of it is a deviating one﴾, that is, one that swerves from the right course and departs from the truth, not leading its traveller to it. It is apparent that the intended meaning is the genus, since partitiveness (*al-baʿḍiyya*) is only achieved on that basis, for the deviating one on the reading of specificity is not part of it but its counterpart. Whoever intends specificity returns the pronoun to the unrestricted (*muṭlaq*) that is contained within that restricted (*muqayyad*), or to what was mentioned, by positing an omitted noun, that is, "and of its kind is a deviating one." Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: it is possible that it refers to the path of the Law, and by this part is meant the sects of misguidance from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), who deviate from the direction of the path. Some claimed that the pronoun refers to creatures, that is, "and of the creatures is one deviating from the truth," and this was supported by the reading of ʿĪsā (Jesus), and it was narrated from Ibn Masʿūd: "and among you" (*wa-minkum*). Ibn al-Anbārī recorded in the *Maṣāḥif* from ʿAlī, may God honour his face, but with *fa* instead of *wa*, and it is not [reliable] for that. The feminine [pronoun] is because *al-sabīl* is both feminine and masculine. The prepositional phrase has been said to be a predicate preceding its subject, with *jā'ir* being a postponed subject. It has also been said that it is in the position of a nominative by way of the subject, either by considering its content, or by positing an omitted noun: "some of the path is deviating," or "some of the path is deviating."

[Page 104]

According to what some of the verifiers chose, the sentence is parenthetical (*iʿtirāḍiyya*), brought in to explain the need for clarification or for the upright-making by establishing proofs, sending messengers, and revealing books, the matters mentioned earlier, and to show the greatness of the blessing in that. This is the guidance explained as indicating what leads to the desired goal, not the guidance that necessitates being guided to it, for that is not upon God, glorified is He, at all, but would violate His wisdom, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿And if He had willed, He would have guided you all﴾.
