Its meaning is: had He willed to guide you to what was mentioned of tawhid with a guidance necessitating being guided to it, He would have done it, but He did not will it, because His will follows wisdom, and there is no wisdom in that will, since what the sphere of obligation revolves around is only free choice, upon which the consequences of deeds are based, by which the reward is connected. The qualifier *ajmaʿīn* (all) is for the negated element, not for the negation, so the meaning is the negation of totality, not the totality of negation.

Some have mentioned that the apparent wording would have been: "And upon God is the direction of the path, and of it is a deviating one," or "and upon Him is its deviating one," but it departed from this to what is in the noble arrangement, because misguidance is not attributed to Him, exalted is He, out of courtesy. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned anger﴾ [al-Fatiha: 7].

Al-Zamakhsharī claimed that the difference between the two sentences' styles is to signal what may be attributed to Him, exalted is He, from the two paths, and what may not. He intended to point to what his Mu'tazili brethren (*al-Muʿtazila*, the rationalist sect) held, namely, that it is not permissible to attribute misguidance to Him, glorified is He, because it is not His creation. They took the verse, with the difference in style, as a proof for this difference. Some of the group answered that what is meant is that it is upon God, by virtue of grace and generosity, to make clear the true religion and the correct doctrine; but as for explaining how misguidance and leading astray occur, it is not upon Him, glorified is He. This was challenged: just as explaining guidance and its path is obligatory, so too is its opposite, and the sending of messengers (peace be upon them) and the revelation of books are only for that.

Ibn al-Munīr said: the difference between the two styles is because the context of the speech is to establish the proof against creatures, namely that God, exalted is He, made clear the straight path and the deviating one, and guided a people who chose guidance, and led astray others who chose misguidance. He verified that every act that proceeds from a servant has two considerations: from the standpoint of its being existent, it is created by God, exalted is He, and is attributed to Him in this respect; and from the standpoint of its being accompanied by the servant's choice of it and its ease for him, it is attributed to the servant. The multiplicity of these two considerations is established in every act, so it was fitting, for the establishment of the proof against the servants, to attribute guidance to God, exalted is He, with respect to His creating it, and to attribute misguidance to the servant with respect to his choosing it. The summary is that in each of the two acts He mentioned a relation different from that mentioned in the other, so that this would suit the establishment of the proof: "Has God not the conclusive argument?" [al-Anʿam: 149].

Some verifiers denied that there is a change of style here for a desired purpose, on the basis that such change occurs only where the apparent meaning requires a particular construction, but one departs from it for a purpose more important than it. The intended meaning of explaining the straight path is not merely informing that it is straight, so that attributing that it is deviating to Him, exalted is He, would be valid, requiring an excuse for not doing so. Moreover, if that were intended, there would be no purpose for changing the style. This has been explained in countless places. Rather, the intended meaning is establishing the proofs for guidance to it, and it is not possible to attribute the like to Him, exalted is He, with respect to the deviating path, by saying "and its deviating one," lest that attribution from Him to other than Him, glorified is He, be needed for some purpose, nor would anyone suppose it, so that the situation would require warding it off by saying "not its deviating one," and then changing the construction of the arrangement for a stronger motive. He mentioned that the sentence is parenthetical, as we quoted earlier. This is a statement that bears the marks of verification. However, one may object: why should it not be permitted that the explanation of the straight path and the explanation of the deviating path mean establishing the proofs indicating the correctness of the first, for guidance to it, and the falsity of the second, so that it be avoided and not relied upon? This is other than the mere informing that he mentioned, and attributing it to Him, exalted is He, is possible. Indeed, some said: the truth is that the meaning is "upon God is the explanation of the way of guidance, so that they may be guided to it, and the explanation of other than it, so that they may beware of it," but He suffices with one of them, because the other is necessarily implied by it.

[Page 105]

In *al-Kashf* (of al-Tibi): the difference between the two styles is also clear according to the doctrine of the people of the Sunna (*ahl al-Sunna*, the orthodox majority), for no one denies that the first is intended for its own sake. The explanation of the path of misguidance in summary, to the extent that the straight path is distinguished from it within the explanation of the straight path, is necessary; but its detailed explanation is not something that must occur, nor is it something the promise has come to. Consider this. Then, this verse openly contradicts what the Mu'tazila claimed, including al-Zajjaj among them, that the attachment of His will, exalted is He, to a thing does not entail its existence. They were compelled to interpret it as "compulsion" (*al-qasriyya*). Abu ʿAlī among them said: the meaning is "if He had willed, He would have guided you to the reward or to Paradise without merit," and all of that contradicts the apparent meaning, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 10:

﴿He it is who sent down water from the sky.﴾ This begins another kind of the blessings that point to His Oneness, glory be to Him. By "water" is meant a particular kind of it, namely rain; and by "sky" is meant either the clouds, by way of metaphor (isti'arah) or the figure of metonymy (majaz mursal), or the known celestial body, the speech being elliptical with an omitted noun, i.e., from the direction of the sky or its side. Taking it in that sense without this [ellipsis] is what the apparent meaning of some reports requires, but I do not say so. The particle "min" (from) in every case is for the beginning of the point (ibtida'iyyah), and it is connected to what comes before it. The postponement of the explicit object from it is so that the mind thirsts for it, so that it settles most firmly when it arrives. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for you﴾ may be a preposed predicate (khabar muqaddam). His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿from it﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿drink﴾, i.e., what you drink, and it is a postponed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), or it is the agent (fa'il) of the first adverbial phrase, and the clause is a qualifier (sifah) of "water". The "min" here is partitive (tab'idiyyah), and there is no implication of restriction (hasr) in placing it first. Whoever imagined that said: there is no harm in it, because all sweet drinking waters are, in origin, from it, as is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He made it into springs in the earth﴾ [al-Zumar: 21], and His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿then We caused it to dwell in the earth﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 18]. It may also be that it is connected to what comes before it. ("And from it is drink") may be a subject and predicate, or "drink" may be the agent of the adverbial phrase, and the clause and the "min" are as previously stated.

It has been objected that placing the accusative between the two genitive phrases, and placing the second of them between "water" and its qualifier, is not becoming of the sublime eloquence of the glorious text. Yet it is so: ﴿and from it are trees﴾, i.e., vegetation in general, whether or not it has a stalk, as transmitted from al-Zajjaj. The word is literally applied to the first sense, and for its use in the second is the verse of the rajaz poet:

"We feed them meat when fodder (shajar) is scarce, and feeding horses meat is harmful."

It is said that "shajar" here means fodder (kala'), because that is what is fed to animals; and likewise al-Nihayah explained it thus in the saying of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: "Do not eat the price of the shajar, for it is unlawful (suht)."

Perhaps this is because the prohibition of withholding surplus water is reported in the hadith, as is withholding surplus fodder, and people's sharing in water, fodder and fire. Some of them kept it to its literal meaning and did not make it an all-encompassing metaphor. The "min" may be partitive by way of metaphor, since the trees, when they come into being through its watering, are treated as if they were from it, like his saying: "the humps of the camels in its rain" (meaning by it the rain by which what camels eat grows, so that their humps become fat). Or it may be for beginning, i.e., "and there comes into being from it trees." The first is better in relation to what precedes it. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is causal (sababiyyah), i.e., and by its cause the growing of trees [takes place], and this indicates that

[Page 106]

﴿He causes to grow for you thereby the crops﴾. Ibn al-Anbari allowed both of the first two interpretations, in line with what the apparent sense of his words requires: the speech is based on an implied elision (*idmar*, "ellipsis of an omitted word"; the elided word is a *mudaf*, a noun governed in a genitive construction), either before the pronoun, meaning "from its direction" or "from its watering," or before *shajar* (trees), meaning "and from it is the drink of trees," like the words of the Exalted: ﴿and they were made to drink the calf into their hearts﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 93), meaning "their love of the calf." End of his words. This, however, is far-fetched. It has been said: ellipsis is preferable to figurative usage (*majaz*, "a word used in a non-literal sense"), not the reverse, as some have held. He held that they are equal, since each of them requires a contextual indicator (*qarina*).

﴿in it you pasture﴾, meaning you graze (your livestock). It is said: *asama al-mashiyata* and *sawwamaha*, meaning he made the livestock graze; and *sama* (intransitive) means they grazed by themselves, so they are *sa'ima* and *sawam*, meaning they grazed wherever they wished. The root of this, according to al-Zajjaj, is *al-sumah*, which is like *al-simah*, "a mark," because livestock leave marks on the ground and in the places where they graze. Zayd ibn Ali (may Allah be pleased with them both) read ﴿tusimun﴾ with a *fatha* on the *ta'*. If *sama* is attested as transitive, then it and *asama* have the same meaning; otherwise, the interpretation is that the speech involves an omitted *mudaf*, meaning "you pasture your livestock."

﴿He causes to grow﴾, i.e., Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is said: *nabata al-shay'* and *anbatahu Allah*, so it is *manbut*, and the analogical form would be *munbat*. It has also been said that *anbata* is used intransitively for *nabata* ("to grow"), and al-Farra' cited:

*"I saw those in need around their tents, dwelling there, until the herbage grew (anbata al-baql)."*

That is, *nabata*. Al-Asma'i used to deny that *anbata* comes in the sense of *nabata*. Abu Bakr read *nunbitu* with the royal plural *nun*. Al-Zuhri read *yunbitu* with the doubling (*tashdid*) of the *ba'*, which, according to one view, indicates multiplication; Abu Hayyan preferred that it indicates intensification of the transitivity. Ubayy read *yanbutu* with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and the coordinated items after it in the nominative as subjects. The clause ﴿He causes to grow for you thereby﴾, meaning by what He sent down from the sky, ﴿the crops, the olives, the palm trees and the grapes﴾, may be a second attribute of *ma'an* (water), or it may be a new, explanatory sentence (*isti'naf bayani*), as if it were said: "Does it have other benefits?" So it was answered: "He causes to grow for you thereby..."

The choice of the present tense (*al-istiqbal*) indicates renewal and continuity, and that growing is the constant practice of Allah, Glorified be He, which runs throughout the ages; or it serves to bring the scene to mind because of its strangeness. The placing of the two adverbial phrases (*al-zarfayn*) before the direct object is for the reason we have mentioned, together with the emphasis conveyed by placing the first of them, which is to bring joy immediately. The placing of the crops before the others is said to be because it is the origin of foods, the pillar of livelihood and the sustenance of most of the world, and because it has a connection with pasture (*al-kala'*, "herbage"). Then the olive, because of its nobility, in that it is a condiment in one respect and a fruit in another. The physicians have mentioned many benefits for it, and a considerable number of them are mentioned in *al-Tadhkira*. The apparent sense of the lexicographers' words is that it is a collective noun (*ism jins jam'i*), whose singular is *zaytuna*, and that it is applied both to the specific tree and to its fruit.

[Page 107]

He held that what is meant here is the first (the tree). Later, if Allah wills, the full discussion of this will come. Most of what it grows in are places where the latitude is high, the cold is intense, and the terrain is mountainous, with white or red soil. Then the palm tree comes before the grapes, because its durability is more evident in comparison to it: a single palm tree often exceeds a hundred years, whereas the grapevine is not like that. Yes, the olive tree is more durable than both, for a single olive tree may last a thousand years, and its fruit is often used as food, so that a report says: *"No house is hungry where there are dates."* (This is a hadith, not a report about the olive; the wording is as it stands in the text.)

Most of what grows in hot, dry lands dominated by sand, such as the Holy City of Medina, Iraq and the outskirts of Egypt. According to al-Raghib, *nakhl* is the plural of *nakhl*, which applies to both the singular and the plural, and for one tree one says *nakhla*. As for *al-a'nab*, it is the plural of *'inaba*, with a *kasra* on the *ayn* and a *fatha* on the *nun* and the *ba'*. Many single nouns have come in this pattern.

The Qamus mentioned a number of them. Al-Jawhari is attributed with a lack of knowledge in his statement that this pattern is rare in the singular, and that *'inaba*, *tiwala*, *hibara*, *tiyaba* and *khiyara* are the only examples. Al-Jawhari also stated that if you want to pluralise it for a small number, you pluralise it with *ta'* and say *'inabat*; for a large number, *'inab* and *a'nab*. End of his words. Consider this together with their listing of *af'al* as plurals of paucity (*jum' qilla*). *Al-'inab*, as al-Raghib said, is applied both to the fruit of the vine and to the vine itself. The apparent meaning is the second.

Abu Hayyan mentioned, as the reason for placing the grapes last, that their fruit is pure fruit. In this there is a problem: if by their fruit he means the grape while still fresh, before it becomes a raisin, this may be accepted; but if he means the raisin, it is not accepted. In the words of many jurists in the chapter on the zakat of fitr (charity at the end of Ramadan), raisins are considered a staple food (*iqtiyat*, "food that serves as a staple"). Indeed, the apparent sense of their words is that in this respect it comes after the date and before rice. The researcher on this matter does not deny that it is a staple, as will not be hidden from anyone who examines the discussion.

In the plural form *al-nakhil wa al-a'nab* there is an indication that its fruits are of different kinds. In *al-Tadhkira*, when mentioning dates, it says that they are varied and of many types, like grapes, until I heard that they exceed fifty kinds. When mentioning grapes, it says that they vary according to size, length, thickness of skin, absence of seeds, abundance of flesh, colour, taste and other features, to many types, like dates. End of its words.

I myself heard from my father (may Allah have mercy on him) that when he came to Egypt after returning from the pilgrimage, to visit his brother who had emigrated there to seek knowledge, he was told that in its regions there are nearly three hundred kinds of dates. The responsibility for this report lies with the one from whom he heard it.

The Allama Abu al-Su'ud has here something whose apparent meaning indicates heedlessness, but glory belongs to the One who is never heedless. It would have been more apparent to place human food first, because of its nobility over the food of the livestock. But it was placed in this order, as the Imam said, to draw attention to noble character, and so that a person's concern for those under his hand may be stronger than his concern for himself. The reverse occurs in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Eat, and let your livestock graze﴾ (Ta-Ha: 54), to indicate that this is not obligatory, though it is among the praiseworthy virtues. This accords with the report: *"Begin with yourself, then with those whom you support."* It has also been said that this is because it is something in which creatures have no part, through sowing or planting, so that the favour in it is stronger. It has also been said that most of those addressed are owners of livestock, who have no crops or anything of what was mentioned. Shihab al-Din said regarding this: "You may say that, since the edible and ridden animals were mentioned, it was appropriate to follow them with mention of their drink and fodder, because this is stronger in conferring favour, for their creation and their sustenance are for the sake of humans. Whoever gives a beast together with its fodder is more gracious, as it is said: 'Among the courtesy of a gift is giving it with its container.'" End of his words. This is not without beauty.

Following this, it is preferable that what is meant by the words of the Exalted ﴿From it for you is a drink﴾ is what is drunk. As for what has been said, that the foods which were mentioned earlier are also for humans, but indirectly, because they are food for their animal food, this does not answer the question, for it may be said afterwards: "It would have been more fitting to mention first what was food for them directly, without intermediary." It cannot be said: "This question is only apt if what is meant by the coordinated items mentioned is their fruits, not what results from them the fruits, because that is not human food." We say: the purpose of mentioning them is only to confer favour through their fruits, but they were mentioned in the same pattern as their predecessor which was mentioned as the food of livestock. What indicates that the favour is through their fruits is His words, glorified be He: ﴿and of all the fruits﴾. Taking the fruits from them from the start, by using one kind of figurative speech (*majaz*) in some of them, is to neglect the observance of other considerations, for which it is good to interpret them in the way we have said rather than otherwise. From it ﴿He causes to grow﴾, since its apparent meaning requires attachment to the tree itself, not to its fruit. So let it be acted upon as its beginning requires, even if its end requires considering something like what was said about: "I fed her straw and cold water." So it was said, and there is room for reflection.

Some have denied that growing is among the things that require the attachment mentioned, for He, Glorified be He, has said: ﴿So We caused to grow therein grain, and grapes and herbage, and olives and palm trees, and gardens dense with trees, and fruit and pasture﴾ (Abasa: 27–31). It is also permitted that what is intended in the things that were counted is not merely their being food, but what includes this and other things, in the sense that He causes to grow thereby, for your benefit, what has been mentioned. Benefit occurs through what has food value and through what does not. The *min* in ﴿من كل الثمرات﴾ is partitive, and the meaning is: He causes to grow for you some of all the fruits. This was said because, as in the *Kashshaf* and elsewhere, all fruits exist only in Paradise, and only some of all of them has been made to grow on earth, as a reminder. One of the eminent scholars said: what is meant is some of what is in the realms of possibility, of the fruit of power which the hand of existence has not yet plucked. This is more evident, more comprehensive and more suited to what has preceded. For just as He, Glorified be He, followed the mention of the animals from which benefit is derived in detail with the words ﴿and He creates what you do not know﴾, so He followed the mention of the fruits from which benefit is derived with something similar:

[Page 108]

﴿Indeed, in that﴾, the aforementioned sending down of water and what He has detailed of its sending down, ﴿is a sign﴾, a great sign indicating the sole divinity of Allah, the Exalted, because it encompasses perfection of knowledge, power and wisdom, ﴿for a people who reflect﴾. For whoever reflects on how the seed and the stone fall into the earth, and moisture reaches them and penetrates them, so that the lower part splits and roots emerge from it that spread into the earth, sometimes spreading even though the earth is hard; and the upper part splits, even if it was upside down when it fell; then a stalk emerges from it and grows, and from it come the leaves, the flowers, the grains and the fruits, containing bodies of different shapes, colours, properties and natures, and containing a seed capable of producing its like in the pattern prescribed, without end, while the water, the earth, the air and the rest are the same for all: he knows that One whose works are these cannot be resembled by anything in any attribute of perfection, let alone share with Him in His most specific attributes, which are divinity and the right to be worshipped. Yet the basest of things, such as inanimate matter, [are worshipped instead]. Exalted is Allah above that, to a great height.

And to Allah, the Exalted, belongs the excellence of the one who said:

*Contemplate the gardens of roses and look*
*At the signs of what the King has made:*

*Eyes of silver, staring,*
*Upon whose lids is refined gold.*

*Upon stems of chrysolite, witnessing*
*That Allah has no partner.*

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 12:**

Since the argument from what has been mentioned involves a hidden matter that requires reflection and contemplation for one who has sound judgment, He concluded the verse with reflection. ﴿And He has subjected to you the night and the day﴾ alternating in succession, for your sleep, your rest, and your striving in your affairs, such as travel and tending to the state of the crops, and the like. ﴿And the sun and the moon﴾ continue in their course and their giving of light, both primarily and secondarily, and in performing what they were appointed to do, such as nurturing trees and crops, ripening fruits and coloring them, and other effects that follow from them, by the leave of Allah, the Exalted, as the early scholars (al-Salaf) say regarding causes and their effects (al-asbab wa al-musabbabat). The intended meaning of subjecting these to those addressed is not that they are empowered to dispose of them however they wish, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 13], and the like. Rather, His, glorified be He, directing of these according to what their benefits and interests require is as if it were a subjection to them and a disposal on their behalf according to their will. This was said by some of the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun).

Others said: The original meaning of taskhir (subjection) is driving by compulsion, and this cannot be intended, because compulsion and domination are not conceivable with respect to what has no awareness, such as inanimate objects like the sun and the moon. Its inconceivability with respect to the night and the day is even more evident. So here it is a metaphor for preparing and readying for what is desired in terms of benefit. In this there is an allusion to the difficulty of grasping what is subjected, relative to those addressed.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) mentioned, regarding the intended meaning of subjection, something similar to what was mentioned first. Then he mentioned another aspect, in which he said: It is only consistent with the doctrine of the astronomers (ashab al-hay'a), who say: The natural motion of the sun and the moon is motion from west to east. So Allah, the Exalted, subjected these stars by means of the motion of the outermost sphere (al-falak al-a'zam) from east to west. Thus this motion is a forced motion, and for this reason the word taskhir occurs with respect to it. He also mentioned that the occurrence of night and day is only by means of the motion of the outermost sphere, not the motion of the sun. As for the sun's motion, it is the cause of the occurrence of the year. For this reason the mention of night and day does not suffice in place of the mention of the sun. End of quotation. This is not objected to by saying that what he mentioned, namely his statement that the occurrence of night and day, and so on to the end, cannot be realized at the latitude of ninety degrees, because night and day only occur through the setting and rising of the sun, and there the sun neither sets nor rises by the motion of the outermost sphere, but by its own particular motion. For this reason the year is one day and one night. That latitude is uninhabited, and so is what is near it, so it does not fall within the scope of the favour being mentioned. Yes, his statement is different according to those who hold firmly to the skirts of the Shari'ah, so let it be examined.

Regarding whether the sun and the moon are among the things that have no awareness, there is a difference of opinion among the scholars. Some held that they are sentient beings ('alamain), and this is what the apparent indications require. This was the view of the Sufis and the philosophers (al-Falasifa). I have not come across any difference of opinion regarding the night and the day having no awareness. However, I saw in al-Bahja al-Qadiriyya, from the Divine Pole (al-Qutb al-Rabbani), Shaykh 'Abd al-Qadir al-Kilani, may his precious secret be sanctified, that the month or the week comes to him in the form of a person and informs him of the events that will happen in it. Perhaps this is in the manner of the Qur'an's appearance on the Day of Resurrection in the form of a pale man, and its saying to one who used to memorize it:

"I am the one who kept you awake through the dark nights, and made you thirsty in the midday heat."

And [in the manner of] death's appearance in the form of a white-horned ram, and its being slaughtered between Paradise and Hell on the Day of Resurrection, as has come in the report. You must believe in what has come from the truthful and the one whose truthfulness is confirmed (ﷺ), and in belief in other than it you have a choice.

The use of the past tense form (sighah al-madi) has been said to indicate that this subjection is one continuous matter, even though its effects are renewed. ﴿And the stars are subjected by His command﴾: it is a subject and predicate (mubtada' wa khabar), meaning: and all the stars, the luminous ones and others, in their motions and their positions which change and do not change, and all their conditions, are subjected to what they were created for, by His, the Exalted's, creation and His governance proceeding according to His will. Thus "al-amr" (the command) is singular, meaning "affairs." It is also permissible that it be singular, meaning "commands," and that by it is meant the command of existence (al-amr al-takwini), according to those who do not hold that the stars are sentient. The meaning is that they are subjected to what they were created for by His, the Exalted's, power and bringing into existence.

It has been said: Since the benefits of the stars do not return to them (humans) in clarity like those of the two previously mentioned luminaries (the sun and the moon), their subjection was not attributed to them with the particle of specification (ada't al-ikhtisas, i.e., "li-"), but was mentioned in a manner that indicates that they are under His dominion, glorified and exalted be He, without indicating anything else. For this reason He turned away from the verbal sentence, which indicates occurrence, to the nominal sentence, which indicates permanence and continuity.

Ibn 'Amir recited ﴿al-shams wa al-qamar﴾ with the nominative as well, so the subject is "al-shams" (the sun), and the rest are conjoined to it, and ﴿musakhkharat﴾ (subjected) is the predicate concerning all of them. The consideration that the manifestation of benefits is not comparable to what preceded, in relation to the whole, cannot be attributed to this reading, as is not hidden, and the consideration that the non-occurrence of the manifestation of benefits is comparable to what came before is in relation to the whole, as you see.

Among the people is one who said regarding this: The intended meaning of the subjection of the night and the day to them is their benefit from both, in that they are times for striving in interests and for rest, and in that the effects that follow from them, through which the benefits of the created beings are attained, become manifest, among which are what is detailed and what is summarized, such as the sun and the moon in them. Ultimately this returns to benefit from these, and this is the meaning of their being subjected to them. Thus the subjection of the night and the day to them includes the subjection of these to them. So since the speech first conveyed this, it dispensed with explicitly stating it a second time, and it explicitly stated what is greater in importance than it, namely that those matters have never ceased and do not cease to be overpowered under His power, submissive to His will and decree, whether you exist or do not exist. So let this be pondered.

The majority (al-Jumhur) recited ﴿wa al-nujum﴾ and ﴿musakhkharat﴾ with the accusative in both, and likewise in what preceded. This is explained by saying that "al-nujum" is the first object of an omitted verb indicated by the verb mentioned, and "musakhkharat" is its second object, meaning: and He made the stars subjected. It is permissible that "ja'ala" (made) means "khalaqa" (created), which takes one object, so "musakhkharat" is a circumstantial accusative (hal). Abu Hayyan preferred that "al-nujum" be conjoined to what precedes without an implied verb, and then "musakhkharat" is a circumstantial clause for all of them. In this case subjection is a metaphor for benefit, meaning: He benefited you with them while they are subjected to what they were created for, which is a means to your benefit. Otherwise, taking it literally indicates that subjection occurs during the state of subjection by His command, and this is not so because the first (the command) is prior. It was also said, for this reason as well: The intended meaning is that they are continuously subjected by His originating command, because bringing into being does not indicate continuity. Some eminent contemporary scholars permitted that it be a confirming circumstantial clause, with the implied "by His command" connected to "yusakhkhiru" (He subjects), and the sentence is of the type of tanazu' (competition between two verbs over one complement). Its acceptance is left to you. It was also said: it is a mimi (noun of place/manner, with the initial mim) verbal noun, such as "mas'ara," in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of the previously mentioned "sakhkhara" (He subjected). And "sakhkharaha musakhkharat" (He subjected them, subjections) is like "darabahu darabat" (he struck him, strikes). The plural is an indication of the difference in kinds. In the mention of the subjection of what was mentioned there is an announcement of the answer to what might be said: The one who influences the growth of plants is the movements and positions of the stars. If that is granted, there is no doubt that they are possible in essence and attributes, and occur in some of the possible ways, so there must be an originator, because the possible in its existence necessarily requires a specifier, lest it follow that occurring in some of the ways while other ways are possible is preference without a choosing preferrer. This is because obligation (ijab) contradicts preference, and the Necessary Existent (wajib al-wujud) is the one who is to be affirmed, in order to avoid circularity (dawr) or infinite regress (tasalsul). So said one of the eminent scholars. Al-Mawla al-'Imadi objected to this, saying: This is based on considering what was mentioned as evidence of the Creator, the Exalted, and His power and choice. But the matter is not like that, for it is something the opponent does not dispute, and does not hesitate in accepting. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth and subjected the sun and the moon?" they would surely say, "Allah." Then how are they deluded?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 61]. And He, glorified be He, said: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who sends down water from the sky and with it revives the earth after its death?" they would surely say, "Allah"﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 63], and so on to the verse. Rather, these are proofs of the Oneness (tawhid), in that one of this description cannot be imagined to share with Him in anything, let alone for an inanimate object to share with Him in divinity. End of quotation. It was objected to that the fact that what was mentioned is proof of Oneness does not preclude that it contains an announcement of the answer to what might be said. What harm is there in something being brought forward for one matter and indicating another matter? By my life, I do not see any merit in this objection after the speaker's statement "it contains an announcement of the answer to what might be said, etc.," since he did not definitively state it and inserted "might" (asa) in between. However, the speaker has a statement that clearly indicates that he considered the aforementioned proofs as proofs of the existence of the Creator, glorified be His affair as well, and al-Imam (al-Razi) had preceded him in this.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, that is, in the subjection related to what was mentioned, ﴿are signs﴾, striking and numerous as the context requires, ﴿for a people who use reason﴾. And since these heavenly effects are many, and the evidence contained in them of great power, knowledge, and wisdom for the Oneness is clearer, He made the signs plural and attached them to mere reason without reflection and contemplation, as if because they are so manifest that they are perceived by the self-evidence of reason, unlike the earthly effects in this regard. So they said. This is evident on the assumption that the argument is for Oneness and not for existence as well. As for if the argument is for that (existence), then in the claim of such manifestness there is discussion, since the discourse drifts to the refutation of infinite regress. How then can the indication be manifest without needing thought? It is answered that the argument from circularity or infinite regress is only after reflection on the beginning of their matter and what arose from it of the variation of their conditions, so understand.

It is also permissible that the intended meaning is "for a people who understand that," and what is pointed to is the ultimate wonders of the subtle details deposited in the heavenly things, indicated by the subjection, which only the skilled ones who have the utmost comprehension among the pillars of the scholars of wisdom attempt to know. In that case He ended the verse here with His saying, glorified be He: (who use reason), to indicate that this requires reflection more than other things. The first is preferable, as is not hidden.

And what He has created (﴿وما ذَرَأ﴾), i.e., created. According to one view, *dhurriyya* (offspring) is included in it. According to some, the conjunction is upon (النُّجُومَ, *al-nujūma*, "the stars") in both the nominative and the accusative, on the basis that it is an object of (جَعَلَ, *ja'ala*, "made"), and *mā* is a relative pronoun, meaning "and He who created it." ﴿For you on the earth﴾ [consisting] of animals and plants. It was said: [it includes] minerals too. There is no harm, in my view, in generalizing, [and it is] in the state of ﴿its colours differing﴾, i.e., its kinds, as a group of exegetes said. This is a well-known figurative usage (*majāz*) in this regard. Al-Raghib said:

"Colours (*al-alwān*) are used to express kinds and types. One says: so-and-so brought types (*alwān*) of speech and food. This is because their differences are mostly by difference in colour." It was also said that the intended meaning is the literal one (*ḥaqīqī*), i.e., differing in colours, from white, black and others. The first is more eloquent, i.e., that it is subjected to God, Exalted is He, or to what He created it for, of properties, states and qualities; or that He made it differing in colours and kinds so that you may enjoy whichever kind of it you wish.

[p. 111]

Some went to the view that the relative (*al-mawṣūl*) is conjoined to "the night." It was objected to this that there is in it a semblance of repetition, based on the view that the *lām* in (لَكم, *lakum*, "for you") denotes benefit, and that (سَخَّرَ لَكُمُ, *sakhkhara lakum*, "He subjected for you") has been explained as "for your benefit." So the meaning comes to "He benefited you with what He created for your benefit." Therefore it is better to take it as being in the place of the accusative, governed by a deleted verb, i.e., "created" or "caused to grow," as Abu al-Baqa' said, and to make ﴿differing﴾ a circumstantial (*ḥāl*) of its object. He defended this by saying that creating something for humans does not necessarily entail subjugating it by rational necessity, since the purpose may fail to be realized, and repetition is not to be denied given the long interval.

It was rebutted: this is heedlessness of the fact that the meaning is "benefited you." What he mentioned as an additional point is based on (لَكم, *lakum*) also being connected to (سَخَّرَ, *sakhkhara*). According to that objector, it is connected, as is evident, to (ذَرَأ, *dhara'a*). In the Shihabi glosses it is stated that this is of no consequence, because repetition for the sake of what was mentioned and for emphasis is an easy matter. The meaning "benefited you" is not ruled out either. Moreover, this verse was brought as a summary (*fadhlaka*) of what precedes it, and therefore it ends with "remember."

It is not for one who distinguishes left from right to say: (ما, *mā*) is a subject (*mubtada'*), (مُخْتَلِفًا, *mukhtalifan*) is a circumstantial from its deleted pronoun, and the clause ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for a people who remember﴾ is its predicate, with the demonstrative noun as the link, along the lines of what was said about His saying ﴿and the garment of piety, that is best﴾ [al-A'raf: 26], as if it were said: "And what He created for you on the earth, indeed in it is a sign." Its gist, Exalted is He, is that in what He created there is a sign. The incongruity of this reading is evident from both the preceding context (*sibāq*) and the broader context (*siyāq*). Indeed, its unsuitability to serve as a vehicle for the sublime speech of God is more evident than that it needs to be pointed out.

(أَلْوانُهُ, *alwānuhu*, "its colours"), i.e., the colours of the possibilities, is in the nominative, governed by (مُخْتَلِفًا, *mukhtalifan*). Some estimated a noun described by it so that its nominative could be governed by it, and said: "i.e., a kind (*ṣinf*) differing in its colours." This is something there is no need for, as is clear to anyone with even slight training in grammar.

Then the referent of "this" is what has been mentioned of subjugation and the like. It was said: the difference of colours. The *tanwīn* (nunation) of (آيَةً, *āyatan*, "a sign") is for magnification (*tafkhīm*): a magnificent sign, clearly indicating that the one whose attribute is this is one who should not be likened to anything in anything. Ending the verse with "remember" is either because of what is in the Shihabi glosses, that it is a summary of what precedes, or to indicate that the matter is so evident that it requires only recollecting knowledge that might be overlooked among the necessary sciences.

Some said: they state that the difference in the natures, forms and shapes of the things mentioned, with the unity of their matter, indicates a wise, choosing Creator. It is evident that what was mentioned is evidence for establishing the existence of the Creator, just as it is evidence for His oneness. This is what the Imam went to, and others followed him. Shaykh al-Islam did not approve of it, on the basis that the opponent does not dispute existence but disputes oneness. Therefore what is accepted by him of the attributes of perfection is brought for inference from it to what necessarily requires His oneness, and the impossibility that anything share with Him in divinity.

Some said: there is no barrier to the intended meaning being inference from the signs mentioned to the totality of existence and oneness, while the opponent denies that, even if he does not deny existence. Taking existence into the objective indicates that affirming it while claiming partnership in divinity is not to be counted, and that there is not much benefit between it and not affirming it. Reflect on that. And may God Most High guide you.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 14 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿It is He who subjected the sea﴾. This begins another kind of blessing, one connected with the sea, following the detailing of the kind connected with the land. Some have made it a counterpart to His saying, ﴿It is He who sends down water from the sky for you﴾. Therefore it came in its style, as a nominal sentence with both parts definite. What occurs in between is either a consequence of that sent-down water or includes a benefit of what results from it. The sea, with what is in the sea, includes both salt and fresh water. The meaning is: He made that for you in such a way that you are able to benefit from it by riding, diving and fishing, ﴿so that you may eat from it fresh flesh﴾, which is fish. Describing it as "flesh" even though it is an animal serves to indicate that its bones are few and weak in most of what is caught for eating, in comparison with livestock, which He favoured them with eating from earlier. It is also said that it hints at the restriction of its benefit to eating.

[p. 112]

The word (مِن) ("from") is connected with ﴿تَأْكُلُوا﴾ ("you eat"), or is a circumstantial element relating to what follows it, and it is then for the beginning of the source (ibtida'iyyah). It is also permitted that it be partitive (tab'idiyyah), and the statement then involves an elided noun, meaning "from its animals". In that case it is permitted that "from the fresh flesh" means the flesh of fish, just as it is permitted that what is meant is fish itself. "Fresh" (ṭarī) is an adjective of the pattern fa'īl from ṭarawa, yaṭrū, ṭarāwah, like sarawa, yasrū, sarāwah. Al-Farra' said: it is from ṭaria, yaṭrā, ṭarā'an and ṭarāwah, like shaqiya, yashqā, shaqā'an and shaqāwah. Freshness (al-ṭarāwah) is the opposite of dryness. Describing it with this indicates its delicacy, and alerts that one should hasten to eat it, for being moist it is ready to change, so decay and spoilage quickly reach it. The physicians have said that eating it after its freshness has gone is among the most harmful things. So there is here an incorporation (idmāj) of a medical ruling. This, as it has been said, does not contradict drying it and eating it lawfully, as has been imagined. And in making "the sea" the subject, the eating of it, on one of the two possibilities, is also a notice of the need to hasten.

Some have claimed that in the description there is also an indication of the perfection of His power, exalted is He, in creating a sweet, fresh thing within water that is bitter and undrinkable. In this there is something that is not hidden. According to us, nothing is eaten of the animals of the sea except fish. This is supported by the explanation of "flesh" as fish, which is related from Qatada and others. And from Malik and a group of the people of knowledge is the permissibility of all that is in the sea. Some excepted the pig, the dog and the human. From al-Shafi'i it is related that he permitted all of it. And what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi supports this: he said, "It is fish and what is in the sea of creatures."

Yes, according to us, eating the floating (ṭāfī) creature is disliked. This is the one that dies in the water of its own accord and then floats on the surface of the water. This is based on the report of Jabir from the Prophet (ﷺ): "What the water recedes from, eat it; what the water casts up, eat it; and what floats, do not eat it." This is the view of a group of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. As for the carrion of the sea, in a report (khabar, a prophetic report): "Its water is pure, its carrion is lawful," it refers to what the sea casts up, so that its death is attributed to it, not what dies in it without a calamity. If a part of an animal is cut off and the rest dies, eating what was severed is lawful, and the remainder is also lawful because its death came from a calamity, and what is severed from a living thing is dead; but if it was already dead, its carrion is lawful. If a fish is found in the belly of another fish, it is edible, because the narrowness of the place is the cause of its death. Likewise, if it is killed by a water bird or something else, or dies in a water container. Likewise, if fish are gathered in an enclosure from which they cannot escape, and it is possible to take them without hunting, and they die in it. If they cannot be taken without hunting, there is no good in eating them, because no cause for their death has appeared. If a fish dies in a net and it is unable to free itself from it, or it eats something that was thrown into the water so that it would eat from it and it dies from it, and that is known, then there is no harm in eating it, because that is in the meaning of what the water recedes from. As for death by heat and cold, there are two reports. One of them, related from Muhammad, is that it is eaten, because it died by a new cause, and it is as if the water had thrown it onto dry land. The other, related from the Imam, is that it is not eaten, because heat and cold are two attributes of time and are not usually among the causes of death. There is no harm in eating the jirrīth and the mārmāhī. It is well known from the Shi'a that eating the first is forbidden; so let it be consulted.

Qatada, as Ibn Abi Shayba transmitted from him, used the verse as evidence for the breaking of an oath by one who swears not to eat meat and then eats fish, because it contains the application of the word "flesh" to it. This is also related from Malik. It is answered that the basis of oaths is what people understand in their custom, not the linguistic literal meaning, nor the usage of the Qur'an. For this reason, when al-Thawri issued a verdict that one breaks the oath in the aforementioned case, citing the verse, and it reached Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, he said to the questioner: "Go back and ask him about one who swears not to sit on a carpet, and then sits on the ground: does he break his oath, on the basis of His saying, ﴿He made the earth for you a carpet﴾ [Nuh: 19]?" He said to him, "Are you not the questioner of yesterday?" He said, "Yes." He said, "He does not break it in this case nor in that," and he retracted what he had first issued as a verdict. The apparent meaning is that the basis of the Imam's position was custom, which Ibn al-Humam also adopted, not what is in al-Hidaya, as he said, namely that the analogy (qiyās) is that the oath is broken. The reasoning for the juristic preference (istihsān) is that the Qur'anic naming is figurative (majāzī), because the origin of flesh is blood, and there is no blood in fish, since it rests in water. This is contradicted by the fat (al-alyah), for it is formed from blood, yet one does not break an oath by eating it.

It is objected that there may be two proofs in the matter that are not contradictory, and the counter-example that was mentioned is refuted by saying that what was mentioned is "every flesh that arises from blood," and it does not necessarily follow that its converse is universal. It is responded that the application of "flesh" to fish in the linguistic sense is beyond doubt, so the counter-example and its converse are contradicted; the objector's intent is therefore a rebuttal of it with an added strengthening of the argument. Yes, it may be said that his intent by the aforementioned figurative usage is that it is a customary figurative usage, like the word "beast" (dābbah) when applied to a human, and his statement then returns to what the Imam said, and in that case there is no objection to it. What he mentioned is an explanation of the reason for the customary usage, so nothing is objected to it, and it is as you see. In the manner of what the Imam said, one may say about a person who swears not to ride a beast and then rides an unbeliever, that he does not break his oath, although Allah, glorified is He, called the unbeliever a beast in His saying, ﴿Indeed the worst of beasts in the sight of Allah are those who disbelieve﴾ [al-Anfal: 55]. In al-Kashshaf, as an explanation that "flesh" is not customarily applied to fish, it is said that if one man says to his servant, "Buy flesh with these dirhams," and he brings fish, he would deserve to be reprimanded, which is evidence that "flesh" is not customarily applied to it. Since oaths are based on custom, one does not break one's oath by eating it. It is objected that if he says to his servant, "Buy meat," and he buys the flesh of a sparrow, he deserves reprimand, while he breaks the oath by eating it. It is responded that the reprimand comes only from the rarity of buying such a thing, since it is not customary; whereas in our case, buying fish and its flesh is customary, so the object of the reprimand is nothing but the non-application of "flesh" to it.

﴿and that you may extract from it ornaments﴾ such as pearls and coral, ﴿which you wear﴾, that is, which your women wear. He directed it in this way: the attribution was made to the men because of their mixing with the women and their being the ones followed, or because they are the cause of women's adornment, for they adorn themselves so as to be beautiful in the eyes of men, and so that adornment is their adornment and their apparel.

Ibn al-Munir said: "By Allah, Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, did well in giving the husband the right to restrain his wife from what is significant of her property, and that is determined by what exceeds a third, for he has a right in it through beautification. Consider the share of men in women's wealth and their adornment, until it was made like the woman's share of her wealth and adornment. So he expressed his share in her wearing it by his wearing it, just as her share is expressed, both being supported by the report transmitted in this chapter." End of quote. It is understood from this that the figurative usage may be considered on the side of the predicate. Some have explicitly stated this and interpreted "you wear" as "you enjoy" and "you take pleasure in". It is also possible that the figurative usage is in the elision, and what appeared in the explanation is what is intended in the wording. It is said: the statement is by way of predominance (taghlīb), or is of the type "the sons of so-and-so killed Zayd," in which the attribution is made to some for all. It is objected that this is a possibility for both views. As for the first, it is because there is no being clothed by the predicate, which is wearing. As for the second, it is because it is not complete without the figurative usage on the side of the predicate, so there is no reason to abandon considering it in the way previously mentioned.

Some have said: there is no need for all of that, for there is no barrier to men adorning themselves with pearls. It is objected that, even after accepting that there is no barrier to it in Law, it is contrary to the constant custom, so the present tense verb, which indicates the opposite, rejects it. And the claim that there is a green gem (zumurrud) from the sea does not hold; and even granting its validity, this would still come in as well. Perhaps, since women are commanded to observe the veil and to conceal adornment from non-mahram men, the explicit attribution of wearing to them was omitted, so that the wording would be like the meaning.

Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on them both, used the verse as evidence that pearls are called an ornament (ḥilyah), so that if one swears not to wear an ornament and then wears it, he breaks the oath. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, says: he does not break it, because pearl alone is not called an ornament in custom, and its seller is not called "seller of ornaments." So it is stated in Ahkam al-Jassas. Some used the verse as evidence that there is no zakat on women's ornaments. Ibn Jarir transmitted from Abu Ja'far that he was asked, "Is there charity on women's ornaments?" He said, "No, it is as Allah said: ﴿an ornament which you wear﴾." And this, as you see, is weak.

Then, fresh flesh comes out of both the sweet sea and the salt sea [p. 114], and ornaments come only out of the salt sea. It is also said that pearls come out of the sweet sea too, except that they are worn only rarely, and most of them are used for medicine. We have not seen anyone mention this in most of the compiled books that deal with such matters.

Al-Bazzar transmitted from Abu Hurayra who said: Allah spoke to the western sea and spoke to the eastern sea. He said to the western sea, "Indeed I am carrying in you some of My servants; what will you do with them?" It said, "I will drown them." He said, "Your might is in your regions," and He forbade it the ornaments and the hunting. Then He spoke to this eastern sea and said, "Indeed I am carrying in you some of My servants; what will you do with them?" It said, "I will carry them on my hands, and I will be for them like a mother to her child." So He, glorified is He, rewarded it with the ornaments and the hunting. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted something similar through the chain of Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As from Ka'b al-Ahbar. Allah, exalted is He, knows best the soundness of this.

The apparent sense of the words of most scholars is that "the sea" in the verse is understood as the salt sea, and it is full of fish. Indeed, it is said that "fish" applies to every animal in it, and that pearls are found only in specific places within it.

﴿And you see the ships﴾, the vessels, ﴿cutting through it﴾, that is, sailing through it. ﴿Mawākhir﴾ is the plural of ﴿mākhirah﴾ in the sense of "sailing". The root meaning of al-makhr is cutting; it is said: "the water cut (makhara) the land" when it cuts through it. Vessels are so named because they cut through the water with their prow. Al-Farra' said: it is the sound of the ship's motion by the winds.

﴿And that you may seek﴾ is coordinated with ﴿you extract﴾ and what is coordinated with it. What lies between them is a parenthetical clause (i'tirāḍ) to prepare the beginnings of seeking and to prevent it from being mistaken as the result of extracting the ornament. He turned away from the pattern of the preceding and following address, namely the plural address, to the singular address, whose intended referent is anyone suitable for address, as a notice that this is not directed at the two previous matters. Ibn al-Anbari permitted that it be coordinated with a hidden cause, meaning "so that you may benefit from that and that you may seek", and that it be connected with a hidden verb, meaning "He did that so that you may seek." This is an artificial reading which Allah, exalted is He, is too great to need.

---

**Note on terms used:** *tafsir* (Qur'anic exegesis), *istihsan* (juristic preference), *qiyas* (analogy), *mahram* (a person one may not marry, permitted to see one without veil), *zakat* (obligatory charity), *khabar* (a prophetic report), *taghlib* (predominance, a grammatical convention of giving precedence to one party in an expression).

**[Part 2 of 2]**

﴿from His bounty﴾: from the abundance of His provision, by means of sailing with them for trade. ﴿And that you may be grateful﴾: that you may fulfil the due of Allah Most High's blessings through obedience and tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness). Perhaps the reason this blessing is singled out to be followed by mention of gratitude is that it is the most important among the blessings of cattle, in that He made the riding of the sea, despite being a cause of potential destruction, since its riders, as ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said, are "a worm on a piece of wood," a means of benefit and the acquisition of livelihood. This is among the perfections of blessing, for it covers a long distance in a short time without the need for the hardship of travel, movement and motion, together with rest and tranquility. How fine is what has been said on this:

*"Indeed we, in this world, are like the passengers of a ship:*
*We think we are standing still, while time is carrying us along."*

The omission of mentioning attainment of the desired goal between the seeking (of bounty) and the gratitude is said to be to indicate that it is needless to state it explicitly, as both occur together.

The verse has been cited as evidence for the permissibility of riding the sea for trade without reprehension, and a group of scholars held this view. ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated from Ibn ʿUmar that he used to dislike riding the sea except for three purposes: for a raider (in holy war), or for a pilgrim (ḥājj), or for one performing the lesser pilgrimage (ʿumrah).

[Page 115 begins mid-passage]

﴿And He cast into the earth firmly set mountains﴾, i.e., firm mountains. The full discussion of this has already passed. ﴿Lest it shake with you﴾, i.e., out of aversion to its shaking, or so that it would not shake. The *mayd* (violent swaying) is the agitation of a great thing. He (al-Alusi) explained how the casting prevents the earth from agitation: the earth is like a ship on the surface of the water. If a ship has no heavy bodies in it, it agitates and tilts from side to side at the slightest thing. If heavy bodies are placed in it, it settles. Likewise, were it not for these mountains upon the earth, it would agitate. The mountains, in relation to the earth, are like heavy bodies placed in a ship in relation to it.

Al-Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) raised objections to this. The first, according to the philosophers (*al-hukama'*) who hold that the motion or rest of bodies is due to their natures, is that the earth is heavier than water, so it must sink into it, not float or be anchored by mountains. This is unlike a ship, which is made of wood

[Page 115 continues]

and has air between its parts that prevents it from settling and would cause it to sway were it not for the heavy weight.

The second, according to the People of Truth (*Ahl al-Haqq*, the Sunnis), who hold that bodies have no natures that necessitate rest or motion, so that no thing rests or moves on land or sea except by the sheer power of God Most High alone. The second objection is that anchoring the earth with mountains so it does not sway and remains standing upon the water's surface is only conceivable if the water on whose surface it rests is still. In that case it is said: if the cause of the water's stillness in its specific place is its specific nature, why not say that the earth's stillness in this place is also due to its specific nature? And if we say that it is due to the sheer power of the Glorified, why not say that the earth's stillness is likewise so? Then anchoring by mountains is inconceivable under either assumption.

The third objection is that it is possible for the earth as a whole to sway without its motion being apparent and without its inhabitants perceiving it. This would be like the motion of a ship without its passenger perceiving it. The perception of its motion is not precluded when vapor gathers within it, because that happens in a small part of it, and it resembles the twitching that occurs in a particular limb of the body.

Then he said: "What I hold concerning this problematic point is this: it is established by certain proofs that the earth is a sphere, and it is established that these mountains on the surface of the sphere function like roughnesses on the face of this sphere. Then we say: if we assume these roughnesses had not existed but the sphere were smooth and free of them, it would become such that it moves in a circle like the celestial spheres because of its simplicity, or it would move from the slightest cause of movement. When these mountains were created and were like roughnesses on its face, its sides became uneven, and the mountains, by their weight, inclined toward the center. So they became like stakes, preventing it from circular motion." End of quote.

Al-Imam followed this solution, and al-'Allama al-Baydawi also followed it. It was objected to him that there is no basis for what he mentioned, either according to the Ahl al-Haqq or according to the philosophers (*falasifa*). As for the first, a thing's essence does not necessitate its motion; rather, that is by the will of God Most High. As for the second, the philosophers did not say that it is the earth's right to move in a circle, because the earth has a straight natural inclination (*mayl mustaqim*), and what is so does not have within it the source of a circular inclination, as they stated in natural philosophy (*al-tabi'i*).

An objection was also raised against the claim that the mountains prevent it from motion: it has been established in geometry (*handasa*) that the greatest mountain on earth, whose height is two and a third farsakhs, relative to the earth's diameter is in the ratio of five-sevenths of the width of a barleycorn to a sphere whose diameter is one cubit (*dhira'*). There is no doubt that this amount of a barleycorn does not take that sphere out of roundness so as to prevent it from motion. The same applies to the mountains in relation to the sphere of the earth.

Then it was said: the correct position is that God Most High created the earth agitated for a wisdom known only to Him, then anchored it with mountains, in accordance with His customary practice of making things dependent upon causes. Some of the verifiers (*al-muhaqqiqin*) said in response: the intended meaning is that the earth, insofar as it is a true simple sphere, setting aside its being an element (*'unsur*), had one of two rights. For from that aspect, it either possesses a circular inclination like the celestial spheres, in which case its right would be to move circularly like them; or it possesses a straight inclination, in which case its right is rest, but it moves from the slightest compelling force (*qasir*). As for rest: a body located in its natural place, if it moves with a natural motion, that motion is instantaneous, because it necessitates leaving its natural place. The earth cannot be conceived as having voluntary motion, since it lacks consciousness. As for moving from the slightest compelling force, whoever has sound imagination judges this necessarily. He clarified this by a true sphere on a true surface, for it touches it only at a point, so by the slightest thing, even a puff of breath, it rolls from its place.

"Yes, what is actually the case is that one of the two is specified, and mentioning both is a broadening of the scope, which is common among them. Thus his statement 'as for the second, the philosophers...' is refuted. As for his statement 'it has been established in geometry...', its answer is that they have stated in the books of cosmography (*hay'a*) that in every climate (*iqlim*) there are thirty mountains or more. So the ratio of each mountain, although it is like the aforementioned ratio, may still be that their collective mass prevents its motion, like a rope made of hairs, whose judgment differs from that of each hair. Moreover, that ratio is considered with respect to volume, while the prevention of its motion is considered with respect to weight, and the weight of these mountains nearly equals the weight of the earth, because mountains are hard stone bodies while the earth is soft and porous, like a wooden ball to which iron grains have been stuck."

As for what is said, that there is something other than this based on the principles of philosophy, it should not be criticized, because that basing is not harmful if it does not contradict the legal principles (*al-qawa'id al-shar'iyya*), as in what we are discussing. An objection was raised against what the objector claimed to be correct, that it is refuted by what he himself raised. But my opinion is that after understanding his intent, nothing of what was mentioned is refuted against him. We have already presented something similar and elaborated on this matter, and from it becomes evident what is most in accord with the principles of Islam.

Then, what the respondent mentioned, that what is explicitly stated in the books of cosmography is that in every climate there are thirty mountains or more, contradicts the well-known view, which is that in the first climate there are twenty, in the second twenty-seven, in the third thirty-three, in the fourth fifty-five, in the fifth thirty, in each of the sixth and seventh eleven. The total is one hundred and eighty-seven mountains. Yet his statement is not free of critique, so reflect.

The meaning of (*alqa*, "cast") according to what Ibn 'Atiyya transmitted from the commentators (*al-mu'awwilin*) is "created" and "made." He himself preferred that it is more specific than that, because it implies that God the Glorified brought the mountains into existence from the sheer power and invention of Himself, not from the earth, and placed them upon it. He supported this with reports they narrated on this point, some of which have already been mentioned. He did not construe it with *'ala* (on), as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39], to indicate the perfection of the mountains, their firmness, and their stability in the earth, so that they are as if nails in a courtyard. Consider whether they are counted as part of the earth, so that one who swears not to sit on the earth would break his oath by sitting on them or not. I have not been informed of anyone who addressed this. The apparent view is the first, because common usage counts them as part of it, even though the apparent meaning of this verse, like others, is that they are not counted.

His statement, the Exalted, ﴿and rivers﴾ is conjoined to *rawasiya* (firm mountains), and the governing element (*'amil*) in it is *alqa* (cast). However, its governing over it is due to what it contains of the meaning of making and creating, or by its being construed as including that meaning. Under either assumption, there is no ellipsis (*idmar*), and this is what many have preferred. It was also permitted that it be an object of a verb that is omitted, but this is not a consensus, contrary to Ibn 'Atiyya. That is: "and He made or created rivers," similar to what was said in the line: "I fed her straw and cold water." Abu al-Baqa' estimated the verb to be "cut" (*shaqq*), and the conjunction in that case is conjunction of clauses (*'atf al-jumal*). It seems that because most sources of rivers are from mountains, He mentioned the rivers after mentioning the mountains.

His statement, the Exalted, ﴿and roads﴾ is conjoined to "rivers," meaning "and He made paths for your destinations." ﴿That you may be guided﴾ to them. So the causal clause, considering His statement ﴿and roads﴾, is as is apparent. It is also permitted that it be a causal clause considering all that was mentioned before, because those great signs indicate the falsehood of abandonment. It was also said: they indicate the existence of a wise Agent. Then in His statement ﴿you may be guided﴾ there is a double meaning (*tawriya*) in this case.

[p. 117]

**"And landmarks"**: these are signs by which the traveller (al-sabilah) is guided, such as a mountain, a watering place, or the smell of the earth. It is related that some people can smell the ground and by its scent know whether the road is travelled or untravelled. For this reason the distance (masafah) is so called, taking it from *al-sawf*, meaning smelling. Ibn Jarir and others related from Ibn ʿAbbas that they are the landmarks of the roads by day. From al-Kalbi it is related that they are the mountains, and from Qatadah that they are the stars. Ibn ʿIsa said: what is meant by them is the things by which one knows what is intended, whether by writing, speech, gesture or appearance. The apparent meaning is what was mentioned first. The strangest and most remote explanation given is that what is meant is long, thin fish, like snakes in their colours and movements, found in the Indian Ocean that is sailed to from Yemen. They were so called because when they appeared they were a sign of arrival at the land of India and an indication of safety.

**"And by the star they are guided"**: by night, on land and at sea. The word "star" here denotes the category, so it includes the *khunnas* (the stars that recede) and others by which one is guided. From al-Suddi it is related that it is restricted to the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), the two Guards (al-Farqadan), the Daughters of the Bier (Banat Naʿsh), and al-Jadi. From al-Farraʾ it is related that it is restricted to al-Jadi and the two Guards. From some of them it is related that it is al-Thurayya, since it has become a proper name for it by dominance. In a hadith: "When the star *tali*ʿ, the affliction is lifted." The poet said:

*Until, when the star settles in the darkness,*
*and the herbage is left withered and reaped.*

From Ibn ʿAbbas it is related that he asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this, and he said: "It is al-Jadi."

If this is sound, it should not be departed from. Al-Jadi is the Jadi of al-Farqad. According to *al-Maghrib*, it is with a fatha on the *jim* and a sukun on the *dal*. The astrologers diminutivise it to distinguish it from the zodiac sign (*al-burj*). It is also said that it is so in the language. As evidence that what is meant is something that includes all of this, one cites what is in *al-Lawaʾih* from al-Hasan, that he read *wa-bi-al-nujum* with two *dammas*, and from Ibn Wththab, that he read it with a *damma* and then a sukun. In both readings it is a plural like *saqf* and *suquf*, *rahn* and *ruhun*. The sukun is said to be for lightness, and it is also said to be a dialect form. The view that it is a plural of the pattern *fuʿul* is preferable to the view that its origin is *al-nujum*, with the *waw* deleted. Ibn ʿUsfur claimed that the saying "al-najm" is a poetic necessity, and he cited:

*Indeed He who decreed this, a judge who ruled,*
*that the water be approached when the star (al-nujum) had set.*

This is like his saying: "Until the throats of the throats became wet."

The pronoun may be general, referring to every traveller by land and sea among those addressed earlier, and the change of expression is for *iltifat* (a shift of address). Placing the prepositional phrase first serves the rhyme (*fasilah*), and the separate pronoun serves emphasis. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to Quraysh, because they were much given to trade journeys and were well known for being guided by the star on their travels. The speech departs from its usual pattern, and placing the prepositional phrase and the pronoun first serves specification, as if it were said: "And by the star, specifically these people, specifically are they guided." Therefore reflection on this and gratitude for it through monotheism is most binding upon them and most incumbent on them.

Some scholars took this verse as a basis for observing the stars in order to know the times, the direction of prayer (*qiblah*), and the routes. There is no harm, then, in learning what gives that knowledge. However, to know the exact direction of the *qiblah* by the stars with certainty is difficult, indeed impossible, as the great scholar Abu al-ʿAbbas Ahmad ibn al-Banna explained. For if one takes as the criterion the stars that lie directly above the heads of the people of Makkah, the point where the perpendicular falls on the plane of Makkah is not the same as the perpendicular falling on the plane of other cities. If one takes al-Jadi as the criterion, it does not follow that if it is on the shoulder or on the side in Makkah, it is so elsewhere, except for one who is on the circle of the meridian passing through the heads of the people of Makkah and of the other town. That is unknown and cannot be reached except by knowing the difference between the longitudes and latitudes, and that is a matter on whose quantity there is disagreement, and the correct figure has not been fixed.

As for the statement of one who said that this is known by the worshipper placing the sun between his eyes, for example, when it is at its zenith on the longest day of the year, so that whenever he does this he has faced the House: if by "its zenith" he means the zenith of the sky of his own town, this is not correct, because the sun does not reach its zenith at one time in two towns that are far apart. If he means the zenith of the sky of Makkah, that cannot be known in another town except by knowing the difference in longitude between the two towns, and you have heard the disagreement about that. The same is said about what resembles this. Indeed, he (may his secret be sanctified) said: knowing it with certainty by what they mention of the Indian circle and the like is also impossible, because the basis of all of that is knowing the longitudes and latitudes, and short of verifying that, it is like gathering thorns with the hand. Therefore the duty of the worshipper should be only to seek out the direction, and knowledge of the direction is obtained by the stars and likewise by other means that are mentioned in their proper place.

[Page 118]

﴿Is then He who creates﴾ the wondrous creatures mentioned (or who creates everything He wills) ﴿like one who creates nothing﴾, whether of great or of small account? This is a rebuke of the disbelievers and a refutation of their associating partners with God, may He be exalted, and of their worship of others besides Him, namely the idols. It denies that they could be likened to Him, which is what their worship implies, after enumerating what plainly requires that He alone be worshipped.

The placing of the interrogative hamza before the fa' (then) directs the denial at the notion that the aforementioned likeness could arise from the great and manifest acts that God alone performs, which are known to be so among them as well, as many verses indicate. Mentioning only creation from among what preceded it is because it is the greatest and most evident, and because the rest follow from it. Or it is because each of those is a particular kind of creation. That is: after the clear evidence that God alone is the origin of these matters, which demonstrate His oneness, His singularity in divinity, and His worthiness of worship, can a likeness be imagined between Him and what is utterly remote from all of that, as your associating partners do?

Strictly speaking, the sentence at first sight should have read: "Is one who does not create like one who creates?" But it has been said: since likening is a relation that holds between the two parties, the noble text was chosen in this form, out of regard for the priority of the positive attribute (malaka) over its absence, and to avoid placing the absence between it and its detailed particulars mentioned before it. It also alerts to the complete ugliness of what they did, since this is not merely removing their idols from their place, but degrading the station of lordship to the level of inanimate matter. There is no doubt that this is worse than the former.

By "one who does not create" is meant everything of this description among rational beings, such as the angels and Jesus, peace be upon them, and others, as well as inanimate things such as the idols. The word "man" (man) is used to give precedence to rational beings over others, together with the correspondence (mushakala) it creates. Alternatively, the reference is to rational beings alone, and the state of the others is understood from them by indication of the text (dalalat al-nass). For if one who creates is not like one who does not create, and the latter is among rational beings, then what of inanimate matter? It has also been said that the reference is to the idols alone, and the use of "man" is either for correspondence or based on what their worshippers believe about them. The first view is preferable. The inclusion of the idols in the ruling of non-likeness is either by way of direct inclusion or by way of implication through the textual indication, according to the demonstrative method, as stated by some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun).

The verse has been cited as evidence against the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), who claim that servants create their own actions.

Al-Shihab (al-Khafaji), after establishing that the object is general in the manner we have mentioned, said: It is also permissible that the generality in it be derived from treating the verb as intransitive, namely that it is understood from this that the verse cannot be used to argue against the Mu'tazila in refuting their view that servants create their actions, as occurs in the books of kalam (theology), because a universal negation does not contradict a particular affirmation. End of quotation, as we found it in the copies in our hands. Perhaps these copies are faulty; otherwise I do not think it is anything but a stumble of a good horse, and this is evident.

﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾ That is: will you not observe, so that you do not recall this? For it is so clear that it requires nothing beyond recollection, which is returning to what was previously conceived and then forgotten. Some have supplied the object as "the non-equality," and said that since it has not previously been established, so that the real sense of recollection could be applied to it by being conceived and then forgotten, they made "recollection" an explicit metaphor (istiara tasrihiyya) for knowledge of it.
