It has also been said that the metaphor is implicit (makniyya) in the supplied object, and the attribution of recollection to it is an imaginative representation (takhyil). So recollect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 18:

﴿And if you were to count the favour of Allah, you could not enumerate it.﴾ This is a general reminder of His favours, exalted is He, after an enumeration of some of them. He separated the two with His words, exalted is He: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who does not create?﴾ as it has been said, in order to hasten the establishment of the proof and to confirm the argument immediately after detailing the acts that were detailed, which are evidences of Tawhid (the oneness of Allah). Their indication of Him, although they are not restricted to the aspect of creation, is evident, since their indication of Him is also apparent from the aspect of bestowing favour. However, since this aspect follows from the first aspect, it was dispensed with stating explicitly. Then its state was explained in a general manner, meaning: if you were to count His favours, exalted is He, which are poured upon you, from what has been mentioned and from what is yet to be mentioned, you would not be able to enumerate them or determine their number, let alone render thanks for them. The discussion on verifying this has preceded, as Allah has granted. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Oft-Forgiving﴾ in that He covers up what has passed from you of disbelief in them and of failing to fulfil their rights, and does not hasten to punish you for that. ﴿Most Merciful﴾ in that He pours them upon you despite your deserving to be cut off and deprived for what you commit and what you leave of kinds of disbelief and disobedience,
[Page 119]
among which is the equating of the Creator with others. Each of those two, the covering and the pouring forth, is among the favours. So the sentence is a reason for the ruling that they cannot be enumerated, and the placing of forgiveness before mercy is due to the precedence of takhliya (clearing away, i.e. removal of defects) over tahliya (adornment, i.e. bestowing virtues).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 19:

﴿And Allah knows what you conceal﴾, i.e., what you harbor of beliefs and deeds, ﴿and what you disclose﴾, i.e., what you manifest of them. The omission of the returning pronoun (al-'a'id) is for the sake of the rhyme (al-fawasil), i.e., both matters are equal in relation to His all-encompassing knowledge, glorified is He. Mentioning the first before the second establishes the equality in the most eloquent manner. In this there is, of threat and of indication of His exclusive possession of the attributes of divinity, what is not hidden. As for the first, the knowledge of the King who is capable of acting regarding the disobedience of His servant necessitates requiting him, and the knowledge and power of Allah the Exalted is often mentioned while that is intended. As for the second, it is based on what has been said: that the fronting of the predicate subject (al-musnad ilayhi) in such a context conveys restriction (al-hasr). From here it has been said: He, glorified is He, refuted their associating idols with Him first by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is He who creates like one who does not create?﴾, and refuted it a second time by His saying, blessed is His name: ﴿And Allah knows﴾, etc., as if it were said: He, the Exalted, is the One who knows that, not what you associate with Him, for it does not know that, rather it does not know anything at all, so how can it be counted as a partner of the Knower of secrets and hidden things?

And in al-Kashshaf: in the first clause there is an indication that He, the Exalted, did not impose upon them the true thanks, due to its impossibility, and that He, glorified is He, passed over the possible to the easy and accessible; and in the second there is what indicates that they fell short even in this accessible matter, and so they deserved reproach.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 20:

﴿And those they invoke﴾ begins the demonstration that their gods are entirely undeserving of worship. It explains this, so that no trace of doubt remains, by enumerating their states that plainly contradict that deserving, and it seems they were described even though their contradiction is evident, in order to draw attention to the complete foolishness of the polytheists, who would not recognise this without explicit statement. That is, "And the gods you worship, O disbelievers, ﴿besides Allah﴾, glory be to Him, ﴿do not create anything﴾ of things at all," meaning that creating is not among their attributes. Some of the eminent scholars said that the mention of this after the denial of similarity and partnership is for the purpose of inference. It is as if it were said: "They do not create anything, and what does not create does not share with what creates," and from the third it follows: "They do not share with the Creator," and it follows from this that the Creator does not share with them. So there is no repetition. It was objected to this: it is based on the assumption that "what creates" and "what does not create" are applied to an unspecified referent. From the preceding words of this scholar it is understood that he took the first to be God, Exalted is He, and the second to be the idols. His argument there would require no need for this premise, since it is known and taken for granted. Therefore the better view is that the repetition is for the sake of matching the words of God, Exalted is He: ﴿and they are created﴾. It was replied that what is explicitly stated in both places is generality, and as for restricting them to what was mentioned, this is because "what creates" is, in actual existence, specific to God, Exalted is He, like the daytime star being specific to the sun, though it is general in its concept. And "what does not create," though general both mentally and externally, is interpreted as "what is worshipped," because the context requires it. The requirement of the argument is not the absence of need for the premise, but rather that it is so evident that it need not be proven, and this justifies its being a part of the proof. When the intended meaning has become clear, the objection is void. End. Perhaps the more apt justification for the mention is what we pointed out first. Since there is absolutely no necessary connection between denying creatorship and being created, He affirmed this for them explicitly, in the sense of their attribute that they create, since being created is the requirement of their essences, because they are contingent and dependent on an agent for their existence and continuance. The construction of the verb in the passive, as some of the eminent scholars said, serves to establish the opposition and contrast between what was affirmed of them and what was denied of them, namely the attributes of creating and being created. It also signals that there is no need to specify the agent, since the exclusivity of His agency, majestic is His majesty, is evident. Perhaps the placing of the pronoun here is merely for emphasis. The meaning of "creating," whether negated or affirmed, is the one that is immediately understood from it.

Page 120

It was also permitted that the second be understood as carving and shaping, on the basis that those invoked are the idols, and that they are referred to with the expression used for rational beings because the worshippers treated them as such. The expression for that as "creating" is for the sake of observing the rhetorical correspondence (mushakala, the matching of one term to another for the sake of symmetry). In this there is an allusion to the extreme feebleness of the polytheists' minds, in that they associated with their Creator those He created. Understanding the first in this sense is also not valid, since the ability to produce such a creation is not at all what the entitlement to worship rests upon.

The majority of reciters (al-jumhur) read with the upper ta' (the letter ت) in «تُسِرُّونَ» (you conceal), «تُعْلِنُونَ» (you declare), and «تَدْعُونَ» (you invoke). This is the reading of Mujahid, al-A'raj, Shayba, Abu Ja'far, and Hubayra from 'Asim. According to the well-known transmission from him, he read with the ya' (the letter ي) at the end for the last word and with the ta' for the first two. All three were also read with the ya' in a transmission from Abu 'Amr and Hamza. Al-A'mash read «واللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ الَّذِي تَبْدُونَ وما تَكْتُمُونَ والَّذِينَ تَدْعُونَ» etc. with the upper ta' in all three verbs. Talha read «ما تُخْفُونَ» (what you hide) and «ما تُعْلِنُونَ» (what you declare), and «تَدْعُونَ» with the ta' likewise. These two readings were taken as explanations, because they differ from the consonantal text of the Mushaf. Muhammad al-Yamani read «يُدْعَوْنَ» (are invoked) with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the 'ain, in the passive, meaning: the disbelievers invoke them and worship them.

﴿Dead﴾ is a second predicate (khabar) of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those"), or the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada', topic), meaning "they are dead." He stated this explicitly because affirming that they are created does not require denying them life, since some created things are living. The meaning of death here, if the thing referred to is the idols, is the absence of life without any addition beyond what is by nature capable of living.

As for His, glorified be He, words ﴿not living﴾, this is also a predicate after a predicate, or an adjective (sifah) of ﴿dead﴾. Its purpose, according to some, is emphasis (ta'kid). Establishing a new meaning (ta'sis) was preferred, because some things that lack life may come to have it, such as a drop of semen. So it was stated to exclude such cases, as if it were said: "They are dead presently, and not capable of life in the future."

It is also permitted that the thing referred to by this description includes all of what they worship, among rational beings and others. In that case ﴿dead﴾ is used in a general metaphorical sense (majaz) to include those who had life and then died, such as 'Uzayr, those who will die, such as 'Isa and the angels, peace be upon them, and those whose nature does not include life at all, such as the idols.

On this view, ﴿not living﴾, if interpreted as "not capable of life," is the attribution of a description of some to all, so that it establishes a meaning in part. If emphasis is intended, the matter is clear. It is also permitted that among those worshipped are the angels, peace be upon them, and that some of the addressees worshipped them. The meaning of their being dead is that they must undergo death. Their being ﴿not living﴾ means that their life is not complete, and complete life is essential life that death cannot befall.

In the reading ﴿والَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ﴾ with the letter ya' (third person), it is also permitted that the dead are the ones who call upon others, and He described them as such to liken them to the dead, since they are astray and not guided. The distance of this interpretation is not hidden.

﴿وما يَشْعُرُونَ أيّانَ يُبْعَثُونَ﴾ (And they do not perceive when they will be raised). The first pronoun refers to the deities, and the second to their worshippers. Shu'ur (perception) means knowledge or its beginnings. Al-Raghib said: "It is said: sha'artu, meaning I reached the hair (sha'r), and from this metaphorically: sha'artu kadha, meaning I knew it with precision, like reaching a hair." It was said: "The poet (sha'ir) was named so for his keen intelligence and precise understanding." Then he mentioned that al-mashá'ir are the senses, and that the meaning of "they do not perceive" is "they do not grasp through the senses." He also said that if it were said in many places where it appears, "they do not perceive," meaning "they do not reason," this would not be correct, since much that is not sensible is rational.

(Ayyana) is an expression for the time of a thing and is close in meaning to (mata, when). Its origin, according to some, is ay aw anna ayya ayyi waqtin, then the alif was dropped, the waw was changed to ya', and they were assimilated. As you see, this is weak.

Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read "إيّانَ" with a kasrah on the hamzah, which is the dialect of his people, Sulaym. The apparent view is that it (ayyana) is governed by (yub'athun, they will be raised), and the clause is in the accusative position as the object of (yash'urun), because it is suspended from operating (mu'allaq 'an al-'amal). That is, those deities do not know when their worshippers will be raised. This is a form of mockery of them, based on the interpretation that the idols are meant, since the perception of inanimate things of obvious matters is clearly impossible for everyone, so how could they perceive what only the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, knows?

In al-Bahr it is stated that there is in this mockery of the polytheists, and that their deities do not know the time of their being raised to be recompensed for their worship of them. Perhaps this applies to all other possibilities regarding the deities. In it there is also an indication that resurrection is among the necessary consequences of moral responsibility (taklif), since it is for recompense, and recompense is for responsibility, so it belongs to it. And that knowing its time is necessary for divinity.

It was also said: the two pronouns in (yash'urun and yub'athun) refer to the deities. The negation of their perception of the time of their being raised entails the negation of their perception of the time of their worshippers' being raised, and this is what the apparent meaning requires. Whoever permits that the dead refers to the disbelieving, misguided ones, makes the two plural pronouns here refer to them, and the statement is in the form of a threat, meaning: "And those polytheists do not perceive when they will be raised for punishment." It was also said: the sentence is complete at His, exalted be He, words ﴿وما يَشْعُرُونَ﴾ (and they do not perceive), and ﴿أيّانَ يُبْعَثُونَ﴾ (when they will be raised) is an adverbial complement (zarf) of His, glorified be He, words that follow.

[Page 121]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 22:

﴿Your God is one God.﴾ This is in the sense that the God is one on the Day of Resurrection, similar to ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ [al-Fatihah: 4]. Abu Hayyan said: "This statement is not sound, because ayyan (when) at that time leaves what it is settled in of being an adverb, whether an interrogative or a conditional, and becomes purely adverbial in the sense of 'time,' governing a clause after it, as in: 'time when Zayd stands, I stand.' Moreover, this connection is itself contrary to what is apparent. The apparent meaning is that His saying, glorified is He, (Your God) is an explicit statement of the claim and a summary of the conclusion after establishing the proof." ﴿So those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ and its conditions, of which the resurrection and what follows it of recompense are part, ﴿their hearts are denying﴾ the oneness, rejecting it, or rejecting the signs that indicate it, ﴿and they are arrogant﴾ toward acknowledging it, or toward the signs that indicate it. The fa' (so) indicates that their persistence in denial and their continuance in arrogance occurred as a consequence of the manifest proofs and the decisive demonstrations; it is thus causal, as in your saying: "I did good to Zayd, so he did good to me." The meaning is that it has been established, by the proofs and arguments that have been set forth, that divinity belongs exclusively to Him, glorified is He; so it followed from this that they persisted in denial and continued in arrogance. The ruling is built upon the relative pronoun to indicate that what falls within its clause is the cause of it, for disbelief in the Hereafter and what it contains of resurrection and recompense, reward for obedience and punishment for disobedience, leads to restricting one's view to the immediate, to not turning to the proofs, which necessitates denying them and denying their substance, and to arrogance against following the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, and believing in him. As for belief in the Hereafter and what is in it, it inevitably calls one to turn to the proofs and reflect upon them, out of desire and fear, and this produces certainty in the oneness and submission to the command of God, exalted is He. This was said by some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun).

Some people said: The meaning of "and they are arrogant" is: arrogant toward belief in the Messenger of God, ﷺ, and following him. Thus the denial is an allusion to their disbelief in God, exalted is He, and the arrogance is an allusion to their disbelief in His Messenger, may God's blessings and peace be upon him. The first is more apparent. Attributing the denial to the hearts is because they are its locus, and this is more eloquent than attributing it to them. Perhaps he did not follow the same mode in attributing the arrogance because it is a manifest effect, as the verse after it indicates. Some scholars have said: every sin can be concealed and hidden, except arrogance, for it is a transgression that necessarily requires being made public.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 23:**

﴿Without doubt﴾, meaning it is true, or truly. ﴿Surely Allah knows what they conceal﴾ of denial, ﴿and what they reveal﴾ of arrogance. Yahya ibn Salam and al-Naqqash said: what is meant here by ﴿what they conceal﴾ is their consultation in Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of Quraysh) about killing the Prophet (ﷺ). This is, as you see, [a weak view]. In any case, the purpose of knowledge of this is the threat of recompense for it. And ﴿anna﴾ and what follows it are in the interpretation of a nominative verbal noun, [functioning as the subject of] ﴿la jaram﴾, according to the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh. The majority hold that ﴿la jaram﴾ is a compound noun, the two words [la and jaram] being compounded like "fifteen" (khamsata 'ashara), and after the compounding its meaning became the meaning of "fa'ala" (he did), namely "haqqa" (it is true). So ﴿anna﴾ is interpreted as [a clause] with "fa'ala" [i.e., as the verb "haqqa" with its clause]. Abu al-Baqa' interprets it as a verbal noun standing in for it, namely "haqqan" (truly). It was also said that it is nominative governed by "jaram" itself, as a past-tense verb meaning "it became established and necessary", with "la" negating an implied statement spoken by the disbelievers, like His saying: ﴿I do not swear﴾ (Al-Qiyamah: 1; Al-Balad: 1), in one of its aspects. Al-Zajjaj held that it is accusative as an object of "jaram", with "jaram" likewise a verb but meaning "kasaba" (he earned), and its subject is a pronoun referring back to what is understood from the context; this is not the case in the preceding view. It was also said that it is the predicate of "la", from which the preposition has been dropped, and "jaram" is its subject, the meaning being: there is no denial and no prohibition regarding the fact that Allah knows, etc. The complete discussion of this has already passed.

Isa al-Thaqafi read ﴿innallaha﴾ with a kasra on the hamza, as a resumption and a break from what precedes it, according to what Abu Hayyan said. It is related from some of them that ﴿la jaram﴾ may serve in place of an oath, as one says: "La jaram la'atiyannaka" (Without doubt, I will surely come to you), and in that case the sentence is the answer to the oath. ﴿Indahu﴾ — He, majestic is His majesty — ﴿does not love the arrogant﴾, meaning absolutely. This includes those who were arrogant toward monotheism or toward the signs that point to it, as a primary inclusion. It is also permitted that it refers specifically to those arrogant ones. The first is preferable. In any case, the form "istif'al" here is not for seeking [something], unlike its use in what came before. It is also permitted that the statement is general while the form "istif'al" is taken in its apparent sense of seeking, meaning: He does not love one who seeks arrogance, let alone one who is characterized by it. Al-Raghib distinguished between "kibr", "takabbur" and "istikbar" after saying that they are close in meaning. The truth is that some of them may be used in place of others. Their discussion will come shortly, if Allah the Exalted wills, and I think it has also passed before. The sentence is a justification for what the preceding speech contained of threat. The meaning of the negation of love is hatred, which some interpret as being about something like retribution and punishment. The reports describing the bad state of the arrogant on the Day of Resurrection are very numerous.

Page 122

Page 123

﴿And when it is said to them﴾, i.e., to those arrogant ones. This is an explanation of their misguidance after the explanation of their error. It is also said that the pronoun refers to the Quraysh disbelievers who, as narrated from Qatadah, would sit on the path of anyone who went to the Prophet ﷺ in order to learn the reality of his affair. When he passed by them, he would say to them: ﴿What has your Lord sent down?﴾ upon Muhammad, peace be upon him. ﴿They say: "Tales of the ancients."﴾ That is, what the ancients wrote. This is like their saying: ﴿"He has had them written, so they are dictated to him"﴾ [al-Furqan: 5]. Thus, asatir (tales) is the plural of asfar, which is the plural of satr (line), so it is a plural of a plural. Al-Mubarrad said: it is the plural of usturah, like urjuhah and arajih. Their intention by this is that there is no verification in it. It is also said that the one who said this to them was some of the Muslims, so that they would reveal what they had. It is also said that the one who said it was some of them, sarcastically, since otherwise he did not believe that anything had been sent down. A similar explanation is given regarding the answer's naming it "al-manzil" (that which is sent down) in the answer, on the basis of the omitted subject in it having that meaning. It is also permissible that they named it by what was mentioned, on the assumption and concession, in order to refute it, like His saying: ﴿"This is my Lord"﴾ [al-An'am: 77, 78]. It is also said that they supposed it to be "sent down" by way of imitation and parallelism.

In al-Kashshaf, it is stated that (madha) is in the accusative governed by (anzala), i.e., "what thing has your Lord sent down?" Or it is in the nominative as the subject, with the meaning "what thing has your Lord sent down?" If you read it in the accusative, the meaning of (tales of the ancients) is "what you claim to have been sent down." And if you read it in the nominative, the meaning is "that which sent it down," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"What should they spend? Say: 'The surplus.'"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219], according to those who read it in the nominative. End. The verification of his purpose has been obscure to some of the verifiers. The author of al-Fara'id said: The correct view is that it is in the nominative as the subject, as evidenced by the nominative of (asatir), for the answer to a nominative is nominative, and the answer to an accusative is accusative. No one has read it here in the accusative.

Page 123

The author of al-Taqrib said: There is an observation in al-Zamakhshari's words, and he explained it with what he explained and answered with what he answered. Al-Tibi extended the discussion on this. The author of al-Kashf has excelled on this point, and said: His statement "or it is in the nominative as the subject, with the meaning 'what thing sent it down'" is a clarification; otherwise the meaning is "what is it that sent it down," as stated explicitly in al-Mufassal, since there is no reason to omit the pronoun without a lengthy construction, and the wording admits the accusative and the nominative equally. In light of this, the difference between the two estimations clearly appears. For although the accusative indicates the establishment of the verb itself, and that the question about the object is less indicative than the nominative, it is known that the clause that serves as a relative clause should be known to the addressee, and where is the accepted and known ruling apart from it? When this is established, it should be known that on both estimations, the answer does not correspond to it, unlike His saying in ﴿"They said: 'Good.'"﴾ [al-Nahl: 30], where the answer corresponds to it. As for (asatir), and His saying here, like His exalted saying: ﴿"What should they spend?"﴾ to the end, in the case of the nominative, is a comparison in the shift to the nominative, not its manner, for the answer there corresponded to the question, unlike what we are dealing with. He estimated "what you claim to have been sent down" according to the accusative reading, because the questioner did not believe in a definite sending down; rather he asked about specifying what he had heard had been sent down in general, so that to return him to the correct view it suffices to say: what you claim to have been sent down is tales. As for the nominative estimation, it indicates that sending down is, in his view, established and accepted without dispute, and that the question is only about specifying what was sent down. He is answered that this established matter in your view is "tales," sarcastically, since it is known that what is sent down cannot be tales. Thus he was overly emphatic in returning him to the correct view by mocking him, and that he decided the ruling as established in a place other than its proper place. So I see that the questioner was answered in appearance, but not in reality; rather, the refutation was intensified. It is likely that the first is an answer to the question among themselves or to the delegates, and the second is an answer to the question of the Muslims, according to what he mentioned of the two possibilities, not the reverse as he supposed. This is the more likely in establishing his statement, which agrees with what he mentioned afterwards, as has passed.

He considered what he mentioned there to be a third aspect, that the answer corresponds to it here. The explanation of the difference between the two estimations, as claimed and as sending down, is by what we have prepared; and although the majority went to it, it is an artificial burden, and one can dispense with it. End. (Asatir) was also read in the accusative, as Abu Hayyan and others stated explicitly. Thus the denial of the author of al-Fara'id stems from a lack of knowledge.

﴿لِيَحْمِلُوا﴾ is connected to ﴿قالُوا﴾, as is the apparent reading. That is, they said this so that they would bear ﴿أوْزارَهُمْ﴾, meaning their own sins, namely the sins of their misguidance. ﴿Awzar﴾ is the plural of ﴿وِزْر﴾, and it is also used for a load, by analogy with the weight of a mountain (wizr al-jabal). Each of the two words is used to mean sin, as in this verse. As for His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿لِيَحْمِلُوا أثْقالَهُمْ﴾, ﴿كامِلَةً﴾ means that nothing is reduced from it and that it is not expiated by something like a calamity that befalls them in this world, or by an accepted act of obedience performed in it, as the sins of the believers are expiated by such things. The Imam said: the meaning is that none of their punishment is lightened, but it reaches them in full. This indicates that God, Exalted is He, may remove part of the punishment from the believers, for if this meaning applied to all, there would be no benefit in singling out these disbelievers for it. The carrying of sins is a metaphor for being punished for them.

Ibn Jarir reported from Zayd ibn Aslam that it reached him that the disbeliever's deed takes the form of the ugliest thing God created in appearance and the foulest in smell. It sits beside him, and whenever something frightens him, it increases his fear, and whenever he fears something, it increases his fear further. He says: "What an evil companion you are! Who are you?" It says: "Do you not recognize me?" He says: "No." It says: "I am your deed. It was ugly, so you see me ugly, and it was foul, so you see me foul. Lower yourself to me so that I may carry you, for you have often carried me in the world." So it carries him. This is the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿لِيَحْمِلُوا أوْزارَهم كامِلَةً﴾ ﴿يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾, where ﴿يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾ is an adverbial complement of time governing ﴿لِيَحْمِلُوا﴾. ﴿ومِن أوْزارِ الَّذِينَ يُضِلُّونَهُمْ﴾ means "and [they will bear] some of the sins of those whom they misguide," that is, some of the sins of those who went astray through their misguidance [of them], in the sense of "and the like of some of their sins." Here ﴿مِن﴾ is partitive (tab'idiyya), because its contrast with His saying ﴿كامِلَةً﴾ determines this.

The intended meaning of this "some" is the share of causation: the misguider and the one misguided are partners. This one misleads and that one obeys, so they both bear the burden, but the one who went astray has other sins beyond this, which are not carried by the misguider. Al-Akhfash said that ﴿مِن﴾ is redundant (za'ida), meaning "and the sins of those who misguide them," in the sense that they will be punished with a punishment equal to the punishment of everyone who followed them. Abu al-Baqa' adopted the view that it is redundant, and he objected to the partitive reading on the grounds that it implies that the misguider does not bear all the sins of the one who went astray, which contradicts the transmitted report: "Whoever establishes an evil practice, upon him is its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it, without that diminishing their burdens in any way."

In reply: the transmitted report indicates partiality, and there is no contradiction between them, as is clear. Because of this supposed contradiction, al-Wahidi said that ﴿مِن﴾ is for the category (li'l-jins), meaning they will bear sins of the kind of the sins of those who follow them. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that the ﴿مِن﴾ which indicates the category cannot be estimated as what was mentioned, but rather as "the sins which are the sins of those who misguide them," so that in meaning it reverts to the view of al-Akhfash, even though they differ in the estimation.

The lam in ﴿لِيَحْمِلُوا﴾ is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), because the carrying is a result of their act and is neither their motive nor their purpose. It is reported from Ibn 'Atiyya that it may be the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), governing an implied verb rather than ﴿قالُوا﴾, meaning that the utterance of that was determined so that they would bear. The question of explaining God's acts by purposes will arise, and you know that there is disagreement on it.

Al-Bahr allowed that it is the jussive imperative lam (lam al-amr al-jazima), in the sense that this carrying is binding upon them, so the sentence is complete at His saying ﴿أساطِيرُ الأوَّلِينَ﴾. But the apparent reading is the lam of consequence. The future form in ﴿يُضِلُّونَهُمْ﴾ indicates the continuity of misguidance, or it is taken with respect to the state of their saying, not the state of the carrying.

﴿بِغَيْرِ عِلْمٍ﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the object, as if it were said: they misguide those who do not know that they are astray in falsehood. This contains a warning that their guile does not succeed upon a person of understanding; rather, only ignorant fools follow them. It also contains increased reproach and blame for them, since it was incumbent upon them to guide the ignorant, not to misguide them. It was also said that it is a circumstantial qualifier of the subject, meaning they misguide while not knowing that what they call to is the path of error. It was also said that the meaning in this case is: they misguide out of ignorance of the severe punishment they deserve for that misguidance. The view that it is a circumstantial qualifier of the subject, with a meaning like this, is attributed to al-Wahidi. Some claimed that this is the correct reading and not the circumstantial qualifier of the object, and they supported it by saying that the concluding statement, His saying ﴿ألا ساءَ ما يَزِرُونَ﴾, and His saying ﴿مِن حَيْثُ لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾, strengthen it. This is not so. What was mentioned as supporting it is thought, by those who made this claim, to mean that if it is made a circumstantial qualifier of the object, it has no connection with what the speech is about concerning the state of the misguiders. You have been shown its correct aspect.

Abu Hayyan preferred it, saying that the one spoken of is the one to whom misguidance is attributed as its agent, so taking him as the bearer of this state is more appropriate. This is answered by the fact that proximity opposes it, so it cannot serve as a preference. It was also said that it is a circumstantial qualifier of the subject of ﴿قالُوا﴾, meaning they said that while not knowing that they would bear on the Day of Resurrection the sins of error and misguidance. This is supported by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وأتاهُمُ العَذابُ مِن حَيْثُ لا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾, in the sense that carrying the mentioned sins of error and misguidance is of the kind of the punishment coming upon them from where they do not perceive. But this is refuted by the fact that the carrying mentioned, as the verse explicitly states, is on the Day of Resurrection, while the punishment mentioned is the punishment of this world, as you will hear, God willing.

It is permitted that it be a circumstantial qualifier of both the subject and the object, as Ibn Jinni said regarding His saying: ﴿فَأتَتْ بِهِ قَوْمَها تَحْمِلُهُ﴾ [Maryam 19:27]. This is contrary to the apparent reading.

The verse has been used as evidence that the one who follows another in taqlid must investigate and distinguish between the one who is right and the one who is wrong, and cannot excuse himself by ignorance. This is clear on the most correct aspect that we have previously mentioned.

﴿ألا ساءَ ما يَزِرُونَ﴾ means: how evil is what they bear and commit of sin, namely their aforementioned action.

[Page 125]

﴿Those before them had already schemed﴾: a threat to them that the harmful consequence of their scheming would rebound upon them, as was the case with the earlier nations who came before them and were struck by the swift punishment. Makr (scheming) means diverting another person from what he intends by a stratagem. Here it is, according to what has been said, a metaphor for actually undertaking its causes and arranging its preliminaries, because what follows indicates that the diversion did not take place. It has also been permitted that the word be taken in its literal sense (tajrid), meaning that they arranged devices and stratagems in order to deceive the Messengers of Allah, peace be upon them. ﴿Then Allah came upon their structure from its foundations﴾: that is, from the direction of the pillars and columns upon which they built, so that it was brought down. Min here is for the beginning of the limit (ibtida'iyyah). Al-bunyan (structure) is a singular masculine noun. Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) related from some lexicographers that it is the plural of bunyanah, like sha'ir and sha'irah, tamr and tamrah, and nakhl and nakhlah; and that this type of plural may be treated as masculine or feminine. The original meaning of ityan (coming), as he said, is arrival with ease, and this is impossible in its apparent sense with respect to Him, the Glorified. For this reason some have needed to posit an elided genitive, meaning "the command of Allah the Exalted," and this was related from Qatadah. In the Kashshaf it is placed under the usage of "time came upon him" meaning it destroyed him and annihilated him, and in that case there is no need to posit an elided genitive.

It was also read as "binyatahum" (their building), which has the same meaning as "bina'ihim." It is said: banaytu abni bina'an and bunyatan, and Banā (ﷺ)... [here the text reads "وبَنى نَعَمْ" which is a scribal or textual oddity; rendered as it stands:] and "banā, na'am" ("he built, yes"), and the term binyah is frequently used to refer to the Ka'bah. Ja'far read "baytahum" (their house), and al-Dahhak read "buyutahum" (their houses). ﴿Then the roof fell down upon them from above them﴾: that is, the roof of their structure fell upon them, since it is not conceivable that it could remain standing after its foundations had collapsed. "Min" (from) is connected to "kharra" (fell), and it is for the beginning of the limit; or it is connected to an elided word, in which case it is a circumstantial (hal) that emphasizes "al-saqf" (the roof). Ibn Atiyyah and Ibn al-A'rabi said that ﴿from above them﴾ is not an emphasis, because the Arabs say: "A roof fell upon us" and "A wall fell upon us" when it collapses on property belonging to the speaker, even if it did not literally fall upon him; so it serves to explain that they were beneath it when it was demolished. Some people have claimed that "ala" (upon) here means "an" (from) and is for causation, and the sentence has an elided genitive, meaning "the roof fell down because of their disbelief." The phrase ﴿from above them﴾ was added with "fell down" to dispel the supposition that it might have fallen while they were not beneath it. It is not hidden that this is a lengthy digression without benefit; indeed, it is speech that no learned person should utter. The statement is an illustration, meaning that their situation, in arranging the constructed devices and stratagems by which they planned to scheme against the Messengers of Allah the Exalted, peace be upon them, and Allah's nullifying them and making them the cause of their destruction, is like the situation of a people who built a structure and supported it with columns; then that structure came from the direction of its columns, by being undermined, so the roof fell upon them and they perished beneath it. The point of resemblance is that what they set up and devised as a means of protection and dominance became a means of ruin and annihilation. So the columns stand in the position of the constructed devices, and their turning back upon them is a destruction, just as those stratagems turned back upon their authors. The "structure" is what they had fabricated and embellished with those constructed devices, and upon which they agreed, an opinion supported by schemes. This resembles their saying: "Whoever digs a pit for his brother falls into it headlong."

Close to this is what has been said, that the meaning is that Allah the Exalted nullified their deeds. It has also been said that the matter is based on its literal sense: Nimrod ibn Kan'an built a tower in Babylon in order to ascend, in his claim, to the heaven, to learn its affairs and fight its inhabitants, and he exceeded in its height, so that its length reached into the heaven, according to what al-Naqqash related, and it is related from Ka'b that it was two farsakhs. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and Wahb said: its height was five thousand cubits and its base three thousand cubits. So Allah sent a wind upon it that demolished it, and its roof fell upon him and upon his followers, and they perished. It has also been said that Jibril, peace be upon him, demolished it with his wing, and when it fell the people were thrown into confusion from fear, so on that day they spoke seventy-three languages; for this reason Babil was so named, and the language of the people before that had been Syriac. There is no concealing the contradiction of this report with the well-known account, for its implication is that Nimrod's destruction took place in the manner mentioned, whereas the well-known view is that he lived after the story of the tower, and Allah the Exalted destroyed him with a gnat that reached his brain, to show the complete baseness and helplessness of his condition; and the Glorified repaid him in kind, because he ascended toward the direction of the heaven with vultures, so Allah the Exalted destroyed him by the most contemptible of birds. What has been mentioned concerning the reason for naming the well-known place Babil is the most famous account. In Mu'jam al-Buldan it is stated that the city of Babil was [the city] of Yuwarasif, the tyrant... [page break]

[Page 126]

...and its name was derived from al-Mushtari (Jupiter), because Babil in the first Babylonian language is a name for Jupiter; and Alexander ruined it. As for what has been mentioned, that the language before that was Syriac, al-Baghawi related it, and al-Khazin examined it, saying that Salih, peace be upon him, and his people came before that and spoke Arabic, and that tribes before Ibrahim, peace be upon him, such as Tasm and Jadis, also spoke Arabic. This may be answered by the consideration of [the matter].

Al-Dahhak said: the verse is an indication of the people of Lut, peace be upon him, and what was done to them and to their towns. The statement is likewise based on its literal sense. A group preferred to base it on illustration, as you have heard. Accordingly, on the preferred view, the meaning of ﴿those who disbelieved before them﴾ includes all the schemers upon whom their structures were demolished and who were thrown into dismay. Al-A'raj read "al-saqf" (the roof), and Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with both of them, and Mujahid read ﴿al-suqf﴾ with a dammah on the sin only. Both are plurals of saqf, and fu'ul and fu'l, according to what Abu Hayyan said, are attested as plural patterns of fa'l, though they are not regular for it; the regular plural is suqf, which is the analogical form. A group read ﴿al-saqf﴾ with a fathah on the sin and a dammah on the qaf, and this is a dialect variant of al-saqf. It is mentioned that the original form has a dammah on the qaf and its sakin form is its lightened form, and that its usage became frequent in reverse of the saying of the Arabs: "rajul" (a man) with a fathah then a dammah, and "rajl" with a fathah then a sukun, and this is a Tamimi dialect. ﴿And the punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive﴾: not by its coming from that direction, but rather they expected the coming of its opposite from what they desired and longed for. By "it" is meant the swift punishment. In the conjoining of this clause to what preceded there is an awe-inspiring magnification of the matter of their destruction, and it indicates that what is meant by it is the swift [punishment].

﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them﴾, that is, He will humiliate them. The apparent meaning is that the plural pronouns refer to those who schemed before them, as if it were said: "Those before them schemed, so Allah punished them in this world, and then He will punish them in the Hereafter." The particle *thumma* ("then") indicates the difference between the two recompenses, together with the temporal distance that it implies. Placing the adverbial phrase before the verb is said to be for restricting the disgracing to the Day of Resurrection, and what is meant by it is what is explained by His saying: ﴿and He will say﴾, that is, to them, as exposure and rebuke: ﴿Where are My partners﴾, to the end of the verse. There is no doubt that this does not happen except on that day. Some verifiers said: the fronting is not for that purpose. Rather, the announcement of their recompense in this world indicates that they have a recompense in the Hereafter, so the soul remains awaiting its arrival, asking about it ("what is it?"), even while being certain that it is in the Hereafter. Therefore the speech is phrased in a way that indicates that what is intended by the mention is their recompense, not the fact that it is in the Hereafter. It is also mentioned that the sentence is a conjunction (*'atf*) upon an implied element (*muqaddar*) to which the speech extends, that is: "this which was understood from the parable concerning the punishment of these schemers, who said about the Mighty Qur'an, 'tales of the ancients,' or something more general than that, and of what was mentioned earlier about the punishment of those schemers: their recompense in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them," to the end. Then he said:

The pronoun is either for those who were deceived regarding the noble Qur'an, or for them and for those among the schemers whom they were likened to. Restricting it to them is refuted by the *sibaq* (the preceding context) and the *siyaq* (the surrounding context). End of quotation.

In this there is a departure from the apparent meaning to the degree that it contains, so let it be considered. Some explained the disgrace as one of the concomitants of punishment by the Fire, because it is the complete instance of it, and Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿Indeed, whoever You admit to the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 192]. It was objected to this that His saying, glorified is He, "Where are My partners," to the end, refutes it, because it occurs before they enter the Fire. It was answered that the *waw* (conjunction) does not require sequence. You know that the better course, even with this, is to interpret it as general humiliation. The attribution of the partners to Himself, Mighty and Majestic, is on account of the slightest association, based on their claim that they are partners of Allah, exalted is He above what they associate. So the verse is like His saying: ﴿Where are your partners whom you used to claim﴾ [Al-An'am: 22].

It is also permissible that what was mentioned is a report from Him, the Exalted, concerning their own attribution, for they used to attribute and say, "partners of Allah, the Exalted," and in that there is an additional rebuke that is not present in "Where are your idols?" for example, if it were said. It is not hidden that this is disgrace and humiliation through speech. So if the disgrace mentioned earlier is explained as punishment by the Fire, the verse points to two disgraces, one practical and one verbal, and I point to the first first, because it is more fitting to what precedes it.

[p. 127]

The majority (*al-Jumhur*) read *shurakā'iya* with the *madd* (elongation) and the hamza, with the *ya'* vowelled with fatha. A group also read it this way, except that they made the *ya'* quiescent (*sakin*), so it drops in continuous recitation due to the meeting of two quiescent letters. Al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, with a variant from him, read it with *qasr* (shortening) and a fatha on the *ya'*. A group denied this and claimed that this reading is not authentically transmitted, because shortening the *madd* is only permissible out of necessity (*darura*). This is not what they said, for it is permissible in latitude (*si'a*). It has also been directed that the hamza with kasra before the *ya'* was dropped for lightness, and this is not like shortening the *madd* in general. Moreover, it has been narrated from Ibn Kathir that he shortened the one in *al-Qasas* and *warā'ī* in Maryam, and from Qunbul that he shortened ﴿that he saw himself free of need﴾ in *al-'Alaq*. So how can that be counted as a necessity?

Yes, Abu Hayyan said: its occurrence in speech is rare. So recognize that, for many people have overlooked it.

﴿Those whom you used to oppose concerning them﴾, that is, you used to dispute and contend with the prophets, peace be upon them, and their followers regarding their affair, and you claimed that they were true partners when they had made clear to you the opposite of that. Some explained *al-mushāqqah* (opposition) as enmity, but explaining it as contention makes the connection of *fīhim* ("concerning them") to it evident, and there is no need to make *fī* causal. It was said: *mushāqqah* is used for contention, taken from splitting the staff (*shaqq al-'aṣā*), or because each of the two contenders is on one side (*shiqq*). The purpose of the interrogative is to summon them as intercessors, by way of mockery and rebuke, for they used to say: "If what you say is true, then the idols will intercede for us." The inquiry about their whereabouts does not necessarily imply their actual absence. It is sufficient for that the fact that they are not present under the title by which they claimed to be characterized, so there are no partners there, nor their places.

It was also said: this implies their absence, and it is said that they will be put between them and their partners at that time, so that they may search for them in a moment in which they had pinned their hopes on them, or because when they did not benefit them, they became like the absent. There is no need for this after what you have learned. Moreover, it was objected to his saying "so that they may search for them," to the end, that it is not sound, for the polytheists will have clearly seen the reality of the matter, and they will have renounced that false claim; so how can a searching for them be conceived from them?

It was answered that it is possible that they will be heedless of that because of the greatness of the terror, so they will search for them. Furthermore, what has been mentioned implies the gathering of the idols, and this is what many verses indicate, such as His saying: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Anbiya': 98], and His saying, glorified is He: (﴿whose fuel is men and stones﴾) [al-Baqarah: 24; al-Tahrim: 6], according to one opinion. I see no obstacle to interpreting "partners" as their false objects of worship, in such a way that it includes rational beings as well.

The majority read *tushāqqūna* with a fatha on the nun, while Nafi' read it with a kasra; this is also narrated from al-Hasan, and the criticism of Abu Hatim is not to be heeded. A group read it with a shadda on the nun, on the basis that the nun of the indicative (*nūn al-rafʿ*) was assimilated into the nun of protection (*nūn al-wiqāyah*). The reading with kasra is on the basis of dropping the *ya'* of the first person and being satisfied with the kasra, meaning: *tushāqqūnanī* ("you oppose me"). Moreover, the opposition to the prophets, peace be upon them, and their followers is like the opposition to Allah, exalted is His affair; and were it not so, it would not be correct to attach the opposition to Him, glorified is He. As for when it means dispute, it is evident that they did not dispute with Allah, the Exalted. As for when it means enmity, it is because they do not believe that they are enemies of Allah, the Exalted. As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do not take My enemy and your enemy as allies﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 1], meaning the polytheists, it is also interpreted without any doubt.

﴿Those who were given knowledge will say﴾, from among the people of the place of standing (*al-mawqif*), and they are the prophets, peace be upon them, and the believers who were given knowledge through the proofs of monotheism. They used to call them in the world to monotheism, and they would argue with them and act arrogantly toward them. Yahya ibn Sallam limited it to the believers, and the matter is easy in this. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they are the angels, peace be upon them. We have not found a qualification of his for them. And from Muqatil that they are the guardians (*al-hafazah*) among them. The speech of some of them suggests that they are the angels of death, since he objected to the view that they are the angels that it would be necessary then to say "they cause them to die" in place of "the angels cause them to die," and that this would entail vagueness in the place of specification and specification in the place of vagueness. Al-Shihab said that this is in utmost weakness. It was also said: the intended meaning is everyone who is characterized by this title, whether angel, human, or otherwise. What the sound heart inclines to is the first view, that is: those (the believers and prophets) will say, rebuking the polytheists, showing their gloating over them, confirming what they used to admonish them with, and affirming what they had threatened them with. The choice of the past tense is to indicate the certainty of its occurrence and its inevitability, as is customary in His, the Exalted, reports, such as His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And the companions of Paradise will call out﴾ [al-A'raf: 44].

﴿Indeed, the disgrace﴾: the humiliation and abasement. Al-Raghib explained it as the humiliation which one is ashamed of. ﴿Today﴾ is in the accusative governed by *al-khizy* (disgrace), according to the view of one who holds that a verbal noun with *al-* (the definite article) can govern, as in the line of poetry: "weak in harming his enemies." Or it is governed by the sense of "being established" in the adverbial phrase that functions as the predicate of *inna*. In this there is a separation between the operator and the operand by the conjoined element, but this is excused in the case of an adverbial phrase. The *alif-lam* here is for presence, that is, "this present day," and its mention is to indicate that they were before that in might and dissent. ﴿And evil﴾: the punishment. Since disgrace is included in it, its mention is for emphasis. ﴿Upon the disbelievers﴾ in Allah, the Exalted, and His signs and His messengers, peace be upon them.

[Page 129 begins at the marked point below.]

﴿Those whom the angels take in death﴾, with the verb feminine. Hamzah and al-A'mash read «yatawaffāhum» with the masculine form here and in what follows, God willing. Both readings are common in such cases.

It is also read with the assimilation (idghām) of the present-tense prefix tā' into the tā' after it. In such a case a connecting hamza (hamzat wasl, the hamza used at the start of a word) is brought in at the beginning, and it drops in continuous speech, even though a connecting hamza is not normally found at the beginning of a present-tense verb. In the Mushaf of 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), there is a single tā' in both places. As for the relative clause, it has three grammatical possibilities: the genitive, as a qualifier of «al-kāfirīn» (the disbelievers), or as a substitute (badal) for it, or as an explicative apposition (bayān) to it. The accusative and the nominative are possible as a "cutting off" (qat') for disparagement (dhamm). Ibn 'Atiyyah allowed that it be nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence, with the clause ﴿So they cast⁠﴾ as its predicate. Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying that adding a fā' (fa) in the predicate is not permitted here except according to the view of al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash al-Awsat), who allowed it, and that its addition in the predicate is general, as in: "Zayd, so he stood," meaning "Zayd stood." He then said: "It should not be supposed that this fā' is the one that enters the predicate of a subject when it is a relative clause and carries the sense of a condition, because it is not permitted for it to enter such a verb together with an explicit conditional particle, so it is not permitted with what carries its meaning." This is his wording. Shihab reported from him that he said: "The prohibition with what carries its meaning is more appropriate." He was criticised: that it is more appropriate is not accepted, because the exclusion of the fā' with it is due to its strength, so that it does not need a linking pronoun when its direct connection to the verb is valid, and what carries its meaning is not like that. His statement which we have quoted does not indicate preference, so perhaps he found another statement of his that indicates it.

He (Abu Hayyan) preferred the genitive as a qualifier. Then he said: "Thus that falls within the speech that is reported, so if the saying is on the Day of Resurrection, «tatawaffāhum» is in the present form as a narration of a past situation. If it is in this world, that is, in relation to what He, glory be to Him, informed that He will disgrace them on the Day of Resurrection, and the Mighty and Majestic will say to them what He says, the people of knowledge said: the disgrace of that Day, of which God, exalted be He, informed that He will disgrace them in it, and the evil upon the disbelievers, will be «tatawaffāhum» in its proper form, and in meaning it includes the one whom she caused to die and the one whom she causes to die." According to what Ibn 'Atiyyah mentioned, it is possible that «alladhīn» (those who) to its end is part of the speech of those who were given knowledge, and that it is a report from Him, exalted be He. The apparent meaning is that the saying is on the Day of Resurrection, so the present form is to bring to mind the image of the angels taking them in death, as was said just before, because of its terror. In the specification of disgrace and evil for those whose disbelief continued until the time of death, and not for those among them who believed even at the very end of their life, there is a rebuke of them that is not hidden. That is, the disbelievers who persisted in disbelief until the angels take them in death, ﴿wronging themselves⁠﴾, that is, while they persisted in polytheism, which is a wrong against themselves. And what a wrong it is, in that they exposed themselves to the enduring punishment. ﴿Then they offer submission⁠﴾, that is, surrender, as al-Akhfash said.

[Page 129 ends here.]

Qatadah said: submission. There is no distance between the two sayings. What is meant by both is that they showed compliance and submission. The original meaning of "casting" (ilqā') concerns physical bodies, but it is used here for their showing compliance, and as an indication of the utmost extent of their submission and compliance, and of treating that as a thing cast before the hands of the mighty and dominant one.

The sentence is said to be coordinated with His saying: ﴿And He says, "Where are My partners?"⁠﴾. What lies between them is a parenthetical sentence (jumlah i'tirāḍiyyah), brought in to confirm the disgrace that befell them in front of all witnesses. The apparent form would have been "then they cast" to its end, but He expressed it with the past form to show the certainty of the occurrence, that is, He, glory be to Him, says that to them, and so they surrender, submit, abandon contention, and come down from what they were upon in this world of arrogance and stubbornness. Perhaps this is the meaning of the one who said that the speech was complete at His saying: ﴿themselves⁠﴾, and then returned to narrating their situation on the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: it is coordinated with «qāla alladhīna» (those who said). Abu al-Baqa' and others allowed coordination with «tatawaffāhum», and Abu Hayyan preferred it. But Shihab said: this is only consistent if «tatawaffāhum» has the meaning of the past, and it has already been stated to you that the sentence is the predicate of «alladhīna» together with what it contains.

The first option was criticised on the ground that His saying: ﴿We used not to do any evil⁠﴾ is either in the accusative governed by a hidden verb, and that verb is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of «alqaw» (they cast), meaning: they cast submission saying "we used not to..." to its end; or it is an explanation (tafsīr) of the submission they cast, on the basis that what is meant by it is the speech indicated by it, with the evidence of the other verse: ﴿and cast to them the word⁠﴾ [al-Naḥl: 86]. Whichever it is, that coordination requires that this saying occur from them on the Day of Resurrection, and that is a plain lie, and it is not permissible for it to occur on that day.

It was answered that what is meant is: "We used not to be doing evil" in our belief, that is, our belief was that our action was not evil. This is similar to what was said in interpreting their saying: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists⁠﴾ [al-An'ām: 23]. It has been objected that the response to them with ﴿Yes, indeed God...⁠﴾ to its end does not suit this, since it is plain that it is a refutation of the negation. And it cannot be said that it is a response to one who denied while his soul was certain, because that would also be a lie, so the interpretation does not benefit.

Some people said that a lie is permissible on the Day of Resurrection, and on that basis there is no difficulty. It is not hidden that this discussion applies also on the supposition that the coordination is with «qāla alladhīna» (those who said), since, as with the first, it requires the occurrence of the saying on the Day of Resurrection, and that is the core of the discussion.

Shaykh al-Islam, may God have mercy on him, preferred the earlier coordination and said: it is an answer to His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Where are My partners?⁠﴾ They meant by "evil" polytheism, denying that it came from them. They expressed it with what was mentioned only as an acknowledgement that it is evil, not as a denial that it is so while acknowledging that it came from them. And that it is not an answer to the saying of those given knowledge is a claim that they do not deserve what overtook them of disgrace and evil. Perhaps this is definite on the supposition of coordination with «qāla alladhīna» to its end. And if the coordination is with «tatawaffāhumu al-malā'ikah» (the angels take them in death), the purpose of their saying this, spoken at the moment of witnessing death, is to seek the compassion of the angels, peace be upon them, by denying that anything was done that would make them deserving of what they were suffering at that time.

It was also said: what is meant by "evil" is an evil act, more general than polytheism and other things, and polytheism enters it as a primary instance, that is: "We used not to do evil," let alone polytheism. ("Min" in every case is extra, and «sū'in» (evil) is the object of «na'malu» (we do).) ﴿Yes⁠﴾ is a refutation of them from God, exalted be He, or from those given knowledge, or from the angels, peace be upon them. The last is definite on the supposition that the saying was at the witnessing of death and its suffering, that is: "Yes, you were doing what you were doing."

﴿Indeed, God is Knowing of what you were doing⁠﴾, so He will recompense you for it, and this is its time.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 29:

﴿So enter the gates of Hell﴾ is an address to each category of them, that each category enter one of the gates of Hell. By "gates" is meant either the outlet (manfadh) or the level (tabaqah). It is not permissible that it be an address to every single individual, lest it entail that an individual disbeliever enter through multiple gates, or that Hell have as many gates as there are individuals. It has also been permitted that by "the gates" is meant the categories of punishment, for the use of "bab" (gate) for "category" has occurred, as one says: "So-and-so looks into a gate of knowledge," meaning a category of it. In that case there is no obstacle to the address being to every individual. And one who said that the meaning of those gates is the graves of the disbelievers, which are filled with punishment, is further removed from the truth, citing what has come: "The grave is either a garden from the gardens of Paradise or a pit from the pits of the Fire."

﴿Abiding therein﴾ is a delayed (muqaddarah) circumstantial clause if by "entering" is meant its occurrence, and a simultaneous (muqarinah) one if by it is meant mere being. The pronoun in "fīhā" ("therein") has been said to refer to "the gates" in the sense of levels, and it has been said to refer to Hell. This latter is adopted, and the circumstance being delayed is among the more remote views. Abiding (khulud) has been interpreted as a long stay, to dispense with this obligation, although its use in their speech is contrary to what is customary in the Noble Qur'an. ﴿So evil is the abode of the arrogant﴾, that is, from monotheism. Their mention by the title of arrogance (takabbur) serves to indicate its causality for their dwelling therein. Exalted is He, in what preceded, described the disbelievers with istikbar, and here with takabbur. Al-Raghib mentioned that these two and kibr are close in meaning: kibr is the state by which a person is distinguished through his self-admiration; istikbar is of two kinds: the first is that a person seeks and strives to become great, and this is when it is according to what he loves, in the place he loves, and at the time he loves, and it is praiseworthy. The second is that he pretends and displays from himself what is not his, and it is blameworthy. Takabbur is also of two kinds: the first is that good deeds are in reality numerous and exceed the virtues of others, and on this basis God Most High is described as al-Mutakabbir. The second is that one be artificial in this and pretend, and this is in the description of most people. Takabbur in the first sense is praiseworthy and in the second blameworthy. The object of the dispraise is omitted, that is, Hell or its gates if they are interpreted as levels. The fa' is conjunctive, and the lam was brought for emphasis, showing concern with the dispraise, since these people are misguided and misguiding, as His saying indicates: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge﴾. For emphasis, showing concern with the praise, the lam was also brought after His saying: ﴿And the Abode of the Hereafter is better, and excellent is the abode of the God-fearing﴾, because those people are the opposite of these, guided and rightly guided. It seems that because this factor is absent in the verses of Surah al-Zumar and al-Mu'min, the lam was not brought. It has been said that the emphasis is directed at what is understood from the sentence, that Hell is their abode; and since it was not understood from the preceding verses here in the way it was understood before the verses of those two surahs, emphasis was used there and not used here, relying on what is almost explicit in conveying that it is their abode, which you will hear, God willing, there.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 30:

﴿And it will be said to those who were mindful of God﴾: that is, the believers. They are described thus to indicate that the answer they gave came from their God-consciousness (taqwa).

﴿"What has your Lord sent down?" They said, "Good."﴾ That is: He sent down good. So "mādhā" is a single compound interrogative meaning "what," in the accusative position as object of "anzala" (sent down), and "khayran" (good) is the object of a verb that has been omitted. The choice of this reading indicates that they did not hesitate in their answer, but matched it to the question, acknowledging the sending down, unlike the disbelievers, who diverted their answer from the question and said: "It is the fables of the ancients" (16:24), which has nothing to do with sending down. Indeed, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him and his father, read "khayrun" in the nominative case. In that case "mā" is an interrogative noun and "dhā" is a relative pronoun meaning "alladhī," so the meaning is: "What is it that your Lord has sent down?" And "khayrun" is the predicate of an omitted subject, so the two sentences of the answer and the question both become nominal sentences. Making "mādhā" accusative as object, as explained above, and making "khayr" nominative as predicate of a subject, is permissible, but it is less preferable. In al-Kashshaf it appears from understanding the intention of the author of al-Kashshaf in this matter that the purpose of the accusative reading, although the nominative is stronger, is to remove ambiguity so that it is explicit regarding what is sought, just as the accusative was preferred in God's saying: ﴿Indeed, We have created everything in measure﴾ (54:49). Its meaning in this respect can be deduced by returning to what we quoted from him earlier and reflecting on it, so reflect, for it is subtle.

Furthermore, we have not found any disagreement here about the questioner, as there was in what preceded. What we have seen in many of the exegetical works we have consulted is that the questioner was the delegation which had asked first in some of the reports related there, and it has been mentioned that it is the questioner in both places. Among them is Ibn Abi Hatim, who transmitted from al-Suddi, who said: The Quraysh gathered and said: "Muhammad (ﷺ) is a man of sweet tongue; when a man speaks with him, he takes away his mind. So look for some of your notable men, known for their lineages, and send them along every road of Makkah at the start of a night or two nights. Whoever comes intending to meet him, turn him away from him." So some of them went out along every road. Whenever a man came as a delegate for his people, they would observe what Muhammad (ﷺ) said, and then descend upon them and say to him: "O so-and-so, son of so-and-so," and he would identify himself by his lineage, and they would say: "I will inform you about Muhammad (ﷺ): he is a liar. None follows him in his affair except the foolish, the slaves, and those with no good in them. As for the elders of his people and their best, they have parted from him." So one of them would return, and this is God's saying: ﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord sent down?" they say, "Fables of the ancients."﴾ But if the delegate was one whom God had determined for guidance, they would say to him the same, and he would say: "Evil is the delegate I am to my people, if I have come until I have reached a day's journey and returned before I meet this man and see what he says, and bring my people the explanation of his affair." Then he would enter Makkah, meet the believers, and ask them: "What does Muhammad (ﷺ) say?" And they would say: "Good," and so on.

Yes, it is rationally possible that the questioner was some of them asking others, so that what they had would be strengthened by the answer, or for similar reasons, such as enjoying hearing the reply. The lover is often asked about what he knows of his beloved's circumstances, delighting in the intoxication of remembering him and in hearing his sweet pearls:

"Ah, pour me wine and tell me it is wine, and do not pour it secretly when it is possible to pour it openly."

Rather, it is also permissible that the questioner was one of the stubborn disbelievers, whose aim in this was mockery and derision.

﴿For those who did good﴾: they performed good, righteous deeds; ﴿in this﴾ ﴿world, there is a good﴾ reward, a good recompense for their goodness. The prepositional phrase is connected to what follows, in the sense that this good belongs to them in this world. What is meant by it, according to what is related from al-Dahhak, is victory and conquest. It was also said: praise and commendation from Him. Al-Imam said: It is possible that it means the opening of the door of unveilings, witnessings, and subtle graces, as in God's saying: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾. It was also said: it is connected to what precedes, and in that case it is possible that the sentence, on a similar construction, is connected to what follows first. Rather, this good which occurs as a reward for their goodness in this world will be in the Hereafter. Some have limited themselves to this possibility. The good in that case means either the great reward which God has prepared on the Day of Resurrection for the doers of good, or the multiplication by ten times its like up to seven hundredfold and beyond, to what no one but Him, exalted is He, knows. Its being connected to what follows was preferred, because it is more in harmony with His saying: ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter is better﴾. The sentence, as the words of several scholars indicate, has an omitted modifier, meaning: and the reward of the abode of the Hereafter, that is, their reward therein, is better than what they were given in this world as reward.

It is also permissible that the meaning is "good" in an absolute sense, so that goodness may be ascribed to the abode of the Hereafter itself. ﴿And how excellent is the abode of the God-conscious﴾: that is, the abode of the Hereafter, omitted because what preceded indicates it, as Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Zajjaj, Ibn al-Anbari and others said. This is a statement beginning a promise from Him to those who were mindful of God, in line with their own words; and in promise here it is like God's saying ﴿that they may bear their burdens in full﴾ in threat earlier. It is also permissible that ﴿khayran﴾ is the object of "qālū" and is governed by it, since it has the sense of a sentence, like "qāla qaṣīdatan" (he said a poem), or a modifier of a verbal noun, meaning "a good saying." This sentence is then either in apposition, so its place is accusative, or explanatory of it, so it has no place in the grammar. In both cases, what they actually said is ﴿for those who did good﴾, except that God, glorified is He, named it "good" and then reported it, as you say: "So-and-so said 'beautiful' to whoever intended us, which makes his right incumbent upon us." According to what has been mentioned, the accusative reading does not indicate what was mentioned earlier for the reason pointed out there; rather, it does so only through God's testimony to the goodness of their saying. It is also possible to make that, as in al-Kashshaf, the object of "anzala," and its naming as "good" is from God, exalted is He, as in His saying: ﴿They will surely say, "The Mighty, the Knowing created them"﴾ (43:9), so that the first thing that strikes the hearing is the correspondence, without looking at understanding its meaning. As for their saying ﴿for those who did good﴾, that is, they said that He sent down this statement, for what is understood from the correspondence after reflecting on the meaning. Some claimed that it is not permissible to make it accusative governed by "anzala," because this statement was not sent down from God, exalted is He, and in that case the correspondence is lost. This is a statement arising from little reflection. In al-Bahr al-Muhit it is said that "for those who..." and so on falls under the saying, and it is an explanation of the good which God, exalted is He, sent down in revelation. Its apparent meaning is that it is another aspect different from what was mentioned, and in it is also a refutation of the claimant. Perhaps their restriction to this among what was sent down is because it is a comprehensive statement, and in it is an encouragement for the questioner. The preferred of these aspects, according to a group, is the first; indeed, it has been said that it is the only aspect.

**Page 133**

﴿Jannatu ʿadn﴾ (Gardens of Eden) is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*), as al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari preferred, meaning: "they are gardens." It is also permissible that it be a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "for them are gardens," or that it is the subject of praise (*al-makhsus bi-l-madh*). ﴿Yadkhuluna-ha﴾ (they enter them) is an attributive clause (*na't*) of ﴿jannat﴾ according to al-Hawfi, on the basis that (ʿadn) is indefinite. Likewise ﴿tajri min tahtiha al-anhar﴾ (rivers flow beneath them). According to more than one scholar, both are circumstantial clauses (*hal*), on the basis that (ʿadn) is a proper name. They also permitted that (jannat) be a subject (*mubtada'*), with the clause (yadkhuluna-ha) as its predicate, and the clause (tajri ilakh) a circumstantial clause (*hal*).

Zayd ibn Thabit and Abu ʿAbd al-Rahman read (jannat) in the accusative (*nasb*) by way of the verbal preoccupation construction (*ishtighal*), meaning: "they enter the Gardens of Eden, they enter them." Abu Hayyan said: this reading strengthens the view that (jannat) is in the nominative as a subject (*mubtada'*), with the clause after it as its predicate.

Zayd ibn ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them both, read ﴿wa-laniʿmatu dari al-muttaqin﴾ (and excellent is the abode of the God-fearing) with a *ta'* marked with a *damma* and *dar* in the genitive (*khafd*). Then (niʿmat) is a subject (*mubtada'*) in construct with (dar), and (jannat) is its predicate.

Ismaʿil ibn Jaʿfar, on the authority of Nafiʿ, read ﴿yadkhulunaha﴾ with a *ya'* (third person), and the verb in the passive voice (*mabni li-l-maf'ul*). This was also reported from Abu Jaʿfar and Shayba.

﴿Lahum fiha﴾ (for them therein): that is, in those gardens, ﴿ma yashaʾun﴾ (whatever they wish). The first adverbial phrase (*zarf*) is the predicate of (*ma*), and the second is a circumstantial element (*hal*) from it. The governing element is what is in the first phrase of the meaning of attainment and settledness, or it is connected to it for this reason, meaning: "there is for them therein whatever they wish of kinds of desirable things." Its placement first is to guard against the misunderstanding that it is connected to the wishing, or because, as has been explained more than once, delaying what by rights should be placed first makes the soul anticipate it, so that when it arrives it is firmly established with especial firmness.

Some scholars mentioned that the placement of (fiha) first is for restriction (*hasr*), and that (ma) is for generality, by the indication of the context. Thus it conveys that a person does not find all that he desires except in Paradise. So reflect on it.

The clause is in the position of a circumstantial element (*hal*), similar to what preceded. It was claimed that (lahum) is connected to (tajri), meaning: the rivers flow beneath them for their benefit. (Wa-fiha ma yashaʾun) (and therein is whatever they wish) is a subject and predicate in the position of a circumstantial element, whose status is not hidden from those of discernment.

﴿Kadhalika﴾ (Thus): like that recompense, the most complete. ﴿Yajzi Allahu al-muttaqin﴾ (Allah rewards the God-fearing): that is, their kind, so it includes everyone who guards himself against polytheism and sins. It was said: against polytheism only. Included in it are the God-fearing mentioned earlier, by primary inclusion, and it contains an incitement for others to piety. Or it refers to those mentioned, and then it contains a rebuke to the disbelievers.

It was said: this clause supports the view that His words, glory be to Him, ﴿li-lladhina ahsanu﴾ (for those who did good) are a promise, for making that a recompense for them looks to the promise of it from Allah, exalted is He. And if it is the content of a statement (*maqul al-qawl*), it would not be from His speech, exalted is He, so that it would be a promise from Him, glory be to Him.

It was also said: it supports the view that (jannat) is the predicate of an omitted subject, not a subject of praise, because if it is the subject of praise, it is nearly explicit that (jannat ʿadn) is a recompense for the God-fearing, and then (kadhalika) etc. would be an emphasis. This is unlike when it is the predicate of an omitted subject, for it is not known explicitly that the Gardens of Eden are a recompense for the God-fearing. There is room for consideration in this, and likewise in what precedes it, except that the expression of perpetuity (*ta'bid*) contains what lightens the matter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 32:

﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are good﴾ is a qualifier (na't) for the God-fearing (al-muttaqin), though it has also been permitted to treat it as a separate clause (qat'). His words, glorified is He, ﴿good﴾ (tayyibin) are a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to their pronoun.
