Its meaning, as transmitted from Abu Mu'adh, is "pure from the defilement of polytheism" (shirk), and this is what fits its being placed in contrast to ﴿those who wrong themselves﴾ in the description of the disbelievers, on the basis that the intended meaning of wrongdoing (zulm) is its greatest form, which is polytheism. However, it has been objected: mentioning purity from polytheism alone has no benefit after describing them as God-fearing.

It is answered that the benefit of this is to indicate that purity from polytheism is the fundamental root. In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, after interpreting wrongdoing as disbelief and interpreting "good" (tayyibayn) as "pure from the defilement of wrongdoing," and making it a circumstantial clause, it says: "Its benefit is the announcement that the essence of the matter in God-fearing is purity from what has been mentioned up until the time of their death. Therefore, there is in it an exhortation to the believers to persist in that, and to others to attain it."

Mujahid said: what is meant by ﴿good﴾ is that "their words and deeds are pure." This is also the meaning of those who said: "pure from wronging themselves through disbelief and sins." To this view al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) went, when he said: "The good person is one who is free from the impurity of ignorance, immorality and vile deeds, and adorned with knowledge, faith and noble deeds." It was these whom He, glorified is He, intended by His words: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are good﴾.

This has been supported by the argument that describing them as God-fearing, promised Paradise in return for their deeds, requires what has been mentioned. They also took the wrongdoing mentioned earlier to encompass both disbelief and sins, because that is answered by their words: ﴿We did not do any evil﴾. Thus the correspondence is not lost in placing this in contrast to that. However, in deriving the general meaning from what is mentioned in the answer, there is what is not hidden. Most commentators, interpreting "good" as "pure from the filth of sins," correspond to ﴿in which there is no impurity﴾. It has also been said: the meaning is "joyful at the glad tidings of the angels, peace be upon them, to them, or at the taking of their souls, because their souls are wholly turned toward the presence of holiness." Thus "good" means "good of soul," and its goodness is an expression of acceptance together with openness of heart.

﴿They say﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the angels. It has also been permitted that "those who" (alladhina) be a subject whose predicate is this sentence, meaning: saying, or they say to them:

﴿Peace be upon you; enter the Garden, which you used to do.﴾

Al-Qurtubi said: al-Bayhaqi narrated something similar from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi: "When the soul of the believer is summoned, the Angel of Death, peace be upon him, comes to him and says: 'Peace be upon you, O friend of God. Indeed God, exalted is He, sends you His greetings, and gives you the glad tidings of Paradise.' ﴿Enter the Garden﴾ which God, exalted is He, has prepared for you and promised you." It seems it was not described because of the fame of its matter.

In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim: the definite article is for specificity, i.e., ("Gardens of Eden") etc., and therefore it is stripped of a qualifier, and this, as you see, is [problematic]. The intended meaning is their entry into it after resurrection, on the basis that the more apparent entry is with bodies and souls. The purpose of the command to that before its time is the glad tidings of Paradise in the most complete manner. It is also permissible to intend entry at the time of death, on the basis of interpreting entry as entry with the souls, as its indication in the report: "The grave is one of the gardens of Paradise."

That the glad tidings are of this rather than of entering Paradise, on the first meaning, does not prevent this; moreover, one may say: the glad tidings of entering Paradise with souls include the glad tidings of entering it with souls and bodies at its time. That this statement, like the preceding one, occurs at the taking of souls is what was related from Ibn Mas'ud and a group of commentators. Muqatil and al-Hasan said: this is on the Day of Resurrection, and the meaning of "taking in death" is the death of gathering (wafat al-hashr), namely, delivering their bodies and bringing them to the place of gathering, from tawaffa al-shay' when one takes it in full. It has been permitted to interpret "taking in death" in its customary sense while the statement occurs on the Day of Resurrection, either by making ﴿Those whom the angels take in death﴾ subject and predicate "they say," or by making "they say" a future circumstantial clause from the angels, with "those who" remaining as it was at first. The state of that is not hidden.

﴿For what you used to do﴾, that is, because of your steadfastness in God-fearing and obedience through what you used to do of that. The "ba'" is causal in the customary sense. In what is in the two Sahihs from his saying, ﷺ: "None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds" (the hadith), it is causal in the true sense, so there is no contradiction between the verse and the hadith. Some have made the "ba'" denote exchange (muqabala) to remove the contradiction.

﴿Do they await﴾ — that is, what are the disbelievers of Makkah, whose mention has preceded, waiting for, ﴿except that the angels come to them﴾ to seize their souls, as narrated from Qatadah and Mujahid. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah and al-A'mash read «yaʾtiyahum» with a *yāʾ* (the third-person masculine prefix) at the beginning of the verb instead of *tāʾ*, ﴿or the command of your Lord comes﴾.

That is, the Resurrection, as also narrated from earlier authorities. Some scholars said that what is meant is the worldly punishment, not the Resurrection, not because waiting for it is incompatible with waiting for the coming of the angels, which makes the conjunction with *aw* ("or", *al-ʿaṭf bi-aw*, coordination by "or") unsuitable, nor because it is not explicit in denial, since it is permissible to consider the prevention of the absence of both (i.e., that one of the two must occur) and to mean by its mention that each of the two is sufficient for their punishment. Rather, it is because the saying of the Exalted in what will come, if God wills: ﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾.

So the phrase ﴿so there befell them﴾ is explicit that what is meant is the worldly punishment that befell them, and in this there is a clear objection. What supports the first interpretation is the use of *yaʾtī* (it comes) rather than *yaʾtiyahum* (it comes to them). It was also said that what is meant by the coming of the angels is their coming to bear witness to the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ), that is: they await nothing regarding your affirmation except that the angels descend and bear witness to your prophethood. This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Why has not an angel been sent down to him?﴾ [al-Anʿam: 8]. The majority hold the first view, and they were described as awaiting this figuratively (*majāzan*), because it reaches them as the awaited matter reaches a person.

It was preferred that this is because of their engagement in the causes of the punishment, which necessitate it and lead to it. Thus it is as if they intend to bring it about and actively seek its arrival. The significance of the expression "the Lord" and its attribution to his pronoun (ﷺ) is not hidden, in terms of the gentleness toward him, upon him be prayers and peace. The connection of the verses will come shortly, if God Exalted wills.

﴿That﴾, that is, the like of that action of polytheism and denial, ﴿did those who passed away before them﴾ from the nations, ﴿and God did not wrong them﴾ when there befell them the recompense of their deeds, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾ by persisting in the commission of the abominations that lead to that. It was said: the apparent wording would have been "but they themselves were the wrongdoers," as in Surat al-Zukhruf, but the noble composition chose what it has in order to convey that the harm of their wronging returns to them, and its consequence is restricted to them, together with the implication that restricting each person's wrongdoing to himself (in terms of its occurrence) entails restricting it to him (in terms of its origin).

[Page 135]

﴿So the evils of what they had done struck them﴾: that is, the requitals of their evil deeds, by way of naming the cause after its effect (ism al-sabab ʿala al-musabbab), to signal how monstrous it was. It has also been said that the speech contains an omission (hadhf al-mudaf, the dropping of a governing noun), so that the meaning is "the requitals of…".

This has been criticised on the ground that it gives the impression that they had deeds other than evil ones, and the critic accepted this implication, as in the case of "the maintaining of family ties." But it is not hard to see that the meaning is not restricted in this way. What prompts one to adopt either of the two positions is that the speech, on its apparent sense, indicates that what struck them was an evil, when it was not one. This need for either position may be dispensed with, as stated above, by holding that what the apparent sense indicates is by way of mushakalah (a figure of speech in which a word is used because of its verbal similarity to a neighbouring word), as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿and the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 4], as in al-Kashshaf.

﴿And there encompassed them﴾: that is, surrounded them. The original sense of ḥayq is encompassing in general, and then in usage it became specific to the encompassing of evil. Thus one does not say "blessing encompassed him" but "retribution encompassed him." This is more emphatic and more monstrous than "struck them."

﴿what they used to mock at﴾: that is, the punishment, as has been said, with ma being a relative pronoun referring to the punishment. There is in the speech no omission and no recourse to metaphor of the kind mentioned just above. It has also been said that ma is a verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah) particle, and the pronoun in (bihi) refers to the Messenger (ﷺ) even though he is not mentioned, and the meaning is: it encompassed them as the requital for their mockery of the Messenger (ﷺ). Or ma is a relative pronoun in general, covering the Messenger (ﷺ) and others, and the pronoun in (bihi) returns to it, and the meaning is likewise "as a requital." What is in this is not hidden. Whichever of these is the case, (bihi) is connected to (yastahzi'un) and has been placed first for the sake of the fasilah (the rhyming end of the verse).

Then, the Exalted's words ﴿Do they await…﴾ etc., according to what is in al-Kashf, return to enumerating what they are in of obstinacy and of rampant corruption, and that they will not desist from this, like their predecessors who passed on until the Day of Calling. What occurred of the states of their opposites in between was for increasing the regret, the rebuke and the loss. In this is an indication that the proof has been completed, and that he (ﷺ) delivered what was incumbent upon him of clear communication.

The Exalted's words ﴿so there struck them﴾ are a conjunction (ʿatf) upon (faʿala alladhina min qablihim, "those before them did"), in a consequential sense, since the meaning is: thus did their forebears act in denial and association of partners, and there struck them what struck them. In this is a warning against what these people did, and a reminder of His, glory be to Him, words: ﴿Those before them had already plotted﴾ [al-Nahl: 26]. The excellence of this sequence is not hidden, because denial and association were the causes of the striking of evils upon those before them.

His, glory be to Him, words "(God did not wrong them)" are a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) that fits its place exactly. Some have made this refer back to what is understood from His, the Exalted's, words ﴿Do they await…﴾, meaning: thus were those before them deniers, the proof was incumbent upon them, awaiting, and there struck them what they had been awaiting. This is a sound and good view, except that the principal reliance of the speech is the first, which is closer in derivation, and the indication of (faʿala) upon it is more apparent. So this is a summation (fadhlakah) which comprised the sum of what they met those blessings and insights with, and within it was woven his (ﷺ) consolation and the good tidings of the turning of the circle of misfortunes upon those who lay in wait for him and his companions, peace be upon him, the misfortunes. It is concluded with what indicates that they were cut off, and they resorted to the last argument that the one who is refuted resorts to, turning over on it, so that he is seen only as one struck dumb and bruised, and this is what it contains.

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 35:

The words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Those who associated partners [with Allah] say: "Had Allah willed, we would not have worshipped anything other than Him, we nor our fathers, nor would we have prohibited anything without Him"﴾, are a continuation of His words ﴿Do they await anything?﴾. Do you not see how He concluded with a similar statement the last of their disputes in Surat al-An'am [6:148], in His words ﴿Those who associated partners will say﴾? The same occurs in Surat al-Zukhruf. You will not find them clinging to the will of Allah except when their proof collapses: ﴿They say: "Had our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels"﴾ [41:14]. What points to the reversal is sufficient in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say: "To Allah belongs the conclusive proof"﴾ [6:149].

In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim (Irshad al-Aql al-Salim, by Abu al-Su'ud), it is stated that this verse explains another aspect of the disbelief of the people of Makkah, and they are the intended referents of the relative pronoun (al-mawsul). The shift from the pronoun to it is to rebuke them for what is in the relative clause (hayyiz al-silah) and to censure them for this from the outset. The meaning is: "Had Allah the Exalted willed that we not worship anything other than Him, the Exalted, as you say, 'We did not worship that,' ﴿we nor our fathers﴾, whom we follow in our religion, ﴿nor did we prohibit anything without Him﴾, of the sawa'ib (free-roaming camels), the bahair (slit-eared camels) and others. So the first ﴿min﴾ is explanatory (bayaniyyah), and the second is superfluous (za'idah), to emphasise comprehensiveness. Likewise the third ﴿min﴾. The word ﴿nahnu [we]﴾ is for emphasising the pronoun in ﴿'abadna [we worshipped]﴾, not for correcting the conjunction, since there is an intervening element, although it does beautify it."

The object of ﴿shā'a [willed]﴾ being the non-worship ('adam al-'ibadah) is what some of them have stated explicitly, though the apparent thing would be to add to it the non-prohibition ('adam al-tahrim). This determination has been objected to on the grounds that non-existence does not need will, as indicated by his statement, ﷺ: "What Allah the Exalted wills occurs, and what He does not will does not occur."

[Page 136]

Since he (peace be upon him) did not say, "What Allah the Exalted wills occurs, and what He wills the non-occurrence of does not occur," but rather the non-will of existence suffices for it, and this is the meaning of their saying: "The cause of non-existence is the absence of the cause of existence." Therefore it is better to determine the object as existential, such as monotheism (al-tawhid), permissibility (al-tahlil), and compliance with what I have brought. The matter in this is simple.

In restricting association (al-shirk) and prohibition to negation, it is because these are the greatest and most well-known of what they were upon. Their aim in this, as some of the researchers (al-muhaqqiqin) have said, is the denial of the Messenger (peace be upon him) and the outright rejection of the message. Its essence is that what Allah the Exalted wills necessarily occurs and what He does not will is impossible. So if He, the Exalted, had willed that we affirm His oneness, not associate anything with Him, permit what He permitted, and not prohibit anything of what we prohibited, as the messengers say, and they convey it from His direction, the matter would have been as He willed: monotheism, negation of association, permissibility of what He permitted, and non-prohibition of any of that. Since it is not so, it is established that He did not will any of that, but rather willed what we are upon. And it becomes clear that what the messengers (peace be upon them) say is from their own selves. Allah the Exalted refuted them with His words, Exalted and Majestic: ﴿Thus﴾, meaning like that abominable act, ﴿did those before them do﴾, from the nations, that is, they associated others with Allah the Exalted and prohibited what they prohibited without Him, and disputed with their messengers in falsehood in order to refute the truth thereby. ﴿Is there then upon the messengers﴾, who were commanded to convey the messages of Allah the Exalted and the firm decrees of His command and prohibition,

﴿anything but clear conveyance?﴾ That is, their duty is nothing but conveying the message, clarifying the path of truth and making manifest the rulings of revelation. Among these, it is necessary that the will of Allah the Exalted be connected to the guidance of the one who directs his power and choice toward attaining the truth, according to the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾ [29:69].

As for compelling them to that and enforcing their saying upon them, whether they will or refuse, as is the implication of their argument, this is not part of their duty nor of the wisdom upon which the sphere of obligation (falak al-taklif) revolves, so that it might be inferred from the non-manifestation of its effects that the messengers (peace be upon them) are not genuine, or that the will of Allah the Exalted is not connected to it. For the actions upon which reward and punishment are based necessarily require, for the connection of His will to their occurrence, that they come about through the voluntary exertion of those agents and the directing of their partial choice toward achieving them. Otherwise, reward and punishment would be compulsory. The fa' according to this is for causation, as if it were said: "Thus did their predecessors, and that is false, for the messengers (peace be upon them) are only concerned with conveying the commands and prohibitions, not with realising their content by force and compulsion." End of quotation. And I see that you do not absolve it from artificiality (takalluf).

It contains a refutation of al-Zamakhshari. In this position he went to excess in speech and deviated from the paths of guidance into the abyss of misguidance. He mentioned that these polytheists did what they did of ugly acts, then attributed their action to Allah the Exalted and said: "Had Allah willed," to the end. This is exactly the doctrine of the Jabriyya (the compulsionists). "Thus did their predecessors." So when they were alerted to the ugliness of their deed and its attribution to their Lord, "Is there then upon the messengers but to convey the truth, and that Allah the Exalted does not will association and sins," by clear proof and evidence, and to inform them of the falsehood and ugliness of association, and of Allah the Exalted's freedom from the actions of servants, and that they perform them by their intention, will and choice, while Allah the Exalted incites them to its good, enables them to it, restrains them from its ugliness, and promises them for it, to the end of what he said of this kind. By my life, he interpreted the verses according to his own desire, and they are against him, not for him, if he had reflected on what they contain. Many of the researchers and eminent meticulous scholars have refuted him and clarified that the verse is far from being evidence for the Mu'tazilah, just as the conditional clause does not yield the conclusion sought by those misguided ones. A portion of discussion on this has already been presented.

Furthermore, that the purpose of the polytheists in the conditional clause is the denial of the messengers (peace be upon them) is one of two possibilities regarding this. The meticulous author of al-Kashf said concerning a similar verse: their saying this is either to claim the legitimacy of what they are upon, as a rejection of the messengers (peace be upon them), or to concede that they are upon falsehood, offering as an excuse that they are compelled. The first is false, because will connects to their legitimate act and to other than it. Whatever Allah the Exalted wills to occur from them as legitimate occurs thus, and whatever Allah the Exalted wills to occur not thus occurs not thus. There is no doubt that whoever imagines that the act being by the will of Allah the Exalted contradicts the coming of the messengers (peace be upon them), in contrast to what the direct agent is upon of disbelief and misguidance, has denied entirely, and he is lying in deducing the intended conclusion from this implication (al-luzumiyyah). The apparent meaning of the verse is directed to this meaning. The second, on what it entails, the attainment of the purpose, which is the acknowledgment of falsehood, is also false, since there is no compulsion. For the will connected to their associating by their own choice, and knowledge connected likewise,

[Page 137]

and likewise regarding prohibition. So this reinforces the removal of excuse, it does not establish it. He mentioned that the meaning of ﴿Is there then upon the messengers﴾ is that what is incumbent upon the messengers is that they convey and clarify the landmarks of guidance by directing to the establishment of the foundations of reflection and supporting with the evidences of hearing and sight. They are not obliged to dispute with one who wants to refute the clear truth with his falsehood, for after that clarification the truth becomes evident to the observers, and the disputation of the obstinate profits nothing. It is also permitted that their saying this is a prevention of sending and obligation, holding to the principle that what Allah the Exalted wills necessarily occurs and what He does not will is impossible, so what is the benefit in them both. Or it is a denial of the ugliness of what he rebuked them for, of association and prohibition, arguing that if that were ugly, Allah the Exalted would not have willed its occurrence from us, or He would have willed its opposite by compulsion. The answer to the first objection is indicated by His words, Exalted: ﴿Is there then upon the messengers﴾ to the end, as if it were said: the benefit of sending is the clear conveyance that makes the truth evident. For what Allah the Exalted wills to exist or not exist is not necessary nor impossible absolutely, as you claim, but may be necessary or impossible through the mediation of other causes that He, the Exalted, has determined. Among these is sending, for it leads to the guidance of whomever Allah the Exalted wills, by way of mediation.

Al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, commentary on Surah 16, verse 36:

As for the second doubt, its answer has been indicated in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation﴾ from the past nations ﴿a messenger, [saying], "Worship Allah" alone, ﴿and avoid the taghut﴾ (the taghut, transliterated as *taghut* [that which is worshipped besides God], is everything that calls to misguidance; al-Hasan said it is Satan). What is meant by avoiding it is avoiding what it calls to.

﴿Among them﴾, that is, among those nations, ﴿are those whom Allah guided﴾ to the truth, of His worship or of avoiding the taghut, by granting them success in that, ﴿and among them are those upon whom misguidance was justly due﴾, meaning it was established and necessary, since He did not grant them success and did not will their guidance. The point of indication is that the realization and persistence of misguidance, insofar as it occurred as a counterpart to guidance, which is by His will and purpose, was itself likewise [by His will and purpose].

As for the claim that willing evil is evil, and so it is impermissible for Allah, glorified is He, to be described by it, this is evidently corrupt, because evil is the acquisition (*kasb*) of evil, and being described by it, not willing and creating it, as has been established in theology (*kalam*). You know that both indications are extremely obscure. Consider what need there is for the restriction and what is meant by it, if ﴿Then upon the messengers is only the clear notification﴾ and so on is taken as indicating the answer to the first doubt.

Al-Imam [al-Razi] said: The polytheists meant by their statement that since everything is from Allah, the Exalted, His sending of the prophets, peace be upon them, would be futile. We say: this is an objection to Allah, the Exalted, and falls under the category of demanding the cause in His rulings and actions, and that is false, since it is for Allah, glorified is He, to do what He wills in His dominion and to decree what He desires, and it is impermissible to say to Him, "Why did You do this, and why did You not do that?" The evidence that the rejection was directed at this meaning is that He, the Exalted, expressed this meaning explicitly in His words, glorified is He: ﴿And We certainly sent﴾ to the end, in which He explained that His practice, glorified is He, regarding His servants is to send messengers to them and command them to worship Him and forbid them from worshipping other than Him. He also conveyed that although He commanded all and forbade them, He, majestic is His majesty, guided some and misguided others. There is no doubt that this proceeds from Him, exalted is He, only by virtue of His being a God, exempt from the objections of objectors and the demands of disputants. So the raising of this question by these disbelievers was a cause of ignorance, misguidance, and distance from Allah, the Most High. Thus it is established that Allah, exalted is He, only censured these speakers because they believed that the matter being so prevents the permissibility of sending messengers, not because they lied in their statement. This is the correct answer on which reliance is placed in this area. The meaning of ﴿Then upon the messengers is only the clear notification﴾ to the end is that He, exalted is He, commanded the messengers, peace be upon them, to convey, and that is what is obligatory upon them. As for whether faith is attained or not, the messengers have no connection to that. Rather, Allah, exalted is He, guides whom He wills by His grace and leads astray whom He wills by His abandonment. End of quotation. And it is as you see.

[Page 138]

Al-Wahidi in *al-Wasit* related from al-Zajjaj that they said that statement in mockery, but many of the verifiers did not accept it, and some of them mentioned that interpreting it that way does not fit the answer. Yes, in *al-Kashshaf*, at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 20], he said that they repelled the statement of the messengers, peace be upon them, calling to His worship, exalted is He, and forbidding them from worshipping other than Him, glorified is He, with this claim, and they are bound by the course of this statement, because if everything is attributed to His will, exalted is He, then He has willed the sending of the messengers, willed their calling of the servants, willed their denial, and willed their entry into the Fire. So the rejection and repelling after this statement is evidence that they said it not out of conviction but out of reckless assertion. In another place, at a parallel of the verse, also, he said: they are liars in this statement, because of their certainty where there is no suspicion at all, let alone knowledge, since it is known that knowledge of Allah's attributes is a branch of knowledge of His essence, and faith in them is likewise, and those who argue with it are disbelieving polytheists, anthropomorphists. He expanded on this discussion in Surah az-Zukhruf.

He also mentioned that their statement involves disabling the Creator by establishing a mutual obstruction between His will and the opposite of what He commanded, so it follows that He does not will except what He commands, and does not forbid except what He does not will. This is disabling in two respects: removing some of the things within the scope of power from being their object, and narrowing the object of His command and prohibition. This is precisely the doctrine of their brothers, the Qadariyya. End of quotation. It may be said that the polytheists only said that as an argument on their own assumption, since they heard from the messengers and their followers that whatever Allah, exalted is He, willed came to be and whatever He did not will did not come to be. Otherwise, they are the most ignorant of creation about their Lord, majestic is His affair, and His attributes: ﴿They are only like livestock; rather, they are further astray﴾ [al-Furqan: 44]. Their aim was to silence the messengers, cut them off from their call to what opposes what they were upon, and to be free of opposing them. So it is as if they said: "You say that whatever Allah, exalted is He, willed came to be, and whatever He did not will did not come to be. So what we are upon is among what Allah willed, and what you call us to is among what He did not will, for otherwise it would have come to be. The fitting course for you is not to confront what opposes the will of Allah, exalted is He, for the duty of the messenger is to proceed according to the will of the sender, since sending is only to execute that will and to achieve what is willed by it." This is ignorance on their part regarding the reality of the matter, the manner in which the will relates, and the purpose of the mission. That is because His will, exalted is He, relates only in accordance with His knowledge, and His knowledge relates only in accordance with what the thing is in itself. So Allah, exalted is He, did not will their polytheism, for example, except after He knew it, and He did not know it except in accordance with what it is in itself in reality. So they are polytheists in pre-eternity and in reality, except that when He, glorified is He, brought them forth in accordance with what He knew about them, if He had left them and their state, they would have had an argument against Him, glorified is He, when He punishes them on the Day of Resurrection, since they would say then: "No warner came to us." So He, majestic is His affair, sent the messengers as bearers of good news and warners, so that people would have no argument against Allah after the messengers. Thus upon the messengers is only the conveyance of the commands and prohibitions, so that the conclusive proof of Allah, exalted is He, may be established. So conveyance is what Allah, exalted is He, wills from the messengers, peace be upon them, in order to establish His proof over His creation by it. His will from His creation is nothing but what they are in reality, whether good or evil.

In a report, Allah, exalted is He, says: "O My servants, I count your deeds for you. Whoever finds good, let him praise Allah, and whoever finds other than that, let him blame none but himself."

There is no contradiction between commanding something and His willing other than it, exalted is He, because the command is according to what befits His majesty and beauty, and the will is according to what the thing in itself requires in the Hereafter. The community (*al-Jama'a*, the majority of Sunni scholars) has affirmed the separation of command from will in the observable world too. Some of the Hanbalis also mentioned separation, but only from the creative will (*al-iradah al-takwiniyya*), not absolutely. The discussion is detailed in its proper place. Knowing this, be aware that His words, glorified is He: ﴿Then upon the messengers is only the clear notification﴾ include an indication of their rejection, as if it were said: "What you pointed to, that the fitting course for the messengers is to abandon calling to what opposes what Allah, exalted is He, willed for us, and to proceed in accordance with the will and be silent about us, is false, because their duty and what is obligatory upon them is the conveyance, and that is what Allah, exalted is He, wills from them, so that the proof of Allah, exalted is He, may be established against you, not silence and abandoning the call." And in His words, glorified is He: ﴿And We certainly sent﴾ etc. there is an indication

[Page 139]

which whoever has a heart will perceive: that the will is according to the disposition (*isti'dad*) in which the person is in reality. So reflect, for this view is not free from remoteness and vagueness. What al-Qadi [al-Baydawi] mentioned regarding His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly sent﴾ etc. is that He explained in it that sending is a matter that the divine practice has followed among all nations, as a cause of guidance for whom He wills to guide and an increase in the misguidance of whom He wills to misguide, like wholesome food that benefits and strengthens a sound constitution, and harms and destroys the deviant one.

In *Irshad al-Aql al-Salim* [Abu al-Su'ud]: it is a verification of the manner in which His will, exalted is He, relates to the acts of the servants, after clarifying that compulsion is not among the functions of messengership, nor is it from the category of the will that relates to what the circle of reward and punishment revolves around, namely the voluntary acts. The meaning is: We sent into every nation a messenger who commands them to worship Allah, exalted is He, and avoid the taghut. So they commanded them, and they divided: among them is one whom Allah guided, after directing his power and partial choice to attaining what he was guided to; and among them is one who persisted in misguidance because of his obstinacy and his not directing his power to attaining the truth. The fa' in ("among them") is for sequence (*nasiha*), as indicated. The apparent form in the second division, "and among them is one whom Allah misguided," would have been expected, but He changed the style to what is in the noble text, to indicate that this is due to their bad choice, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when I am ill, it is He who heals me﴾ [ash-Shu'ara: 80]. And "that" (*an*) may be interpreted as explanatory of the sense of saying in the sending, and it may be a verbal particle (*masdariyya*) with the preposition omitted, meaning "that [worship Allah]." ﴿So travel﴾, O polytheists who deny and say, "If Allah had willed, we would not have worshipped other than Him," ﴿in the land and see how was the end of the deniers﴾, from 'Ad and Thamud and whoever traveled their path among those upon whom misguidance was justly due, and say as you say, "Perhaps you will take heed." The ordering of the command to travel upon the mere report that misguidance has been established upon them, without reporting that punishment has descended, is to signal that this is too evident to need explanation. In the coordination of the second command with fa' there is an indication of the obligation to hasten to reflection and reasoning, which save from misguidance.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 37:

﴿If you are eager for their guidance﴾ is addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Al-hirs (eagerness) is excessive desire. Al-Nakha'i read "wa-in" with an added waw, and he, al-Hasan and Abu Haywa read "tahras" with a fatha on the ra', the present tense of harisa with a kasra on the ra', and this is a dialect (lughah). The majority read ﴿tahris﴾ with a kasra on the ra', the present tense of harasa with a fatha on the ra', and this is the dialect of the Hijaz. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide those who go astray﴾ is the response to the condition, with the meaning "then know this," or it is the reason (illah) for the omitted response, meaning: if you are eager for their guidance, your eagerness will benefit nothing, for Allah, exalted is He, does not guide those who go astray. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is intended to refer to the Quraysh, who were referred to earlier as "those who associated partners." The relative pronoun was placed in the position of their pronoun to specify that they are among those upon whom misguidance has been decreed, and to indicate the cause of the ruling. It is also permissible that it refers to whatever includes them, and they enter it in the first instance. The meaning of the verse, according to what has been said, is: He, glorified is He, does not create guidance by compulsion and force in one whom He creates misguidance in, due to his own bad choice. Some interpretation of this kind is necessary, because the ruling without it is something that is hardly ever unknown. ("Man") in this case is the object of (yahdi), as is apparent. It has also been said that yahdi is the present tense of hada in the sense of ihtada, and so it is intransitive, with ("man") as its subject, and the pronoun of the subject in (yudilla) refers to Allah, exalted is He, and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: whom He misguides. Al-Farra' has related the use of hada in the sense of ihtada. Several of the Seven Readers, al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Mujahid, Ibn Sirin, al-Utaridi, Muzahim al-Khurasani and others read "la yuhda" in the passive voice, with "man" as the deputy of the subject, and the returning pronoun and the pronoun of the subject are as previously mentioned. This reading is more eloquent than the first, because it indicates that whomever Allah has misguided, no one at all can guide him, unlike the first reading, which indicates only that Allah does not guide him, though whoever Allah does not guide has no guide. This, according to what has been said, applies if we do not hold that hada is necessarily intransitive; but if we do hold that, then the two are of one meaning, except that this reading is explicit in the generality of the agent, unlike that one, although the transitive use is the more common. A group among them, including Abdullah, read "la yahiddi" with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the ha' and the dal, with shadda on it, and its origin is yahtadi, which was assimilated, as in your saying "yakhtasimu" becoming "yakhissimu."

Another group read "la yuhdi" with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the dal. Ibn 'Atiyya said: It is weak. Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr criticized him, saying that if hada is established as intransitive in the sense of ihtada, it is not weak, because he has added the causative hamza to the intransitive, so the meaning is: he does not make one who is guided out of one whom He has misguided.

It may be answered that the weakness in his view may be because the form ahda, derived from it, is not well known.

"Yadilla" was read with a fatha on the ya'. In the codex of Ubayy: "Indeed Allah does not guide one who has misguided."

﴿And they have no helpers﴾ who would help them in guidance, or repel punishment from them. This is a completion (tatmim) by nullifying the assumption that their gods benefit them in any way. The pronoun in (lahum) refers to the meaning of (man). The plural form in (nasirin) is due to the plurality in the pronoun, for the juxtaposition of plural with plural indicates the distribution of individuals over individuals, not that the intended meaning is the negation of a group of helpers from each of them.

Tafsir of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 16, verse 38:

Then, the beginning of these verses may seem to support the school of the Mu'tazila (Mu'tazilism), but their end contains many indications that support the school of the People of the Truth, as the Imam (al-Razi) said. The matter is probably too clear to need explanation, and all praise is due to God, the Exalted, for this. ﴿They swore by Allah﴾ begins the explanation of another category of their falsehoods, which is their denial of the resurrection (al-ba'th). According to al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari) and others, this clause is coordinated (ma'tuf) with the words of God, the Exalted: ﴿Those who associated partners with Allah said﴾. It has been said: because the first clause includes the denial of monotheism (tawhid), and this clause is the denial of the resurrection, and both are great matters of disbelief and ignorance, the coordination between them is fitting. The pronoun (in "they swore") also refers to the people of Makkah. That is, they swore by Allah ﴿with their most earnest oaths (jahd aymanihim)﴾. Jahd aymanihim is a verbal noun (masdar) in the accusative, functioning as a circumstantial qualifier (hal), meaning: exerting themselves in their oaths. ﴿Allah will not raise up those who die.﴾ This is based on the view that the dead is annihilated and perishes, that the resurrection is his re-creation, and that the re-creation of the non-existent (i'adat al-ma'dum) is impossible. The philosophers held this impossibility, and none of the theologians (mutakallimun) agreed with them in this claim except the Karramiyya and Abu al-Husayn al-Basri of the Mu'tazila. They argued for it with arguments that the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) refuted. Some of them claimed that this is a matter of necessary knowledge (darura), and that what is mentioned in its explanation are merely reminders of it. The Imam (al-Razi) quoted from Shaykh Abu 'Ali ibn Sina that he said: Everyone who returns to his sound nature, and sets aside inclination and partisanship, will find that his clear intellect testifies that the re-creation of the very same non-existent thing is impossible. In the oath of these disbelievers that there will be no resurrection there is an indication, as he said in the tafsir, that they claim knowledge of this as a necessary truth.

You know that if the re-creation of the very same non-existent thing is permitted, as is the view of the majority of theologians, then there is no difficulty regarding the resurrection at all. As for if we say that re-creation is impermissible because of a decisive proof (al-qati') establishing this, it has been said: we maintain that no part of the bodies is annihilated, so that the resurrection would require the re-creation of the non-existent. Rather, dispersal (al-tafarruq) has only befallen them, and gathering (al-ijtima') will befall them in the resurrection, so there is no re-creation of a non-existent. But there is a discussion in this, even if it is supported by the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. From here, Mawla Mirzajan said: There is no escape except by saying that the detached soul (al-nafs al-mujarrada) remains, and that the body that is raised up is like the body that was in this world, but not the very same individual body. This does not contradict the law of justice (qanun al-'adala), since the agent is none other than the soul, and the body is in relation to the act like a knife is in relation to cutting. Just as the effect that follows from cutting, namely praise, blame, reward and punishment, belongs only to the cutter and not to the knife, so the effect that follows from human actions belongs only to the soul, which is the one who experiences pleasure and pain, whether intellectual or sensory. Therefore, there is no violation of justice. As for the apparent texts that indicate the return of that very same individual, they are interpreted (mu'awwala) on the assumption of a decisive proof showing impossibility, namely by saying: what is meant is the re-creation of its matter (madda) together with a form that was closest in resemblance to the first form. So reflect. If Allah the Exalted wills, the verification of this matter will come in Surah Ya Sin in the most complete manner.

It is reported from Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu al-'Aliya that this verse was revealed because a man from among the Muslims demanded a debt from a man among the polytheists. Among what the Muslim said was: "And I hope for what is after death." The polytheist said: "Will you indeed be raised after death?" and he swore by Allah that Allah would not raise up those who die. So Allah, the Exalted, related that and refuted it in the most eloquent refutation, with His words, glorified is He: ﴿Yes (bala)﴾, where bala is used to affirm the negation. That is: Yes, He will raise them up. ( wa'dan ) is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing what is indicated by ( bala ), since its meaning is nothing but the promise of resurrection and the report about it. This kind of construction is called emphasis of the thing itself (mu'akkid li-nafsihi). It is also permitted that it be a verbal noun for an omitted verb, meaning: He promised that as a promise. ( 'alayhi ) is a qualifier (sifa) of ( wa'dan ). The intended meaning is a promise that is binding upon Him to fulfil it; otherwise the promise itself is not binding upon Him. The binding character of its fulfilment is due to the impossibility of breaking His promise, or because resurrection is one of the requirements of wisdom.

﴿True (haqqan)﴾ is another qualifier of wa'dan. It is emphatic if it means established and realized, and it is affirmative (mu'assisa) if it means not false. Or it is in the accusative as a verbal noun with an omitted verb, meaning: it is truly right, haqqa haqqan. ﴿But most people﴾ do not know, because of their ignorance of the affairs of Allah, the Exalted, such as His knowledge, power, wisdom and other attributes of perfection, and of what is permissible for Him and what is not, and because they do not understand the secret of creation and its ultimate purpose, and that resurrection is among the things required by wisdom. They ( do not know ) that He, the Exalted, will raise them up. He blamed them for not knowing the resurrection, rather than for knowing its non-occurrence, which they claim, as the apparent meaning of their oath requires, so that the denial of that is understood by implication.

It is also permitted that this is to indicate that what they possess is far from being called knowledge; rather, it is pure delusion and absolute ignorance. The most suitable reading of the object of ( yalamun ) in this context is: what you know. It is also permitted that the sense is: they do not know that it is a promise from Him which is true, so they deny it, saying: ﴿We and our fathers were promised this before; this is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 83; al-Naml: 68].

﴿That He may make clear to them﴾ is connected to what is implied by ﴿Yes﴾, which is "He will resurrect them." The pronoun refers to "whoever dies," which includes both believers and disbelievers, since the making clear also applies to the believers. Although they already know this, when they witness the reality of the situation the matter becomes manifest, and their knowledge reaches the level of ʿayn al-yaqīn (certainty by direct witnessing). That is, He resurrects them so that He may make clear to them, by this and by what they gain through beholding the circumstances as they are and witnessing them in their true forms, ﴿the matter about which they differ﴾, namely the truth, which encompasses everything that they opposed of what the messengers who were sent to them brought. The resurrection enters into this in the first instance. Expressing this by the relative pronoun serves to indicate its magnitude and to signal that what is mentioned in the relative clause is the cause of the making clear. The fronting of the prepositional phrase serves the rhyme endings (ruʾūs al-āy). ﴿And that those who disbelieved may know﴾ in God Most High, by associating partners with Him, denying the bodily resurrection, and denying the messengers, peace be upon them, ﴿that they were liars﴾ in everything they say. In the first instance, this includes their saying: ﴿God will not resurrect whoever dies﴾.

It has been transmitted in al-Baḥr (Tafsīr al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ) that ﴿That He may make clear﴾ etc. is connected to the words of God Most High: ﴿And We certainly sent into every community a messenger﴾, meaning: We sent him so that he might make clear to them what they differed about, and that they were upon misguidance before his coming, fabricating lies against God, glorified be He. It is not obscure that this is far-fetched, given what precedes. The making clear and the knowledge mentioned have been made the purpose of the resurrection, as in Irshād al-ʿAql al-Salīm (Tafsīr Abī al-Suʿūd), on the basis that it occurs in the context of refuting the opponents and nullifying the claims of the obstinate, which calls for addressing what would deter them from opposition and lead them to submit to the truth. For when the disbelievers know that the realization of the resurrection is for the purpose of making clear that it is true, and so that they may know that they are liars in denying it, this is more effective in restraining them from denying it, and more conducive to acknowledging it. This is because it indicates the sincerity of the resolve to realize it, just as you say to one who denies that you pray: "I will certainly pray, in spite of your nose and to expose your lie." Also, because the repetition of purposes is more indicative of the occurrence of what they are the purposes of. Otherwise, the original purpose of the resurrection, considered in itself, is the recompense, which is the ultimate end of creation, the end being knowledge of Him, Mighty and Majestic, and His worship. It was not mentioned because it is repeatedly mentioned in many places and is well known. In this there is also the point that the liars among the disbelievers were not placed under the making clear by saying, for example: "And indeed those who disbelieved were liars," but rather the form of knowledge was used, because that is not among the things to which making clear, which is the disclosure of what was previously obscure by informing about it, applies, so that people then differ about it, as with the resurrection which the Qur'an spoke of and about which the disputants differed. As for the lying of the disbelievers, it is not of this kind. It may be inferred from the investigation of a parallel to this case that, since the content of a report is truth or falsehood, which are rational possibilities, and the meaning of making the truth clear is disclosing that content and cutting off the possibility of its opposite after it had been rationally possible, it was appropriate to connect the making clear to "that about which they differ" of the truth. There is not much difference between truth and sincerity. Since lying is an occurring matter, and the report does not indicate it so as to be connected to by making clear and disclosure, but is rather its opposite, what is connected to it becomes a new knowledge. So it was appropriate to connect knowledge to "that they were liars." So reflect.

It has been said: because knowledge of what is mentioned is among the concomitants of that making clear, it was said ﴿and that those who disbelieved may know﴾ rather than "and that He may make those who disbelieved knowers," and the attribution was restricted to them by not saying "and that they may know that those who disbelieved were liars," to indicate that their knowledge is the more important. It has also been said: He did not say that because the knowledge of the believers of what is mentioned already exists before that too. It has been objected that the attainment of one level of knowledge does not preclude the attainment of a higher level than it, so why was it not said, to announce the attainment of this level of knowledge for them at that time? Perhaps there is inattention to the intent of the speaker in this. It has also been allowed that by the knowledge of the disbelievers that they were liars is meant their punishment for their lying, so it is as if it were said: that the truth may become manifest to believers and disbelievers, and that the disbelievers may be punished for their lying in what they used to say, that God does not resurrect whoever dies and the like. This is like saying to a criminal: "Tomorrow you will know your crime." In that case the reason for restricting the attribution to them is clear. But it is, as you see, far-fetched.

Some of the Shiʿa claimed that the verse concerns ʿAlī, may God ennoble his face, and the Imams from his descendants, may God be pleased with them, and that it is among the proofs of the return (raʿja, the belief that the dead will return to the world before the Day of Resurrection), which most of them hold. This claim is false. The doctrine of the return is pure foolishness, and one who believes in the resurrection hardly holds it. This has been clarified most thoroughly in al-Tuḥfa al-Ithnā ʿAsharīyya (of Shah ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz al-Dihlawī). Perhaps the occasion will lead, God willing, to explaining it. As for what Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from ʿAlī, may God ennoble his face, that he said: "Indeed His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they swore by God﴾ etc. was revealed concerning something not established as sound." And even on the assumption of its soundness, there is no evidence in it for what they claim of the return, by saying that he, may God be pleased with him, meant that it was revealed on account of him, and that he, may God be pleased with him, was the man who sued a man among the polytheists for a debt owed to him, and that man said what he said, as has passed from Ibn al-Jawzī and Abū al-ʿĀliyah. Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also transmitted it from Abū al-ʿĀliyah.

Shaykh Bahāʾ al-Dīn (al-ʿĀmilī) deduced from the verse an evidence that lying is the contradiction of reality, and belief is not considered. This is evident, so understand.

Page 142

[Page 143]

﴿Indeed, Our saying﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a new sentence that resumes the discussion) explaining the act of bringing things into existence in general, whether at the outset or as a re-creation after the reminder of the immediacy of resurrection. From this it becomes known how it is done. ﴿mā﴾ is *kāffah* (a particle that "restrains" the particle *inna* from governing the noun after it, so that it can precede a verb). ﴿qawlunā﴾ is the subject (mubtada'). The words of the Exalted, ﴿for a thing﴾, are connected to it. The *lām* is the *lām* of communication (li'l-tablīgh), as in your saying: "I said to Zayd, 'Stand,' and he stood." Al-Zajjāj said: it is the *lām* of causation, meaning "for the sake of bringing a thing into existence." This was criticized as not clear, since the thing that comes to mind from the word *shay'* ("thing") here is the non-existent, which is one of its usages.

Shaykh Ibrāhīm al-Kūrānī, may Allah have mercy on him, has proven that applying the term *shay'* to the non-existent is literal, just as applying it to the existent is. He composed a noble treatise on this titled *Jalā' al-Fuhūm* ("The Clarification of Understandings"). From it, it is known that the view of this usage is not specific to the Mu'tazilah, as is commonly thought. For this reason, some of the scholars who did not reach the verification (of this matter) interpreted it here, saying: the expression of it as such is in view of its existence at the moment the Exalted's will is directed toward it, not that it was a thing before that.

In al-Bahr, quoting Ibn 'Atiyyah, there are two aspects to the words of the Exalted, ﴿for a thing﴾: the first is that since its existence is certain, it may be called a "thing" even while in the state of non-existence. The second is that this is an indication of the examples being considered, and that whatever among them is existent is intended, and it is said to it, "Be," and it is. Thus it becomes an example of what is later among matters by what came before. In this there is an escape from calling the non-existent a "thing." End of quote. But in it there is what is in it of obscurity.

Whatever the case, the tanwīn (nunation) is for indefiniteness, meaning "for a thing, whatever thing it may be," of what is precious or insignificant. ﴿when We intend it﴾ is an adverbial clause (*zarf*) modifying ﴿Our saying﴾, meaning: at the time the directing of Our will to bringing it into existence occurs. ﴿that We say to it, "Be"﴾ is in the sense of a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) serving as the predicate of the subject. The *lām* in ﴿to it﴾ is like the *lām* in ﴿for a thing, so it is﴾. It is either a conjunction with an implied element that the *fā'* (so) reveals and that the speech extends to, meaning: "so We say that, and so it is," or it is the answer to an implied condition, meaning: "so when We say that, then it is." It is also said that, after supposing *huwa* ("it") in front of *takūnu* ("it is"), the clause is a predicate of an implied subject, meaning: "what We intended, so it is." In both positions *kāna* is complete (tāmmah, i.e., meaning "to come into being" rather than linking a predicate).

The view taken by most of the verifying scholars, and which Shaykh al-Islām mentioned while restricting himself to it, is that there is no saying, nor one to whom it is said, nor a command, nor one commanded, so as to be asked: this entails one of two impossibilities, either addressing the non-existent or obtaining what is already obtained. Or it may be said: the word *innamā* ("only") requires that the Exalted's statement be restricted to His saying "Be," and it does not follow from this that the causes of creation are restricted to it, as the Exalted's words indicate: ﴿Indeed, His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 82]. The meaning of "command" here is affair (sha'n), which includes speech and act. Restricting it to the phrase "Be" necessarily entails restricting its causes absolutely to that. Rather, it is only an illustration of the ease with which decreed things come about in accordance with the directing of His will, and a depiction of the speed of their occurrence through what is an analogy in that from the obedience of the obedient subordinate to the command of the obeyed commander. So the meaning is: "Indeed Our bringing a thing into existence, when Our will is directed to it, is that We bring it into existence in the quickest manner." Since He expressed it with the command, which is a specific kind of saying, it was necessary to express the absolute act of bringing into existence with the absolute saying.

It has been said: the speech is on its literal basis, and by that the divine custom has proceeded, and this is attributed to the early scholars (al-salaf). And an answer has been given on their behalf to the objection of the necessity of one of the two impossibilities: first, that the address is existential (takwīnī) and there is no harm in its being directed to the non-existent. This was criticized as a view that it is an allegory (tamthīl). Second, that the non-existent is established in knowledge, and that suffices for the validity of addressing it with that, to the point that some said it is seen by Him in its state of non-existence. This was criticized with lengthy argument. As for the objection regarding restriction, they said the matter there is simple. Some of the discussion at this point has already passed.

Some of the Ahl al-Sunnah (the people of the Sunnah, the orthodox majority), taking the verse literally, used it as evidence for the eternity of the Qur'an. He said: It indicates that when He intends to bring something into being, He says to it "Be." So if "Be" were originated, it would entail an infinite regress (tasalsul), which is impossible. So it is eternal. And whoever says that some of it is eternal must say that all of it is eternal. This was criticized: the word *idhā* ("when") does not indicate repetition. For this reason, if a man says to his wife, "When you enter the house, you are divorced," and she enters many times, she is divorced only once. So it does not follow that every originated thing is originated by the word "Be." Hence no infinite regress is entailed. Moreover, the view that the "Be" is eternal is necessarily false, because of what it contains of the sequencing of letters. The same applies to all verbal speech.

The Imam (al-Rāzī) said: the verse indicates that speech is originated in several ways. The first: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, Our saying to a thing, when We intend it﴾, requires that the saying occurs by the will, and whatever is so is originated. The second: He linked the saying to the word *idhā* ("when"), which, without doubt, is for the future. The third: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿that We say﴾, there is no disagreement that it indicates the future. The fourth: the saying of the Exalted, ﴿"Be," so it is﴾, the "Be" precedes the coming into being of the created thing, even if only by a single moment, and what precedes the originated is likewise originated. So it is necessary to affirm that speech is originated.

[Page 144]

Yes, it indicates the origination of the verbal speech that the Hanābilah (Hanbalis) and those who agree with them hold, but it does not indicate the origination of the inner speech (kalām nafsī, the speech of the soul). The Ash'ariyyah, as is known of their position, claim only the eternity of the inner speech and deny the eternity of the verbal speech. This is a matter on which they lengthened the discussion, so let it be consulted.

As for what was mentioned about the indication of *idhā* and *naqūlu* (we say) to the future, this is what more than one scholar stated. However, Abū Ḥayyān quoted Ibn 'Atiyyah as saying: what is in the words of this verse of the meaning of the future and resumption refers only to the intended object, not to the will. That is because the things intended and brought into existence, in their coming into being, are a resumption and a future, not in the will to that nor in the command to it, for these two are eternal. So for the sake of the object He expressed it with *idhā* and *naqūlu*. You know that there is no dispute over the eternity of the will. But they differed over whether it has an originated connection (ta'alluq ḥādith) or not. Some said the first, and others said: it has only an eternal connection, but with the existence of contingent things at the time each is destined for it. So the Exalted's will connected, from eternity, to the existence of Zayd, for example, on such-and-such a day, and to the existence of 'Amr on such-and-such a day, and so on. There is no need for an originated connection on that day. As for the command, the inner command is eternal and the verbal command is originated according to those who hold that verbal speech is originated. As for time, it is often not taken into account regarding the acts attributed to the Exalted. He considered the statement "Allah was, and nothing was with Him," and "Allah created the world," and similar. I do not see this ruling as specific to the case where time is interpreted as the philosophers held, but rather it applies to that and also where time is interpreted as the theologians held. So reflect. And Allah the Exalted is the Guide.

More than one scholar made the verse an explanation of the possibility of resurrection. Its explanation is that Allah the Exalted's bringing things into being by pure power and will does not depend on prior materials and supply, for otherwise it would entail an infinite regress. Just as He is able to bring things into being at the outset without a prior material or model, He is able to bring them into being again after that. Its apparent meaning is that it is a statement of the re-creation of the non-existent. And the apparent meanings of many texts indicate that resurrection is the gathering of scattered parts. The verification of this will come, as I promised you just now, if Allah the Exalted wills.

Ibn 'Āmir and al-Kisā'ī read here and in [Yā-Sīn: 82] ﴿fa-yakūna﴾ with the accusative (naṣb). Al-Zajjāj interpreted it as conjoined to ﴿naqūlu﴾, meaning "so that it may be," or as the answer to "Be." This was rejected by al-Radī and others, on the ground that the accusative after an imperative is conditional upon the verbal noun of the first being the cause of the second, and this is not possible here because the two are identical. So that does not hold. It was explained that his meaning is that it is put in the accusative because it resembles the answer to the imperative, since it comes after it, and it is not really an answer to it in meaning, for there is no sense in your saying: "I said to Zayd, 'Strike,' you strike."

This was criticized: its weakness is not hidden, and it entails cancelling the mentioned condition. Then it was said: the more apparent way to interpret it is that when the like of this comes from an eloquent speaker, intending an illustration of the speed of effect through the quickness of the subordinate in obeying, the meaning is: "If I say to you, 'Strike,' you will quickly obey." So the verbal noun caused by it is formed from the pattern (hay'ah) and not from the root (māddah), and the verbal noun of the second is from the root, or is the resultant meaning. By this the difference between the two verbal nouns is achieved, and the causal and caused relation becomes clear. Some of them said: the intent of whoever says that the accusative is for resemblance to the answer to the imperative is that *fa-yakūna*, as in the reading of the nominative, is conjoined to what the speech extends to, or it is by implication "so it is," the predicate of an implied subject, except that it was put in the accusative because of this resemblance. In this there is what there is.

"Those who emigrated for the sake of Allah" — ﴿وَالَّذِينَ هَاجَرُوا فِي اللَّهِ﴾ — meaning: for His right (fi haqqihi). Taken literally, "fi" (in) indicates that this emigration is firmly rooted, in the way a container is firmly within what it contains, so the "fi" is figurative in its sense of location. Or, "fi" here indicates cause (lil-ta'lil), for the sake of His good pleasure, as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat."

Emigration (muhajara) originally means cutting off from and abandoning another, and it has been used for leaving the land of disbelief for the land of faith. So the meaning is: "Those who abandoned their homelands, left them for Allah, the Exalted, and went out ﴿after they had been wronged﴾," i.e., after the wrongdoing of the disbelievers against them.

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah, who said: They are the companions of Muhammad (ﷺ). The people of Makkah wronged them, so they went out from their homes until groups of them reached the land of Abyssinia. Then Allah, the Exalted, settled them in Madinah after that, as He promised, glorified is He, in His saying, "We will surely settle them in this world in a good place" — ﴿لَنُبَوِّئَنَّهُمْ فِي الدُّنْيَا حَسَنَةً﴾. That is, a good abode; the sum of it is: "We will surely lodge them in this world in a good dwelling." It is reported from al-Hasan: "a good house." The first estimate is more evident because the verb indicates it, and the second is more in harmony with His saying, "They settled in the abode" (Al-Hashr 9).

Whichever it is, "hasanah" is an attribute of an omitted noun in the accusative, functioning as an adverbial accusative (nasb al-zuruf). It is also permissible for it to be a second object of "linubawwi'annahum," in the sense of "We will surely give them a good station." This was interpreted as domination over the people of Makkah who wronged them and over the Arabs entirely. It was also said: it is what remained for them in this world of praise, and what came to their descendants of nobility. From Mujahid: the estimate is "a good livelihood," i.e., good provision. It was also said: the estimate is "a good gift," and "the gift" means "the thing given," which is interpreted as every good thing that the emigrants attained in this world. Some estimated "a good settling" (tabwi'ah hasanah), so it is an attribute of an omitted verbal noun. This settling may be considered as encompassing the granting of every good thing that came to the emigrants, in the manner of the previous.

In al-Bahr: the apparent view is that "hasanah" is in the accusative as a verbal noun not of the same root (masdar ghayr al-sadr), because the meaning of "linubawwi'annahum" is "We will surely treat them well," so "hasanah" means "ihsanan" (kindness). In all the estimates, "alladhina hajaru" is the subject (mubtada'), and the clause "linubawwi'annahum" is its predicate (khabar).

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "alladhina" be in the accusative governed by an omitted verb which the mentioned one explains. The first is determined according to Abu Hayyan, who said: In this is evidence for the validity of an oath clause occurring as the predicate of a subject, contrary to Tha'lab. What some verifying scholars have held is that the predicate in such a case is only the answer clause, emphasized by the oath, and it is declarative, not performative. Abu al-Baqa's second view was objected to on the grounds that the accusative governed by an omitted verb is only permissible where the mentioned verb could govern that accusative, so that it may be an explanation. What is here is not so: "Zaydan la-adribanna" is not permitted, so "Zaydan la-adribannahu" is not permitted. The prepositional phrase is attached to what is before it. It was also said: it is attached to an omitted element which occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) of "hasanah." This is it.

It is related from Ibn Abbas that the verse was revealed concerning Suhayb, Bilal, Ammar, Khabbab, Abis, Jubayr, and Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl, whom the polytheists seized and began torturing to turn them back from Islam. As for Suhayb, he said to them: "I am an old man; if I am with you, I will not benefit you, and if I am against you, I will not harm you." So he ransomed himself from them with his wealth and emigrated. When Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) saw him, he said: "The sale has profited, O Suhayb!" And Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "What a fine servant is Suhayb! Had he not feared Allah, he would not have disobeyed Him."

The majority hold to what was reported from Qatadah. Ibn Atiyyah even said: it is the sound view, and we have not found for this report from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) a chain of narration that can be relied upon. Shaykh Baha' al-Din al-Subki, in his commentary on al-Talkhis, mentioned, as did others among the later scholars such as the hafiz and allamah Zayn al-Din Abd al-Rahim al-Iraqi and his son the jurist and hafiz Abu Zur'ah and others, regarding what is attributed to Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) in it, from his saying "What a fine servant is Suhayb" to its end, that we have not found it in any book of hadith after an intense search. This casts strong doubt upon the soundness of that. Yes, in al-Durr al-Manthur: Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) that he said concerning those who emigrated: "They are a people from the people of Makkah who emigrated to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after their wronging." Then he said: "And their wronging is shirk." But this, by its apparent meaning, indicates that he (may Allah be pleased with him) was reading "zalamu" in the active voice.

Objection was raised to both reports: it has been said that the surah is Makkan except for three verses at its end, which are Madani. If the report is sound, it requires going to the view that there is another Madani portion besides that; or saying that what is meant by Makkan is what was revealed concerning the people of Makkah; or that this verse was not revealed in Madinah, and that the Makkan is what was revealed outside it; or saying that this is information about something before it occurs. All of these, as you see, are weak. It is not objected to the first view, upon which the majority rests, that it contradicts the well-known view about the surah, because the emigration to Abyssinia was before the emigration to Madinah, so there is no obstacle to the verse being Makkan in the well-known sense. However, it was said: Qatadah, the one who holds the view mentioned earlier, holds that this verse to the end of the surah is Madani, and he refuses what was mentioned. From here some scholars interpreted what was reported from him earlier as meaning that its revelation was between the two emigrations in Madinah. These views cannot be reconciled at all. What should be relied upon is that the surah is Makkan except for the verses, which are not among them; rather they are Makkan, revealed between the two emigrations, concerning those whom the majority mentioned. And Allah knows best the reality of the matter.

Some said: "Alladhina hajaru" is general, applying to emigrants whoever they were, so it includes the first of them and the last of them. This was, from its speaker, a consideration of the generality of the wording, not of the particularity of the occasion of revelation, as is established among them.

Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) and Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with him), Nu'aym ibn Maysarah, and al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham read ﴿لَنُثْوِيَنَّهُمْ﴾ with the letter thaʼ (ث), from athwa, the causative form (with the hamzah of transitivity) of thawa bi-l-makan, meaning "stayed in it." In al-Bahr: The accusative of "hasanah" is either by estimating "ithwa'atan hasanah," or by removing the preposition, i.e., "in a good abode," "in a good dwelling," or "in a good station." There is no obstacle, according to what has been said, to considering the verb as containing the meaning of "nu'tihim" (We will give them), as was indicated earlier.

The verse has been used as evidence for one of the views on the nobility of Madinah and the nobility of sincerely performing deeds for Allah, the Exalted. ﴿وَلَأَجْرُ الْآخِرَةِ أَكْبَرُ﴾ — that is, the reward of their deeds mentioned, in the Hereafter, is greater than what is hastened for them in this world. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Umar ibn al-Khattab that whenever he gave a man among the emigrants a gift, he would say to him: "Take it; may Allah bless you. This is what Allah promised you in this world, and what He has deferred for you in the Hereafter is better." Then he would recite this verse. It was also said: what is meant is that it is greater than anyone can know before witnessing it. The emphasis of this promise's style, differing from what precedes it, is not hidden. ﴿لَوْ كَانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ — the pronoun refers to the disbelieving wrongdoers: if they knew that Allah, the Exalted, gathers for these emigrants the good of both abodes, they would have agreed with them in the religion. It was also said: it refers to the emigrants, i.e., if they knew that, they would have increased in striving, would not have been pained by what befell them of emigration and its hardships, and would have grown even more joyful. In al-Ma'alim: that is not permissible, because the emigrants know it. This was answered by saying that what is meant is knowledge of witnessing, and report is not like direct observation; or what is meant is detailed knowledge. It was also permitted that the pronoun refers to those who stayed behind from emigration, meaning: if those who stayed behind from emigration knew what honor the emigrants have, they would have agreed with them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 42:

﴿Those who were patient﴾ over what injustice befell them, and did not turn back (*al-qahqara*, going backwards), and [were patient] over leaving the homeland, which is the sanctuary of God, glorified is He, beloved to every believer, let alone one who was born there, and [were patient] over bearing estrangement among people who are unrelated to them by lineage and whom they were not accustomed to, and over other than that. The relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) may be in the accusative by implying *a'ni* ("I mean"), or in the nominative by implying *hum* ("they"). It may also be a follower of *alladhina hajaru* ("those who emigrated") as a substitute (*badal*), an explanatory apposition (*bayan*), or a qualifying adjective (*na't*).

﴿And upon their Lord they rely﴾: cut off from everything else towards Him, turning away from whatever is other than Him, and entrusting Him with the whole matter, as the omission of the object of *al-tawakkul* (reliance) indicates. It has been said that the fronting of the prepositional phrase (*al-jar wa'l-majrur*), which signifies restriction (*al-hasr*), is for the sake of the rhyme-endings (*al-fawasil*, the verse-final sounds), though this is not definitively required. The imperfect form (*sighat al-istiqbal*) is either for continuity or to bring that wondrous image to mind. The clause is either conjoined to the relative clause (*al-sila*) or is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *sabaru* ("they were patient").

[Page 147]

﴿We sent none before you but men to whom We revealed⦆ is a rebuttal to the Quraysh, who denied the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "God, exalted is He, is too great for His messenger to be a human being. Why did He not send an angel to us?" The meaning is that God's established practice, as wisdom requires, is that we send for the general call only human beings, to whom We reveal, usually through an angel, the commands and prohibitions so that they may convey them. By "the general call" we exclude the sending of an angel to the prophets (peace be upon them) for conveying a message, or for other purposes, such as His sending to Maryam to give her good news. And "usually" indicates that some kinds of revelation did not come through an angel, as His words indicate: ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should speak to him except by revelation, or from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger who reveals by His permission what He wills﴾ [al-Shura 51]. The majority of readers recited «yūḥā» with a ya and a fatha on the ha. A group recited it with a ya and a kasra on the ha, and so did ʿAbdullah, al-Sulami and Talha. Ḥafṣ recited it with a nun and a kasra. In this there is an evident exaltation of the matter of revelation. Since the intended address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was to alert the disbelievers to its content, the address was turned to them, and so it says: ﴿So ask the people of the Reminder⦆, meaning the People of the Book, from among the Jews and Christians. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Ḥasan, al-Suddi and others. The naming of the Book will be explained in what follows, God willing. It is reported from Mujahid that it was specific to the Torah, based on His words: ﴿And We had written in the Psalms after the Reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya 105]. So its people are the Jews.

Al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit) says: The intended people are those among the People of the Book who have not become Muslims, because they are the ones who are not suspected by the people of Makkah when they report that the messengers (peace be upon them) were men. Thus their report is a proof against them. The purpose is to break their argument and bind them, for otherwise the truth is clear in itself and does not need the report of these people. The polytheists sent, after this verse was revealed, to the people of Yathrib to ask them about this.
