Al-Aʿmash, Ibn ʿUyayna and Ibn Jubayr said: The intended people are those among them who became Muslims, such as ʿAbdullah ibn Salam and Salman al-Farisi, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others.

This is weakened by the fact that the statement of one who became Muslim is not a proof against the disbelievers. From this we know the weakness of what Abu Jaʿfar and Ibn Zayd said, that the Reminder means the Qur'an, because Allah has called it a reminder in several places, among which is what will come, God willing, shortly. On this view, the people of the Reminder are Muslims in general. Some of the Imamiyya restricted it to the Imams, the People of the House, citing what Jabir and Muhammad ibn Muslim narrated, one of them from Abu Jaʿfar (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "We are the People of the Reminder." Some interpreted the Reminder as the Prophet (ﷺ), based on His words: ﴿a reminder, a messenger﴾ [al-Talaq 10–11], according to one view. It is said, on the basis of what is in al-Bahr: How could the disbelievers of Makkah be convinced by the report of the People of the House on this matter, when they are not more truthful than the Messenger of Allah in their eyes, and he (peace be upon him) was well known among them as "the Trustworthy"? Perhaps what Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, which agrees outwardly with what that group among the Imamiyya claims, is: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'A man may pray, fast, perform Hajj and ʿUmrah, and yet he is a hypocrite.' It was said: 'O Messenger of Allah, by what did hypocrisy enter into him?' He said: 'By criticising his imam, and his imam is the one whom Allah mentioned in His Book: ﴿So ask the people of the Reminder⦆ to the end of the verse.'"

This is not sound. I say: It is permissible that the people of the Reminder mean the people of the Qur'an, although Abu Hayyan said what he said, and you will know its aspect shortly, God willing, the Bestower. Al-Rummani, al-Zajjaj and al-Azhari said: The people of the Reminder are the scholars of the reports of past nations, whoever they may be. Here "reminder" means preservation, as if it were said: "Ask those who are informed of the reports of the nations, and they will inform you of that, ﴿if you do not know⦆." The answer to "if" is either omitted, because what precedes it indicates it, meaning "then ask," or it is what precedes it itself, based on the permissibility of placing the answer before the condition. The verse has been used as evidence that Allah did not send a woman or a child as a messenger, and this does not conflict with the prophethood of ʿIsa (peace be upon him) in the cradle, because prophethood is more general than messengerhood. Nor does it imply the validity of the claim that Maryam was also a prophet, because at most it negates the messengerhood of a woman, and this does not necessitate establishing her prophethood. A group went to the validity of the prophethood of women, and Ibn al-Sayyid affirmed it. What the verse indicates regarding the negation of sending angels (peace be upon them) does not conflict with His words: ﴿Who made the angels messengers⦆ [Fatir 1], because the intended meaning is that He made them messengers to the angels or to the prophets (peace be upon them), not for the general call, and this is what is claimed, as you have understood. So "messenger" is either in its technical sense or in its linguistic sense. Al-Jubba'i said: The angels (peace be upon them) were not sent to the prophets (peace be upon them) except in the form of men. This was refuted by what is narrated: "Our Prophet (ﷺ) saw Jibril (peace be upon him) in his own form twice."

This objection is directed at the restriction, which implies generality, so it is not refuted by the claim that there is no indication in what was narrated of the seeing by those before our Prophet (peace be upon him) of Jibril (peace be upon him) in his own form. Moreover, if this is established for the Prophet (ﷺ) and it is not established that it is among his particular privileges (peace be upon him), then there is no barrier to its being established for others. This was said by al-Shihab. He also mentions that al-Imam narrated from al-Qadi that what al-Jubba'i meant is that they were not sent to the prophets (peace be upon them) in the presence of their nations except while they were in the forms of men, as it is narrated that Jibril (peace be upon him) came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the presence of his Companions in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi, and in the form of Suraqa, and in the form of a Bedouin whom they did not recognise.

The verse has also been used as evidence for the obligation of consulting scholars in matters that are not known.

In al-Iklil of al-Jalal al-Suyuti it is said that it has been used as evidence for the permissibility of taqlid (following a jurist's opinion without independent verification) by the layman in the branches of law. Consider the restriction to the branches of law, for the apparent meaning is generality, especially if we say that the matters about which the people are commanded to consult and ask are among the roots of the faith. This is supported by what is transmitted from al-Jalal al-Mahalli: that a non-mujtahid, whether a layman or otherwise, is required to follow a mujtahid (one qualified to derive rulings through ijtihad, independent legal reasoning), based on His words: ﴿So ask the people of the Reminder if you do not know⦆. The correct view is that there is no difference between doctrinal matters and others, nor between the mujtahid being alive or dead. End of quotation.

He and others affirmed the impermissibility of taqlid for the mujtahid absolutely, whether he has a definitive proof or not, and whether he is a mujtahid in actuality or has the capacity for ijtihad. The implication of their statements is that there is no difference between following one of the four imams of the schools and following another mujtahid. However, the scholar Ibn Hajar and others mentioned that for following another it is a condition that his school be recorded and its conditions and authoritative principles preserved. So al-Subki's statement that one who opposes the four schools is like one who opposes consensus is to be understood as applying to schools whose transmitters have ceased and whose books have been lost, and whose conditions and other authoritative principles are not preserved, such as the school of al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Ibn Abi Layla and others. Then, the following of another, with its condition, is permitted only in acting; but for issuing fatwas and judging, one of the four schools is required. Al-ʿAllama Ibn Qasim al-ʿAbbadi raised a question about this distinction. It was answered that the distinction may be that caution is exercised in these two, since their scope extends beyond what is exercised caution in when acting, so they are abandoned for the slightest risk, even if merely possible. A parallel to this is what some Shafiʿis mention regarding two equally balanced opinions: that one does not issue a fatwa according to either of them nor judge by either, for it is possible that it is the weaker one, though it is permissible to act upon it. Al-Imam mentioned that some people permitted taqlid for the mujtahid on the basis of this verse, saying: Since one of the mujtahids was not knowledgeable, he was obliged to refer to a knowledgeable mujtahid, based on His words: ﴿So ask⦆, the verse. If he does not do so, then at least it is permissible. This was supported by the fact that some mujtahids transmitted the views of some Companions and confirmed the ruling according to them. The correct view is what you heard at first, and what was mentioned is not taqlid, but rather is an instance of one ijtihad agreeing with another ijtihad.

Those who deny qiyas (analogical reasoning) also used the verse as evidence. They said: When an accountable person faces an event, if he knows its ruling, then he may not use qiyas; otherwise, he is obliged to ask one who knows it, according to the apparent meaning of the verse. If qiyas were a valid proof, it would not be obligatory for him to ask, because he could derive that ruling by qiyas. Thus it is established that permitting acting on qiyas necessitates abandoning acting on the apparent meaning of the verse, so it must not be permitted. This was answered: The permissibility of acting on qiyas has been established by the consensus of the Companions, and consensus is stronger than this argument.

Some of them said: If the accountable person is one who is able to perform qiyas, then he is one who knows, and so it is not obligatory for him to ask. So reflect.

[p. 149]

﴿with the clear proofs and the scriptures﴾: that is, with the miracles and the books. The first is for showing the truthfulness (of the messengers), and the second is for explaining the laws and obligations. Whoever explains the two of them as the technical usage of the people of crafts (*ahl al-hiraf*) has strayed from the truth. The prepositional phrase (*al-jar wa'l-majrur*) is connected to an implied verb (*muqaddar*) indicated by what precedes it. It serves as an answer to the question of one who asks: "With what were they sent?" So it is said: "They were sent ﴿with the clear proofs and the scriptures﴾."

Al-Zamakhshari and al-Hawfi permitted its connection to the preceding "We sent" (*arsalna*), falling under the exceptive restriction along with "men" (*rijalan*). That is: "And We did not send except men with the clear proofs." It has the meaning of your saying: "We did not send a group of groups with anything of things except men with the clear proofs," and like your saying: "I did not strike except Zayd with a whip." This is based on what some grammarians permitted, namely that two things may be excepted by one particle without a conjunction, and that this applies in the *istithna' mufarragh* (exceptive construction with the excepted element omitted). Most grammarians, however, prohibit it, as stated by the author of *al-Tashil* and others.

In *al-Kashf*, it says: "The truth is that it is not permitted, because *illa* (except) is part of what it enters upon, like a component of it, and because of the necessity of causing confusion (*ilbas*), or the requirement that everything that comes after *illa* be restricted, and that it would require something like 'I did not strike except Zayd, Amr' if the restriction is intended for both, and there would be no difference between this and that. All of this is clearly untenable." Al-Zamakhshari permitted it and stated it explicitly in several places in his *Kashshaf*, and it has been argued for by the fact that the original of "I did not strike except Zayd with a whip" is "I struck Zayd with a whip." He meant that the addition of *ma* and *illa* is only for emphasis, so it should be emphasized, since the original structure of the speech is that. This is good, were it not that usage and analogy refuse it.

Some of them said that it is connected to it (*bihi*) without entering together with "men" under the exceptive restriction, on the basis that its original form is: "We did not send with the clear proofs and the scriptures except men."

This was objected to: it is not permitted according to the school of the Basrans, since they do not allow that after *illa* there should come an excepted element, an element from which something is excepted, or a follower (*tabi'*), and whatever is thought to be other than these three as an operand of what precedes *illa* requires a governing element to be supposed for it. Al-Kisa'i permitted that after it there come an operand of what precedes it in the accusative, as in "Only Zayd struck Amr," and in the genitive, as in "Only Zayd (struck) with Amr," and "None punishes with the Fire except Allah," and in the nominative, as in "Only Zayd was struck by Amr." Ibn al-Anbari agreed with him regarding the nominative, and al-Akhfash regarding the adverbial complement, the prepositional phrase and the circumstantial (*zarf, jar, hal*). So what has been mentioned is based on the school of al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash. However, al-Shihab said: "It contradicts the apparent sense of the speech and takes it out of the normal arrangement." Most grammarians hold that this is prohibited.

It is also permitted that it be connected to what is raised (*ma rufi'*) as a qualifier (*sifa*) of "men," meaning: "men associated with the clear proofs." It did not come as a circumstantial (*hal*) of him. It was said: because it is an indefinite noun placed before (its qualifier). Yes, it was said that it is permitted for it to come as a circumstantial of the pronoun of "men" in "to them" (*ilayhim*). It was also said: it is permitted that it be a circumstantial of "men" (*rijalan*), because it is a qualified indefinite noun. Abu Hayyan preferred the coming of a circumstantial from an indefinite noun without a justifying factor, as frequent and analogical, and he transmitted it from Sibawayh, though it is weaker than the following (of the adjective) in strength.

It is also permitted that it be connected to "We revealed" (*nuhi*). The words of the Exalted: ﴿so ask the people of the reminder﴾ are a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*) on the preceding aspects, or on other than the first. The introduction of a parenthetical clause with *fa* (then) is stated explicitly in *al-Tashil* and elsewhere, and what was transmitted of its prohibition is not established. Then, if it is a parenthetical insertion intervening between the two parts of the restrictive particle, its meaning is: "Ask the people of the reminder if you do not know that We sent men with the clear proofs." And if it is in the descriptive sense: "if you do not know that they were men associated with the clear proofs." On this basis the parenthetical insertion is understood as suitable to what intervenes between the two. The most fitting of the aspects is that it be in two statements, so that the parenthetical insertion falls in its appropriate place both verbally and in meaning. This is what he said in *al-Kashf*.

It is also permitted that it be connected to "you know" (*ta'lamun*), and then there is no parenthetical insertion. In the conditional there is a sense of rebuke and obligation, as in the words of a hired worker: "If I have worked for you, then give me my right." For the worker does not doubt that he worked, but he has expressed the speech in the form of doubt, because the treatment he receives, such as procrastination, is the treatment of one who thinks his worker did not work. So he, in that respect, holds the other to what he has acknowledged of work, and rebukes him for negligence, making him ignorant. Likewise here: there is no doubt that the Quraysh had no share in the knowledge of the clear proofs and the scriptures. So he says: "That the messengers, peace be upon them, were men is a manifest matter with no doubt about it. So ask the people of the reminder, if you are not of their kind, and they will explain to you." He means that your denial, while you do not know...

[p. 150]

...while you do not know, is not correct. The proper course is that you ask the people of the reminder, not that you deny their statement. For your denial contradicts what your situation requires of asking. So it is a rebuke in terms of acknowledging your lack of knowledge, and the way of the ignorant is to ask one who knows, not to deny him. This too is stated in *al-Kashf*. Then he said: "I do not restrict the people of the reminder to the People of the Two Books, so that it includes the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions. Even if it were restricted, it would be permissible, because they agree in that, so their denial is their denial. Then the rebuke is directed at turning away from asking to denial; they asked first." Ended. From this it is known that it is permissible to mean by the people of the reminder the people of the Qur'an. What Abu Hayyan mentioned in weakening this, that there is no proof in their information and no obligation, arises from not having grasped this elegant investigation.

This is evident on the assumption that "with the clear proofs" is connected to "you know," and the preposition (*ba'*) on this assumption is causal, and the object is omitted according to some. Another claimed that it is superfluous and that "the clear proofs" is the object. So understand that, and may Allah the Exalted guide you.

﴿And We revealed to you the Reminder﴾: that is, the Qur'an. It derives from *tadhkir* (reminding), either in the sense of admonition or in the sense of awakening from the drowsiness of heedlessness. Its application to the Qur'an is either because it includes what has been mentioned, or because it is a cause of it. From this is known the reason for calling the Torah and similar books "reminder." It was said: the intended meaning of the reminder is knowledge, but this is not the case. ﴿so that you may explain to mankind﴾, all of them, and the people of Makkah enter among them first and foremost, ﴿what has been sent down to them﴾ in that reminder of laws and legislation and other matters concerning the conditions of the destroyed generations with various kinds of punishment, according to their deeds with their prophets, peace be upon them, which necessitated that, in detail, with a sufficient explanation, as the form of the verb (*tafil*) in both verbs indicates, especially after the second has come first in the form of verbs. It is related from Mujahid that the intended meaning of this explanation is the interpretation of the ambiguous and the clarification of what is difficult, since these two are what need explaining, while the explicit text and the apparent meaning do not need it.

It was said: the intended meaning is making them stand upon their differing capacities, regarding what is hidden from them of the secrets of the Qur'an and its countless sciences. This is not limited to explaining the lawful and the unlawful and the conditions of the past generations and bygone nations. He took as evidence for this what al-Hakim transmitted and authenticated from Hudhayfah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood among us in a station in which he informed us of what would happen until the Day of Resurrection. Whoever among us retained it, retained it, and whoever forgot it, forgot it."

This is in the sense of what more than one has mentioned: that explanation is more general than explicit statement of the intended meaning, and than guidance to what indicates it. It includes analogy (*qiyas*), the indication of the text (*isharat al-nass*), its implication (*dalalatuhu*), and what is derived from it of doctrines, realities and secrets. Perhaps His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿and perhaps they will reflect﴾ is an allusion to that, meaning: and that they should contemplate it, so that they become aware of the realities and the lessons in it, and guard against what leads to the punishment that befell the former peoples. Some of the Mu'tazilah said: that is, the desire that they reflect on that, so that they know the truth. Then he said: In it is evidence that Allah the Exalted desired from all people reflection and contemplation leading to knowledge, unlike what the people of compulsion (*jabr*) say. We have no need to estimate the will by estimating the request, and whoever estimates it among us, wills it from it. Otherwise it would follow that some do not reflect, and they are probably the majority. And according to the correct doctrine, the desired thing is not separated from the will, so it is necessary to turn away from it to its opposite. It was said: he meant that the will is connected to a part, namely the one who reflects, and not to all. Some supported that the intended meaning is the Companions, or whoever includes them and the Prophet ﷺ, among the people of the reminder mentioned earlier, by the mention of this verse after it. But this is not of strong evidence.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 16, verse 45:

﴿Do those who devise evil schemes feel secure﴾ According to most commentators (*mufassirun*), they are the people of Mecca who schemed against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and who sought to turn his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, away from faith. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir (al-Tabari) and others related from Mujahid that they were Nimrod ibn Kan'an and his people. Some commentators generalized, saying: they are those who plotted to destroy the prophets, peace be upon them. This was objected to on the grounds that the purpose is to warn the people of Mecca against suffering what befell the earlier peoples of various kinds of punishment that are well known. So what the majority hold is the reliance. [Page 151]

The word «السَّيِّئاتِ» (*al-sayyi'at*, "the evil [deeds/schemes]") is an adjective (*na't*) modifying an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning: they devised the evil schemes that have been related about them. Or it is the direct object of the mentioned verb, with the verb taken to include the sense of a transitive verb such as «عَمِلَ» ('amila, "to do"), meaning: they did evil deeds while scheming.

Then the words ﴿that Allah should cause the earth to swallow them﴾ are the object of «أَمِنَ» (amina, "to feel secure"). Or «السَّيِّئاتِ» is the object of «أَمِنَ», with an implied noun (*mudaf*) or a figurative usage, meaning: the punishment of the evil deeds. Or «السَّيِّئاتِ» means the punishments that will harm them. The phrase «أَنْ يَخْسِفَ» is then a substitute (*badal*) for that.

In every case, the «فاء» (fa', "so/then") is for coordination (*lil-'atf*) with an implied element that the noble text's context requires, meaning: We sent down the Reminder to you so that you would make its content clear to them, which includes the accounts of the destroyed nations with their various punishments, and so that they would reflect upon it. Did they not reflect? So those who devised evil schemes feel secure... The denial is directed at the two conjoined elements. Or the meaning is: "Did they reflect, and so feel secure?" with the denial directed at the conjoined element. It has also been said that the «فاء» coordinates with an implied element indicated by the relative clause: "Did they scheme, so that those who devised evil schemes feel secure..."

The verb «خَسَفَ» (khasafa, "to sink, to cause to sink") is used both intransitively and transitively. As al-Raghib said: "Allah sank him (*khasafahu Allah*), and he sank (*khusifa huwa*)." Both usages are possible here. Accordingly, the «ب» in «بِهِمُ» is either for transitivity (making the verb transitive) or for accompaniment (*lil-mula'abah*, "meaning 'together with them'"). The word «الأَرْضَ» (*al-ard*, "the earth") is either the direct object, or accusative after the removal of the preposition, meaning: that Allah should cause them to vanish into the earth, or that He should cause the earth to swallow them, as He did with Qarun.

﴿Or that punishment should come upon them from where they do not perceive﴾ meaning: from a direction they do not realize punishment could come from, such as the direction of their place of safety, or the direction from which they hope that what they desire will come. Al-Baydawi said: that is, suddenly, from the side of the sky, as was done to the people of Lot. The specification of "the side of the sky" seems to be because what comes from there is usually not perceived, unlike what comes from the earth, which is usually perceptible. Taking it this way is perhaps more fitting for the contrast. It is possible that his meaning by "from the side of the sky" is whatever does not occur at the hand of a created being, whether it arises from the earth or from the sky, as has been said:

"Leave it heavenly, running by decree."

In that case it is metaphorical. But it has been objected that this does not fit the example, though it does not restrict the meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 46:

﴿Or He seizes them﴾ i.e., the punishment, or Allah, Exalted is He. The first is preferred for its proximity, and the second for the frequency with which the Qur'an attributes the act of seizing (akhdh) to Allah, Exalted is He, although He, majestic is His affair, is the true Agent of it.

﴿In their going to and fro﴾ i.e., their movement, going forth and returning. The meaning, as Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Qatadah, and as is reported from Ibn Abbas, is "in their travels." The Imam said that this interpretation is derived from the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Let not the going to and fro of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 196]. Or the meaning is: while they are moving about in the pursuit of their plotting and striving to carry it out. It was also said: the meaning is while they turn over on their beds, right and left, which has the same sense as what is reported from Ibn Abbas, also, "in their sleep," but I do not think this is authentic.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning encompasses all their movements in their affairs, by night or by day. The majority hold the first view. Akhdh (seizing) originally means taking possession of a thing and acquiring it, and here it means subjugation and destruction. The prepositional phrase is either in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) or is connected to the verb before it. The first is preferred, in view of the similar phrase that comes later, if Allah wills; yet the apparent sense of what precedes it is the second.

﴿So they cannot escape﴾ i.e., they cannot escape Allah, Exalted, by flight or fleeing, as the state of going to and fro and traveling might suggest; or: they cannot resist Him, as their scheming and their turning about in it might suggest. The particle "fa" (so) is said to indicate either the cause of the seizing, or the consequence of their inability to escape from it, showing its severity and terror, in accordance with the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah gives respite to the wrongdoer, until when He seizes him, He does not let him go."

The nominal sentence serves to indicate the continuity of the negation, and emphasis also returns to this.

Page 152

﴿Or that He seize them with a gradual wasting away﴾, meaning with fear and dread of destruction and punishment: that He destroy a people before them, or bring about conditions of which they would be afraid, other than that, such as violent winds, thunderbolts and earthquakes, so that they become fearful and He seizes them with punishment while they are in a state of fear. A similar view is narrated from al-Dahhak. It is, as al-Zamakhshari said, and as the words of Ibn Bahr imply, contrary to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿from where they do not perceive﴾.

Many of the eminent scholars said: [it means] that He diminishes them little by little in their persons and their wealth, until they perish, from the verb takhawwafa, meaning that it diminishes him (tanaqqasahu). This interpretation is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak as well.

Al-Haytham ibn 'Adi mentioned that diminishing in this sense is the dialect (lughah, a regional form of speech) of Azd Shanu'ah. It is also narrated that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said from the pulpit: "What do you say about this verse and the word 'takhawwuf' in it?" They were silent. Then a shaykh from Hudhayl stood up and said: "This is our dialect: takhawwuf means tanaqqus (diminishing)." He said: "Do the Arabs know that in their poetry?" He said: "Yes. Our poet Abu Kabir said, describing his she-camel:

"The saddle wasted her away, a hump-backed, bony one,
as the wood of the nab'ah-tree wastes away the ships."

'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Keep to your dīwān (the collected poetry of your people) so that you do not go astray." They said: "And what is our dīwān?" He said: "The poetry of the Jahiliyyah, for in it is the explanation of your Book and the meanings of your speech."

The prepositional phrase ['alā takhawwuf] Abu al-Baqa' said is in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause, describing the state of the subject or object) relative to the subject or object in ﴿yaʾkhudhahum﴾.

Al-Khafaji said: "The apparent meaning is that it is a ḥāl relative to the object, and it seems he intended it according to the two interpretations of takhawwuf: according to the second interpretation, it is from the fear (jaza') of it." The purpose of mentioning these conjoined possibilities is to show Allah's power to destroy them in any manner, not to restrict it. Then some scholars considered, regarding the contrast between the two [verses], that what is meant by the earth swallowing them is their destruction from beneath them, and by the coming of punishment ﴿from where they do not perceive﴾ their destruction from above them. Since they are paired with their destruction during their movement and travels, the condition considered in them is their settling in their dwellings and homelands. The contrast between seizing them with takhawwuf in the first sense and seizing them suddenly, which is indicated by ﴿from where they do not perceive﴾, is clear. The non-perception in the seizing during movement and in the swallowing is considered on the basis of the indication of seizing with takhawwuf in that sense, and the rest of them are understood as the punishment of total annihilation (istiʾsal), not seizing with takhawwuf in the second sense. The summary of this is that in each pair of the four, the prohibition of combining is considered, provided that the general one of the two is intended, for the sake of contrast, to be what is other than the specific one, whether the two have a general-and-specific relation from one aspect or an absolute one.

Al-Imam [al-Razi] and Ibn al-Khazin mentioned, regarding the essence of the verse, that He, the Exalted, frightened them with a fear that arises on the earth through a punishment descending from the sky, or through calamities that occur suddenly, or through calamities that come gradually until destruction reaches the last of them. The apparent wording of the verse would have been: "or punish them from where they do not perceive," to fit what comes before and after it, on the basis that the attribution of the verb in both to Him, and in what precedes it alone, while the attribution in what follows to the punishment, despite it being shorter than the sublime composition, is a deviation from it to that because it is more forceful in frightening and more indicative of deserving punishment, since it implies that there is an existing punishment, prepared, which needs only to arrive and not to be created. There is no such implication in "yu'adhdhibuhum" (He punishes them). Moreover, the sublime composition is further from having an incorrect meaning imputed to it, as might be imputed to the supposed substitute (badal), where it might be imagined that He, glory be to Him, punishes them with punishment from where they do not perceive; and this, as you see, is [unacceptable]. Since the two states of movement and takhawwuf are a context (maẓinnah) for flight, He expressed the striking of punishment in them by seizing (akhdh), and its striking in a state of heedlessness, which indicates settling, by coming (ityan). Fi was used with movement and ʿalā with takhawwuf. It was said: because in movement there are two motions, so the person moving is between them, whereas this is not so in takhawwuf. It was also said: since movement occupies the person with all his limbs, to the extent that it encompasses him while he is enclosed within it, a negation (fi) was used with it. And takhawwuf, meaning fear, arises only in one of his organs, namely the heart, which is encompassed by the human body; therefore ʿalā was used with it. It was also said: ʿalā here means maʿa (with), as in His saying: ﴿and gave wealth despite love for it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177], meaning: He seizes them while accompanied by it. Since takhawwuf itself is a kind of punishment, because of the pain of the heart and the preoccupation of the mind, and seizing indicates another kind of punishment too, ʿalā in the sense of maʿa was used, so that the meaning would be: He punishes them along with their punishment. This was not considered with movement, meaning turning back and forth in travels and trade, even though it has been reported: "Travel is a piece of torment," because they do not count that as punishment. There is something in the heart about this, so reflect and consider, for the secrets of the Book of Allah cannot be counted.

﴿Indeed your Lord is Most Gentle, Most Merciful﴾. Ibn Bahr made this a reason (taʿlil) for seizing with takhawwuf, on the basis that what is meant by it is seizing them upon the occurrence of conditions that cause fear, such as violent winds, thunderbolts and earthquakes, not suddenly. In that there is an extension of time and a respite in which escape is possible. It is as if it were said: "or seize them with takhawwuf, and not surprise them, because He, glory be to Him, is Most Gentle, Most Merciful," and that is more fitting to His gentleness and mercy, exalted is He. It is also permitted that it be a reason for that according to the last meaning, since in their diminishing little by little, rather than being seized all at once, there is a respite in general, and that is, absolutely, one of the effects of mercy. It was also said: it is a reason for what is understood from the verse, that He, glory be to Him, is able to destroy them in any manner, but He, exalted is He, did not do so. It was also said: it is like a reason for the safety that is questioned about. The expression through the title of Lordship, with its attribution to the pronoun of address, is one of the effects of His mercy, exalted is His majesty.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 48 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Have they not seen﴾ The hamza is for rebuke, and the waw is for conjunction with an implied clause required by the context. The seeing is visual (baṣariyyah), leading to reflection (tafakkur). The pronoun refers to "those who plotted evil deeds," meaning: have not these plotters looked and seen, turning toward ﴿what God has created﴾.

It has been said that the pronoun refers to people in general, which includes those and others, and the rebuke is with respect to them. al-Sulami, al-A'raj and the two Akhawan (Hamzah and al-Kisa'i) read "awa lam tarawu" with the taa' of address, following the style of His saying: ﴿for your Lord﴾. Likewise, the majority read with the yaa', following the style of His saying: ﴿Do those who plotted evil feel secure﴾. al-Khafaji and others mention that the reading with the taa' is by iltifat (shift of address), or with the implied "say" (qul), or the address in it is general to all creation. "Ma" is a relative pronoun, indefinite. His saying ﴿of a thing﴾ is an explanation of it, but in terms of its attribute, which is His saying ﴿whose shadows turn around﴾; so it is the one explained in reality, and the qualified noun is a preparation for it, for otherwise what explanation would it give to itself?

Tafayyu' is a tafa''ul form from fa'a yafi'u fay'an, when it returned. Fa'a is intransitive, and when made transitive it is by hamza or doubling, as in af'aahu Allah and fay'ahu, so tafayya' is its intransitive reflexive. Abu Tammam used it transitively in his line from a qasidah praising Khalid ibn Yazid al-Shaybani:

You sought the spring of its spring, the one that was sought for it,
and it sought shade for it, extended.

That requires transmission from Arabic speech. The zilal are the plural of zill, which in the view of some is what is in the morning, that is what the sun has not reached, and fay' is what is in the evening, that is what the sun has moved away from. They cite the saying of Humayd ibn Thawr, describing a sidr tree and metaphorically a woman:

So neither does the shade from the chill of forenoon suit it,
nor does the fay' from the chill of evening taste it.

Tha'lab transmitted from Ru'bah: what the sun was upon and then left is fay' and zill, and what it was not upon is zill. So zill is more general than fay'. It has been said: they are synonyms, each applied to what was before noon and to its opposite. Abu Zayd recited, for al-Nabighah al-Ja'di:

So the peace of God comes to them in the morning,
and the fuyuf of Paradise, with its shade.

It is well-known that fay' occurs only after noon. From here al-Azhari said: the tafayyu' of shadows is their return after midday. Abu Hayyan said: the consideration is from the beginning of the day to its end. The idafah of dalal to a pronoun of the singular is because its referent, though singular in wording, is plural in meaning, and parallels to this are more than can be counted.

The meaning: have they not seen the things whose shadows return and move ﴿from the right and the left﴾. By these are meant the dense things, of mountains, trees and others, whether inanimate or human, according to some exegetes. Some restricted it to inanimate things whose shadows show no effect other than tafayyu' through the sun, as you will learn God willing, excluding what includes animals whose shadow moves with their movement. Both opinions hold on the assumption that min is explanatory, as you have heard. Some scholars went to generality but made min initial, connected to "created"; the intended by what He created of a thing is the world of bodies, opposite the world of spirit, and the matter which was not created from a thing but came into being by the command "Be," as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Verily, His is the creation and the command﴾ [al-A'raf: 54]. Its remoteness is not hidden. It was also objected that the heavens and jinn are of the world of bodies and creation and have no shadow, and the implication of the generality is that nothing is free of it, unlike when min is made explanatory and "tafayya'u" is a qualifier of "shay'" specifying it. It was answered that the clause ﴿tafayya'u﴾ then is not a qualifier of "shay'," since the intent is to affirm that for what God created of a thing there are shadows turning, and it is not a qualifier of "ma" because they differ in definiteness and indefiniteness; rather it is a new clause establishing that He has shadows that turn, and the generality of "ma" does not require that the meaning be that each one has this attribute.

It was criticized: if it is meant that it does not imply generality apparently, that is disputed; and if it is meant that it may admit it, it is not a rebuttal, because it is built on the apparent and immediate sense. The meaning of "right and left," as said, is the two sides of a thing, a metaphor from the right and left of a human, or a metonymy by the restricted for the general: have they not seen the things that have shadows turning from each side of each one, returning from side to side by the rising and setting of the sun, or by the difference of its risings and settings, for they have risings and settings according to their daily orbits, while the shadows are ﴿prostrating to God﴾, that is, submissive to Him, moving according to what He wills of extension, contraction and other things, not resisting Him, glorified is He, in what He has subjected them to. This is the meaning of their prostration. It may also be explained as adhering to the earth, that is, while they are clinging to the earth in the posture of one prostrating. His saying ﴿while they are humbled﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of "zilaluhu," referring to "shay'," and the plural is by consideration of meaning. It is valid for a circumstantial clause to come from the genitive because it is like a part. The use of the form specific to rational beings is because humbling (dukhur) is among their characteristics, being smallness and abasement. Dhu al-Rummah said:

So there remained only one humbled in a tamed pen,
and one confined in other than your land, in a hollow.

So the statement is by metaphor, or because among that group there is one who reasons, so the masculine plural was given precedence. The reason for the expression with them is known from what has been mentioned. It is permissible to consider its aspect first and make what follows conform to it by parallelism, that is: and the state is that the owners of those shadows are abased, submissive to His judgment; describing them with humbling suffices in place of describing their shadows with it. It was also allowed that "sujjadan" and the clause be two circumstantial clauses from the pronoun, that is, the shadows of those bodies return while those bodies are submissive to Him, glorified is He, and humbled; so describing them with both suffices in place of describing their shadows with both.

By prostration is also meant submission, whether it is by nature, by compulsion, or by will. So it is not objected, on the possibility that "ma khalaqa" includes rational and other beings, how can it be "sujjadan" as a circumstantial clause from its pronoun, since the prostration of rational beings differs from the prostration of others.

What we have pointed to in summary is that this is of the generality of metaphor, and the matter is apparent on the supposition that the inanimate things are intended. Some claimed that prostration is literal in every case, namely falling upon the earth with the intention of worship, and that this requires life and knowledge in order for worship to be intended; but this is nothing, as is not hidden. Then, if we say on this view that the waw is circumstantial, as indicated, the two circumstances are synonymous, and multiplicity of circumstances is permissible according to the majority. Whoever does not permit making the second a substitution of inclusion or a substitution of whole for whole, as Samin explained. If we say that it is conjunctive, then the circumstance is not synonymous but coordinated. Abu al-Baqa' said: "sujjadan" is a circumstance of the shadows, and "wa hum dakhirun" is a circumstance of the pronoun in "sujjadan," and it is permissible that it be a second coordinated circumstance. In this there is the view of interpolation, which is possible on the supposition that "sujjadan" is a circumstance of the pronoun in "zilaluhu." The first opinion is the one chosen by al-Zamakhshari, and he preferred it in al-Kashf, saying: the submission of the shadow and the owner of the shadow is sought; do you not see His saying: ﴿and their shadows in the mornings and evenings﴾ [al-Ra'd: 15]? So making both a circumstance of the pronoun in "zilaluhu" is a deficiency. In it there is a fine completion: when He described the shadows with prostration, He described their owners with humbling, which is more eloquent, since it is forced submission together with the attribute of the one submitting. It was not made a circumstance of the returning pronoun in the relative "khalaqa Allah," because the meaning is on depicting the prostration of the shadow and its owner and their concurrence in existence, not on the concurrence of creation and humbling. The operator of the second circumstance is "yatafayya'," according to what Ibn Malik said in His saying: ﴿but rather the creed of Abraham, a hanif﴾ [al-Baqarah: 135]. From this it is known what is in Abu al-Baqa's parsing. Indeed, in this view there is a verbal remoteness, and the matter there is easy. As for making ﴿wa hum dakhirun﴾ a circumstance of the verb of seeing ("yara")? That is impossible in any way, as is not hidden.

Here al-Imam mentioned two other opinions about the right and left, besides those already passed. The first: that by them is meant east and west, likening them to a human's right and left, since the daily motion takes its start from the east, which is the stronger of the two sides, so it is the right, and the other side is the left. So the shadows at the beginning of the day begin from the east, falling upon the western quarter of the earth, and at midday they begin from the west, falling upon the eastern quarter. The second: the right and left of the town, that is, the right and left of a town whose latitude is less than the amount of the total declination, which is "kajal yiz" or "kahlah," according to differences of observations. In summer the sun lies on the right of that town, and then the shadows fall on its left, and in winter the reverse. What is in the second is not hidden, for it is specific to a particular region, while the speech is apparently general. It was also said: by right and left is meant the right and left of one facing south. "'An," as al-Hawfi said, is connected to "yatafayya'," and Abu al-Baqa' said it is connected to an omitted element which stands as a circumstance. It was also said: it is a noun meaning "side," so it is in the place of an accusative as an adverb of place. Regarding the singularity of "al-yamin" and the plurality of "al-shama'il," which is a non-analogical plural, there is a long discussion.

It was said: when the Arabs mention two plural forms, they express one of them with the singular, as in His saying: ﴿and made the darknesses and the light﴾ [al-An'am: 1] and ﴿God has sealed upon their hearts and upon their hearing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7]. It was also said: when we explain "yamin" as the east, the point which is the rising of the sun is one and the same, so the right is one; as for the left, it is an expression for the deviations occurring in those shadows after they fall upon the earth, and these are many, so it is expressed by the plural form. It was said: "yamin" is singular in wording but plural in meaning, so it agrees with "shama'il" in meaning. al-Farra' said: it may be singular and plural; if singular, it goes to one of the shadows themselves, and if plural, it goes to all of them, because "ma khalaqa Allah" is singular in wording and plural in meaning. al-Kirmani said: it may be meant by "shama'il" the left, the front, and the back, since the shadow turns from all directions; so he began with the right, because the beginning of turning is from it, or out of desire to start with its mention; then he made the rest follow the wording of "shimal," because of the contrariety between left and right, and he treated the back and front

the position of the left, for what lies between them and the right is a matter of difference, and this is close to the first view. It has been objected that this involves the combining of a word according to its literal and figurative senses, and its soundness is disputed. It was also said: the intended "right" is the right side of one standing facing the east, which is called the south, and "left" is its left, which is the north. So it is as if it were said: its shadows turn from the south toward the north and from the north toward the south. Since most of the inhabited world lies to the north, and its shadows are likewise, He used the plural for "left" but not for "right." This, as you see, is not satisfactory. Abu Hayyan transmitted from his teacher Abu al-Hasan Ali ibn al-Sa'igh that the singular and plural were used with regard to the two extremes, because the shadow of the morning diminishes until little of it remains, so it seems to be in a single direction, whereas in the evening it is the reverse, since it spreads over all directions; thus both extremes are taken into account. This is in terms of meaning. As for wording, the second was made plural to agree with "prostrating" (sujjadan), which is adjacent to it on the left, just as the first was made singular to agree with the pronoun in "its shadows" (zilaluhu), which is adjacent to it on the right. There is no concealing the fine point in the order of mention, which also observes the principal and the subordinate. Thus the verse achieves agreement of wording with meaning. The direction of the east is the right, and the direction of the west is the left; since the first direction is the rising place of light and the second is its setting place and the locus of darkness, He used the singular for what indicates the first direction, just as "light" (al-nur) is used in the singular throughout the Qur'an, and the plural for what indicates the second, just as "darkness" (al-zulumat) is used in the plural. The discussion of the singular "light" and plural "darknesses" has already been treated. It may also be said that the plural "shadows" alongside the singular before and after it is because a shadow is darkness produced by a dense body blocking the sun, for example, from its light falling on what lies opposite it; therefore "shadows" is pluralized just as "darknesses" is. This is not undermined by the fact that "easts" (al-mashariq) is pluralized in the Qur'an just as "wests" (al-magharib) is, since a matter is often adopted for a reason in one context and not adopted for it in another. There is also another consideration: since the right signifies the direction of the east, which is the origin of the shadow, and is singular in that it alone corresponds to the singularity of the true Origin, namely God, exalted is He, whereas the direction of the west does not share this, and a similar observance does not suit the left, as you will be guided to this by His saying: "Both His hands are right" (kilta yadayhi yamin), and the attribution of creation to Him, exalted is He, helps in noticing this originating character. There is also another: the shadow coming from the direction of the east has no legal ruling attached to it, whereas the shadow coming from the direction of the west does have such a ruling attached. For the time of the noon prayer begins at the first emergence of that shadow from that direction, upon the sun's passing the zenith; the time of the afternoon prayer begins when the shadow becomes equal to the object or twice its length, after the shadow of noon, in regions where the sun inclines; and the time of the maghrib prayer begins with the spreading of the shadow over the whole earth at sunset. How delicate is the placement of "prostrating" after "the left" in light of this. There is also another, which is more consistent with the approach of allusion (ishara), and which, God willing, will come later, and the Opener (al-Fattah) knows best. The path of the mind has latitude, so reflect; perhaps what I have mentioned will not satisfy you.

The Imam has clarified that the variation of shadows is evidence that they are subject to God, exalted is He, submissive to His decree and His governance, glorified is He. Then he said:

If it is said: why is it not permissible to say that their variation is caused by the variation of the sun? We reply: We have shown that a body is not moving by its own essence, so its motion must come from something else, and in the end it must rest upon the Necessary Being, majestic is His majesty; thus the matter of the variation of shadows returns to Him, exalted is He, on this assumption.

You know that there should be no doubt that the apparent cause of shadows is the sun and the like, and the density of the object casting them. Yes, whether that is ultimately ascribed to Him, exalted is He, directly or through an intermediary, is a matter of disagreement, and the position of the early scholars (al-salaf) is not hidden from you, for we have indicated it more than once, so recall it if it is not already in your memory. Then, the apparent meaning is that "shadows" refers to the spread shadows, which are called the level ones (al-mustawiya); and it is permissible that it be taken to include the inverted shadows, for these too turn away from the right and the left, so understand this and do not be negligent.

Abu 'Amr, 'Isa and Ya'qub read "tatafayya'u" with the taa' for the feminine. The matter of feminine and masculine in the verb ascribed to a plural such as the one mentioned is evident.

'Isa read "zululuhu," which is the plural of zullah, like hullah and hulal. The author of al-Lawami' said: "zullah" with a damma means cloud, whereas with a kasra it means shade; the first is a body and the second an accident. So 'Isa saw that the "tafayyu'" which is the return of bodies is more appropriate. As for the common reading, it is by metaphor. End quote. This seems to suggest reading by opinion. Some people explained "zilal" in the common reading as "persons (ashkhas)," so that it would be like the reading of 'Isa. They cited as evidence for the use of "zilal" in that sense the verse of 'Abadah:

When we halt, we raise the shade of tents, and the cooking pots bubble for the people with meat.

For he is speaking of raising tents, not of the shade which is the shade. And the verse of another:

He follows the shades of shadows in the evening.

He meant the shades of persons. Al-Raghib objected to this, saying there is no proof in what was cited. For his saying "we raised the shade of tents" means "we raised the tents, so by it we raised their shade," as if he raised the shade. And his saying "the shades of shadows": "shadows" here is general and "shade" is specific, and the idafa is from the idafa of a thing to its genus. Some said: what is meant by "zullah" in the reading of 'Isa is the shadow resembling a canopy, and what is meant by it is something like the form of a shelter in benefiting from it. It was also said: the discourse in that reading is by omission of a modifier, i.e., "shadows of its canopies," and "zullah" is explained as that which is like a shelter; and the understanding from "zill" in that case is the inverted shadow.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 49:

Then, after He, exalted is He, had mentioned what He mentioned, He followed it with what reinforces it, as an emphasis, together with the addition of the prostration of what has no shadow. So He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿And to Allah prostrate whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾. Or, after He, glory be to Him, had explained the prostration of the shadows and their possessors from the lower bodies that are fixed in their places and their hollows, He, glory be to Him, turned to the matter of the prostration of the created beings that move by will, whether or not they have shadows. So He, mighty is the One who speaks, said what He said. By prostration, according to what many have mentioned, is meant submission (inqiyad), whether it is submission to His will and its effect by nature, or submission to His command and His charge willingly, so that its attribution may be valid to the general population of the heavens and the earth without combining the literal and the figurative. And because the verse is a verse of prostration (ayat sajdah), it must indicate the well-known prostration, even if implicitly. The noble Name is connected to "yasjudu" (prostrates). The construction is for the purpose of restriction (qasr), and it can cover both restriction of the genus (qalb) and restriction of the individual (ifrad). However, what is more suitable to the state of the addressees is restriction of the individual, as is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah said: Do not take two gods﴾. That is, to Him alone, exalted is He, submit and humble themselves all that is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. ﴿Of living creature﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of what is in them, based on the premise that crawling (dabib) is bodily movement, whether it is on earth or in the sky. The angels are subtle bodies that are not purely immaterial. Restricting "crawling" to being on the surface of the earth is either for its manifestness or because it is the origin of its meaning, and it is general here by the indication of what is being explained. His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿And the angels﴾ is a conjunction (atf) upon the position (mahall) of "dabbah" which is explained by it, and that position is nominative, as it is the predicate of a deleted subject, because the explanatory "min" (min al-bayaniyyah) cannot be an adverbial complement (zarf laghw). This is conjunction of the specific upon the general, for the sake of conveying the great status of the angels, peace be upon them. It is also permitted that it be conjunction of the distinct (min 'atf al-mubayin), based on the premise that what is in the heavens is intended to mean corporeal beings, and one commits to the view that the angels, peace be upon them, are immaterial, so they do not enter into what is in the heavens, because immaterial beings are not in a place or a direction. Some of them (scholars) used the verse as evidence for the immateriality of the angels, based on the premise that "what is in the heavens and what is on the earth" are divided, one by the creature that crawls and the other by the angels, and the basic principle in opposition is difference. The moving creature has a bodily movement, so its opposite is not among the bodies, and that the body must have bodily movement in it. It is not hidden that this is a persuasive proof (dalil iqna'i), since it allows that it is a specification after generalization, as you have heard just now, or that it is an explanation of what is on the earth. "Dabbah" is a name for what crawls on the earth. ("And the angels") is a conjunction upon "what is in the heavens," and it is a repetition of it, and a specification for the sake of honour and magnification. Many have mentioned that it is conjunction of the specific upon the general for this reason as well. It is also permitted that what is in the heavens means the creatures called the Spirit (ar-Ruh)

[Page 158]

and one commits to the view that they are other than the angels, peace be upon them, so it is conjunction of the distinct, or the two of them are an explanation of what is on the earth. What is meant by the angels, peace be upon them, is angels who are in the heavens, like the guardians (al-hafazah) and the noble recording angels (al-kiram al-katibin), and "dabbah" is not meant to include them. As for "ma" (what): if we say that it is specific to non-rational beings, as the report of Ibn al-Za'bara supports, then its use here for rational beings and others is by way of predominance (taghlib). But if we say that its original use is for non-rational beings and for what covers rational beings and others, like a visible apparition whose rationality is not known at first, then it is applied to it literally, so the matter, as it has been said, does not need predominance. In Anwar al-Tanzil: when "ma" was used for rational beings as it is used for others, its use where both categories are gathered is preferable to the use of "man" by predominance. In al-Kashshaf: if "man" had been used, there would have been no indication of predominance, so it would have been restricted to rational beings alone. Therefore "ma," which is suitable for both rational beings and others, was used, intending generality. This is an answer concerning the reason for choosing "ma" over "man." Its summary, according to al-Kashf, is that "man" is for rational beings, and predominance is a metaphor; so if it were used without any indicator, the literal meaning would be fixed, while the context requires generality, so "ma," which covers both, was used. He meant that there is no evidence in the wording, and the indicator of generality in the preceding part is not sufficient to permit specifying them out from the whole after generalization. Moreover, the context requiring generality and what predominance contains of specificity is sufficient for the shift. End. It was said, based on the premise that "ma" is specific to non-rational beings and "man" is specific to rational beings, that bringing "ma" and performing predominance is more fitting to the magnification of Allah, exalted is He, than bringing "man" and doing that. So let this be understood. ﴿And they﴾, that is, the angels, despite the loftiness of their status, do not ( yastakbirun ) become proud of worshipping Him, exalted is His glory, and of prostrating to Him. The placing of the pronoun first is not for restriction, and the sin (in yastakbirun) is not for requesting. It was said: it is for the meaning that they do not seek that, let alone perform it and be characterized by it.

And if we say that the form of the present tense (mudari') is for continuous renewed duration, then what is meant is the continuity of the negation. The clause is either a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of "yasjudu" as it is attributed to the angels, or a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) to inform about them with that. The pronoun was not made to refer to "ma" because it is specific to those possessing knowledge, and the context is not one of predominance. Some of them disagreed on this and made it refer to the angels, and likewise the pronoun in His, glory be to Him, saying:

[p. 159]

**﴿they fear their Lord﴾.** Among those who explicitly stated that the pronoun refers to the Lord is Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Abu Hayyan said that this is the apparent meaning. Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil adopted the view we have stated, namely that the meaning is: they fear the Owner of their affairs. **﴿from above them﴾**: this may be related to *yakhafuna* ("they fear"), and the fear of their Lord is then a metonymy for fear of His punishment. Or the phrase may imply an omitted noun, "the punishment," which is the apparent meaning. Or it may be attached to an omitted word that functions as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) modifying *rabbahum* ("their Lord"), meaning: existing from above them. The meaning of His, glorified be He, being above them is His dominance and overpowering might, because spatial "aboveness" is impossible with respect to Him, exalted be He. The position of the early generation (*salaf*) on this matter I have already set out for you, and I think it is in your memory.

The clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *la yastakbiruna* ("they are not arrogant"). It has also been permitted that it be an explanation of the negation of arrogance and an affirmation of it, because whoever fears God, exalted be He, is not arrogant toward His worship. Ibn al-Munir chose this view and said: "This is the only correct reading, so that arrogance is not restricted, and so that this attribute is also shown to be established absolutely." It must be said, on the assumption that it is a circumstantial clause, that it is a non-continuous circumstantial clause (*hal ghayr muntaqila*). Such clauses occur in eloquent Arabic, indeed in its most eloquent usage, according to the sound view. In choosing the title of Lordship there is a cultivation of awe and an indication of the reason for the ruling.

**﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾**, that is, what they are commanded to do of acts of obedience and of the affairs they manage. The use of the verb in the passive voice follows the customary forms of majesty, and it signifies that there is no need to name the agent, because it is impossible for the act to be attributed to anyone other than Him, glorified be He. The verse has been cited as evidence that the angels are morally responsible (*mukallafun*) and that they are balanced between fear and hope. As for its indication of responsibility, this is by virtue of the imperative. As for its indication of fear, this is clearer than to be hidden. As for its indication of hope, this is by way of the implication of fear, as has been said. It has also been said that their attribute of hope is because whoever serves the most noble of the noble has a firm place in hope. Some have claimed that their fear is nothing but the fear of reverence and awe, not the fear of threat and punishment. This is refuted by His, exalted be He, saying: **﴿and they are apprehensive out of awe of Him﴾** and **﴿Whoever among them should say, "I am a god besides Him," We shall repay him with Hell﴾** [al-Anbiya' 21:28–29]. This does not contradict their infallibility (*'isma*). The Imam said: "The more correct view is that this fear is the fear of reverence." It has been mentioned that this was transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, and it has been argued for with His, exalted be He, saying: **﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾** [Fatir 35:28]. There is something troubling in the heart about this. The truth is that the verse is not fit to serve as evidence that the angels are superior to humans. A group has argued for this superiority from it in four respects, which the Imam mentioned, but he did not follow them with any objection, because he is among those who hold this superiority. The place for verifying this is the books of theology (*kalam*).

* * *

Furthermore, among the allusive (*ishari*) interpretations of these verses is: **﴿The command of God has come﴾**, which is the Greatest Resurrection, in which the veil of particular determinations is lifted and the apparent multiplicity vanishes. Since the Prophet (ﷺ) was witnessing this in the state of unity (*'ayn al-jam'*), he said "has come" (*ataa*, past tense). Since its manifestation in detail, such that it becomes visible to all, will occur only after a while, He said: **﴿So do not seek to hasten it﴾**, because this is not the time of its manifestation. Then He affirmed his witnessing of the Face of God, exalted be He, and the annihilation of creation at the Resurrection: **﴿Glorified be He and exalted above what they associate﴾**, by affirming the existence of other than God. Then He detailed what he had witnessed in the state of unity, because he was in the station of distinction after unity, neither veiled by oneness from multiplicity nor the reverse. So He said: **﴿He sends down the angels with the Spirit﴾**, which is the knowledge by which hearts live, **﴿upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾**, who are those sincere to Him, **﴿that you warn that there is no god but Me, so fear Me﴾**. Some have said: that is, warn the creatures against the base thoughts mixed with regard for other than Me, and [warn them of] their fear of My great majesty. This is a revelation of conveyance (*wahy tabligh*), which is specific to the messengers, peace be upon them. They have mentioned that revelation, when it is not of this kind, is not specific to them but also belongs to the saints (*awliya'*): **﴿Those who say, "Our Lord is God," and then remain upright, upon them the angels descend, [saying], "Do not fear, nor grieve"﴾** [Fussilat 41:30]. It has been transmitted from one of the imams of the Household of the Prophet that the angels crowd them in their assemblies.

Then He, exalted be He, enumerated the attributes and detailed the blessings, saying: **﴿He created the heavens and the earth in truth﴾**, and so on. In His, glorified be He, saying: **﴿and He carries your burdens﴾**, and so on, there is an allusion, as transmitted from al-Junayd, may God sanctify his secret, that whoever wishes to reach his goal should make the beginning of his affair and intention striving and diligence, so that the blessing of that brings him to his goal. They have mentioned that those who are carried by God's servants to their goals are of several kinds, and so is the one who carries them. One is carried by the light of the act, one by the light of the attribute, and one by the light of the essence. The one carried by the light of the act has as his land the station of fear and hope, his dwelling is the sincerity of certainty, and his house is the quadrangle of witnessing. The one carried by the light of the attribute has as his land the station of gnosis, his dwelling is the purity of intimate friendship, and his house is the abode of love. The one carried by the light of the essence has as his land the unity of God, his dwelling is annihilation (*fana'*), and his house is subsistence (*baqa'*). These kinds pertain to the wayfarer (*salik*). As for the one who is drawn (*majdhub*), he is carried upon the mount of grace to the land of contemplation.

In His, glorified be He, saying: **﴿and He creates﴾** what **﴿you do not know﴾** there is bewilderment for minds and an expression of incapacity, that is, an incapacity to grasp the King, the All-Knowing. Some have said: in it is an instruction to stop at what the intellect cannot grasp of the traces of the Maker's craftsmanship and the varieties of knowledge, and not to meet that with denial. For He, glorified be He, informed that He creates what is not known according to the customary human faculties, and it is known only by divine power and eternal (*samadiyya*) providence. Do you not see how the Sufis, upon whom God has bestowed what He has bestowed, knew great worlds, the relation of the world of witnessing to them being like the relation of an atom to a great mountain? And among those who claimed to be in their company, such as the Kafshiyya, who style themselves the Kashfiyya (the Unveilers), is one who mentioned about this things that no sensible person doubts have no basis. Rather, if their statements on this were presented to children or madmen, they would not doubt that it is a tale of nonsense issuing purely from imagination. I ask God, exalted be He, not to afflict any Muslim with the like of what He has afflicted them with. I had resolved, when I saw some of their books, composed by some of our contemporaries, which contain such things, to do something similar, opposing falsehood with its like. But shame before God and occupation with serving His, glorified be He, speech held me back, along with the knowledge that such nonsense is not marketed except to those deprived of perception and confined to the inanimate.

Al-Wasiti said about the verse: the meaning is: He creates in you of acts what you do not know whether it is for you or against you. **﴿And upon God is the direction of the way﴾**, that is, the straight way, which is monotheism (*tawhid*). **﴿And of it is the deviant﴾**, which is everything other than that. **﴿Had He willed, He would have guided you all﴾**, but He did not will it, because of your lack of readiness, and so that the attributes of His beauty and majesty, glorified be He, might be manifested. **﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains﴾**, which are the pegs (*awtad*), the masters of establishment (*tamkin*), **﴿lest it shake with you﴾**, that is, lest it be agitated. Among the well-known sayings on people's tongues is: "If they were absent, [the earth] would be overturned." **﴿And rivers﴾**, which are the scholars by whose sweet waters the trees of hearts live. **﴿And roads﴾**, which are the guides who call to Him, exalted be He. **﴿And landmarks﴾**, which are the signs of the horizons and of the souls. **﴿And by the star they are guided﴾**, which are the lights that shine upon the wayfarer from the world of the unseen.

Some have said: He cast into the earth of hearts the firm mountains of unseen knowledge and everlasting gnosis, and made flow in them the rivers of the lights of knowledge, unveiling, love, longing, passion, wisdom, and discernment, and He clarified roads for the spirits, the intellects, and the secrets. The way of the spirits is to the lights of the attributes, the way of the intellects is to the lights of the signs, and the way of the secrets is to the lights of the essence. The roads are, in reality, endless. Among their sayings is: "The paths to God, exalted be He, are as numerous as the breaths of creatures." The landmarks, outwardly, are the lights of the acts, in general; and the most particular of the landmarks in the world are the saints. The stars are the people of gnosis who swim in the orbits of perpetuity with their spirits, hearts, and secrets. Whoever follows them is guided to his everlasting goal. And in a hadith: "My companions are like the stars: whichever of them you follow, you will be guided."

By them is meant their elite, so that the address may be coherent. It is also permissible that all of them be meant, and the address be to us; and there is no obstacle to that according to the way of this people. **﴿And those they call upon besides God create nothing, and they are created﴾** **﴿dead, not living; and they do not perceive when they will be raised﴾**. How magnificent a sign this is in forbidding one who seeks help from other than God, exalted be He, from inanimate things and the dead, and asks of Him what he cannot bring to himself or repel from himself.

Some of the great masters among the Sufi leaders, may God, exalted be He, sanctify their secrets, said: seeking help from the saints is forbidden, except by a gnostic who distinguishes between origination and eternity, so that he seeks help from the saint not from his own self but from the perspective of the manifestation of the Truth in him; for that is not forbidden, since it is then seeking help from the Truth. I say: if the matter is so, what is the motive for turning away from seeking help from the Truth from the outset? Also, if seeking help from the saint is permissible from this perspective, then prayer, fasting, and all other kinds of worship should likewise be permissible to him from that perspective. Perhaps the one who says this would say this as well. Indeed, I have seen some of them say something whose mention my pen can scarcely bring itself to write, or my mouth to utter. So the path that is safe in the eyes of every rightly guided person is seeking help and assistance from God, mighty and majestic, for He, glorified be He, is the Living, the Powerful, the Knowing of the interests of His servants. So beware of being counted among those who hope for benefit from other than God, exalted be He.

**﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are wronging themselves﴾**. They have mentioned that the foremost monotheists, God, exalted be He, takes in death Himself, by His essence. As for the righteous and the blessed, they are of two kinds. Whoever ascends beyond the station of the self by detachment and reaches the station of the heart by knowledge and virtues, is taken in death by the Angel of Death. Whoever is in the station of the self, among the worshippers, the pious, and the ascetics who observe the Law, who have not detached themselves from the ties of the body by adornment and purification, is taken in death by the angels of mercy. As for the wicked and the wretched, they are taken by the angels as well, but they are angels of punishment, and they appear to them in the form of their blameworthy characters, just as the angels of mercy appear to those who preceded in the form of their good characters.

**﴿Those whom the angels take in death, good﴾** [i.e., pure]: their souls are good in the service of their Master, their hearts are good in love of their Lord, their spirits are good in the goodness of contemplating their Lord, and their secrets are good in the goodness of the lights. It has also been said: their bodies and spirits are good through constant service and abandonment of desires. It has been said: their spirits are good at death, because it is the gate of union and the cause of eternal life.

**﴿Those who associated said, "Had God willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him, neither we nor our fathers﴾** [al-Nahl 16:35]. They said this as an argument against the monotheists, according to their claim, and they did not realize that it is a proof against them, because He, exalted be He, wills only what He knows, and He knows only what the thing is in itself. So had they not in reality been polytheists, God, exalted be He, would not have willed that. **﴿So ask the people of remembrance, if you do not know﴾** [al-Nahl 16:43]. They are the people of the Qur'an, who are characterized by its character, who uphold its command and prohibition, and who are acquainted with the secrets and unseen matters it contains. But they are few. Thus "remembrance" here means the Qur'an, as in His, exalted be He, saying: **﴿And We have sent down to you the Remembrance, that you may clarify to people what has been sent down to them, and perhaps they will reflect﴾** [al-Nahl 16:44].

In it there is an indication that God, exalted is He, did not reveal the hidden secrets of His Book except to His Prophet ﷺ. He, peace and blessings be upon him, is the trustworthy one, entrusted with secrets. God, glorified is He, pointed to him, peace and blessings be upon him, to clarify this, and he did so, but in accordance with the capacities of the recipients: "Do not withhold wisdom from its people, lest you wrong them, and do not bestow it on those who are not its people, lest you wrong it. Secrets are only entrusted to the noble-minded." This is because they are a trust, and if they are deposited with others, one cannot be secure from their betrayal. Betrayal of them is their disclosure, and disclosing them is a great danger. Hence it has been said:

Those whom they consulted, and who revealed the secret openly,
they did not trust with secrets for as long as he lived.
They kept away from him, and he did not find happiness in their nearness,
and they exchanged the intimacy for estrangement.
They do not associate with one who spreads some of their secret;
far be it, far be it that their affection should be of that kind.

﴿Have they not looked at what God has created of a thing﴾, i.e., of any existent created entity, whatever it may be, ﴿whose shadows turn about﴾. It has been said: i.e., whose forms and manifestations are reflected, ﴿from the right﴾, the direction of good, ﴿and the left﴾, the directions of evil. Since the direction of the right indicates the direction of good, which is attributed only to Him, exalted is He, the word "right" is in the singular. Since the direction of the left indicates the direction of evil, which should not be attributed to Him, exalted is He, as His saying indicates: "And evil is not attributed to You, but is attributed to other than Him, glorified is He." And since there is an evident multiplicity in "other," the left is in the plural. It has also been said regarding the singular and plural: all existent things share in one kind of good, from which they cannot turn away, namely love (ʿishq). Ibn Sina (Avicenna) demonstrated the pervasion of the power of love in each of the individual entities. They do not, however, share in a single kind of evil, so what they turn away from in evil can only be multiple; hence He used the plural for the left. This is not the case with what they turn away from in good; hence He used the singular for the right. So let this be considered.

﴿And to God prostrates﴾, i.e., submits, ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth of creatures﴾, i.e., every existent that moves and crawls from non-existence into existence, ﴿and the angels, and they are not arrogant﴾, i.e., they do not refrain from submission and humbling themselves to His command. ﴿They fear their Lord above them﴾, because He is the Subduer, the One who has power over them, ﴿and they do what they are commanded﴾, willingly and in submission. And God, exalted is He, is the Guide to the straight path.

[Page 162]

Then, after He, may He be exalted, had shown that all existent things are submissive and subject to Him, may He be exalted, He followed this with relating His prohibition, glory be to Him, to those who are accountable, of associating partners with Him. So He, mighty is He, said, saying: ﴿And Allah said﴾, coordinated with His words, glory be to Him: ﴿And to Allah prostrates﴾. It has also been permitted that it be coordinated with ﴿And We have sent down to you the Reminder﴾. It has been said that it is coordinated with "what Allah created" in the style of the line of poetry:

*"I fed her chaff and cold water."*

That is, "Have they not looked at what Allah created, and have they not listened to what Allah said?" Its strain is not hidden.
