The explicit mention of the agent (Allah) and the singling out of the name of majesty (Allah) by mention serve to announce that He, may He be exalted, is the one whose divinity is fixed, and that what is forbidden is associating partners with Him, not that what is forbidden is the mere taking of a god in such a way that abstention is realized by rejecting either of them. The one addressed is not mentioned, for generality; that is, He, may He be exalted, said to all those who are accountable, through the messengers, peace be upon them:

﴿Do not take two gods.﴾

It is well known that *"two"* (*ithnayn*) is an attribute of *"gods"* (*ilahayn*), and likewise *"one"* (*wahid*) in His words, glory be to Him:

﴿He is only one God.﴾

is an attribute of *"God"* (*ilah*). Both were brought for clarification and explanation, not for emphasis, although emphasis is also achieved. The explanation of this is that the word *"two gods"* carries the meaning of the genus (*jinsiyya*), namely divinity, and the meaning of number, namely duality. Likewise the word *"God"* carries the meaning of genus and unity. The purpose for which the speech is directed is, in the first, the prohibition of taking two gods, not the prohibition of taking the genus of god; and in the second, the affirmation of one god, not the affirmation of its genus. So *"two gods"* is described by *"two"* and *"God"* by *"one,"* for clarifying this purpose and explaining it. For the singular may be intended as the genus, as in *"the man is excellent, Zayd"* (*ni'ma al-rajulu Zaydun*). Likewise the dual, as in the line:

*"Fire is kindled by two sticks, and war begins with words."*

This is the view of the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari). What might be understood from it as emphasis means that it is established and affirmed by the one it follows; so it is linguistic emphasis (*ta'kid lughawi*), not that it emphasizes the matter of the one it follows in the relation or in comprehensiveness, so as to be technical emphasis (*ta'kid sina'i*). How could it be so, since that comes only by affirming the followed term itself, or by something agreeing with it in meaning, or by words that are preserved? Therefore what has been said, that his doctrine is that this is technical emphasis, is nothing, since there is no indication in his words of that. Al-Sakkaki (al-Sakkaki, the author of Miftah al-'Ulum) cited the verse in the chapter on explicative apposition (*'atf al-bayan*), explicitly stating that it belongs to this category. So some have supposed from this that he holds that it is technical explicative apposition. This is what the scholar al-Qutb (al-Qutb al-Razi) chose in his commentary on the Miftah, denying that it is an attribute, and he argued for that by saying that the meaning of the saying of the grammarians, "the attribute is a follower that indicates a meaning in its followed term," is that it is a follower mentioned to indicate a meaning in its followed term, as transmitted from Ibn al-Hajib. But *"two"* and *"one"* were not mentioned to indicate the duality and unity that are in their followed terms, so that they would be attributes. Rather they were mentioned to indicate that the intention of their followed terms is one of their two parts, namely duality and unity, and not the other part, namely the genus. So each of them is a follower, not an attribute, which clarifies its followed term, and so it is explicative apposition, not an attribute.

The second scholar (al-Taftazani) said: There is nothing in al-Sakkaki's words that indicates that it is technical explicative apposition, since it is possible that he meant that it belongs to the category of clarification and explanation even if it is a technical attribute. And his mention of it in that discussion is like his mention of "every excellent man" and "every human, an animal" in the discussion of emphasis, and such is his usual practice. The first scholar was answered: If it is meant that it was mentioned only to indicate a meaning in its followed term, then the definition does not apply to any attribute, because attributes are always for specification, or emphasis, or praise, or the like. If it is meant that it was mentioned to indicate this meaning, and the purpose of its indicating it is something else, such as specification, emphasis, or other things, then it is permissible that the mention of *"two"* (*ithnayn*) and *"one"* (*wahid*) is to indicate duality and unity, and the purpose from this is to show what is intended and explain it, just as *"al-dabir"* in *"yesterday al-dabir"* was mentioned to indicate the meaning of "past," and its purpose is emphasis. Indeed, the matter is so upon careful examination. Do you not see that al-Sakkaki counted among attributes that which is revealing and clarifying, and did not on this account leave the category of attributes? It was answered: We choose the second alternative and say: the scholar's meaning in his words "mentioned to indicate a meaning in its followed term" is that the intention in mentioning the indication of the occurrence of the meaning in the followed term is to use that to reach specification, or clarification, or praise, or blame, or other things. The mention of *"two"* and *"one"* is not to indicate the occurrence of duality and unity in their described terms, but to determine the intended one of their two parts. So they are not attributes. And *"al-dabir"* was mentioned to indicate the occurrence of "past" in "yesterday," and then through that one reaches emphasis; and likewise in the revealing attribute. This differs from what we are discussing, so reflect on it, for it is obscure.

The first scholar did not permit that it be a substitute (*badal*), and said: As for it not being a substitute, that is evident, because it does not stand in the place of what it substitutes.

The second scholar examined this, saying: We do not concede that a substitute must be such that it can stand in the place of what it substitutes. Al-Zamakhshari made *"the jinn"* in His words, may He be exalted, ﴿And they made the jinn partners to Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 100] a substitute for *"partners,"* and it is known that there is no sense in our saying "and they made the jinn to Allah." Then he said: Rather, it is not far-fetched to say: the better view is that it is a substitute, because it is the intended term with respect to the relation, since the prohibition is of taking two gods, as its explanation has passed. It was answered that al-Radi (Radi al-Din al-Astarabadi) mentioned that since the substitute is not a meaning in the followed term such that it needs the followed term as an attribute does, and its meaning is not understood from the followed term as is understood in emphasis, it is permissible to regard it as independent in wording, that is, suitable to stand in the place of the followed term. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that the validity of its standing in place with this meaning does not require that the sense of the speech be complete without it, so as to refute what was objected. It has been said that the mention of *"two"* is to indicate that duality is incompatible with divinity, and the mention of unity is to draw attention to the fact that it is one of the necessary attributes of divinity.

Some have made this one of the implications of the indication that what is mentioned is in the context of prohibition and affirmation, and this is the apparent view, even though what has been said about it has been said. Some have claimed that *"take"* (*tattakhidhu*) is transitive to two objects, and that *"two"* (*ithnayn*) is its first object and *"gods"* (*ilahayn*) its second, the sense being: do not take two gods as two. It has been said: the first is the first object and the second is the second. It has been said that *"gods"* (*ilahayn*) is its first object, while *"two"* (*ithnayn*) remains as an attribute and emphasis, and the second object is omitted, that is, "worshipped ones." But what is in this is not hidden. The affirmation of unity for Him, although the specific named being is not multiplied, in the sense that He has no partner in His attributes and His divinity, means that the predicate is not vain. There is no need to make the pronoun refer to the worshipped one by the truth of the concept understood from the name of majesty, by way of *istikhdam* (a device in which a word is used in one sense and its pronoun in another), as has been said. This will come, if God the Exalted wills, in its verification in the surah of Sincerity (al-Ikhlas).

In the expression by the pronoun placed for the absent there is an *iltifat* (shift of person) from speaking to absence, according to the view of al-Sakkaki, who is content that the style from which one turned is the proper form of speech, even if mention did not precede in that way. As for His words, may He be exalted: ﴿So fear Me alone﴾, there is in it an *iltifat* from absence to speaking according to the view of the majority as well. The point in it, after the general point, namely awakening and renewing attentiveness, is intensifying the warning and dread. For warning a present person face to face is more forceful than warning an absent one, especially after describing Him with unity and divinity, which entail greatness and complete power to take vengeance.

The *fa* in *"fa-iyya-ya"* (so Me) is in the response to an assumed condition, and *"iyya-ya"* (Me) is the object of a verb omitted and to be understood after it, indicated by *"fa-rhabun"* (so fear): that is, "if you fear anything, then fear Me." As for the statement of Ibn 'Atiyya that *"iyya-ya"* is governed by a hidden verb whose estimate is "fear Me, so fear" (*farhabu iyya-ya farhabun*), it is a lapse from the grammatical rule, which is that when the object is a detached pronoun and the verb is transitive to one object which is that pronoun, the verb must come after it, as in ﴿You alone do we worship﴾ [al-Fatiha: 5]. It is not permitted for it to come first except in poetic necessity, as in the line:

*"To you, until I reached you (iyyaka)."*

And coordinating the explicit explained term with the omitted explained term by *fa* is because the intended meaning is fear after fear. It has been said: because the explained term should be mentioned after the explainer. It is not hidden that the separation and fronting of the pronoun conveys restriction, that is, "fear Me alone, not other than Me," for I am that One God, able to take vengeance.

[p. 164]

﴿And to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Indeed, He is but one God﴾. Or it is coordinated with the predicate (khabar), or it is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) brought to establish the reason why everything in them submits to Him alone, and to confirm the restriction of awe to Him, exalted is He. The prepositional phrase is placed first to strengthen the sense of exclusivity contained in the lam. The same applies to what follows, meaning: to Him alone, exalted is He, belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, in creation and in dominion. ﴿And to Him﴾ alone ﴿belongs the religion﴾, that is, obedience and submission, as is one of its meanings. It is reported from Ibn ʿAtiyya and others that ﴿perpetual﴾ means obligatory and constant, having no cessation, because it is established that He, glorified is He, is the God alone who deserves to be feared.

[p. 164]

The interpretation of ﴿perpetual﴾ as stated above is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, ʿIkrima, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and a group. They recited for Abu al-Aswad al-Duʾali:

I do not seek a praise whose duration is brief, [even if] all of it, by a day's blame of time, is perpetual.

Ibn al-Anbari said: it derives from waṣab, meaning fatigue or its intensity, and the form is of the relative type (nisba), as in His saying:

And my heart became smitten with her, meaning, possessed of waṣab and kalafa (hardship and burden). From this, religion (dīn) was called taklīf (obligation).

al-Rabiʿ ibn Anas said: ﴿perpetual﴾ means pure. This is also related from al-Farraʾ. It was also said: the dīn is dominion (mulk) and the wāṣib is the everlasting. This is made remote by the words of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

And to Him belongs the dīn, perpetual, and to Him the dominion and praise in every state.

It was also said: the dīn is recompense, and the wāṣib is as in the preceding interpretation, meaning: to Him, exalted is He, belongs recompense perpetually, its reward for the obedient never ceasing and its punishment for the disobedient. In any case, the accusative of ﴿perpetual﴾ is either a circumstantial state (ḥal) from the pronoun in the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) that is implicit in ﴿the religion﴾, with the adverbial phrase being the governing element for it; or it is a state from ﴿the religion﴾, with the adverbial phrase being the governing element according to the view of those who permit the governing element of the state to differ from the governing element of its subject. The verse has been cited as evidence that the acts of servants are created by God, exalted is He.

﴿Is it other than God you fear?﴾ The hamza is interrogative of denial, and the fāʾ indicates sequence, meaning: after what has been established of the restriction of all existing things to prostration before Him, exalted is He, that all of that belongs to Him, glorified is He, and His prohibition against taking two gods, and that the religion is His perpetually, which necessitates restricting taqwā (fear and God-consciousness) to Him, exalted is He, will you fear other than Him? What is denied is fearing other than God, exalted is He, not taqwā in general; therefore the other is placed first. The hamza is placed first not for restriction, so that it would not be objected that denying the restriction of taqwā to other than Him, glorified is He, does not preclude its permissibility. It was also said: it is valid to consider the restriction as applying to the denial, so that the placement is for restricting the denial, not for denying the restriction. In al-Bahr it is stated that this question includes reproach and wonder, meaning: after you have come to know His oneness, glorified is He, and that all else belongs to Him and is in need of Him, how can you fear and be wary of other than Him?

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 53:**

﴿And whatever blessing you have, it is from Allah.﴾ That is: whatever thing attaches to you and accompanies you of blessing, of whatever kind it may be, it is from Him, exalted is He. Here *ma* (مَا) is a relative pronoun serving as the subject (mubtada'), containing the meaning of a conditional (shart). *Min Allah* ("from Allah") is its predicate (khabar), and the *fa'* (ف) is inserted into the predicate because of that containing of the conditional meaning. (*Min ni'mah*, "of blessing") is an explanation (bayan) of the relative pronoun, and ﴿bikum﴾ ("you have") is its relative clause (silah).

Al-Farra' permitted, and al-Hawfi followed him, that *ma* be a conditional particle, with the conditional verb (fi'l al-shart) omitted, meaning: "and whatever blessing may be with you, etc." Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that the conditional verb is not omitted except after *in* (إنْ), specifically in two positions: the construction of *al-ishtighal* (a construction in which the verb is occupied with a pronoun referring back to a preceding noun), such as in ﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection﴾ [al-Tawbah: 6], and where the conditional *in* is followed by *la* (لا) of negation, and the condition is indicated by what precedes it, as in the line of poetry:

"So divorce her, for you are not a match for her; otherwise, let the sword rise over your head."

Omitting it outside what has been mentioned is a case of poetic necessity (darurah), as in the line:

"The daughters of my uncle said: 'O Salma, even if he is poor and destitute?' She said: 'Even if...'"

And his saying:

"Wherever the wind inclines it, it inclines."

It is answered that al-Farra' does not accept this, so what he permitted is based on his own school of thought.

The question of the conditional construction arises in both interpretations, in that the condition must be a cause of the consequence, as you say: "If you submit, you will enter Paradise," since submission is a cause of entering Paradise. Here, however, it is the reverse: the first, which is the settling of the blessing upon the addressees, cannot be a cause of the second, which is its being from Allah, in the sense that it is a consequence of Him. Ibn al-Hajib answered in *Idah al-Mufassal* that the verse was revealed to inform a people upon whom blessings had settled, who did not know their Giver, or doubted Him, or did what leads to their being doubters. So the settling of the blessings upon them, while unknown or doubted, is a cause for the information that they are from Allah, the Exalted. Thus it is established that the condition and the conditioned are in accordance with the known pattern, in which the first is the cause and the second the caused. Whoever said that the condition may be the caused has erred.

In *al-Kashf* it is said that the condition and the consequence are not in their apparent sense, since the first is not a cause of the second; rather the matter is the reverse. But what is intended by it is to remind them and make them aware, so the connection is the cause of knowledge that they are from Allah, the Exalted. This is preferable to what Ibn al-Hajib assumed, that it is the cause of the notification that they are from Him, because it concerns a people upon whom blessings have settled while they did not know their Giver or doubted Him. Do you not see what follows after *kayfa* (how), which indicates that they know that He, glorified is He, is the Bestower, but they are compelled to Him at times of distress and disbelieve after deliverance? The end.

In it, it is said that this refutes what he mentioned, because their knowledge is treated as having no standing, and their practice that contradicts it is treated as ignorance; so they are informed of this, just as you say to one whom you rebuke: "Did I not give you such-and-such? Did I not, did I not?"

﴿Then when harm touches you﴾ with a slight touching, ﴿to Him you cry out for help﴾: you entreat Him to remove it, not to other than Him, as the fronting of the prepositional phrase (*ilayhi*, "to Him") indicates. *Al-Ju'ar* (الجُؤار) originally means the cry of wild animals, and it is used for raising the voice in supplication and seeking help. Al-A'sha said, describing a monk:

"He persists in the prayers of the King, at times prostrating, at times crying out."

Al-Zuhri read *tajarun* (تَجَرُونَ) by dropping the hamzah and placing its vowel on the *jim*.

In mentioning *al-massu* (المَسُّ), which indicates the slightest contact, and in its being expressed by a verbal sentence which indicates occurrence, together with *thumma* (ثُمَّ, "then"), which indicates its occurrence after a period of time, and in the definite article of *al-darr* (الضُّرُّ, "harm") as the article of the genus, which indicates the slightest contact to which the name of the genus applies, along with the expression of the blessing by a nominal sentence, which indicates continuity, and the expression of its attachment to the addressees by the preposition *ba'* of accompaniment, and the use of *ma* (مَا), which expresses generality, in both of its possible readings, there is considerable eloquence and grandeur that is not hidden.

Perhaps the use of *idha* (إذا) rather than *an* (أنْ) is to make the occurrence of the response certain, as said by Mawla Abu al-Su'ud. There is in this what is recognized, with its answer, upon slight reflection. It would have been more apparent, according to what has been said, to say after ﴿Then is it other than Allah that you fear?﴾: "And there is no harm upon you except from Him," so as to strengthen the denial of fearing other than Him, glorified is He. But He mentioned the benefit by which harm is understood, and restricted Himself to it, as an indication of the precedence of His mercy and its comprehensiveness. With this meaning in view, it has been said: the connection of "And whatever blessing you have, it is from Allah" with what precedes it becomes evident. What relates to that will come soon, if Allah the Exalted wills.

The verse has been cited as evidence that Allah, the Exalted, bestows blessing upon the disbeliever, and that faith is created by Him, the Exalted.

(Commentary of al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on surah 16, verse 54)

﴿Then when He removes the harm from you﴾, meaning: He lifts the harm that touched you. ﴿Behold, a group of you associate others with their Lord﴾, meaning: their association of others with Him, the Exalted, by worshipping other than Him, the Glorified, is renewed. If the address in the verse is general, then *min* (from) is partitive (*li-l-tab'id*), and the "group" refers to the disbelievers. If the address is specific to the polytheists, as al-Zamakhshari's *al-Kashshaf* inclines, then *min* is explanatory (*li-l-bayan*) by way of abstraction (*tajrid*), so that it is apt; otherwise it is not in its proper place, as has been said. The meaning is: "when a group, namely you, associate others." It is also permitted, on this possibility of the address, for *min* to be partitive as well, because among the polytheists are those who turn back from their polytheism when they witness severe harm, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when He delivers them to the land, some of them are moderate﴾ [Luqman: 32], on the assumption that *al-iqtisad* (moderation) is interpreted as monotheism and not as lack of extremism in disbelief.

The first *idha* is conditional, and the second is sudden (*fuja'iyyah*), and the clause after it is the answer of the condition. Abu Hayyan argued from its being joined with the sudden *idha* that the conditional *idha* is not governed by the answer, because what follows the sudden *idha* does not govern what precedes it. ﴿Their Lord﴾ is connected to *yushrikun* (associate), and its fronting is for the sake of the ends of verses (*ru'us al-ayy*, the rhyming endings). Mentioning the attribute of lordship is to signal the complete ugliness of their committing association, which is an extreme form of ingratitude.

Al-Alusi said, in *Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*: *thumma* here is not for the lapse of a long period between the touching of harm and the occurrence of relief, but rather to indicate the distance in rank of what follows from it, namely the sudden onset of association, for its occurrence after that is at the furthest extreme of misguidance.

(page 166)

In *al-Kashshaf*, while criticising the author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari), he said that he did not mention the purpose of the wording in His saying, Exalted is He: "*Thumma idha massakum*, *thumma idha kashafa*" (then when harm touches you, then when He removes it). It has two aspects, and God, Exalted is He, knows best.

The first is that His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿And whatever good you have is from God﴾ is a continuation of what precedes, in the sense of denying the seeking of protection from other than God, the Exalted, while they know that everything they enjoy is from His blessing, and He, Glorified is He, is able to take it away. Then He denounced their singling out of Him for supplication in times of harm, in contrast to their singling out of others for protection, then their associating others with Him, the Exalted, as ingratitude for that blessing. *Thumma* is used to show the difference between the two denunciations, for seeking protection from other than the Benefactor is closer [to the wrong] than turning away from Him while one is constantly enveloped in His blessings. Then [there is] the turning to this One who is denied, alone, when in need. More distant than this is turning away, while his foot has not dried from the dew of salvation.

The second is that it is an independent sentence coming as a rebuke. *Thumma* in the first case is for the lapse of time, indicating that they overlooked those blessings and did not cease in that state until the time of being compelled. It also includes a hint of the distance in rank as an indication. In the second case it is for the distance in rank alone. End of quotation. It is a precious statement. Al-Tibi has a lengthy discussion on this matter, which you may consult if you wish.

Al-Zuhri read *thumma idha kashafa* (with *fa'ala* in the form of *fa'ala*), and here *faa'ala* has the meaning of *fa'ala*. The verse contains an indication that the practice of most of the common people today, of imploring other than God, the Exalted, those who possess no benefit or harm for them, nor even for themselves, when harm befalls them, and their turning away from calling upon Him, the Exalted, at that time entirely, is great foolishness and a new misguidance, yet it is worse than the ancient misguidance. Among things that make the skin shudder and cheeks turn away is that these are worse than the disbelievers, the People of the Trench (*ashab al-ukhdud*), let alone the believers in the promised Day. Some of those who pose as shaykhs said to me when I was young: "Beware, then beware, of seeking help from God, the Exalted, when a calamity strikes you, for God, the Exalted, does not hasten to relieve you, nor is He concerned with the badness of your condition. Rather, resort to seeking help from the past saints, for they hasten to relieve your distress and are concerned with what has befallen you." That statement repelled my hearing and my tears flowed, and I asked God to protect me and the Muslims from such manifest misguidance. Many of the shaykhs of today have sayings similar to that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 55:

﴿So that they may deny what We have given them﴾ of the blessing of having the affliction removed from them. Here "disbelief" (kufr) means ingratitude for the blessing (kufran al-ni'mah), and the lam is the lam of consequence and outcome (lam al-'aqibah wa al-sayrurah). This is a metaphor of the subordinate kind (isti'arah tab'iyyah), for when their disbelief and polytheism produced nothing but ingratitude for the blessings God the Exalted had bestowed upon them, it was treated as though it were a final cause intended by it. It is also permissible for kufr to mean denial (al-juhud), that is, denying that this blessing came from God the Exalted, and the lam then remains the lam (of purpose); the two meanings are close to each other.

﴿So enjoy yourselves﴾ is an imperative of threat, as is one of the figurative senses of the imperative according to the majority (al-jumhur), as when a master says to his slave: "Do what you wish." The shift to the second-person address is to signal that wrath has reached its limit.

Abu al-'Aliyah read "(fa-yumma'u)" with a dammah on the yaa' (the underlying form), a sakin on the meem, a fathah on the taa', the imperfect of mata'a in its unemphatic form, in the passive voice. Makhul al-Shami related this from Abu Rafi', the freedman of the Prophet (ﷺ). It is coordinated with (yakfuru) so that both verbs are presented to them as an exposure to polytheism. It is also permissible for the lam in (li-yakfuru) to be the lam of command, and the intended meaning is a threat, by leaving them to what they are in, as a way of abandoning them. In that case the fa' comes in response to the command, and what follows it is in the subjunctive by dropping the nun. It is also permissible to read it in the jussive by coordination, just as it is put in the subjunctive by coordination when the lam is a preposition.

﴿Then you will come to know﴾ the outcome of your affair and the punishment that will descend upon you. This contains a severe warning, since the object is not mentioned, signalling that it cannot be described.

Abu al-'Aliyah also read "ya'lamuna" with a yaa' (third person), and Makhul related this from Abu Rafi' as well.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 16, verse 56:**

﴿And they assign﴾ It has been said that it is coordinated with ﴿they associate partners﴾ (*ma'tuf 'ala*, "coordinated with"), but this is not correct. It has also been said that it may be coordinated with what precedes it in meaning, as an enumeration of their crimes, meaning: they do what they do, of what has been related to you, and they assign ﴿to what they do not know﴾, that is, to their gods about whose conditions they have no knowledge, and that they neither harm nor benefit. This is on the basis that *ma* is a relative pronoun (*ma mawsulah*) and the returning pronoun (*al-'a'id*) is omitted. The plural pronoun refers either to the disbelievers, or to their gods, which have no knowledge of anything and are inanimate. This is on the basis that *ma* is also a relative pronoun referring to the gods, and the pronoun in (﴿they know﴾) returns to it. The object of (*they know*) is left unstated for the purpose of generality. It is also permitted for the verb to be treated as intransitive, meaning that knowledge is not among their attributes. The form of the plural used for rational beings is used because the gods are described with their attributes. It is also permitted for *ma* to be a verbal noun (*ma masdariyyah*), with the plural pronoun referring to the polytheists, and the *lam* is causal (*lam ta'liliyyah*), not the object of the verb "assign," as in the first two interpretations. Its complement is for the knowledge of them, meaning: they assign to their gods, because of their ignorance of them, ﴿a share of what We have provided them with﴾, from the tilth and livestock and other things, which they have created, seeking nearness to them. ﴿By God, you will certainly be questioned﴾: this is a questioning of rebuke and reproach in the Hereafter. It has been said that it occurs at the punishment of the grave, and it has been said that it occurs near death. ﴿About what you used to fabricate﴾ before, namely that they are truly gods deserving of being drawn near to. The introduction of the sentence with an oath, and the shift of speech from the third person to the second person, which indicates complete anger because of the severity of the threat, is evident.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 57:

﴿And they attribute to Allah daughters﴾. These are the Khuza'a and Kinana, who used to say: "The angels are the daughters of Allah, exalted is He." Out of their ignorance, it seems, they supposed that the angels are female and are His offspring. The Imam said: "I think they applied the term 'daughters' to the angels because they are hidden from the eyes, as women are. For this reason, when the disc of the sun was considered to be like something hidden from the eyes because of its dazzling light and overpowering brightness, they applied the feminine term to it."

This is not refuted by the fact that the jinn are likewise hidden, because the rule of consistency (ittirad) is not required in such matters. It has also been said that they applied this term to the angels because of their being hidden while located in a place that others cannot reach. Thus they are like the daughters of a man whom he guards jealously, housing them in a secure place and a firm position. The jinn are hidden too, but not in this manner. This explanation is better than what the Imam mentioned. As for the lack of procreation, it does not fit this interpretation.

﴿Glorified is He﴾: this is a declaration of His transcendence and holiness, exalted is His station, above the content of their statement. Or it expresses wonder at their audacity in uttering such a grave thing. In the first sense it is literal, and in the second it is figurative.

﴿And for them is what they desire﴾, meaning sons. The word (ما) (ma, "what") is in the nominative position, as the subject (mubtada', the noun that begins a nominal sentence), and the preposed prepositional phrase is its predicate (khabar). The whole clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). "Glorified is He" is an interjected parenthetical phrase, placed in the middle of the sentence. Al-Farra' and al-Hawfi permitted that (ما) is in the accusative position, coordinated with (البَنات) "the daughters", as if it were said: "and they attribute to them what they desire." Al-Zajjaj and others objected to this, on the grounds that it contravenes the grammatical rule that it is not permitted for a verb whose subject is an attached pronoun, and likewise a noun, to transitively govern its attached pronoun, whether the transitivity is direct or through a preposition. The exception is the verbs of belief (zanna) and what is attached to them of the verbs of loss and absence. So one may not say "Zayd darabahu" meaning "Zayd struck himself," nor "Zayd marra bihi" meaning "Zayd passed by himself." But one may say "Zayd zannahu qā'iman" (Zayd thought him standing) and "Zayd faqadahu" (Zayd lacked him). If the pronoun were replaced by an explicit noun such as "nafs" (self), as in "Zayd darab nafsahu" (Zayd struck himself), or by a separate pronoun, as in "Zayd ma darab illa iyyahu" (Zayd did not strike except himself), it would be permitted. Therefore, if (ما) is coordinated with (البَنات), this leads to the transitive governing of the verb of the attached pronoun, namely the waw of (يَجْعَلُونَ) "they make", over its attached pronoun, namely (هُمْ) "them", which is in the genitive after the preposition lam, in cases other than the excepted ones. This is forbidden according to the Basran grammarians and weak according to others. Its correct form would have been to say "li-anfusihim" (for themselves). It is answered that what is forbidden is only the verb governing something in the sense that the action falls upon it, or upon what is governed by a preposition, as in "Zayd marra bihi" (Zayd was passed by), since the passing falls upon Zayd. What we have here is not of this kind, for the making does not fall upon those who make, but upon what they desire. Its summary, as al-Khafaji said, is that prohibition applies to the directly transitive verb absolutely, while the detailed treatment of the verb transitive by a preposition distinguishes between what is intended to fall upon the object and what is not. It is prohibited in the first case but not the second, because it is not customary for a person to act upon himself. Abu Hayyan raised an objection to the rule with the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree﴾ (Maryam 19:25), and ﴿And draw your wing close to you﴾ (al-Qasas 28:32). The Allama al-Baydawi answered with another explanation, namely that the prohibition applies only when the verb is transitive in the first place, not in the second and subordinate place. Subordinate elements are permitted what is not permitted for the principal element. Some scholars restricted this to the verb transitive directly and permitted it for the verb transitive by a preposition, as here. Al-Shatibi preferred this view in his commentary on the Alfiyya. Al-Khafaji said: "It is strong in my opinion, but it is not hidden that coordinating here, after all this debate, leads to making the verb 'ja'ala' (make) carry a meaning that includes both assertion (za'm) and choice (ikhtiyar)."

**Ruh al-Ma'ani (al-Alusi) on Surah 16, verse 58:**

﴿When one of them is given the good news of a female﴾, i.e., he is informed of her birth. The original meaning of *bishara* (good news) is the report of something that gladdens. However, since the birth of a female grieves them, the word was applied to the mere act of informing. It is also permissible that this be called *bishara* with regard to the birth itself, regardless of its nature. It has been said that it is literally *bishara* when viewed in terms of the actual state of what is announced in reality. Whichever is the case, the speech is according to an omitted noun (*mudaf*), as we have indicated. ﴿His face becomes dark﴾, i.e., becomes ﴿darkened﴾ from grief and from shame before people. The original meaning of *zalla* (to remain/become) is to stay during the day in the state attributed to the subject. Since the giving of good news may occur at night or during the day, it is explained by what has been mentioned. It may also be that the predominant situation is intended, on the basis that most births occur at night, and the one who is informed of the birth delays the news until daytime, especially in the case of a female. Thus his remaining in that state throughout the day, and the blackening of the face, is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for frowning, distress, pensiveness and the aversion that befalls him at the birth of a female. It has been said: when joy is strong, the spirit of the heart expands from within and reaches the extremities, especially the face, due to the strong connection between the heart and the brain, so it is seen radiant and gleaming. When grief is strong, the spirit is confined to the inner heart and leaves no strong trace on the outer face, so it turns pale, changes, becomes yellowish, blackens, and the mark of earthliness appears on it. Thus it is a necessary consequence of joy that the face becomes luminous and shining, and a necessary consequence of grief and sorrow that it becomes dusky and blackened. Therefore joy is expressed metonymically by illumination, and grief by blackening. Even if it were said to be a metaphor (*majaz*), it would not be far-fetched; indeed, some have said, "It is the apparent meaning." The apparent meaning is that (*wajhuhu*) is the subject of *zalla* and (*muswaddan*) is its predicate. It is also permissible that the subject be a pronoun referring to *ahad*, with *wajhuhu* in apposition (*badal*) to it. If (*muswaddan*) were put in the nominative, with (*wajhuhu*) as a subject and it as its predicate, the clause being the predicate of *zalla*, it would be correct, but it has not been read that way here. ﴿And he is suppressing [his anger]﴾, i.e., full of rage. The original meaning of *kazm* is the outlet of breath. One says, "He took him by his *kazm*," when he is seized by the outlet of his breath. From this comes *kazm al-ghayz* (suppressing anger): its concealment and its restraint from reaching its outlet.

*Fa'il* is either in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive), as indicated, or is an intensive form (*sigha mubalagha*). The apparent meaning is that this anger is directed at the woman, since she bore a female and not a male. This is supported by what al-Asma'i narrated: a woman gave birth to a daughter and named her al-Dhalfa'; then her husband deserted her, and she recited:

What is with Abu al-Dhalfa'? He does not come to us,
He stays in the room that is nearest to us.
He is indignant that we do not bear sons,
Whereas we only take what he gives us.

And indeed you have seen the one who divorced his wife because she bore a female. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in (*zalla*). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from *wajh*, and others also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (*muswaddan*).

﴿يَتَوارى مِنَ القَوْمِ﴾ يَسْتَخْفِي مِن قَوْمِهِ ﴿مِن سُوءِ ما بُشِّرَ بِهِ﴾ عُرْفًا (by custom) وهو الأُنْثى، والتَّعْبِيرُ عَنْهُما بِـ«ما» لِإسْقاطِها بِزَعْمِهِمْ عَنْ دَرَجَةِ العُقَلاءِ، والجُمْلَةُ مُسْتَأْنَفَةٌ أوْ حالٌ عَلى الأوْجُهِ السّابِقَةِ في ﴿وهو كَظِيمٌ﴾ إلّا كَوْنَهُ مِن وجْهِهِ، والجارّانِ مُتَعَلِّقانِ بِـ«يَتَوارى» («مِن» الأولى ابْتِدائِيَّةٌ، والثّانِيَةُ تَعْلِيلِيَّةٌ، أيْ يَتَوارى مِن أجْلِ ذَلِكَ). ويُرْوى أنَّ بَعْضَ الجاهِلِيَّةِ (Jahiliyyah: the age of ignorance before Islam) كانَ يَتَوارى في حالِ الطَّلْقِ، فَإنْ

[صفحة 169]

أُخْبِرَ بِذَكَرٍ ابْتَهَجَ، أوْ بِأُنْثى حَزِنَ، وبَقِيَ مُتَوارِيًا أيّامًا يُدَبِّرُ فِيها ما يَصْنَعُ. ﴿أيُمْسِكُهُ﴾ أيَتْرُكُهُ ويُرَبِّيهِ ﴿عَلى هُونٍ﴾ أيْ عَلى ذُلٍّ، والجارُّ والمَجْرُورُ في مَوْضِعِ الحالِ مِنَ الفاعِلِ، ولِذا قالَ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ تَعالى عَنْهُما: مَعْناهُ أيُمْسِكُهُ مَعَ رِضاهُ بِهَوانِ نَفْسِهِ وعَلى رَغْمِ أنْفِهِ. وقِيلَ: هو حالٌ مِنَ المَفْعُولِ بِهِ، أيْ أيُمْسِكُ المُبَشَّرُ بِهِ، وهو الأُنْثى، مُهانًا ذَلِيلًا. وجُمْلَةُ ﴿أيُمْسِكُهُ﴾ مَعْمُولَةٌ لِمَحْذُوفٍ مُعَلَّقٍ بِالِاسْتِفْهامِ عَنْها، وقَعَ حالًا مِن فاعِلِ ﴿يَتَوارى﴾، أيْ مُحَدِّثًا نَفْسَهُ مُتَفَكِّرًا في أنْ يَتْرُكَهُ ﴿أمْ يَدُسُّهُ﴾ يُخْفِيهِ ﴿فِي التُّرابِ﴾، والمُرادُ يَئِدُهُ ويَدْفِنُهُ حَيًّا حَتّى يَمُوتَ، وإلى هَذا ذَهَبَ السُّدِّيُّ وقَتادَةُ وابْنُ جُرَيْجٍ وغَيْرُهُمْ. وقِيلَ: المُرادُ إهْلاكُهُ، سَواءٌ كانَ بِالدَّفْنِ حَيًّا أمْ بِأمْرٍ آخَرَ، فَقَدْ كانَ بَعْضُهم يُلْقِي الأُنْثى مِن شاهِقٍ.

رُوِيَ أنَّ رَجُلًا قالَ: يا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ، والَّذِي بَعَثَكَ بِالحَقِّ ما أجِدُ حَلاوَةَ الإسْلامِ مُنْذُ أسْلَمْتُ، وقَدْ كانَتْ لِي في الجاهِلِيَّةِ بِنْتٌ، وأمَرْتُ امْرَأتِي أنْ تُزَيِّنَها وأخْرَجْتُها، فَلَمّا انْتَهَيْتُ إلى وادٍ بَعِيدِ القَعْرِ ألْقَيْتُها، فَقالَتْ: يا أبَتِ قَتَلْتَنِي. فَكُلَّما ذَكَرْتُ قَوْلَها لَمْ يَنْفَعْنِي شَيْءٌ. فَقالَ (ﷺ): «ما في الجاهِلِيَّةِ فَقَدْ هَدَمَهُ الإسْلامُ، وما في الإسْلامِ يَهْدِمُهُ الِاسْتِغْفارُ».

وكانَ بَعْضُهم يُغْرِقُها، وبَعْضُهم يَذْبَحُها، إلى غَيْرِ ذَلِكَ، ولَمّا كانَ الكُلُّ إماتَةً تُفْضِي إلى الدَّفْنِ في التُّرابِ قِيلَ: ﴿أمْ يَدُسُّهُ في التُّرابِ﴾. وقِيلَ: المُرادُ إخْفاؤُهُ عَنِ النّاسِ حَتّى لا يُعْرَفَ، كالمَدْسُوسِ في التُّرابِ. وتَذْكِيرُ الضَّمِيرَيْنِ لِلَّفْظِ «ما». وقَرَأ الجَحْدَرِيُّ (al-Jahdari, a reciter) بِالتَّأْنِيثِ فِيهِما عَوْدًا عَلى قَوْلِهِ سُبْحانَهُ: ﴿بِالأُنْثى﴾، أوْ عَلى مَعْنى «ما». وقُرِئَ بِتَذْكِيرِ الأوَّلِ وتَأْنِيثِ الثّانِي. وقَرَأ الجَحْدَرِيُّ أيْضًا، وعِيسى: «هَوانٍ» بِفَتْحِ الهاءِ وألِفٍ بَعْدَ الواوِ. وقُرِئَ: «عَلى هَوْنٍ» بِفَتْحِ الهاءِ وإسْكانِ الواوِ، وهو بِمَعْنى الذُّلِّ أيْضًا، ويَكُونُ بِمَعْنى الرِّفْقِ واللِّينِ، ولَيْسَ بِمُرادٍ. وقَرَأ الأعْمَشُ: «عَلى سُوءٍ»، وهي عِنْدَ أبِي حَيّانَ تَفْسِيرٌ لا قِراءَةٌ، لِمُخالَفَتِها السَّوادَ (the consonantal text of the Qur'an). ﴿ألا ساءَ ما يَحْكُمُونَ﴾ حَيْثُ يَجْعَلُونَ لِمَن تَنَزَّهَ عَنِ الصّاحِبَةِ والوَلَدِ ما هَذا شَأْنُهُ عِنْدَهم، والحالُ أنَّهم يَتَحاشَوْنَ عَنْهُ، ويَخْتارُونَ لِأنْفُسِهِمُ البَنِينَ. فَمَدارُ الخَطَأِ جَعْلُهم ذَلِكَ لِلَّهِ تَعالى شَأْنُهُ مَعَ إبائِهِمْ إيّاهُ، لا جَعْلُهُمُ البَنِينَ لِأنْفُسِهِمْ ولا عَدَمُ جَعْلِهِمْ لَهُ سُبْحانَهُ. وجُوِّزَ أنْ يَكُونَ مَدارُهُ التَّعْكِيسَ، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿تِلْكَ إذًا قِسْمَةٌ ضِيزى﴾. وقالَ ابْنُ عَطِيَّةَ: هَذا اسْتِقْباحٌ مِنهُ تَعالى شَأْنُهُ لِسُوءِ فِعْلِهِمْ وحُكْمِهِمْ في بَناتِهِمْ، بِالإمْساكِ عَلى هُونٍ أوِ الوَأْدِ، مَعَ أنَّ رِزْقَ الجَمِيعِ عَلى اللَّهِ سُبْحانَهُ، فَكَأنَّهُ قِيلَ: ألا ساءَ ما يَحْكُمُونَ في بَناتِهِمْ. وهو خِلافُ الظّاهِرِ جِدًّا. ورُوِيَ الأوَّلُ عَنِ السُّدِّيِّ، وعَلَيْهِ الجُمْهُورُ. والآيَةُ ظاهِرَةٌ في ذَمِّ مَن يَحْزَنُ إذا بُشِّرَ بِالأُنْثى، حَيْثُ أخْبَرَتْ أنَّ ذَلِكَ فِعْلُ الكَفَرَةِ. وقَدْ أخْرَجَ ابْنُ جَرِيرٍ (Ibn Jarir al-Tabari) وغَيْرُهُ عَنْ قَتادَةَ أنَّهُ قالَ في قَوْلِهِ سُبْحانَهُ: ﴿وإذا بُشِّرَ﴾ إلَخْ: هَذا صَنِيعُ مُشْرِكِي العَرَبِ، أخْبَرَكُمُ اللَّهُ تَعالى بِخُبْثِهِ. فَأمّا المُؤْمِنُ فَهو حَقِيقٌ أنْ يَرْضى بِما قَسَمَ اللَّهُ تَعالى لَهُ، وقَضاءُ اللَّهِ تَعالى خَيْرٌ مِن قَضاءِ المَرْءِ لِنَفْسِهِ. ولَعَمْرِي ما نَدْرِي أيَّ خَبَرٍ لَرُبَّ جارِيَةٍ خَيْرٌ لِأهْلِها مِن غُلامٍ، وإنَّما أخْبَرَكُمُ اللَّهُ عَزَّ وجَلَّ بِصَنِيعِهِمْ لِتَجْتَنِبُوهُ ولِتَنْتَهُوا عَنْهُ.

واسْتَدَلَّ القاضِي (al-Qadi, i.e., al-Baydawi, a judge and exegete) بِالآيَةِ عَلى بُطْلانِ مَذْهَبِ القائِلِينَ بِنِسْبَةِ أفْعالِ العِبادِ إلَيْهِ تَعالى، لِأنَّ في ذَلِكَ إضافَةَ فَواحِشَ، لَوْ أُضِيفَتْ إلى أحَدِهِمْ أجْهَدَ نَفْسَهُ في البَراءَةِ مِنها والتَّباعُدِ عَنْها. قالَ: فَحُكْمُ هَؤُلاءِ القائِلِينَ مُشابِهٌ لِحُكْمِ هَؤُلاءِ المُشْرِكِينَ، بَلْ أعْظَمُ، لِأنَّ إضافَةَ البَناتِ إلَيْهِ سُبْحانَهُ إضافَةٌ لِقَبِيحٍ واحِدٍ، وهو أسْهَلُ مِن إضافَةِ كُلِّ القَبائِحِ والفَواحِشِ إلَيْهِ عَزَّ وجَلَّ. وأُجِيبَ عَنْ ذَلِكَ بِأنَّهُ لَمّا ثَبَتَ بِالدَّلِيلِ اسْتِحالَةُ الصّاحِبَةِ والوَلَدِ عَلَيْهِ سُبْحانَهُ، أرْدَفَهُ عَزَّ وجَلَّ بِذِكْرِ هَذا الوَجْهِ الإقْناعِيِّ، وإلّا فَلَيْسَ كُلُّ ما قَبُحَ مِنّا في العُرْفِ قَبُحَ مِنهُ تَعالى. ألا تَرى أنَّ رَجُلًا لَوْ زَيَّنَ إماءَهُ وعَبِيدَهُ، وبالَغَ في تَحْسِينِ صُوَرِهِمْ وصُوَرِهِنَّ، ثُمَّ بالَغَ في تَقْوِيَةِ

[صفحة 170]

الشَّهْوَةِ فِيهِمْ وفِيهِنَّ، ثُمَّ جَمَعَ بَيْنَ الكُلِّ، وأزالَ الحائِلَ والمانِعَ، وبَقِيَ يَنْظُرُ ما يَحْدُثُ بَيْنَهم مِنَ الوِقاعِ وغَيْرِهِ، عُدَّ مِن أسْفَهِ السُّفَهاءِ، وعُدَّ صَنِيعُهُ أقْبَحَ كُلِّ صَنِيعٍ، مَعَ أنَّ ذَلِكَ لا يُقْبَحُ مِنهُ تَعالى، بَلْ قَدْ صَنَعَهُ جَلَّ جَلالُهُ. فَعُلِمَ أنَّ التَّعْوِيلَ عَلى مِثْلِ هَذِهِ الوُجُوهِ المَبْنِيَّةِ عَلى العُرْفِ إنَّما يَحْسُنُ إذا كانَتْ مَسْبُوقَةً بِالدَّلائِلِ القَطْعِيَّةِ، وقَدْ ثَبَتَ بِها امْتِناعُ الوَلَدِ عَلَيْهِ سُبْحانَهُ، فَلا جَرَمَ حَسُنَتْ تَقْوِيَتُها لِهَذِهِ الوُجُوهِ الإقْناعِيَّةِ. وأمّا أفْعالُ العِبادِ، فَقَدْ ثَبَتَ بِالدَّلائِلِ القاطِعَةِ أنَّ خالِقَها هو اللَّهُ تَعالى، فَكَيْفَ يُمْكِنُ إلْحاقُ أحَدِ البابَيْنِ بِالآخَرِ لَوْلا سُوءُ التَّعَصُّبِ؟

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 60:

﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ — of those whose ugly qualities were mentioned — ﴿is the evil similitude﴾: the evil attribute, which is like a similitude in ugliness, namely the need for a son to take their place after their death and so that their remembrance may endure through him; the preference for males for the sake of support; and the burying of daughters, either to avert shame or out of fear of poverty, depending on the differing aims of those who bury them. Each of these is proclaimed as weakness, deficiency and extreme stinginess.

It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that ﴿the evil similitude﴾ is the Fire. I think this is not authentically transmitted from him, may Allah be pleased with him. Among those who hold this view is Ibn 'Atiyyah, who took the word "mathal" (similitude) to mean "attribute" and said: it is not necessary to resort to this, because it is a departure from the wording; rather it retains its own sense. This is because they said that the daughters belong to Allah, the Exalted, so they ascribed to Allah, Glorified is He, a similitude. Daughters are among humans, and a multitude of daughters is considered disliked and blameworthy by them. Thus it is the evil similitude which Allah, Exalted, informed is theirs. It is not limited to daughters alone; rather, when they ascribed daughters to Him, Glorified is He, He made for them, Glorified is He, every evil in an absolute sense, and there is no greater end than the torment of the Fire. End of quote. In my view, however, this resembles gibberish, as is not hidden.

The placing of the relative pronoun in the position of the pronoun indicates that the basis of their being characterised by those ugly qualities is their disbelief in the Hereafter.

﴿And to Allah belongs the highest similitude﴾: that is, the wondrous attribute of supreme standing which is a similitude in absolute exaltedness, namely necessary existence in Himself, absolute self-sufficiency, vast generosity, and freedom from the attributes of created beings. Included in it is His exaltedness above what they say, a great exaltedness. Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Qatadah that the highest similitude is the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and this is a narration from Ibn 'Abbas. What al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat and others transmitted from him is ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾. ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾: the one singular in perfect power over everything, and among that is His seizing them for their ugly deeds. It is also said: He is the one for whom there is no equal. ﴿The Wise﴾: the one who does everything He does in accordance with perfect wisdom.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 16, verse 61:

﴿Had God been going to seize people﴾ for their wrongdoing absolutely. It has been said: by [their] disbelief. The word *mu'akhadhah* (seizing to account) is a *mufa'alah* form from *fa'ala*, meaning the same as *fa'ala*, and this is the apparent meaning. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is a metaphor, as if the servant takes God's right by his disobedience, and God takes from him by his punishment. The same applies to people seizing one another. ﴿for their wrongdoing﴾, that is, because of their disbelief and their sins, based on the view that *zulm* (wrongdoing) is doing what is not fitting and placing something in other than its proper place. It may also be specified as disbelief and transgression against others, and it includes whatever is counted among ugly deeds. This is an explicit statement of what His words ﴿And He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾ convey, and an indication that what these disbelievers have done of ugly deeds has reached a limit beyond which there is no end. ﴿He would not have left upon it﴾, that is, upon the earth, which is indicated by "people" and by His words ﴿any creature﴾, based on the well-known fact that crawling takes place on the earth. That is, He would not have left upon it any creature of the living beings at all, but would have destroyed them entirely. As for the wrongdoer, he is seized for his wrongdoing; as for others, it is by the ill consequence of that. For He, glorified is He, has said: ﴿And beware of a trial that will not strike exclusively those of you who have done wrong﴾.

Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shu'ab* and others related from Abu Hurayrah that he heard a man say: "The wrongdoer harms only himself." He said: "Nay, by God, the bustard dies of starvation in its nest because of the wrongdoing of the wrongdoer."

He (al-Suyuti) also related, and so did others, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The dung beetle nearly was punished in its hole for the sin of the son of Adam." Then he recited the verse. Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* related from him that he said: "The sins of the son of Adam kill the dung beetle in its hole." Then he said: "Yes, by God, at the time of the drowning of the people of Noah, peace be upon him."

It has been said: the intended meaning of "creature" is a wrongdoing creature, with the nunation indicating a kind, and this is specific to disbelievers and sinners among mankind. It has been said: [it includes] them and the jinn. It has been said: the intended meaning is a wrongdoing creature, that is, one that does what is not fitting according to the law or custom, so that some creatures are included when they harm others. A group, among them Ibn 'Abbas, said: the intended meaning of "creature" is the polytheist, for He, exalted is He, has said: ﴿Indeed, the worst of creatures in the sight of God are those who disbelieve﴾. Al-Jubba'i said: "creature" is in its generality, so it includes all animals. The intended meaning of "people" is wrongdoers absolutely. The reason for the necessary connection is that if God were to seize them for what they earned of disbelief or disobedience, He would hasten their destruction, and then no offspring would remain for them. It is known that there is no one except that among his forefathers there is someone who deserves punishment. If they were all destroyed and their offspring cut off, no one among mankind would remain. Then the creatures would perish too, because they were created for the benefits and welfare of the servants, as His words indicate: ﴿He created for you all that is on the earth﴾. By specifying "people," the argument from this verse for the non-infallibility of the prophets, peace be upon them, falls away.

Some of the verifiers said: there is no need for specification in this matter, and the verse is of the type of "The Banu Tamim killed a slain man," since the proofs and texts for the infallibility (*'ismah*) of the prophets, peace be upon them, are abundant. So it is not said: "The original principle is to interpret it literally."

Some have argued for the specification by His words: ﴿Then We gave the Book as inheritance to those We chose from among Our servants. Among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾. Otherwise the division would be corrupted. It may be said: there is no one except that he is characterized by some wrongdoing, but his ranks differ. So the good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near. The infallibility claimed for the prophets, peace be upon them, is only infallibility from what is counted as a sin in relation to others. As for infallibility from what is counted as a sin in relation to their station and rank, it is not claimed for them, since that has occurred from them, as many verses bear witness.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'If God were to seize me and Jesus son of Mary for our sins'—and in another wording, 'for what these two fingers committed, the thumb and the one next to it'—'He would punish us, and He would not be wronging us at all.'"

Yes, it is not said of a prophet that he is a wrongdoer, nor of the prophets, peace be upon them, that they are wrongdoers, but it is said that people are wrongdoers. This is like their saying: it is not said of God, glorified is He, that He is the creator of monkeys and pigs, but it is said that He is the creator of everything. Many a thing is permissible as a follower but not permissible independently. The matter of division is easy for the one who reflects, so let him reflect.

Some people have argued from the verse that the original principle concerning harms is prohibition. For if harm were lawful, it would either be lawful in a way that is a retribution for a crime or not. Both alternatives are invalid. As for the first, the verse refutes it, and that in two respects:

First, "if" (*law*) implies that God did not seize people for their wrongdoing, and that He left upon its back a creature.

Second, the requirement of seizing is that no creature be left upon its back, yet we witness that He, glorified is He, has left many creatures. So it must be concluded with certainty that He did not seize for wrongdoing.

As for the second alternative, it is invalid by consensus (*ijma'*). Thus it is established, by the requirement of the verse prohibiting harms, and other verses and reports confirm this. Then it is said: when an incident occurs that involves harm in every respect, if we find a text indicating that it is lawful, we rule accordingly, giving precedence to the specific over the general. Otherwise we rule that it is prohibited, based on the principle that has been established.

The Mu'tazila (a theological school) also argued from it that servants create their own actions. The argument, along with its refutation, is clear enough not to need explanation.

﴿But﴾ He does not seize them for that. Rather, ﴿He defers them until an appointed term﴾, which He, glorified is He, has named and fixed for their deeds or for their punishment, so that they may multiply or so that their punishment may increase. ﴿So when their term comes﴾ that is appointed, ﴿they cannot delay it﴾ ﴿by an hour﴾, the least period, ﴿nor can they advance it﴾ beyond it. The discussion of a similar passage has already passed.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 62:

﴿And they attribute to Allah﴾ i.e., they affirm for Him, glorified is He,
page 172
[that which they dislike], namely what they themselves dislike, of daughters. The expression "má" (what), according to Abu Hayyan, is intended to denote the category. This, as I have heard, is a repetition of what preceded, a second statement for rebuke and a preparation for His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿and their tongues describe the lie﴾, i.e., they assign to Allah, exalted is He, what they assign, and yet their tongues describe the lie, which is ﴿that for them is the best﴾, i.e., the best outcome with Allah, mighty and majestic. It is not necessarily intended that this means Paradise.

It is reported from some of them that what is meant by it is that, on the basis that some of them acknowledge the Resurrection, and this applies to them, or that it is on the assumption and supposition, as it is reported that they said: "If Muhammad (ﷺ) is truthful about the Resurrection, then we will have Paradise on account of what we are upon." It was said: this is the suitable reading in light of His, exalted is He, later saying: ﴿Certainly, for them is the Fire﴾, because its indication is evident that they judged for themselves Paradise. So it is not objected that how could they say that while they deny the Resurrection. And it is reported from Mujahid that they intended by "the best" the sons, but this is not so. Some of the verifiers said: what is meant by [that which they dislike] is more general than what preceded, so it includes daughters, and their dislike of them is known, as is their attributing them to Allah according to their claim, and partners in leadership, for one of them does not accept that he be made a partner in that and claim a partner for Him, glorified is He, and the belittling of the messengers of Allah, peace be upon them. For they become angry if a messenger they sent on a matter for others is belittled, yet they belittle the messengers of Allah, peace be upon them, and the vile types of wealth. For when they saw what they designated for Allah from their livestock as better, they replaced it with what was for their idols, and when they saw what was for their idols as better, they left it for them. And if something like that were done to them, they would be angry. On this basis "making" (ja'l) is interpreted in a way that covers both claim and choice, and "what" covers the qila' and others. The speech is not free of a kind of repetition. And what is meant by ﴿their tongues describe the lie﴾ is "they lie," and this is from the eloquent and wondrous speech. Similar to it is their saying: "Her eye describes magic," i.e., she is a sorceress, and "her slender body describes slenderness," i.e., she is slender, and the words of Abu al-'Ala' al-Ma'arri:

The lightning of al-Ma'arra travelled after weakness, so it spent the night at Barrama describing fatigue.

The complete discussion of this will come, God willing, shortly. The apparent reading is that "the lie" (al-kadhib) is the object of "describes" and that "for them" (lahum) is a substitute for it, or with the implied "bi-anna lahum" (that for them). When the preposition is omitted, it occupies a position of accusative according to Sibawayh, and according to al-Khalil it is in a position of genitive. It is permitted that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, as we indicated in explaining the meaning. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that "the lie" be a substitute for [that which they dislike], and it is, as you see, far-fetched. Al-Hasan and Mujahid read "alsinatuhum" with the omission of the ta' (feminine marker), and this is the dialect of Tamim. The word lisan (tongue) is masculine and feminine. It was said: the masculine is pluralized as alsina, like himar and ahmira, and the feminine as alsun, like dhira' and adhru'. Mu'adh ibn Jabal and some people of Syria read "al-kudhub" with three dammas, and it is the plural of kadhub, like subur and sabur, and this is regular. It was also said that it is the plural of kadhib, like sharif and shuruf, which is not regular. He made it a description of the tongues. Then "that for them is the best" is the object of "describes." "Certainly" (la jaram), i.e., truly, "that for them," in place of what they claimed of the best, "is the Fire," which has no punishment beyond its punishment, and it is a sign of the worst outcome. The word "la" is a rejection of a statement, and "jaram" means "earned," and "that for them" is in a position of accusative as an object, i.e., they earned what proceeded from them, that for them is that.

This is the view of al-Zajjaj. Qutrub said: "jaram" means "established and necessary," and "that for them" is in a position of nominative as its subject. It was said: "la jaram" means "truly," and "that for them" is the subject of the omitted "haqqa." The complete discussion of this has passed, and it is sufficient. Al-Hasan and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read "inna lahum" with a kasra on the hamza, making the sentence the answer of an oath, which "la jaram" has replaced. Likewise they both read with a kasra in His saying: ﴿and that they are made to hasten forward﴾, i.e., they are sent ahead, brought forward to it, as reported from al-Hasan and Qatada, from afratuhu ila kadha (I made him precede to such-and-such), and it is transitive with the hamza from faraṭa ila kadha (he preceded to such-and-such). From it is the hadith: "I am your forerunner (faraṭ) at the Pool," i.e., one who goes ahead of you. It is often said of one who goes ahead to the water to prepare, such as a bucket: fariṭ and farṭ. They recited for al-Qutami:

They hastened us, and they were of our companions, as the forerunners hasten to the watering.

Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, and Ibn Abi Hind said: i.e., they are left behind in the Fire, forgotten there forever, from afratu fulanan khalfi when you leave him behind and forget him. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Raja', Shayba, Nafi' and most of the people of Madina read ﴿mufritun﴾ with a kasra on the ra', as an active participle from afrata, intransitive, when he exceeded the limit, i.e., those who exceed the bounds in disobedience to Allah, exalted is He. Abu Ja'far read "mufarrituna" with a shadda on the ra' and kasra, from farrata in such-and-such, when he fell short, i.e., those who fall short in obeying Allah, exalted is He. And it is reported from him that he read "mufarratun" with a shadda and fatha on the ra', from farratahu, the transitive form with doubling from farrata meaning "preceded," i.e., those who are made to precede to the Fire.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 63:

﴿By Allah, We certainly sent [messengers] to communities before you﴾. This is a consolation to the Messenger (ﷺ) for what he suffered from the ignorance of his disbelieving people, and a warning to them for that. The great emphasis contained in this is not hidden; that is, We sent messengers to communities before your community, or before your being sent to these people, and they called them to the truth. ﴿But Satan made their deeds appear fair to them﴾, the ugly deeds, so they did not abandon them nor comply with the call of the messengers, peace be upon them. The discussion of attributing the adornment to Satan has already passed. ﴿So he is their walī (protector/patron)﴾, that is, the companion of the communities, and what an evil companion; or the one who takes charge of their misguidance and turning them away from the truth. ﴿Today﴾, that is, the day on which Satan made their deeds appear fair to them. Although it is past, and "the day" with the definite article refers to the present time, like "now", it is portrayed in the form of the present so that the listener may bring that wondrous scene to mind and be amazed by it. Such usage is called the narration of a past situation (ḥikāyat al-ḥāl al-māḍiyah), and it is a metaphor (isti'arah) from external presence to mental presence. Or the intended meaning of "the day" is the duration of the world, because it is like the present time in relation to the Hereafter, and it includes the past, the future, and what lies between them; that is, he is their walī in the world. ﴿And for them﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿is a painful punishment﴾, which is the punishment of the Fire. The use of "day" for its duration occurs frequently, so it is a common figurative usage, and there is no narration of the past in it. Or the "day" is the Day of Resurrection, in which their punishment occurs, but it is portrayed in the form of the present to bring it to mind, as in the first aspect, except that it is a narration of a future event, whereas in the first it is a narration of a past situation; and the first does not involve a metaphor.

On this view, the walī means the helper; that is, there is no helper for them on that day other than him. This is a negation of any helper in the most emphatic manner, in the manner of his saying:

"A land in which there is no companion except the gazelles and the camels."

It is not permissible for it to mean the one who takes charge of misleading, since there is no misleading there, nor to mean the companion, since he is in the lowest level of the Fire. Some have permitted it on the basis that he is with them in the Fire in general, and the disagreement over the levels does not matter. The apparent meaning is that all the plural pronouns refer to the communities, as we indicated in some of them. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the pronoun in "their walī" (the one attached as a genitive) refers to the Quraysh, not the communities; and "today" means the time in which the address takes place. That is, Satan made the deeds of the earlier disbelievers appear fair to them, so he is the walī of these people, because they are of them.

And that the pronoun refers to the earlier ones, with the sentence having an elided genitive construction; that is, the walī of their likes, and the intended "likes" are the Quraysh.

Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying that it is remote, since the pronouns differ without any need for that nor for the assumption of an elided term. It was answered that the word "today" necessitates it. Al-Tibi said: the preferable view, and the one on which the excellent composition rests, is that in opening the oath with His saying, the Exalted, ﴿By Allah﴾, after their denial of the message and enumeration of their ugly deeds, there is an indication that what was mentioned serves as consolation. It is as if it were said: the earlier communities, together with the earlier messengers, did not cease to be in this same manner; so you have an example in the messengers, peace be upon them, and your people are successors to those communities. Therefore do not be concerned about that, for your Lord will avenge you upon them in this world and the Hereafter. So occupy yourself with conveying what has been sent down to you, and with establishing the various proofs set up for the Oneness of God, and with alerting to the giving of thanks for the manifest blessings of God, the Exalted. End.

Al-Kashshaf says: there is no preference for this view in terms of consolation, since all of them convey consolation in a clear manner; the preference lies only in the view that leads to bringing the situation to mind, because of the greater satisfaction it provides. End.

The truth is that what al-Zamakhshari mentioned is not apparent, and what has been said, that the word "today" necessitates it, is not acceptable. At most it can be said: the presence of a context that makes it valid, not one that makes it preferable.

Al-Kashshaf also mentions, in explaining the connection of the verses, that His saying, the Glorified: ﴿And they assign to what they do not know﴾ up to this point is another category of their disbelief and enumeration of their ugly deeds. It may be a continuation of what precedes it, in the same pattern as ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾, except that it is built on the third person to indicate that it is a different category. This is the closer meaning. It is also permissible to make it a conjunction with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they swear by Allah﴾, since what comes after it, from what is said, is part of it, as an interjection and digression, as if it were said: that is their belief about the return, and this is about the beginning; and they, in between, profess this upright religion; and despite the difference of belief regarding the origin and the return, they claim that the best reward is theirs, so the opposite of that is rightfully due to them. Then he said:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 64:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And We have not sent down to you the Book except that you may make clear to them that about which they differ﴾, is highly fitting according to this interpretation, because of His saying, glorified is He, in another place: ﴿That He may make clear to them that about which they differ﴾, and because of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Reminder that you may make clear to mankind what has been sent down to them﴾. In it is the meaning that whoever has had guidance made clear to him by this clarification has no need of that clarification, since it benefits him only to know its falsehood. And this is more suitable for the composition of the verse. Ends.

You know that the possibility of coordination (ʿaṭf) is remote. The "Book" here means the Qur'an, for it is most deserving of this name. The exception is a "mufarragh" (an exception with the preceding element left unstated) from the most general category of causes (ʿilal), meaning: We did not send it down to you for any cause among the causes except that you may make clear to them what they differed about, namely the resurrection (al-baʿth), and it was the case that among them were some who believed in it, and matters of permitted and forbidden, affirmation and denial. The rule of returning the preceding pronouns to the earlier nations requires that the pronoun in (ilayhim) and (ikhtalafu) also return to them, but what prevents this is that the clarification of "that about which they differed" cannot be made to apply to them. Some of the scholars therefore made it refer to the Quraysh, because the discussion concerns them; and others made it refer to people in general, since that is not restricted to the Quraysh, and they enter into it in a primary way.

﴿And as a guidance and a mercy﴾, great ones, ﴿for a people who believe﴾. He singled them out for mention because they are the ones who seize its fruits. The two nouns — Abu Hayyan said — are in the accusative position, as objects of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), with the governing verb being (anzalna). Since the agent is one in both the cause and the effect, the verb reached both directly; but since it was not one in (li-tubayyina), because the agent of the sending down is God, exalted is He, not the Messenger, peace be upon him, the cause was connected by the particle.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "They are both coordinated with the position (maḥall) of (li-tubayyina)," and this is not correct, because its position is not accusative, so that an accusative noun could be coordinated with it. Do you not see that if it were accusative it would not be permitted, due to the difference of agent? End. It has been objected that the meaning of its being in an accusative position is that it is in a position which, if free of impediments, would show its accusative case, and here it is so for whoever reflects. So his saying "it is not correct, because its position is not accusative" is not in accordance with what is proper.

Al-Halabi said: That is disallowed, since there is no disagreement that the position of a prepositional phrase (jar and majrur) is accusative; and for this reason they permitted "I passed by Zayd and ʿAmran" with coordination on the positions. Al-Khafaji has a discussion here; if you want it, return to it and consult it.

Perhaps the reason the cause of clarification was placed before the two causes of guidance and mercy is that it precedes them in existence in terms of the order of occurrence.

﴿And Allah sends down water from the sky﴾: water whose like has already been discussed. According to what has been said, this is a repetition of what came before, to affirm its content and to emphasise the Oneness (tawhid) of what follows of the proofs of God's Oneness. ﴿and He revives thereby the earth﴾ by what He causes to grow in it of various kinds of plants, ﴿after its death﴾, after its dryness. Thus "reviving" and "death" are a metaphor (isti'arah) for growth and dryness. The intended meaning is not the restoration of what has dried, but the growth of its like. The "fa" (then) denotes customary sequence (al-ta'qib al-'adi), so the interval between the two conjoined clauses does not contradict it. A parallel is: "He married, and then a child was born to him." This verse is evidence for those who say that effects (musabbabat) come about through their causes but not by them, and whoever says this has interpreted it accordingly. ﴿Indeed, in that﴾, i.e., in the sending down of water from the sky and the reviving of the dead earth, ﴿is surely a sign﴾. What a sign it is, indicating His Oneness, knowledge, power and wisdom, exalted is His majesty. The use of a demonstrative that denotes distance is either to magnify the thing indicated or because it has not been mentioned explicitly. ﴿for a people who hear﴾. Al-Mawla Ibn al-Kamal said: "By hearing is meant acceptance, as in 'God hears whoever praises Him' (sami'a Allahu liman hamidah), i.e., for a people who reflect upon them, understand the manner of their indication, and accept what they indicate. He specified that it is a sign for them only because others do not benefit from it. This is like the specification in His words, exalted is He: ﴿a guidance and a mercy for a people who believe﴾. And by what we have established, the reason for the shift from 'yubsirun' (see) to ﴿yasma'un﴾ (hear) becomes clear." End of quotation. Al-Khafaji said: "What is fitting to the context is what the two shaykhs mentioned. Its explanation is that when He, exalted is He, mentioned that He had sent to the earlier nations messengers and books, and they disbelieved in them, and so they suffered disgrace in this world and the Hereafter, He followed this by stating that He sent him, peace be upon him, with the master of books, so that it became the very essence of guidance and mercy for those to whom he was sent. This is an indication that the opposition of his community to those before them brings them close to the happiness of both abodes, and it is good news for him, peace and blessings be upon him, of the abundance of his followers and the fewness of his opponents, and that they will enter his religion in multitudes. Then He followed this, by way of illustration of His sending down that mercy which revived from the death of misguidance, with the sending down of rains which revived the dead lands. He is the One who sends down the rain after they had despaired (42:28). Had it not been so, His words, exalted is He, ﴿And Allah sends down water from the sky﴾, would be extraneous to what precedes and follows it. His words, glorified is He, ﴿Indeed, in that is surely a sign﴾ and so on, are a completion of His words ﴿And We did not send down﴾ and so on, and of the principal purpose of it. Therefore the fitting word is (yasma'un) 'hear', not (yubsirun) 'see'. Even if it were a completion of a nearer clause concerning growth, the word 'yasma'un' in the sense of 'accept' would not be fitting." Then he said: "Whoever does not grasp the focal point of their view says in reply: it is possible to take the phrase 'Allah sends down' and so on as the referent of 'yasma'un', since it is masculine and prompts reflection on its meaning." End of quotation. In his statement that follows, "that He sent him, peace be upon him, with the master of books, so that it became the very essence of guidance and mercy, is an indication" and so on, there is obscurity, as is not hidden. And if it is a completion of His words ﴿And We did not send down﴾ and so on, it does not become evident that the thing indicated is what you have heard, which is the apparent meaning. In al-Bahr it is said: when He, exalted is He, mentioned the sending down of the Book for clarification, the Qur'an was life for souls and a cure for what is in the breasts of defects of belief. For this reason He concluded with His words, glorified is He, ﴿for a people who believe﴾, i.e., who affirm, and affirmation has its locus in the heart. He mentioned the sending down of rain, which is the life of bodies and the cause of their survival. Then, by the reviving of the earth after its death, He indicated the reviving of hearts through the Qur'an, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life﴾ (6:122). Just as the earth becomes green with plants, fresh after its stillness, so the heart lives by the Qur'an after having been dead through ignorance. For this reason God, exalted is He, concluded with His words, glorified is He: ﴿who hear﴾, i.e., who hear this indicated comparison, and the meaning is hearing with fairness and contemplation. And in observance of this meaning, and God knows best, He did not conclude with ﴿for a people who see﴾, although the sending down of rain is something that is seen and witnessed." End of quotation.

In addition to this, there is in it [i.e., in al-Bahr's view] some of the same artificiality. I say: perhaps the more evident view is that the thing indicated is what has been mentioned, namely the sending down, the reviving and the hearing, taken in its apparent sense, and that the discourse is a completion of what is adjacent to it. The shift from "yubsirun" to "yasma'un" serves to indicate that this consideration is evident in it, that it requires neither looking nor reflection, but only that the one being admonished hear the word alone. And it suffices, for linking the verse to what precedes it, that the Book and the rain share in reviving: in that is the reviving of hearts, and in this the reviving of the parched earth. So reflect.

﴿وإنَّ لَكم في الأنْعامِ لَعِبْرَةً﴾ ﴿And indeed, in the livestock there is surely a lesson for you.﴾ That is, a means of crossing (ma'bar) by which one passes from ignorance to knowledge. The root meaning of ʿibrah and ʿubur is crossing from one place to another. al-Raghib said: ʿubur is specifically crossing water by swimming or the like. The more well-known usage is that it is general, so the term ʿibrah is applied to that by which one takes a lesson, as mentioned. However, it has become a conventional term in the usage of the language. The indefiniteness of ʿibrah is for emphasis, meaning a great lesson. ﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ﴾ ﴿We give you to drink﴾ is a explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), as if it were asked: "What is the lesson in them?" So it is said: "We give you to drink ﴿مِمّا في بُطُونِهِ﴾ from what is in their bellies." Some have assumed here an implied subject, "hiya" (it is) — "hiya nusqikum" — but there is no need for this. The pronoun in ﴿بُطُونِهِ﴾ (its bellies) refers to al-anʿam, which is a collective noun (ism jam'). A collective noun may be treated as masculine and singular with regard to its wording, or feminine and plural with regard to its meaning. For this reason both forms occur in the Qur'an and in Arabic speech, so it is said.

It is related from Sibawayh (the great grammarian, d. c. 180 AH) that he considered al-anʿam to be singular. His statement, may God have mercy on him, is apparently contradictory, for he said in the chapter on words of the pattern mafaʿil and mafaʿil, the following text: "As for ajmal and fulus, they are declinable (tanṣarif) and similar words, because they resemble the singular. Do you not see that you say: aqwal and aqawil, aʿrab and aʿarib, and aydin and ayadin? These letters go to the patterns mafaʿil and mafaʿil just as the singular goes to them when it is made plural. As for mafaʿil and mafaʿil, they are not broken so that the plural goes to a pattern other than this, because this is the final form. So when they resembled the singular, they became declinable." Then he said: "Likewise faʿul, if it is broken like fulus, you bring it to fa'a'il, as you say: judud and jada'id, and rukub and raka'ib.
