If you did that with mafaʿil and mafaʿil, it would not go beyond this pattern. What strengthens this is that some Arabs say: atā (a type of) for the singular, with a ḍamma on the alif. As for afʿal, it may occur for the singular, and some Arabs say: huwa al-anʿam." He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿نُسْقِيكم مِمّا في بُطُونِهِ﴾. And Abu al-Khattab said: "I heard the Arabs say: hadha thawb akyas" — end of quotation.

He, may God have mercy on him, also said in the chapter on triliteral forms that received additional letters: "In speech there is no afʿil, afʿul, afʿal, or afʿal, except that collective nouns are broken according to it" — end of quotation. People have differed in reconciling his two statements. Abu Hayyan went to interpret the first, and to keep the second on its apparent meaning, namely that afʿal is not one of the patterns of the singular. So he took his earlier statement, "As for afʿal, it may occur for the singular, etc.," to mean that some Arabs use it for the singular figuratively, like al-anʿam in the sense of al-niʿam (blessings), as the poet said:

"We left the horses and the cherished camels,
and we said to the women: 'Stay here with them.'"

His meaning is not that it is singular in form and in lexical origin, as is shown by what he stated in another place, that it occurs only as a plural. It was objected to him that Sibawayh's intention in what he mentioned first was to distinguish between the two forms of the final plural patterns (mafaʿil and mafaʿil) and afʿal and fuʿul, where the first two are not declinable while the last two are, for several reasons. Among them: the first two do not apply to the singular, unlike the latter two, as he explained. So if the application of afʿal to the singular were not lexically established, the distinction would not be achieved, and the intended purpose would not be complete. Yes, there is no disagreement about the contradiction between his two statements. Also, if it were so, it would not be restricted to some of them. And also, the figurative use of the plural for the singular is valid in every plural, even the two final plural patterns.

al-Khafaji responded to this, saying: "The truth is that there is no contradiction between his two statements. He distinguished between the two forms of the final plural patterns and the last two forms in that the first two are not pluralized, while the last two are pluralized, so they resemble individual nouns. Then he strengthened this by noting that a group of Arabs used atā, which is on the pattern fuʿul, as truly singular, and some used al-anʿam, which is on the pattern afʿal, in the same way. He indicated that this is a rare dialect (lughah) in a few cases. What he mentioned afterwards is based on the common dialect. As for his statement that his intention at first was the distinction by several aspects, there is no basis for this, as the bearers of the book know." — end of quotation. It is known from this that the return of the masculine singular pronoun to al-anʿam, according to Sibawayh, is by considering that it is singular in the dialect of some Arabs. As for the one who says it is the plural of naʿam, he made the pronoun refer to a part, either a part that is implied, i.e., some of the livestock, or what is understood from them, or to the livestock with regard to some of them, namely the females from which milk comes, or to their singular, as in the statement of Ibn al-Hajib: "al-marfuʿat is what includes the sign of the doer (fa'iliyyah), or it has the meaning." Because the definite article of genus (al al-jinsiyyah) makes singular and plural equal in meaning, so it is permissible for the pronoun of each of them to return to the other. In al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's commentary), he returned the pronoun in the masculine out of consideration of the genus, because if the singular that indicates the genus can validly stand in place of its plural, it is permissible for the pronoun to return to it in the masculine, as in their saying: huwa ahsan al-fityan (he is the best of the youths) and abtaluh (its/his...), because it is valid to say huwa ahsan fata (he is the best youth). Although this is not analogous according to Sibawayh.

It was said: a plural of multiplicity (jam' al-taktir) for non-rational things is treated like a group and like a plural, so the pronoun returns to it in the singular, as in his statement:

"In them are lines of black and white,
as if on the skin is the pattern of leprosy."

This is valid in the Qur'an, and from it is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿كَلا إنَّهُ تَذْكِرَةٌ﴾ "Nay, indeed it is a reminder," ﴿فَمَن شاءَ ذَكَرَهُ﴾ "so whoever wills may remember it," and ﴿فَلَمّا رَأى الشَّمْسَ بازِغَةً قالَ هَذا رَبِّي﴾ "So when he saw the sun rising, he said: 'This is my lord.'" This happens only with figurative feminine, so one may not say: jariyatuka dhahaba (your female servant went) — where the verb must agree.

It was objected: how is naʿam pluralized, when it is restricted to camels, while al-anʿam is said of cattle, sheep and camels? Even if it were restricted, it would be equal. It was answered: the one who regards it as a plural of it either restricts al-anʿam or generalizes naʿam, and makes the distinction arise from usage, and makes the plural indicate the multiplicity of types.

Ibn Masʿud, in one report from him, and al-Hasan, and Zayd ibn ʿAli, may God be pleased with them both, and Ibn ʿAmir, Nafiʿ, Abu Bakr, and the people of Madina read (nasqikum) with a fatḥa on the nun here and in al-Muʾminun, as the present tense of saqā, which is a dialect of asqā according to a group. They recited the verse of Labid:

"Saqa qawmi Bani Majdin wa-asqa
Numayran wal-qabaʾila min Hilal."

("He gave drink to my people, the Banu Majd, and gave drink to Numayr and the tribes of Hilal.")

Some said: one says saqaytuhu for his lips, and asqaytuhu for his livestock and his land. It was said: saqāhu means he irrigated him with water, and asqāhu means he made it a drink prepared for him. There is more discussion on this later, so reflect on it. Abu Raja' read yusqikum with a ḍamma on the yāʾ, with the pronoun referring to God, exalted is He.

The author of al-Lawami said: it is permissible for it to refer to al-niʿam (blessings), and it is masculine because niʿam can be masculine or feminine, and the meaning is: "Indeed for you in the livestock are blessings; He gives you to drink," i.e., He makes for you giving to drink. "And this is, as you see, [weak]." A group, including Abu Jaʿfar, read tasqikum with a fawqiyyah tāʾ with a fatḥa. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "This is a weak reading" — end of quotation. He did not clarify the reason for its weakness. It seems, and God knows best, that he meant the combination of the feminine in tasqikum with the masculine in ﴿بُطُونِهِ﴾, and he overlooked that such a thing is not considered a weakness, because the feminine and masculine are considered from two aspects.

﴿مِن بَيْنِ فَرْثٍ ودَمٍ لَبَنًا﴾ ﴿from between dung and blood, milk﴾. al-Farth, according to what is in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari), is the digestive matter (sirjin) as long as it is in the rumen (kirsh), and its plural is furuth. In al-Bahr: it is the dense residue of what remains of the food in the rumen or the intestines. And bayn requires more than one, and here it is the dung and the blood. So the apparent sense of the structure requires that milk be in the middle between them. al-Kalbi related this from Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: "When the beast is fed and the fodder is cooked in its rumen, its lowest part becomes dung, its middle becomes milk, and its highest becomes blood." A similar report is related from Ibn Jubayr. So the "betweenness" (bayniyyah) is in its literal and apparent sense.

Imam al-Razi criticized this, saying: "One may say: milk and blood are not generated in the rumen, and the evidence for this is sensory observation, for animals are slaughtered constantly and nothing of that is seen in their rumen. If what is mentioned were generated there, it would have to be observed at some times. And a thing whose falsity is shown by observation may not be relied upon. Rather, the truth is that when an animal takes nourishment, it reaches its stomach and its rumen, if it is among the livestock or other animals. When it is cooked and the first digestion takes place in it, what is pure of it is drawn to the liver, and what is thick descends to the intestines. Then what is obtained in the liver ripens and becomes blood, and that is the second digestion, and it is mixed with yellow bile, black bile, and an increase of watery matter. As for yellow bile, it goes to the gall bladder, and black bile to the spleen, and water to the kidney, and from it to the bladder. As for that blood, it enters the veins and arteries that sprout from the liver, and there occurs the third digestion. Between the liver and the udder there are many veins, so the blood pours from those veins into the udder. The udder is a soft, white glandular flesh, so God, exalted is He, transforms the blood in it into the form of milk. It may be said: this meaning exists in the male animal, so why does milk not come from it? We say: the divine wisdom required that everything be arranged in the manner appropriate to it and conducive to its benefit. So it made the temperament of the male hot and dry, and the temperament of the female cold and moist, since the offspring is generated within the body of the female. So it was fitting for her to be specially characterized by moisture, to become the material for generation and a cause for receiving expansion, so that she could accommodate the offspring. Then, after the separation of the fetus, that moisture pours into the udder and becomes material for its nourishment, as it was likewise in the womb before. Whoever reflects on the marvels of God's creation in what has been mentioned of the humors and milks, and the preparation of their channels and passages, and the causes that generate them, and the forces that dispose them at every time in the manner appropriate, will be compelled to acknowledge the perfection of His knowledge, power, wisdom, and the limitless mercy and compassion:

'Wisdoms in which the created beings are bewildered,
and it is fitting that they be bewildered.'"

The essence of what they mentioned is that when food reaches the rumen, it is cooked in it, and delicate parts are distinguished from it that are drawn to the liver, where they are cooked, so blood is produced. Then parts of it flow to the udder and turn into milk by the arrangement of the Wise, the All-Knowing. In that case, the meaning is that milk comes from between the parts of the dung, then from between the parts of the blood. So the "betweenness" in this view is figurative. In Irshad al-ʿAql al-Salim (Abu al-Suʿud's commentary) and others: "Perhaps what is related from Ibn ʿAbbas means that its middle is the material of milk, and its highest is the material of blood which nourishes the body, for the non-formation of these two in the rumen is undoubted. The reason for this interpretation is the contradiction between what the apparent sense requires and what the senses observe, and what the sages, the anatomists, have stated. And what supports what they mentioned is what someone I trust told me: that he witnessed blood coming out from the udder after milk when milking is pushed to the extreme. And God knows best."

(The first "min") is partitive (tabʿiyyah), since milk is part of what is in the bellies of the livestock, because it is made from some of the parts of the blood that is generated from the delicate parts that are in the dung, as you have heard. And these two are attached to nusqikum. The second "min" is initial (ibtida'iyyah), and it too is attached to nusqikum, for between the blood and the dung is the place from which the giving to drink begins. And their attachment to one governing element is due to the difference in their meanings. (Laban) is the second object of nusqikum. Placing it before (the other elements) is because, as has been stated many times, placing what should be delayed first arouses in the soul a longing for what is delayed, making its firm establishment upon its arrival more valuable, especially when the advanced element includes a description contrary to the description of the delayed element, as in the case under discussion. For between the descriptions of the advanced and the delayed there is opposition and distance, such that their fires cannot be seen from each other. This increases the longing and anticipation for the delayed element. It is also permitted that (min bayni) be a circumstantial clause (hal) of (laban), placed before it because it is indefinite, and to draw attention to the fact that this is the place of the lesson.

[p. 178]

Part 2 of 2 of the commentary (al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 16, verse 66.

It is also permissible that the first (min) be ibtida'iyyah (indicating origin), like the second, so that "min bayni" (from between) is a substitute of inclusion for what precedes it. ﴿Pure﴾: purified of whatever accompanies it of dense parts, by narrowing its outlet, or clear, not accompanied by the color of blood or the smell of dung. ﴿Palatable to those who drink﴾: easy to pass down their throats because of its smoothness (duhniyyah).

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Yahya ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Labibah, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "No one drinks milk and then chokes on it, [for] Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿pure milk, palatable to those who drink﴾."

A group read "sayghan" with a shadda on the ya. Isa ibn Umar read "saygh" without shadda, from sayyigh, like hayn from hayyin (the lightened form).

The verse has been used as evidence for the purity of the milk of animals whose meat is eaten and the permissibility of drinking it. Some who hold that semen is pure have argued against those who consider it impure, because it passes through the urinary passage as well, and that it is not unlikely that it should pass through the route of urine while being pure, just as milk came out pure from between dung and blood.

In al-Tafsir al-Kabir, the people of verification said: considering the origination of milk, as it indicates the existence of the Creator who chooses, also indicates the possibility of resurrection and rising again. This is because this grass that the animal eats is only produced from water and earth. The Creator of the world arranged an arrangement by which it turned into milk, then arranged another arrangement by which butter and cheese came about from that milk. This shows that He, exalted is He, is able to turn these bodies from one attribute to another and from one state to another. When this is so, it is also not impossible that He is able to turn the parts of the bodies of the dead back to the attribute of life and intellect as they were before. Thus this consideration indicates, from this aspect, that resurrection and the Last Day are a possible matter, not impossible.

And from the fruits of the date-palms and grapes" is governed by a verb that has been omitted, its implied sense being "and We give you to drink from the fruits of the date-palms and grapes," meaning from their juice (ʿaṣīr). The verb is omitted because "nusqīkum" (We give you to drink) mentioned earlier indicates it. The words "You take from it an intoxicant and good provision" (﴿تَتَّخِذُونَ مِنهُ سَكَرًا ورِزْقًا حَسَنًا﴾) are an explanation and clarification of the nature of the giving to drink. Alternatively, "from it" (minhu) may be attached to "you take" (tattakhidhūna), with the prepositional phrase repeated for emphasis, as in your saying, "Zayd is in the house, in it." Or it may be the predicate of an omitted subject whose description is "you take" (tattakhidhūna), meaning: "And from the fruits of the date-palms and grapes there is a fruit from which you take..." The pronoun in "from it" refers either to the omitted noun that was suppressed (the juice) or to "fruits," which is interpreted as "fruit," since it is a definite plural used to denote the genus. The purpose of the form is to point to the enumeration of kinds. It may also refer to the omitted "fruit" (thamar).

"Intoxicant" (al-sakar) means wine. Al-Akhṭal said:

"Evil are the sober, and evil is their drinking, when the mizzā' and the sukkar flow among them."

Originally it is the verbal noun of sakira, sukran and sakaran, like rashida, rushdan and rashadan. It is cited as evidence with the verse:

"They came to us with intoxication upon us, so today the clear-headed one has been revealed, and the drunkard is sober."

The commentators explained "good provision" (rizqan ḥasanan) as vinegar, date-syrup, raisins, and other things. This is the view of the author of al-Kashshāf (al-Zamakhsharī). He mentioned in the i'rāb (grammatical analysis) of the verse what we have mentioned. He gave priority to the first of his three possible readings, and this clearly indicates his preference for it. Al-Ṭībī stated this explicitly and clarified it with what he clarified. He placed the third reading last, and it is clear that it is inferior to the other two.

In al-Kashf, after quoting his words on the first reading, it says: "In it there is an implied ʿaṣīr (juice), and it is not suitable as a conjunction with the preceding in an apparent sense, since it is not suitable as an explanation of the lesson in the livestock." And it says: "In this there is a problem, for 'you take' (tattakhidhūna) is not suitable as a clarification of the nature of the giving to drink, especially since 'good provision' has been interpreted as dates and raisins as well. What relation has the juice to this? And how far is this explanation from the explanation by His saying, 'We give you to drink' (nusqīkum), for it to be made the grounds for preferring it?" Thus this is an inferior reading, to be interpreted as being conjoined to the entire preceding phrase. The verbal sentence was chosen because of its proximity to "We give you to drink." His saying, "You take from it an intoxicant" (﴿تَتَّخِذُونَ مِنهُ سَكَرًا﴾), is where the explanation is complete for him, and then an additional benefit is added. The most evident reading is the last one mentioned, meaning: "And from the fruits of the date-palms and grapes there is a fruit from which you take..." so that a nominal sentence is conjoined to a nominal sentence, namely His saying, "Indeed, in the livestock there is a lesson for you" (﴿وإنَّ لَكم في الأنْعامِ لَعِبْرَةً﴾). Since the lesson in it is not the same as in the first, it suffices to make it a conjunction to what is a lesson, without stating it explicitly. The partitive (min) indicates that among their fruits there are some that are eaten before ripening, some that are spoiled, and some that are eaten by wild animals, and other things. End of quotation.

What he mentioned in the interpretation about the explanation of the explanation at "intoxicant" requires making "provision" (rizqan) an object of another governing word, and its remoteness is not hidden. The evident point is that he does not deny this. The most evident reading that he mentioned was also mentioned by al-Ḥawfī, like his companion (al-Zamakhsharī). It is not objected to it that it involves omitting the described noun with a clause, because that is regular when the described noun is part of a genitive phrase introduced by "min" or "fī" preceding it, such as "Among us is one who stood, and among us is one who journeyed," meaning "a group." It may also omit a described noun with a clause in other cases, as in the verse of the rajaz poet:

"You have nothing with me except an arrow and a stone, and other than a loose-stringed bow with a tight string. It gave with my hand, and he was among the best archers of mankind."

meaning "a man." Yes.

Al-Ṭabarī said: the estimate is "And from the fruits of the date-palms and grapes, what you take from it..." Abū Ḥayyān criticized this by saying that this is not permitted according to the school of the Basrans, and it seems he considered "what" (mā) a relative pronoun, and omitting the relative pronoun while keeping the relative clause is not permitted according to them. Perhaps they distinguish between the relative pronoun and the described noun in what has been mentioned.

The scholar Ibn Kamāl said in some of his treatises: "There is no benefit in what the author of al-Kashshāf chose, namely linking the prepositional phrase to the omitted 'We give you to drink' and estimating 'juice' as an added noun, because then it does not include the edible, and the edible is the greater of the two kinds of their fruits, meaning the date-palms and grapes. The context is one of bestowing favor, and its requirement is to include both kinds." Then he said: "It is strange that he and those who followed him, like al-Bayḍāwī, agreed on interpreting 'good provision' as including dates and raisins, and yet they say that the meaning is 'and from its juice you take an intoxicant and good provision.' There is no coherence between these two statements. The correct reading is that the prepositional phrase is linked to 'you take,' and 'from it' is a repetition of the adverbial phrase for emphasis." End of quotation. This is what Abū Ḥayyān preferred, and the objection along with what was said in response to it has been mentioned before. It is also reported from him that he made it dependent on what is in "giving to drink" of the meaning of "feeding": that is, "We feed you from the fruits of the date-palms and grapes," so that the edible from them and the drink prepared from their juice are included together. There is much remoteness in this.

You know that the estimate of juice according to the first reading is necessary according to those who hold it, and its estimate according to the second reading is permissible according to them as well, but it is not permissible according to the objector. Abū al-Baqāʾ preferred making it dependent on "He created for you" or "He made," but this is not correct. It was also said that it is conjoined to "livestock," meaning: "And from the fruits of the date-palms and grapes there is a lesson," and "you take" is an explanation of it. This is different from the reading that the author of al-Kashf preferred. The evident would be "in" instead of "from." The pronoun in "from it" is not restricted to what you have heard, as is not hidden to you after you have learned the variant opinions about the pronoun in "their bellies" (﴿بُطُونِهِ﴾).

The interpretation of "intoxicant" as wine is what is related from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿUmar, Abū Razīn, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, al-Shaʿbī, al-Nakhaʿī, Ibn Abī Layla, Abū Thawr, al-Kalbī, and Ibn Jubayr, along with many others. The verse was revealed in Mecca, and wine at that time was lawful, drunk by the righteous and the wicked. Its prohibition took place in Medina by consensus. They differed as to whether it was before Uḥud or after it. The verse that prohibits it is: "O you who believe, wine, gambling, idols and divining arrows are only an abomination of Satan's work, so avoid it" (﴿يا أيُّها الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إنَّما الخَمْرُ والمَيْسِرُ والأنْصابُ والأزْلامُ رِجْسٌ مِن عَمَلِ الشَّيْطانِ فاجْتَنِبُوهُ﴾), according to the view of a group. Thus what is here is abrogated (mansūkh, abrogated by naskh, meaning the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation) by it. This was narrated by more than one of those mentioned earlier, such as al-Nakhaʿī, Abū Thawr, and Ibn Jubayr. It was also said that it was revealed before, and there is no abrogation, based on what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that "intoxicant" is vinegar in the language of Abyssinia, or on what is reported from Abū ʿUbayda that "intoxicant" is food eaten for enjoyment, like a dessert, and he recited:

"She made the honor of the noble ones an intoxicant."

It was objected that the meaning of "intoxicant" as wine in this is more fitting than as food. The meaning is that, because of his eagerness for backbiting and tearing people's honor, this became for him like intoxicating wine. Perhaps for this reason al-Zajjāj said: "Abū ʿUbayda's view is not correct." It is also objected that what is known about backbiting is calling it a dessert, and that is why it was said: "Backbiting is the fruit of the reciters." The followers of the Ḥanafī school went to the view of no abrogation and said: the intended "intoxicant" is what does not intoxicate of the beverages (anbidhah, fermented drinks). They used as evidence that God Most High bestowed favor upon His servants with what He created for them of that, and a favor is not given except through something lawful. Therefore this is evidence of the permissibility of drinking what is less than intoxicating from the nabīdh (date-wine). When it reaches intoxication, it is not permitted. They supported this from the Sunnah with what was narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "God Most High prohibited wine itself, its little and its much, and intoxication from every drink." Reported by al-Dāraquṭnī.

The permissibility of drinking nabīdh as long as it does not reach intoxication was held by Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, Abū Jaʿfar al-Ṭaḥāwī, who was the imam of the people of his time, and Sufyān al-Thawrī, the one you know. May God have mercy on him, he used to drink it, as al-Qurṭubī mentioned in his tafsir. After al-Bayḍāwī interpreted "intoxicant" as wine, he hesitated about the time of its revelation and said: "However, if the verse preceded the prohibition of wine, it indicates its disapproval; otherwise it combines reproach and favor." The indication of disapproval is that wine is placed in opposition to "good," and this requires its ugliness, and what is ugly is not free from disapproval even if it is free from prohibition. This was objected to, on the grounds that his hesitation here about its preceding the prohibition of wine contradicts what was said in Sūrat al-Baqarah. For he states definitively, at the beginning of this sūrah, that it is Meccan except for three verses at its end.

In al-Kashshāf, after interpreting "intoxicant" also with what was mentioned, he said: "In it there are two views: one is that it is abrogated, and the second is that it combines reproach and favor." Al-Kashf reports that the view that it is abrogated is the best of the opinions. Then he said: "In the verse there is evidence of the ugliness of consuming it, by implication, from restricting the contrast to 'good.'" This is the view of those who held that it combines reproach and favor. On the first view, it is a symbol that intoxicant, although permissible, is something one should avoid. End of quotation.

Ibn Kamāl argued for its revelation before the prohibition by saying that the context does not allow reproach, for the flow of speech is on what its context indicates and what follows it, in enumerating great blessings. He mentioned that the words of al-Zamakhsharī and those who followed him arise from neglecting this. Perhaps the reason that "intoxicant" is not described with what follows it is that God Most High knew that it would become an abomination (rijs) which the Sharīʿah rules to be prohibited. Al-Zamakhsharī permitted that intoxicant be made "good provision," as if it were said: "You take from it what is intoxicating and good provision," meaning that the conjunction is of attributes. You know that conjunction apparently implies difference.

Now, since milk is a great blessing in which the act of creation has no part, He, glorified, attributed the giving to drink to Himself by His saying, "We give you to drink" (﴿نُسْقِيكُمْ﴾), in contrast to the making of intoxicant. This has been stated explicitly in al-Baḥr, so reflect upon it. "Indeed in that is a sign" (﴿إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لآيَةً﴾), a manifest one, "for a people who reason" (﴿لِقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ﴾), who use their intellects by considering and reflecting upon the signs. Thus the verb is treated as intransitive. Abū Ḥayyān said: Since the opening of the speech was "Indeed, in the livestock there is a lesson for you" (﴿وإنَّ لَكم في الأنْعامِ لَعِبْرَةً﴾), it is fitting to conclude with His, glorified, saying "they reason," for only those possessing intellects take heed. I say: If the verse contains an allusion to belittling the matter of intoxicant, then the concluding phrase mentioned strengthens this, and it has a place in souls. What a place it has, since wine, as they say, is a fetter for the intellects:

"When the cupbearers circulate it with their hands, they have given the intellects as a bridal gift in exchange for its betrothal."

So understand this, and God Most High guides you.

[Page 182]

**Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 68:**

﴿And your Lord inspired the bee﴾: He inspired it (*alhamaha*), cast it into its heart (*alqa fi ruʿiha*), and taught it in a manner that none knows except the Subtle, the All-Aware. Some interpreters (*fassara*) explained the inspiration to it as its being subjugated (*taskhir*) to what is wanted from it. They rejected that the intended meaning be literal inspiration, because inspiration (*al-iya'*) belongs only to rational beings, and the bee is not one of them. Yes, there proceed from it actions and there are found in it states by which one imagines that it has intellects and a virtue that males fall short of. Thus you see that among them there is one like a chief, the largest of them in body, whose command is binding over all the rest, and all of them serve him and carry for him. He is called *al-yaʿsub* (the leader of the bees) and *al-amir* (the commander). They also mention that when they leave their hive (*wakr*) and go off with their collective body to another place, then, when they want them to return to their hive, they strike drums and musical instruments for them, and by means of those melodies they return them to their hive. They build hexagonal houses of equal sides, which rational beings cannot manage except with instruments such as the ruler (*mistara*) and the compass (*farjar*). They prefer these over other houses shaped in other forms such as triangles, squares, pentagons and others. In this there is a subtle secret, for they have said: it is established in geometry (*handasa*) that if they were shaped in other forms, there would necessarily remain between them empty, wasted gaps, and they have other wondrous states besides this, which many people have witnessed. Glory be to Him who gave everything its creation, then guided it.

The Sufis, as al-Sha'rani mentions in more than one place, do not prevent the intended meaning from being literal. They have affirmed, among all animals, messengers and prophets, while the Shariʿa rejects that. Some of the Ishraqi sages (*hukama' al-ishraq*, the Illuminationists) held that the rational soul (*al-nafs al-natiqa*) exists in all animals, and I nearly grant them that. We have not heard of anyone other than the Sufis saying what I have heard from them.

The bee (*al-nahl*) is a collective noun whose singular is *nahla*, and it is feminine in the dialect of the Hijaz. For this reason He, glory be to Him, said: ﴿that take for yourselves﴾ (*ani ittakhidhi*). Ibn Wththab read *al-nahal* with two fatahs, and this may be a dialectal form or a following of the vowel of the *nun*. ( *Ani* ) is either a verbal particle (*masdariyya*), with the preposition of accompaniment (*ba' al-mulabasa*) understood, meaning "by [means of] taking," or it is explanatory (*tafsiriyya*), and what follows it explains the inspiration, because it contains, according to its well-known meaning, the sense of speech without its letters, and that is sufficient for making it explanatory. Abu Hayyan either overlooked this or did not take it into account, and he said: that is a consideration because inspiration here means *ilham* (intuitive inspiration) by consensus, and in *ilham* there is no sense of speech. ﴿From the mountains, houses﴾ (*min al-jibal buyutan*): nests (*awkar*). The original sense of *bayt* is a person's dwelling, and it is used here for the nest that the bee builds to make honey in, by way of comparison with what a person builds, because of its fine workmanship and arrangement, as you have heard. It is also read *biyutan* with a kasra on the *ba'* for the sake of harmony with the *ya'*; otherwise the plural of *fiʿl* would be *fuʿul* with a damma.

﴿And from the trees and from what they erect﴾ (*wa min al-shajar wa mimma yaʿrishun*): that is, what people trellis (*yuʿarrishuh al-nas*), i.e., what they raise, of vines, as is reported from Ibn Zayd and others; or the roofs, as is transmitted from al-Tabari; or something more general than both, as some have said. ( *Min* ) in the three places is partitive (*lil-tabʿid*) with respect to individuals and with respect to parts, for the bee does not build in every tree, every mountain, and everything that is trellised, nor in every place of those. Some said that *min* is partitive only with respect to individuals, and the other meaning is known from outside, not from the signification of *min*, since it is not permissible to use it in both senses. Master Ibn Kamal has a separate monograph on the question, so let it be consulted. In any case, there is in it, together with what comes shortly after, God willing, from the rhetorical devices (*badi*) the figure of *tibaq* (antithesis). The interpretation of *buyut* as what they build is the one taken by more than one scholar. Abu Hayyan said: the apparent meaning is that it refers to the openings (*kuwa*) in mountains, in the hollows of trees, and the hives that Adam's son makes for the bees, and the openings in walls. Since the bee has two kinds: one kind is in its abode in the mountains and thickets, and no one tends it; and another kind is in people's houses and is tended in hives and the like, the command to "take" (houses) covers both kinds.

[p. 183]

﴿Then eat of all the fruits﴾, i.e., of all of them. The word *thamarat* (fruits) is the plural of *thamara*, with a vowelled stem, meaning the produce of a tree. Ibn 'Atiyya took the apparent sense of this and said: "It is only the blossoms of trees that the bee eats." It is also said that *al-thamara* can refer to the tree itself, as in the *Qamus* (the dictionary *al-Qamus al-Muhit*). It has been said that this is the appropriate reading here, since restricting the verse to the fruit of trees contradicts the reality, given that the bee eats from leaves, blossoms and fruits in general. It has been objected that it is not hidden that applying *thamara* to the tree is a figurative usage that is not well known, and that the bee's eating from other than the tree is not established, nor does it contradict limiting its eating to what grows on the tree. The generality in "all" is, according to what some have indicated, customary (*'urfi*). It has also been permitted that it be restricted by custom, i.e., "eat from every fruit that you desire." It has also been said that it is for multiplicity. Al-Khafaji said: "Even if it is kept on its apparent sense, it is permissible, because it does not follow from the command to eat from all the fruits that she eats from them all, since the command is for permission and allowance." In any case, *min* (from) is partitive (*lil-tab'idh*).

[p. 183 continued] Al-Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) said: "I have seen in the books of medicine that God, exalted is He, arranged this world in such a way that in the nights a subtle shade arises in the air and falls upon the leaves of trees. Sometimes those parts are subtle and small, scattered over the leaves and blossoms, and sometimes they are so numerous that perceptible parts gather from them. This is like *al-taranjabin* (a sweet exudate, similar to manna), for it is a shade that descends from the air and gathers on the tips of branches in some lands. As for the first kind, it is what God inspired in the bee, so that it gathers it from the blossoms and the leaves of trees with its mouths, and feeds on it. When it is satisfied, it gathers again with its mouth some of those parts and carries them to its hives, and places them there, as though it were trying to store its food for itself. What gathers from that is honey. Among people there is one who says that the bee eats from fragrant blossoms and sweet-smelling leaves certain things, and then God, exalted is He, transforms those bodies inside its body into honey, and then it vomits it up. The first view is closer to reason and more suitable to induction, for the nature of *al-taranjabin* is close to honey in taste and form, and there is no doubt that it is a shade that arises in the air and falls on the tips of trees and blossoms, so likewise here. Also, we observe that bees feed on honey, to the extent that when we take honey out of their hives we leave some of it for their food. In that case, *min* (from) is for the beginning of the end (*li-ibtida' al-ghayah*)." End of the Imam's words.

[p. 183–184] You know that the apparent sense of ﴿Eat﴾ supports the second view, and it supports it more strongly than the similarity of *al-taranjabin* to honey in taste and form supports the first view, especially since the natures of honey and *al-taranjabin* differ. Some eminent physicians have stated that honey is hot in the third degree and dry in the second, while *al-taranjabin* is hot in the first degree and moist in the second, or temperate. Yes, because of that resemblance it is called by the name of honey, for *taranjabin* is a Persian word meaning "moist honey," not "dew of the dawn" as is claimed. Although they say that in reality it is a dew that falls on the *al-'aqul* plant (a shrub) in Fars and is gathered like manna, and from Tikrur there is brought something called in their language *tanit*, which is most similar to it in appearance and effect but is coarser. The matter of observing their feeding on honey is easy, for it is not constant. It is reported of some birds that hide in winter that they feed on excrement. In support of the well-known view is what is reported from the Commander Ali, may God ennoble his face, in belittling the world: "The noblest garment of the son of Adam contains the saliva of a worm, and the noblest of his drinks is the excrement of bees." It is also reported from him, may God ennoble his face: "As for honey, it is the vomit of flies."

To interpret it as a metaphor is contrary to the apparent sense, and on this poetry has been composed. Al-Ma'arri said:

"The bee gathers bitter things from the blossoms of the *ruba*, and they return as honey in the passage of its saliva."

And al-Hariri said:

"You say: this is the bee's honey, you praise it; / and if you wish to disparage it, it is the vomit of wasps."

And someone whom I trust informed me that he had observed many times their carrying leaves and blossoms in their mouths to their hives, and this is something that supports the eating. Also, God willing, what supports it will come later. ﴿Then go along the ways of your Lord﴾, i.e., His paths, glorified is He, returning to your hives after eating. So by *subul* (ways) is meant their courses in returning. It is related that sometimes the land around them becomes barren, so they seek distant places for pasture, and then they return to their hives without losing their way. In the attribution of the ways to the Lord, who is attributed to her pronoun, there is an indication that He, glorified is He, is the one who prepares that, facilitates it, and takes charge of her affairs and livelihood. It has been said: by the ways is meant the paths of going to the places where it eats, and in that case the meaning of ﴿eat﴾ is "aim to eat." It has also been said: the ways are a metaphor for the paths of work and their kinds, i.e., "go along the paths that your Lord inspired you to follow in making honey." It has also been said: a metaphor for the means by which food is transformed into honey. And *uslukī* (go along) is transitive, from *salakattu al-khayt fi al-ibrah* (I threaded the thread through the needle), and not intransitive from *salaka fi al-tariq* (he walked in the way). Its object is omitted, i.e., "go along what you have eaten through its channels, in which by His power the bitter nectar becomes honey within your bodies."

[p. 184] It has been objected that threading in those channels is not up to her choice, so that she should be commanded to do it, so the command must be creational. It was answered that this is worthless, because the entering is by her choice, so it does not harm her that the transformation that follows from it is not by her choice, and this is clear. So that is not as claimed.

﴿Docile﴾, i.e., made easy, which God made smooth and facilitated for you. It is the plural of *dhalul* (tame, docile), and it is a state (*hal*) of "ways." This was related from Mujahid.

Ibn 'Abd al-Salam made the description of the ways as *dhull* (smooth) an evidence that the ways are the channels of food, not the paths of going or returning. He said: "Because bees go and return in the air, and the air is not paths that are smooth, for the smooth (*dhalul*) is that which is made smooth by frequent treading, and the air is not like that." There is a point to be considered in this.

Qatada said: "*Ay* (i.e., 'docile') means obedient and submissive." So it is a state of the pronoun in ﴿go along﴾.

﴿From their bellies there comes forth﴾: this is a resumed sentence (*isti'naf*), in which He turned from addressing the bee to speaking with people, to explain what appears from them of the marvels of God's creation, which are a place of lesson for them, after she was commanded what she was commanded.

﴿A drink﴾, meaning honey. It was named so because it is drunk, to the extent that it has been said: one does not say "I ate honey," but "I drank honey." It seems that He, glorified is He, did not express it with the verb of bringing out directly attributed to Himself, but was content with attributing the inspiration of the beginnings to Him, exalted is His majesty. In this there is an announcement of His great power, glorious and exalted is He, such that what indicates the will for a thing suffices for its occurrence.

[*min*] (from) is for the beginning of the end. He mentioned the beginning of the first end, which is the bellies, and did not mention the beginning of the final end, glorified is He. The majority hold that it comes out of their mouths. Some claimed that this is more expressive of power, and al-Hariri's verse supports it, as does al-Hasan's saying: "The essence of righteousness is by the saliva of bees, with pure ghee, which no Muslim finds fault with."

It has also been said: from their backsides (*adbar*), which is the apparent sense of what is reported from the Leader of the Believers, may God ennoble his face.

Others said: "We do not know except what God, exalted is He, mentioned." It is related that Sulayman, peace be upon him, Alexander, and Aristotle made for them hives of glass in order to look at how they make it, and whether the honey comes out of their mouths or from elsewhere. But they did not put any honey in it until they smeared the inside of the glass with clay in a way that prevented observation.

Some said: by *buṭūn* (bellies) is meant the mouths. The mouth is called a belly because it is in its position, and because it is something that is concealed and not visible. This is the interpretation of those who held that they gather small particles from the dew and store them in their hives, and that is the honey. You know that the apparent sense of *baṭn* (belly) is the well-known organ, so the verse supports the well-known view about the formation of honey. In the *Kashshaf* (of al-Zamakhshari) it is said that in God's words ﴿Then eat﴾ there is an indication that the bee's stomach has an effect in this, and this is the view preferred by the researching philosophers. As for those who made honey purely vegetable and interpreted the bellies as the mouths of bees, I wonder what they would do with His words, glorified is He, ﴿Then eat﴾. It was answered that he interprets eating as gathering, and this, as you see, is a weak answer, for removing the corruption does not remove the improbability. Among people there is one who claims that they gather blossoms and dew; what is gathered from the blossom itself becomes honey, and what is gathered from the dew becomes *mum* (wax-like substance). The reason permits the reverse, and perhaps this is closer than that.

﴿Its colours vary﴾, in white, yellow, red and black, either purely by the will of the Wise Creator, glorified is His majesty, or because of the difference in pasture, or because of the difference in seasons, or because of the difference in the age of the bees: the white is for the young, the yellow for the mature, the red for the aged, and the black for one who is very old.

It has been objected that this is something for which there is no evidence. I asked a group whom I trust, who had tested their conditions, and they reported that they had investigated and examined, and found that the strongest apparent cause of the difference in colours is the difference in age. Indeed, some of them said: "We know of no cause for that except this, by induction." In that case, what has been mentioned supports the well-known view about the formation of honey, as is not hidden from anyone with the least discernment.

﴿In it is healing for people﴾, either by itself, as in phlegmatic diseases, or together with other things, as in the rest of diseases, for there is hardly any electuary (*ma'jun*) that does not contain honey. So it has a share in most of what healing is obtained from in electuaries and compounds. It has been objected to this that its entering into those does not require that it have a share in the healing, but rather that it does no harm, since it has been said that its inclusion in the compounds is to preserve them, and for this reason sugar has taken its place in that. What we have seen in many books of medicine is that it preserves the powers of medicines for a long time and conveys their benefits. It is not hidden from the fair-minded that what preserves the powers and conveys the benefits of a medicine is truly said to have a share in the healing. It is not known that sugar takes its place in that.

In the *Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) it is said: honey is found abundantly in most lands, but as for sugar, it is specific to some lands, and it is a recent manufactured product for humans. In former times nothing was put into medicines and drinks except honey. End of quote.

In the *Sharh al-Shama'il* (commentary on al-Tirmidhi's *Shama'il*) it is said that he, may blessings and peace be upon him, did not eat sugar. Many have mentioned that the word "people" here does not mean all people, because many diseases do not have honey in their treatment, such as diseases of yellow bile, for it is harmful to the bilious. And even if we grant that *sakanjabin* (a drink of vinegar and honey), which, as its original meaning indicates, is vinegar and honey, is beneficial for them, the beneficial one is another type of *sakanjabin*, for it has been transferred to what is compounded of sour and sweet, and it has many kinds, on whose collection treatises have been written, to the extent that they said it is forbidden to take it in that form. What is meant by "people" is those for whom honey is beneficial in their diseases.

The indefinite form in ﴿healing﴾ (*shifa'un*) is either for magnification, i.e., "a healing, what a healing," or for partiality, i.e., "in it is some healing." So it does not imply that every healing is in it, nor that everyone is healed by it.

It may be objected that milk is also like this. Rather, hardly is there any medicinal substance that does not contain healing for people in this sense. When it was said that the explicit statement of this ruling is meant to convey something that seems improbable: that what comes out, in its various colors, from these worms (which most resemble venomous creatures, and which may themselves be venomous, since they sting and cause pain, and the skin may swell from their sting) contains **"healing for mankind."** This clearly indicates that they are venomous. Some reports also suggest that the statement is general. Humayd ibn Zanjawayh narrated from Nafi' that Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) would not complain of any sore or anything else without applying honey to it. Even for a boil (dumul), if he had one, he would apply honey to it. We said to him: "You treat a boil with honey?" He said: "Does not Allah, exalted is He, say, **'In it is healing for mankind'**?"

You know that there is no harm in treating a boil with honey, for the physicians have mentioned that it cleanses wounds, helps them heal, and consumes excess flesh.

The truth is that there is no room for generality, for there is no doubt that there is a disease in which honey does not help. As for the reports that imply generality, Allah knows best their soundness. As for what Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, my brother's bowels are loose.' He said: 'Give him honey to drink.' So he gave him honey to drink. Then he came and said: 'I gave him honey, but it only increased his looseness.' He said: 'Go and give him honey again.' So he gave him honey, then he came and said: 'It only increased his looseness.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Allah has spoken the truth, and your brother's belly has lied. Go and give him honey.' So he went and gave him, and he was healed."

This is not explicit about generality, since it is possible that the Prophet (ﷺ) was taught by Allah, glorified is He, that this man's ailment of looseness of the bowels is among those cured by honey. Indeed, some kinds of looseness of the bowels can be cured by honey. The physicians' writings state that the Prophet (ﷺ) only said this because he knew that in the stomach of the patient there were thick, viscous humors which had made his stomach slippery. Whenever some astringent medicine passed through him, it had no effect, since the humors remained in their state, and food slid off them. So the looseness persisted. When he took honey, it dissolved those humors and dislodged them, so the looseness increased at first as they were expelled. This continued until the humor was entirely drained, and his looseness ceased and he was healed. Thus the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying, **"Allah has spoken the truth,"** means by the knowledge which Allah taught His Prophet (ﷺ).

And his saying, **"your brother's belly has lied,"** means what appeared from his belly of looseness and its abundance was by way of accident, and was not a real looseness or real illness. So his belly was "lying." End of quote. Some of them said: what is meant by "Allah has spoken the truth" is that Allah, glorified is He, spoke the truth that honey contains healing. The Prophet's (ﷺ) saying, **"your brother's belly has lied,"** is an instance of *al-Mushakala al-Didiyya* (harmonization by contrast), like their saying: "Whoever has a long beard, his intellect is short." On the first explanation it is a metaphor based on likening the belly to a liar, in that what appears of its looseness is not a real matter but something that befell it. On this basis is also the physicians' saying: "a false straining (zahir kadhib) and a true straining (zahir sadiq)." Some of them denied this type of *mushakala* and said: it is not well known, and he only expressed it that way because his belly was, as it were, denying Allah's word with the tongue of its state. This is from a lack of familiarity.

A parallel to this story occurred in the time of al-Ma'mun. Thumama al-'Absi, who was among his close associates, fell ill with looseness of the bowels, so that he would go to the toilet a hundred times in a day and a night. The physicians were unable to treat him. Yazid ibn Yuhanna, al-Ma'mun's physician, treated him with a purgative as well, and he was healed. The physicians had thought he would die because of this and would not survive until the next day. When al-Ma'mun asked the physician about the wisdom behind what he had done, he said that there was in the man's body a corrupt *kaymus* (chyme), so that no food or medicine entered it without corrupting it. So I knew there was no cure for it except to expel it through looseness of the bowels. From this it is known that what the Prophet (ﷺ) did was among his miracles, which show his knowledge of the subtleties of medicine without having been taught. Likewise it is known that what some atheists, and those with sickness in their hearts, have criticized, namely how one could treat looseness of the bowels with honey when it is a laxative by the agreement of the physicians, arises from ignorance of the subtleties and from failing to grasp the realities.

It is also reported from Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Farra', and Ibn Kaysan, and it is a narration from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan, that the pronoun in **"in it"** refers to the Qur'an, and that the meaning is that in the Qur'an there is healing for the diseases of ignorance and polytheism, and guidance and mercy. Ibn al-Nahhas approved of this.

But al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: I think this view cannot be validly transmitted from these men, and even if it were validly transmitted, it would not be sound in reason. For the whole context of the discourse concerns honey, and there is no mention of the Qur'an in it. Also, the pronoun referring to the Book in His saying, glorified is He, **"And We have not sent down the Book to you except that you may make clear to them that about which they differ"** is something that men like these noble and eminent scholars would hardly say. Yes, the Qur'an being a healing is not in question, and al-Tabarani and others narrated from Ibn Mas'ud: "Upon you are the two healings: honey and the Qur'an." End of quote.

Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the sending down of water first, because water is more complete in benefit and greater in importance, and it is the fundamental origin for the formation of milk and what follows it. Then milk is mentioned, because people need it more than the other things mentioned after it. It may suffice to drink it instead of drinking water, as we have witnessed among some of the ascetics of our time, who gave up drinking water for several years and were content with drinking milk. We have heard similar things about some Bedouin chiefs. This is also an indication of natural disposition (fitra). For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) chose it when he was taken on the Night Journey, and milk, wine and honey were offered to him. Then wine is placed next because it is closer to water than honey is, for it is the water of grapes. But it is not customary to make it a condiment as honey is, for bread is often eaten with honey as a relish. Between wine and milk there is a kind of resemblance, in that each of them comes out from between dense parts, and its heaviness is like that of dung. If the ease of swallowing is considered for milk and its absence for wine, according to what they say, that wine is not easy to pass down the throat, and therefore its drinker frowns when drinking and may even choke on it, then there is a kind of opposition between them. And it is fitting to place an opposite after an opposite, just as it is fitting to place a like after a like. And if their final ruling in the Sharia is considered, you will see that wine has not remained lawful to drink since the verse about it was revealed, while drinking milk has always remained lawful. By this the opposition is strengthened. It is further strengthened by the fact that milk comes out of the belly of an animal with no role of human action in it, whereas wine is not like that.

As for the mention of "good provision" after wine and its placement before honey, the reason for it is quite evident. And perhaps what we have considered as the reason for placing wine before honey and mentioning it after milk is stronger than what can validly be considered as a reason for placing honey before wine and mentioning it after milk. So it cannot be objected that in every direction there is a precedence, and that considering it in one of them and not the other is preference without a preferring factor. The mention of water, milk, wine and honey in the description of Paradise has come in this same order. He, exalted is He, said: **"In it are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, delicious to drinkers, and rivers of honey, purified"** [Muhammad: 15]. So reflect. The path of the mind is broad, and Allah, exalted is He, knows best the secrets of His Book.

**"Indeed in that"**, meaning in what has been mentioned of the signs of Allah's power, **"is a sign"** great, **"for a people who give thought."** For whoever reflects on the fact that the bee is specially endowed with those subtle knowledges and wondrous actions that were previously pointed out, and on the emergence of this sweet drink of varied colors containing healing, is certain beyond doubt that it has a wise, powerful Lord who inspired it with what it was inspired and deposited in it what He deposited. And since its condition in this matter is wondrous and needs further reflection, Allah, glorified is He, concluded the verse with reflection.

Among the strange interpretations of the Rafidah (Shi'a), mentioned in al-Kashshaf, is that the bee refers to 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) and his people. And it is reported from one of them that he said in the presence of al-Mahdi: "The bees are only the Banu Hashim, from whose bellies knowledge comes out." A man said to him: "Allah has made your food and drink come from what comes out of their bellies!" So al-Mahdi laughed, and he related it to al-Mansur, and they made it one of their jokes. You will hear, if Allah wills, what the Sufis, may Allah sanctify their secrets, say in the chapter on allusion (ishara).

[Page 188]

Then, when He, glorified be He, mentioned some of the wonders of the states of water, plants, livestock and bees that He had mentioned, He pointed to some of the wonders of the states of mankind, from the beginning of his life to its end and the various changes between them. So He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And Allah created you, then He takes you back in death﴾, according to what His will requires, a will founded on consummate wisdoms, with differing terms of life. The indication that this is intended is His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject age﴾. For this reason it has been said that it is connected (ma'tuf) to an implied clause, meaning: "So among you is one whose death is hastened, and among you [is one who...]" etc. (*Arzal al-'Umr*) means its most abject and worthless part, and it is the time of decrepitude in which the powers decline, the senses deteriorate, and the person's condition in it becomes like his condition in childhood, with weakness of intellect and strength. From here the "return" (radd) is conceived. This is like His, exalted be He, saying: ﴿And whoever We grant long life, We reverse him in creation﴾ [Ya-Sin: 68]. So there is a metaphor (majaz) in it. Ibn Jarir reported from Ali, may Allah ennoble his countenance, that "the most abject age" is seventy-five years, and from Qatadah that it is ninety, and it has been said ninety-five. A group chose to interpret it by what preceded, and it varies with the differences in temperaments: many a person who lives long has not had his powers diminished, and one whose powers are diminished has not lived long. Perhaps restricting it to a specific age is based on what is most common, according to those who restricted it.

If the address is to those present at the time of revelation, then the use of the past and future tenses in it is evident. If it is general, then the past tense is relative to the time of their existence and the future is relative to the creation as a whole. According to the apparent reading, ( whoever is returned to the most abject age) encompasses the believer absolutely and the disbeliever. It has been said that it is specific to the disbeliever, and that the Muslim is not returned to the most abject age, because of His, exalted be He, saying: ﴿Then We return him to the lowest of the low﴾ ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ [al-Tin: 5, 6]. Ibn al-Mundhir and others reported from Ikrimah that he said: "Whoever recites the Qur'an will not be returned to the most abject age." Observation contradicts both statements, for we have seen many a Muslim who recites the Qur'an who has been returned to that state, and deriving the opposite from the verse is questionable. Among his supplications (ﷺ), as al-Bukhari and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Anas, was: "I seek refuge with You from stinginess, laziness, the most abject age, the punishment of the grave, the trial of the Dajjal, and the trial of life and death."

﴿so that he will not know anything after having known﴾. The lam here is the lam of outcome and consequence (*lam al-sayrura wa-l-'aqibah*), though originally it is the lam of causation. Kay is a verbal particle (masdariyyah), the verb is put in the subjunctive after it, and the resulting verbal noun (al-munsabik) is in the genitive after the lam, and the prepositional phrase is attached to *yuradd* ("is returned"). Al-Hawfi claimed that the lam is the lam of kay that entered upon kay for emphasis, but this is nothing. "Knowledge" here means "awareness" (ma'rifah), and the statement is a metonymy (kinayah) for the extreme of forgetfulness, meaning: so that he becomes forgetful, such that when he acquires knowledge of something, he soon forgets it and his knowledge departs from him at once. He says to you: "Who is this?" and you say: "So-and-so," and he does not pause a moment before asking you about him again. It has been said that the meaning is: so that he does not know an increase in knowledge beyond his knowledge. It has also been said: so that he does not understand anything after his first understanding; thus "knowledge" here means "understanding" (*'aql*), not its literal meaning, as in the preceding case. In this there is an indication of his incapacity, and that he cannot attain additional knowledge. The adopted view is the first. *Shay'an* ("anything") is put in the accusative either as an absolute object (masdar) or as a direct object (maf'ul bih). It has been permitted that there be a dispute (tanazu') over it between *ya'lama* and *'ilm*, and that the object of *'ilm* be omitted for the sake of generality, meaning: he does not know anything after knowing many things. ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing﴾ of everything, and among that is the wisdom in creation, in causing death, and in returning to the most abject age. ﴿All-Powerful﴾ over everything, and among that is whatever He, glorified be He, wills of such matters. It has been said: He is All-Knowing of the measures of your lifespans, All-Powerful over everything, Who causes the vigorous youth to die and preserves the decrepit one who is perishing. In this there is an alert that the difference in terms of life is only by the decree of a powerful and wise One, who arranged the structures and balanced the temperaments to a known measure; and had that been what the natural constitutions required, it would not have reached this extent. It has also been said: when He, exalted be His majesty, mentioned what befalls a person in decrepitude of weakened powers and ability and the absence of knowledge, He mentioned that He, exalted be His majesty, is constant in perfect knowledge and perfect power, which do not change with the passage of time as human knowledge and ability change. The nominal sentence (*al-jumlah al-ismiyyah*) conveys continuity, and perfection is expressed by the pattern *fa'il* (in *'Alim* and *Qadir*). He placed the attribute of knowledge first, because the absence of knowledge is addressed to those being addressed, although the relation of the attribute of knowledge to a thing comes before its relation to the attribute of power. The best of the three is not hidden from you, so reflect.

[Page 189]

*Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 16, verse 71:*

﴿And Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision.﴾ That is, He made you differ in it, so He gave you more than what He gave your slaves. ﴿Yet those who were favoured﴾ in it over others, namely the owners, ﴿do not give﴾ (*bi-raddi*, "giving back," i.e., "by giving") ﴿their provision﴾ that Allah provided them ﴿to those whom their right hands possess,﴾ meaning their slaves, who are their partners in being created and in being provided for. ﴿So they are equal in it,﴾ that is, the owners who were favoured and the slaves (*fa-hum*, "they"), ﴿in it,﴾ that is, in the provision (*fihi*), ﴿equal,﴾ meaning there is no disparity between them. The phrase (*sawa'un*) is a nominal sentence occupying the position of a verb in the subjunctive, as an answer to the negation. That is, they do not return it to them, so that they would be equal in it and share it. It has also been permitted that it be taken as having the sense of a verb in the nominative, coordinated with the words of Exalted Allah (*bi-raddi*). That is, they do not give it back to them, so they are not equal. The purpose of this is to rebuke those who associate with Allah, glorified is He, some of His creatures, to reprimand them, and to alert them to the utter ugliness of their act. It is as if it were said: You do not accept that your slaves be partners with you in anything that is not exclusive to you, but rather encompasses you and them, of the provision in which they are your equals in deserving it, and they are like you in being human and created by Allah, mighty is His authority. So how can you associate with Him, glorified and exalted is He, in matters that befit none but Him, exalted is His majesty, of divinity
صفحة 189
and of exclusive worship that belongs to His own Essence, exalted is He, for His own sake, some of His creatures, which is far beyond the level of consideration? This, as a group has stated, is in the manner of His words: ﴿Allah has coined for you a parable from yourselves: Do you have among those whom your right hands possess any partners in what We have provided you, so that you are equal therein?﴾ [Ar-Rum: 28]. They mean by this that it is a parable coined to show the utmost ugliness of what they did. In His words ﴿Then is it the favour of Allah they deny?﴾ there is an indication, as it has been said, of this. Likewise in His words ﴿So do not strike forth comparisons for Allah,﴾ there is an implied element, and it is in reality attached to the verb, I mean (*yajhadun*, "they deny"). Because denial (*al-juhud*) includes the meaning of disbelief, the preposition (*bi*) was used with its object placed first, either for emphasis, or to imply exclusivity as an intensification, or for the sake of the rhyme endings (*ru'us al-ayi*). As for the meaning of "favour" (*ni'mah*), it has been said to be provision. It has also been said, and this is perhaps the better view, that it includes that and other favours overflowing upon them from Him, glorified is He. That is, they associate with Allah, exalted is He, and so they deny His favour, exalted is He, in that they do what they do of associating others with Him. For that entails that they attribute what was bestowed upon them by Allah, exalted is He, of favours, to their partners, and deny that they come from Him, majestic and exalted is He. It has also been permitted that the meaning of the favour of Allah, exalted is He, is what He, glorified is He, bestowed through establishing proofs, clarifying the paths, and sending the Messengers, peace be upon them, and there is no favour greater than that. So the meaning of their denial of that is rejecting it and not paying heed to it. The third-person form is for the sake of consistency with (*fa-ma alladhina*, "then what of those who"). Abu Bakr, from Asim, Abu Abd al-Rahman, and al-A'raj, in one of the transmissions from him, read ﴿tajhadun﴾ with the letter *ta'*, in the second-person form, for the sake of consistency with (*li-ba'dikum*, "some of you"). This is what has been said. It has also been permitted that the meaning of the verse is that Allah, exalted is He, favoured some over others in provision, and that those who were favoured do not give any of their provision to those beneath them, and that I am the one who provides for them. So the owner and the owned are equal in the basic provision, even though they differ in quantity and quality. The intended meaning is a prohibition against self-admiration and boasting, which are the two precursors of ingratitude.

The coordination is also with an implied element, that is, do they admire and boast, and so deny the favour of Allah, exalted is He, upon them? It has been said that the implied meaning is: do they not understand, and so deny? In *al-Kashshaf* (by al-Zamakhshari), he preferred that the meaning is that He, glorified is He, made you differ in provision, and gave you more than what He gave your slaves, who are humans like you and your brothers. It would have been fitting for you to return the surplus of what you were given to them, until you were equal in clothing and food in quantity, as is related from Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, that he heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "They are only your brothers, so clothe them with what you wear, and feed them with what you eat."

Therefore, his slave was never seen afterwards except that his cloak was his cloak and his garment was his garment, without any difference. Its summary is that Allah, exalted is He, favoured you over your likes, so it was incumbent upon you to return some of that surplus to them, in gratitude for His favour, exalted is He, so that you would be equal in that surplus, and the surplus of bestowing and conferring would remain for you. So the verse is an exhortation to good treatment of those one owns. It also incorporates that they and their slaves are nurtured by His favour, exalted is He, despite their fluctuating in it, so that this would serve as a preparation for their ingratitude for His abundant blessings, glorified is He, to the point that they made for Him, mighty and majestic is He, equals that do not own for themselves any harm or benefit, so they worshipped them as they worship Him, exalted is He, or even more intensely and more firmly. There is in this much remoteness. The coordination here is also with an implied element, as in: do they not know that, and so deny?

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 72 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And Allah has made for you, from yourselves,﴾ i.e., from your own kind and species. This is a figurative usage (*majaz*) in that sense. The most common meaning of *nafs* is the essence (*dhat*), and it does not fit here as it does elsewhere, so the figurative usage was adopted. The figure may be either in the singular or the plural. Some scholars have used this to argue that it is not permissible for a human to marry from among the jinn, ﴿spouses﴾, so that you may find tranquility in them, and so that you may thereby maintain your welfare, and your children may be like you.

Ghayr wahid (many scholars) reported from Qatadah that this refers to the creation of Adam and Hawwa' (peace be upon them), for Hawwa' was created from his own self (peace be upon him). It was objected that this does not suit the plural forms *anfus* and *azwaj*, and that taking it as *taghlib* (predominance of one term over the other, using the masculine or the more prominent form to cover both) is a strained interpretation that does not suit the context. Likewise, saying that what is meant by them is some of the selves and some of the spouses is also not suitable.

﴿And He has made for you, from your spouses,﴾ i.e., from them. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun (*fa-wada'a al-zahir mawdi' al-damir*) to indicate that what is meant is that He made for you, from among you, one whose spouse is of you, not from the spouse of another. ﴿Sons﴾, and also to indicate that the result of marriage is procreation. ﴿And grandchildren (*hafadah*)﴾, the plural of *hafid*, like *katib* and *katabah*. It derives from their saying *hafada yahfidu hafdan, huchudan*, and *hafadanan*, meaning he hastened in service and obedience. In the hadith: "To You we hasten and serve (*nahfid*)." Jamil said:

*The maidservants hastened around them,*
*and surrendered with their hands the reins of the camels.*

The verb has been used both intransitively and transitively, as in his saying:

*They serve the guest in their tents,*
*out of generosity, that from them is without humiliation.*

It came in a dialect, as Abu 'Ubaydah said, as *ahfada ihfadan*. It was said: *al-hafd* is rapidity of cutting, and it was said: it is closeness of stride. What is meant by *hafadah*, according to what is reported from al-Hasan and al-Azhari, and reported in one narration from Ibn 'Abbas and chosen by Ibn al-'Arabi, is the children's children, and their being among the spouses in that case is through an intermediary. It was also said: the daughters, who are so described because in general they serve most fully in the houses. It was said: *banun* (sons) and the conjunction is for the difference of the two attributes, sonship and service, and this is treated as the difference of essences, and its parallel has passed. So this is a favour in giving one who combines these two noble qualities, as if it were said: and He made for you from them children who are sons and who are *hafadah*, i.e., combining these two matters. Close to this is what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, that the *banun* are the young children and the *hafadah* are the older ones, and similarly what is related from Muqatil with the reverse. It seems that Ibn 'Abbas considered that the older ones are stronger for service, while Muqatil considered that the young ones are more readily compliant with it and with obeying the command, and he took *hafd* in the sense of closeness of stride. It was also said: they are the woman's children from a first husband, and Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported it from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Tabarani, al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan*, al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, reported from Ibn Mas'ud that they are *al-akhtan* (in-laws). What is meant by them, as has been said, is the husbands of the daughters, who are called *ashhar* (in-laws by marriage). They recited:

*If my self had obeyed me, it would have become*
*for her many grandchildren, countable in number.*
*But it is a self that is proud against me,*
*my eyes turn toward the in-laws of the base.*

The accusative case on this view is by a verb understood, i.e., *and He made for you hafadah*, not by coordination with *banin*, because when a restriction (*qayd*) is placed before the two conjoined items, it applies to both, and the husbands of the daughters are not among the spouses. This was judged weak, since there is no indication that requires supposing a meaning contrary to the apparent one, and in it there is a subtle point that is not hidden.

It was said: there is no obstacle to coordination, provided that *al-akhtan* is taken to mean the woman's relatives, such as her father and brother, not the husbands of the daughters, for the application of the term *akhtan* to them is only among the common people, whereas among the Arabs it is not so, as in *al-Sihah*. And *min* is taken as causal. There is no doubt that spouses are a cause for the making of *hafadah* in this sense, and this, as you see, is weak. The interpretation of it as *akhtan* and *rabaib* (stepdaughters) was also objected to: that the context is one of favour, and one is not favoured by that. It was answered that the favour is considered in terms of service, and it is not hidden that this is a correct (*musahhah*) but not a preferred (*murajjah*) reading.

It was said: *hafadah* are the servants and helpers, and this is the well-known meaning of the word linguistically. The accusative case here too is by an understood verb, i.e., *and He made for you servants who serve in your interests and assist you in your affairs*.

Ibn 'Atiyyah, after citing several opinions about the meaning of this, said: "These opinions are based on the premise that each person was given, from his wife, sons and grandchildren, and it is not hidden that this is in consideration of the majority. It is possible that His words, *from your spouses*, be taken in a general and shared sense, i.e., He made from the spouses of mankind sons and grandchildren, and on this basis it is correct to apply *hafadah* in its linguistic sense, since mankind as a whole does not do without grandchildren." Then the matter does not need a supposed verb, but it is not hidden that there is a remoteness in it. The placing of the accusative objects in both places after the prepositional phrase is for what has passed many times, namely the creation of suspense (*tashwiq*). Placing the prepositional phrase with *li* (for) before the one with *min* (from) is to indicate from the beginning that the benefit of the making returns to them, providing support for the suspense and strengthening it.

﴿And provided you with good things (*tayyibat*)﴾, i.e., delicacies, and this is its linguistic meaning. It was permitted that what is meant by *tayyib* is what is customary in the language of the Shari'ah, namely what is lawful (*halal*). Abu Hayyan objected to this: the addressees here are the disbelievers, who have no Shari'ah, so interpreting it in that way is not evident. It was answered that they are obligated with the branches (*furu'*) just as with the roots (*usul*), so lawful and unlawful apply to them; and also they are provided with much of the lawful, of which they have eaten some, and this does not entail that they believe in its lawfulness or the like. And *min* is partitive (*lil-tab'id*), for what they were provided with is a part of all the good things, since what is in this world of them in its entirety is a model (*unmudhaj*) of what is in the Hereafter, for there are in it things that no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and that have not occurred to the heart of any human, while much of what is in this world has not reached them. The apparent meaning, as we have said, is the generality of *tayyibat* to plants, fruits, grains, drinks, and animals. It was said: what is meant by them is what comes without toil. It was said: the spoils of war. But this is nothing.

﴿Then do they believe in falsehood (*al-batil*)﴾, which is the benefit and blessing of the idols, and that is nothing but a false delusion, for they did not arrive at it by proof or sign. The prepositional phrase is connected to His words, ﴿they believe﴾. It was placed first for restriction (*hasr*), which conveys that they have no faith except in that, as if it were a known and certain matter. ﴿And in the blessing of Allah﴾, the visible and manifest one, about which there is no doubt for one of intellect and discernment, of what has been mentioned and of what the circle of expression cannot encompass, ﴿they disbelieve﴾, i.e., they persist in disbelief in it and denial of it, as one denies what is impossible that the intellects cannot conceive. And this is by attributing it to their idols.
