It was said: *al-batil* is what Satan adorns for them of the prohibition of the *bahirah* and *sa'ibah* and others, and the blessing of Allah the Exalted is what He made lawful for them. On this view the verse is evidently connected only to His words, ﴿and provided you with good things﴾, and not to what precedes it, but the apparent view is that it is connected to both. From this there appears the state of what Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn Jurayj, that the falsehood is Satan and the blessing of Allah the Exalted is Muhammad (ﷺ). What we have mentioned has been stated for the most part by al-Zamakhshari. The deduction of restriction from the fronting is evident. As for "as if it were a known and certain matter," it is deduced from their restricting faith to what was mentioned, because that is the attitude of one who believes in it, especially since they were restricted. Also, the contrast of the perceived, sensible reality, namely the blessing of Allah the Exalted, indicates their reversal, so it indicates that they made the imagined to be like the certain and vice versa. The *fa'* which indicates reversal is very strong in indicating this matter. Taking it as coordination with something omitted is not the proper reading, as in the *Kashf*. In this there is a rebuttal of what has been said, that in both constructions there is emphasis and restriction: restriction in both through the fronting of the complement, and emphasis in the first because the *fa'* requires an antecedent, whose estimate is: "Do they disbelieve in the truth and believe in falsehood?" and disbelief in the truth entails belief in falsehood, so belief in falsehood has been repeated, and repetition conveys emphasis. Emphasis in the second is from building *yakfuruna* on *hum*, which conveys the strengthening of the judgment. The words of al-Zamakhshari were taken as pointing to all of this, so reflect on it.

What has been mentioned, that the fronting of the prepositional phrase in both constructions is for restriction, is something that more than one has stated explicitly. The Allamah al-Baydawi permitted this, but he introduced the notion of implicit indication (*iham*) here, in the same way as we did in what preceded just now. The reasoning is that the situation is not one of restriction in the strict sense, since their belief in falsehood is not exclusive to them, nor is their disbelief in the blessings of Allah the Exalted. He did not introduce it in explaining the parallel of this in *al-'Ankabut*. If it is argued that when they believe in falsehood, their belief in other than it is like non-existence, and that all blessings are from Allah the Exalted, either directly or through intermediaries, so their disbelief is only in His blessings, as is said: "He who does not thank people does not thank Allah," the discrepancy remains. It was answered that if one looks at the actual reality, there is no restriction in it, but if what has been mentioned is considered, the restriction is claimed (*ida'iyy*), and this is the meaning of implicit indication for the sake of emphasis, so there is no contradiction. It was also permitted that the fronting is for the sake of importance, since the matter intended by the denial, to which the speech was directed, is the connection of their disbelief to the blessing of Allah the Exalted and their adherence to falsehood, not the absolute of faith and disbelief. It was also permitted that it is for the sake of observing the rhyme (*fawasil*), but this is below the two points. And the shift to the third person is to indicate that their condition deserves turning away from them and directing the address to other listeners, to marvel at them for what they did.

In al-Bahr it is related that al-Sulami read *tu'minun* with the *ta'*, in the second person, and that he narrated this from 'Asim. On this reading, the sentence that follows it is, as al-Bahr inclined to think, free of the disbelievers and not included in the rebuke. There remains the matter that in *al-'Ankabut* it occurs: ﴿Then do they believe in falsehood, and in the blessing of Allah do they disbelieve?﴾ without the pronoun, while here what you have heard occurs with the pronoun. Al-Khafaji explained the secret of this: since in this surah there was already His words, ﴿Then in the blessing of Allah do they deny?﴾, i.e., disbelieve, as has passed, if what we are dealing with were mentioned without the pronoun, the verse would be a repetition in appearance. So He came with the pronoun, which indicates intensification and emphasis, so that it would be an escalation in censure, far from being purposeless. Then he said: It was also said that it is conformed to the custom of people, when they report about someone a disapproved matter, finding an aversion, and then they report about his other state with a statement more emphatic than the first. It is not hidden that this is only useful if one is asked why it was said, "Then do they believe in falsehood," without the pronoun, and "And in the blessing of Allah, they disbelieve in it." As for the distinction between what is here and what is there, it is not useful. It was also said: the verses of *al-'Ankabut* continued in the third person, so there was no need to add the third-person pronoun, while the verse we are dealing with has many preceding second-person addresses, so the third-person pronoun emphasizing it was necessary, lest it be confused with the address. The singling out of this verse for the addition, rather than "Then do they believe in falsehood," although the latter is apparently more deserving of it because it comes first, is so that the first clause does not become longer than the second. It was objected to this: it is not hidden that there is no requirement for the third person to be necessary, nor is there any confusion if the pronoun were left out.

It may be said: the reason the pronoun is not used in the verse of al-Ankabut, with the verb built upon it, is to express intensification (al-taqawwi), relying on the repetition of what conveys the disbelief of the people in the blessings, given its proximity to that verse, from which it is not far. Moreover, there has already appeared there something from which both clauses draw support in the most complete manner, though there is in it a kind of distance and some difference. That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who believe in falsehood and disbelieve in Allah, those are the losers﴾ [al-Ankabut: 52]. Since the verse of al-Nahl, as mentioned, is not at this level, what conveys intensification has been brought in it. Or it may be said: since the enumeration of the blessings here is in a manifest manner regarding their reaching them and the bestowal of them upon them, it is more fitting that what conveys their disbelief in them be brought in a way that indicates the improbability of its occurring from them, so the pronoun was brought in it. And since what is there is not like that, the pronoun was not brought in it with what was mentioned. Perhaps the expression here, "yakfuruna" (they disbelieve), and earlier, "yajhadun" (they deny), is because what precedes was, as has been said, preceded by the striking of a parable for the complete ugliness of what they did, and denial (al-juhud) is more fitting for that, since the complete ugliness in it is more perfect; this is not the case in what is under discussion. Thus it has been said, so understand. And Allah, exalted is He, is most knowing of the secrets of His Book.

[Page 193]

Abu Hayyan said: It is a resumptive statement (istinaf, a new sentence that is not grammatically linked to what precedes it), informing about their condition in worshipping idols. It also clarifies His saying, ﴿Do they then believe in falsehood?﴾

Some of the eminent verifiers (muhaqqiqun) said: It may be coordinated (ʿatf) with "they disbelieve" (yakfuruna), falling under the reproachful rebuke (inkar tawbikhi). That is: ﴿Do they disbelieve in the blessing of God and worship, besides Him, what does not possess for them any provision from the heavens and the earth, anything?﴾ That is, what is not able to provide them with anything, neither rain from the heavens nor vegetation from the earth.

"Rizqan" (provision) is a verbal noun (masdar). "Shay'an" (anything) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu, the object indicating the reason). This is the view of Abu ʿAli and others. Ibn al-Tarawa objected to this, saying that rizq (with a kasra) is the thing provided, like ruʿy (pasturage) and tahn (grinding), and that the verbal noun is rizq with a fatha on the ra', like ruʿy and tahn. It was answered that rizq with a kasra on the ra' is also a verbal noun, like ʿilm (knowledge), and it has been heard with this form, so it is valid for it to govern the object. It was also said that it is an ism masdar (a noun functioning as a verbal noun), and the Kufan grammarians permit its governing the object; so "shay'an" is its object according to their opinion.

It is also permitted that "rizqan" means "marzuq" (what is provided), and "shay'an" is then a substitute (badal) of it, meaning: it does not possess for them anything. Al-Samin and Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that it is not beneficial, since it is known that provision is among things, and a substitute comes for one of two purposes, explanation (bayan) or emphasis (taʾkid), and neither is present here. It was answered that the tanwin (nunation) of "shay'an" indicates minimization and belittling. If the tanwin of "rizqan" is of the same kind, then it is an emphasis; otherwise it is an explanation. In that case it is valid for it to be a substitute of part or of whole, and there is no difficulty.

It is also permitted that "shay'an" is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of "yamliku" (does not possess), meaning: it does not possess anything of possession. "Min al-samawat" (from the heavens) is either connected to His saying "does not possess," or to an omitted word that functions as a qualifier of "rizqan," meaning: a provision existing from both of them. The application of "rizq" to rain is because it arises from it.

﴿And they are not able﴾: It is permitted that this be coordinated with the relative clause of "ma" (what), or that it be a resumptive statement informing about the condition of the gods. "Istataʿa" (to be able) is transitive, and its object is omitted, which is the pronoun referring to possession; that is: they are not able to possess that, and it is not possible for them. So the sentence completes what precedes it, and it contains the progression (tarakki) that it contains. Thus the denial of the ability to possess is not unnecessary after the denial of possessing provision. If the object is taken to be the pronoun referring to provision, as the Kashshaf permitted, then this denial is an emphasis of what precedes it.

It was objected that the rhetoricians have established that a conjunction does not enter between the emphasizing and the emphasized, because of the complete connection between them. It was answered that this is not accepted by the grammarians, and it is not absolute according to the rhetoricians. Do you not see His saying: ﴿No! They will soon know﴾, ﴿Then no! They will soon know﴾ [An-Naba' 78:4-5]. Yes, the hadith that "establishing (ta'sis) is better than emphasis (ta'kid)" does object to this. It is also permitted, and perhaps it is the better view, that the verb is treated as intransitive, so the meaning is the negation of ability from them absolutely, in a manner that gives and withholds (yuʿti wa yamna'). The meaning is that they are dead, with no power at all. Then it is a concluding statement (tadhyil) for the preceding speech. In this there is what there is in the first view, plus something more.

The pronoun in it is plural and in "la yamliku" it is singular, out of consideration first for the wording and then for the meaning, since "ma" is singular in form while meaning gods. Such consideration occurs in eloquent speech, even though some have denied it because of the ambiguity that follows explanation, which contradicts eloquence. But that is rejected, as explained in its proper place. The expression also takes into account the actual state of what they worship: they are stones and inanimate things, so it refers to them with "ma," which in the common usage is for non-rational beings. And their state according to their belief that they are gods is referred to with the plural pronoun, which is for rational beings. This is when "ma" means idols. The situation is not hidden from you when "ma" means false objects of worship in general, whether they are angels, humans, stones, or others.

It is also permitted that the plural pronoun refers to the disbelievers, like the pronoun in "ya'buduna" (they worship), and "ma" is in its well-known meaning. The sense is that they, despite being living beings who manage affairs, are not able to do any of that, so how about an inanimate thing that has no sense? Thus the clause "la yastatiʿuna" (they are not able) is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) to emphasize the denial of possession from the gods, and the object is omitted as indicated. Although this is contrary to the apparent meaning, it is free from contradicting the well-known view of agreement in meaning after observing the wording.

[Page 194]

﴿So do not strike out similitudes for God﴾ is a shift to direct address (iltifat, a shift in grammatical person), to signal the importance of the prohibition. The fa' (the conjunctive "so") indicates that the prohibition follows from what was enumerated: the blessings God has poured out upon them, and that their gods are powerless to provide them with any sustenance, let alone surplus. Al-amthal is the plural of mathal, like 'alam. The meaning of ḍarb (striking) here is ja'l (making, setting up), so it is as if it were said: "Do not make for God, exalted is He, similitudes and equals." The verse is thus like His saying: ﴿So do not set up rivals to God﴾. This is what the apparent meaning of Ibn 'Abbas's words requires, for Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim report from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said regarding the verse: "He, glorified is He, says: Do not make a god alongside Me, for there is no god other than Me."

Some have read kathir al-amthal as the plural of mathal with a vowel change (mathal, pronounced with a fatha on the second letter), and the meaning of striking a similitude for God, glorified is He, is associating partners with Him and likening Him to His creation, which is by way of metaphor of representation (al-isti'arah al-tamthiliyyah, an extended metaphor drawn from a whole scene). In al-Kashf it is said that God has made the associated partner whom they liken to Him, by His creation, in the position of the one who strikes the similitude, for the deluded one who likens compares one attribute to another attribute and one essence to another essence, just as the one who strikes the similitude does. It is as if it were said: "Do not associate anything with God, glorified is He." He turned away from this to the indefinite form (al-munazzal) to indicate generality in the prohibition against comparison, both in attributes and in essence. The word "al-amthal" (the similitudes), applied to One who has no likeness whatsoever, contains a severe rebuke of them for their evil conduct. Within it is also an idmaj (an embedded implication, a subtle inclusion of a further point), namely that the names are tawqifiyyah (determined only by revelation, not by human choice). This is the apparent meaning, given the indication of the fa' and the absence of any previous mention of a similitude struck by them. This is the view chosen by al-Zamakhshari, and the words of the scholar (al-hibr), may Allah be pleased with him, do not contradict it. Thus His saying ﴿Indeed God knows, and you do not know﴾ is the justification (ta'lil) for the prohibition, meaning: He knows the true nature and magnitude of what you do, and He will punish you for it with the greatest punishment, while you do not know its true nature or the true nature of its punishment. That is why it has come from you and you have ventured upon it boldly.

It is also permitted that the meaning is a prohibition against measuring God by analogy with others, by making the striking of a similitude a metaphor for qiyas (analogy). Qiyas is the joining of one thing to another, and in its reality it is the comparison of a compound with a compound. The difference between this and the previous view is slight, and the matter of the justification remains as it is. Al-Zamakhshari and others also permitted that the meaning is a prohibition against striking similitudes for God, glorified is He, in the literal sense, so that the meaning is: "Do not strike for God, exalted is He, the similitudes that some of you strike for others. Indeed God knows how similitudes are struck, and you do not know." The reasoning behind the justification is clear. In all the other interpretations, the lam (of li-Allah) is connected to tadribu (strike).

Ibn al-Munir claimed that it is connected to al-amthal when the meaning is the representation of association and likening, and then said: "It is as if it were said: 'Do not represent God, exalted is He, and do not liken Him.'" And its connection to tadribu on this interpretation, then he said: "It is as if it were said: 'Do not represent for God, exalted is He, the similitudes, for striking a similitude is only used by one who knows toward one who does not know, to clarify for him what is hidden from him, and God, exalted is He, is the All-Knowing, while you do not know. So representing one who does not know for one who knows is the reverse of reality.'" But this is not right. The meaning he mentioned, on the assumption that it is connected to the verb, contradicts what the context requires, even though the justification is more evident on it. For this reason the meticulous scholar in al-Kashf said, after stating that God forbade the literal striking of similitudes: "It seems that the intent is to stress that they should not deviate in His names and attributes, for when the striking of a similitude and the metaphors are not permitted, the existence of some resemblance suffices for them, and the use of a relation of this kind is sufficient. Thus the impermissibility of applying names without prior instruction from Him, and affirming attributes, is more fitting and still more fitting."

The connection of His words, ﴿God strikes a parable﴾ and so on, according to the meticulous scholar (al-Mudaqqiq), is this: after He forbade them from striking parables for Him, glory be to Him, He struck a parable by which He showed that they are not fit for that. And if they are at this level of knowledge, imitation, or obstinacy, then they have no capacity for striking exact parables, which require acuity and guidance to the right path. Another scholar said about this, and it is probably more evident than the former, that when He mentioned that He knows how parables are struck, and that they do not know how parables are struck in this matter, He said, ﴿God strikes [a parable]﴾ and so on.

The connection according to what preceded, namely that the prohibition concerns associating partners with God, is that when He, glory be to Him, forbade them from striking the practical parable, which is association, He followed it with an unveiling, for the one who has insight, of the corruption of what they had committed, by His words, glory be to Him, ﴿God strikes﴾ and so on, that is, He presented and mentioned what can be used as evidence for the difference in condition between His exalted Presence and what they associated with Him, and it calls out clearly to the corruption of what they are upon. ﴿A slave owned, who has power over nothing﴾ is a substitute for "a parable" and an explanation of it. The parable in reality is his condition that befalls him, of being owned and of complete incapacity, and according to it the parable of his self is struck. He described the slave by being owned in order to distinguish him from the free person, since they share in being slaves of God, exalted is He. It has been said that it includes, according to what is said, that all are slaves of Him, exalted is He. The lack of power is for distinguishing him from the mukatab (the slave contracted to buy his freedom) and the ma'dhun (the licensed slave), who have some disposal. In the vagueness of the parable at first, then its clarification with what is mentioned, there is a sublimity that is not hidden.

﴿And one whom We have provided﴾: "man" is an indefinite qualified noun, according to what al-Zamakhshari inclined to, so that it corresponds with ﴿a slave﴾, for it too is an indefinite qualified noun, and Abu al-Baqa' went to this. Al-Hawfi said it is a relative noun, and Abu Hayyan preferred it. Some claimed that this is because its use as a relative noun is more frequent than its use as a qualified noun. The first is the choice of the majority, that is, a free person whom We have provided with a provision by way of ownership. The shift to the first person plural is to indicate the difference between the condition of striking the parable and that of the provision. In choosing the pronoun of majesty there is an exaltation of the matter of that provision, and His words, glory be to Him, ﴿from Us﴾, increase that exaltation, that is, from Our great and exalted Presence, ﴿a good provision﴾, lawful and good, or approved, praised by people. From it, according to what is said, is derived that it is abundant, by Our reckoning, on the basis that scarcity, which is the sister of nonexistence, has no goodness in itself. ﴿So he spends from it﴾, out of bounty and benevolence. The fa' is for the consequence of spending upon provision, as if it were said: and whoever We have provided with a good provision from Us, and he spends. The choice of the verbal sentence, derived from the nominal sentence whose predicate is a verb, indicates the constancy and continuity of spending as a renewing act. ﴿Secretly and openly﴾, that is, in the state of secrecy and the state of openness, or the spending of secrecy and the spending of openness. The purpose is to explain the generality of his spending across times and the comprehensiveness of his benefaction, even to those who shun accepting it openly.

It is permissible that the description of him with abundance is taken from this, on the basis that what is meant by it is "however he wills," and this indicates the modes of disposal and the breadth of the one who disposes. The precedence of secrecy over openness is to announce its superiority over it. The discussion of this has already passed. Deviating from matching the two correlates by saying "and free, owning wealth" is more indicative of the difference in condition between him and his counterpart, because in the guidance of the sound intellect there is an aim at establishing the truth, that free persons too are under the yoke of His servitude, exalted is He, and that their ownership of what they own is only by God, exalted is He, granting it to them, without any part of their own in that. And it also seeks to intensify the indication of what the parable aims at, the difference in condition between the two parties being compared. For if the slave owned is not like the owning slave, then what do you think of the inanimate and of the Owner of the kingdom, the Creator of the worlds?

﴿Are they equal?﴾ The pronoun is plural although two are mentioned before it, and the expected form would have been "are equal" in dual. This is to indicate that what is meant by what is mentioned is whoever is characterized by the mentioned attributes from the two mentioned kinds, not two specific individuals from them. Although Ibn 'Asakir and a group transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that the verse was revealed concerning Hisham ibn 'Amr, who spent his wealth secretly and openly, and concerning his slave Abu al-Jawza', who used to forbid him, and God knows best its authenticity. It was also said that it was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may God be pleased with him, and a slave of his, but its chain is not sound, as in al-Bahr. In it is that it may be that the plural is by the consideration that what is meant by "whom" is the plural, and that it may be by the consideration of the pronoun returning to the slaves and the free, even though no mention of them has preceded, due to the indication of "a slave owned." And "whom We have provided" refers to both of them. What is relied upon is what was mentioned first. The meaning is: are the slaves and the free persons described by what was mentioned of the attributes equal, while both groups are equal in being human and created by God, glory be to Him, and what the free spend is not something they have any part in producing or owning, but rather it is what God, exalted is He, has given them? Since the two groups are not equal, then what do you think of you, the Lord of the worlds, when you associate with Him what is not more humble than Him, which are the idols?

It was said that this is a parable for the disbelieving forsaken person and the believing successful person. The former is likened to a slave who has no disposal, because of the nullification of his deeds, the non-regard for his actions, and his following of his desire, like the submissive slave who is joined with the beasts, unlike the believing successful person. Making it a parable for that is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, and Qatada. Nor is there any specification in it, even though it was said that the verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, and Abu Jahl. Abu Hayyan said that this attribution is not sound. Then know that they differed concerning whether a slave can own property or not. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: the apparent doctrine is that he cannot, and al-Shafi'i said so. Ibn al-Munir, as summarized in al-Kashf from a long discussion, said that ownership is valid for him according to Malik. The apparent meaning of the verse supports this, because He established incapacity for him by His words, ﴿owned﴾, then He negated the power that is accidental through the owner's granting of ownership, by His words, glory be to Him, ﴿who has power over nothing﴾. The meaning is not the power of disposal, because its counterpart is ﴿and whom We have provided from Us with a good provision﴾. And taking it as excluding the mukatab, despite its oddity, is concise but deficient, as Imam al-Haramayn, may God have mercy on him, said concerning: "Any woman who is married without the permission of her guardian..." The taking of it as referring to the contracted slave is far-fetched and not permissible, and the licensed slave is not excluded, for the reason already mentioned, that what is meant by power is what it is. It is not for one to say that it is a necessary, clarifying attribute, and that the basic principle regarding attributes is restriction. End of quote.

The meticulous scholar followed this with his words: The answer is that the meaning is the negation of power over disposal. The verse is revealed concerning the depiction of the condition of the idols by comparison with Him, exalted is He far above that, and whenever the helplessness of the one compared is emphasized and the perfection of the counterpart is emphasized, it indicates in the one compared as well that same thing. So what fits the context is power over disposal, and it stands opposite His words, ﴿he spends from it secretly and openly﴾. What he mentioned has no substance, and there is no deficiency in excluding the mukatab, since the wording includes it, and the context is one of emphasis, so what is supposed to enter by its aspect should be negated. How is this comparable to what he quoted from Imam al-Haramayn? End of quote. It is also argued from the verse that the slave also does not own divorce, and this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from him that he said: a slave has no divorce except with the permission of his master, and he recited the verse. The rulings of slaves have been detailed in the law of jurisprudence in the most complete manner.

﴿All praise is for God﴾, that is, all of it belongs to Him, glory be to Him, and no one deserves it other than Him, exalted is He, because He, exalted is His majesty, is the bestower of blessings, even if they appear at the hands of some intermediaries, let alone the deserving of worship.

In it is guidance to what is the truth, that what appears at the hand of one who spends in the aforementioned manner returns to Him, exalted is He, as He alluded to by ﴿We have provided﴾. Many said: this is praise for the clarity of the path and the strength of this proof. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ what has been mentioned, so they attribute His blessings to others and worship them for their sake, or they do not know the clarity of that and the strength of what is there, so they remain in their association and error. The negation of knowledge from most of them is to indicate that some of them know that, but they did not act upon its requirement out of obstinacy. It was said: what is meant by "most" is all, as if it were said: they do not know. And it was said: the pronoun in "they" refers to creation, and "most" are the polytheists. Both opinions are contrary to the apparent meaning.

[Page 197]

﴿And God strikes a parable﴾: that is, another parable, which indicates what the previous parable indicates, but in a more manifest and clearer way. He first left it indefinite and then clarified it with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿two men, one of whom is dumb﴾, corresponding to what preceded. "Al-bukm" (dumbness) is the muteness that accompanies one's creation, and it entails deafness. So the dumb man does not understand because he cannot hear, and others do not understand him because he cannot speak. Gesture is not taken into account, because it does not convey meaning fully and clearly to everyone. It is as if it were said: one of them is mute and deaf, and neither understands nor is understood. ﴿He has no power over anything﴾ among the matters related to himself or to others, whether by conjecture or by insight, because of the poverty of his understanding and perception. ﴿And he is a burden﴾, a heavy weight and a dependant ﴿upon his master﴾, upon the one who supports him and takes charge of his affairs. This is an explanation of his inability to manage his own interests, after the mention of his general inability. Then comes His saying, glorified be He:

[Page 198 is not a separate break in the text; continuing]

﴿Wherever he directs him, he brings no good﴾: that is, wherever his master sends him on a matter, he does not return with success or with the fulfilment of an important task. This is an explanation of his inability to serve his master's interests. ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) is reported in one transmission to have read "tuwajjihhu" (in the second person, as a verb addressed to the master). ʿAlqama, Ibn Ribʿ, Mujahid and Talha, and in another transmission from ʿAbd Allah, read "yuwajjih" with the active voice and the jussive. This is explained on the basis that the subject refers back to the master, and the object is omitted, namely the pronoun referring to the dumb man, that is, "yuwajjihuhu" (he directs him). It is also permissible that the pronoun of the subject refers back to the dumb man, and the verb is intransitive, with "wajjaha" meaning "tawajjaha" (to turn or set out). On this usage comes the saying of al-Adba' ibn Qarīʿ al-Saʿdī:

"Wherever I set out, you will find Saʿd..."

and ʿAlqama, ʿĀʾisha, and Ibn Thabbab also read "yuwajjah" with the jussive and the passive voice. In another transmission from ʿAlqama and Talha, they read "yuwajjihu" with a kasra on the jim and a damma on the ha. The author of al-Lawami' said: if this is authentic, then the ha which is the final radical of the verb has been omitted to avoid the doubling, or the word "ayna-ma" is not intended as a conditional particle, and the meaning is "wherever he is directed," with the object pronoun omitted; so the ya' is dropped from the end of "ya'ti" for lightness. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that "ayna" does not leave the sense of a conditional or interrogative. It is reported from Abu Hatim that this reading is weak, because the jussive is required. Then he said: what this reading may be justified by is that "ayna-ma" is a conditional, treated as "idha" (when) by virtue of what they share of the conditional sense; then the ya' of "ya'ti" was dropped for lightness, or it was put in the jussive on the assumption that "ayna-ma" was used as a jussive particle, as in the reading of one who reads "innahu man yattaqi wa yasbir" in one of its two possibilities. The meaning of "yuwajjih" is "yatawajjah" (he turns), as mentioned just before.

﴿Are the two equal?﴾: that is, is that dumb man, described by those attributes mentioned, ﴿and one who commands justice﴾, who is articulate, understanding, possessing sound judgement and right guidance, who suffices people in their important matters and benefits them by urging them to justice, which gathers all the virtues, ﴿and he﴾ in himself, along with what has been mentioned of his particular and general benefit, ﴿is on a straight path﴾, not turning to any aim without reaching it by the nearest effort. So the clause is a circumstantial clause, explaining his perfection in himself. Since this perfection precedes his perfecting others, it is expressed as a nominal sentence, for it indicates that, together with its permanence, it is concurrent with the state of its subject. So it should not be said: the more fitting arrangement would have been to place it earlier in the noble structure. The contrast between those four attributes and these two descriptions is because these two are the completion and the culmination of what corresponds to them; so the last of the attributes of the perfect is chosen, which entails what has been mentioned and goes further, since he is made a guide who is himself guided. The change of style, in not saying "and the other commands justice" and so on, is to preserve harmony between it and the purpose of showing the contrast between the two groups. It may be said here, as was said of the previous parable: since the two groups are not equal in excellence and honour, though they are equal in essence and form, then how much more so is it that the idol, which does not speak or hear, is powerless, has no power over anything, and is a burden upon its worshipper, needing to be carried, set down, have harm wiped from it when it falls, and be served; and if one directs it to any of one's needs, it does not benefit him nor bring him anything. Such a thing is not equal to the Lord of the worlds, and He is far more deserving and worthier of being worshipped. It has also been said that this is a parable for the believer and the disbeliever: the dumb man is the disbeliever, and the one who commands justice is the believer. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both. Whatever the case, the intended "two men" are not two specific individuals, but two men characterized by the attributes mentioned, in general. As for what is reported, that the dumb man was Abu Jahl and the one commanding justice was ʿAmmar, or that the dumb man was Ubayy ibn Khalaf and the one commanding justice was ʿUthman ibn Maz'un, Abu Hayyan said: its chain of transmission is not sound. And what Ibn Jarir, Ibn ʿAsakir and others narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, that he said: this verse, "And God strikes a parable, two men..." and so on, was revealed concerning ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan and a non-Muslim client of his, who was Usayd ibn Abi al-ʿIs, who disliked Islam. ʿUthman used to support him, provide for him, and relieve him of his burdens, while the other would forbid him from charity and good works; so this verse was revealed about them both. After verifying its authenticity, it does not harm us in taking the two described individuals in general, such that those mentioned enter into them, for the scholars have stated that the specificity of a cause does not negate the generality of the ruling.

This is what Shaykh al-Islam confined himself to, namely that the purpose of the two parables is to deny equality between Him, may His majesty be exalted, and what they associate with Him. This is evidence that it is his preferred view. Then he said: know that neither of the two verbs is intended to narrate a past striking, but rather their intent is the initiation of the parable with what is mentioned after it. It is not far-fetched to say that God, exalted be He, struck a parable through the creation of the two groups as they are, so their creation was such, in order to deduce from their non-equality the perfection of the equality between Him, glorified and exalted be He, and what they associate with Him. Thus each of the two verbs is a narration of a past striking. End of quotation. It is not hidden that there is no dispute about the goodness of his choice, but there is something in my soul about his saying "it is not far-fetched."

**Ruh al-Ma'ani** of al-Alusi, on surah 16, verse 77:

﴿To Allah﴾, exalted is He, exclusively, not to anyone else, either independently or as a partner, ﴿belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning all the matters hidden from the knowledge of created beings, such that there is no way for them to perceive them by the senses or comprehend them by the intellect. The meaning of the idafah (possessive construction) to them both is that the unseen is connected to them, either in terms of its occurring within them, presently or eventually, or in terms of its being hidden from their inhabitants. There is no need to supply an elided term for this mudaf (the first term of the construction). The intended meaning is to show that the unseen is exclusive to Him, exalted is He, in terms of its being known, as indicated by the title "the unseen," and not in terms of its being created and owned, although that is also the case in reality. It implies, as in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim (Abu al-Su'ud's commentary), that His knowledge, exalted is He, is presential (huduri, knowledge that is immediately present to its object), and that the unseen things are realized in themselves in relation to Him, glorified is He. For this reason He did not say, "and to Allah belongs the knowledge of the unseen of the heavens and the earth." It has also been said that what is meant by the unseen of the heavens and the earth is what is mentioned in His words, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour and sends down the rain﴾ [Luqman: 34], etc. It has also been said that it means the Day of Resurrection. It is not hidden that the view of generality is preferable.

﴿And the matter of the Hour﴾, which is the greatest of the unseen matters connected to the heavens and the earth about which disputes arise, in terms of its being hidden from their inhabitants, or in terms of the manifestation of its effects in them at the time of its occurrence, meaning: and its affair in terms of the speed of its coming, ﴿is but as a glance of the eye﴾, meaning like the return of the glance from the top of the eyeball to its bottom. In al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's al-Bahr al-Muhit), it is said that al-lamh is a rapid look; one says, "He glanced at it (lamahahu) with a glance (lamhan) and a rapid glance (lamahanan) when he looked at it quickly." ﴿Or it is nearer﴾, meaning its affair is nearer than that and quicker, in that it occurs within some part of its time. For the return of the glance from the top of the eyeball to its bottom, however brief, is a motion in place which has a continuous identity, coinciding with a time which itself is of this kind, capable of division into parts that are themselves times. Rather, it occurs within what is called an instant (an), which is an indivisible part of time, like the instant at which motion begins. As for ﴿أو (aw)﴾, al-Farra' said it means "bal" (rather).

Abu Hayyan refuted this in al-Bahr, saying that bal is for idrab (a turning away from one statement to another), and this does not hold here in either of its two forms. As for abtal (cancellation of the prior statement), it leads to the conclusion that the preceding judgment does not correspond to reality, so that reporting it would be a lie, and Allah, glorified is He, is exalted above that. As for intiqal (transition to a further statement), it entails a contradiction between reporting that it is like the glance of the eye and reporting that it is nearer, so both cannot be true together, and it entails the impossible falsehood. It was answered that the second (intiqal) is intended, and there is no contradiction between comparing it in speed to the utmost that people know in this regard, and its being in reality nearer than that. This was built on the premise that the purpose of the comparison is to show its speed, not to specify the quantity of the time of its occurrence and its limit. It was also answered with what validates it in both its parts: that it came according to the custom of people, meaning that when they are asked about its matter, it is said of it, "it is like the glance of the eye," and then one turns from it to what is nearer. It has been said that ﴿أو﴾ is for choice (takhyir). Abu Hayyan also refuted this in al-Bahr, saying that it is only used in prohibited matters, such as "take from my wealth a dinar or a dirham," or in obligations, such as the verse of expiations. It was answered that this is based on the view of Ibn Malik that ﴿أو﴾ comes for choice, and that this is not restricted to occurring after a request, but occurs in a declarative statement and is frequent in comparison, to the point that some have restricted it to that.

Page 199

In Sharh al-Hadi, it is said: know that choice (takhyir) and permission (ibahah) are restricted to commands, since they have no meaning in declarative statements, just as doubt and uncertainty are restricted to declarative statements. Permission has come in other than commands, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The likeness of those who kindled a fire﴾ to His saying, glorified is He: ﴿or like a rain-cloud from the sky﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17–19], meaning: with either of these two you have compared, you are correct, and likewise if you compare with both together. Similar examples in poetry are numerous. It has also been said that what is meant is the choice given to the addressee after supposing a request and question, so there is no need to base it on what was mentioned, and this is, as you see, [weak]. Some have claimed that choice is problematic from another angle: that one of the two matters, being like the glance of the eye or nearer, does not correspond to reality, so how could Allah, exalted is He, give a choice between what does not correspond to it? It is answered that what is meant is choice in the comparison, and what harm is there in the non-occurrence of the thing compared to it? Indeed, the non-occurrence may even be considered beautiful in it, as in the saying:

Banners of ruby, displayed upon spears of emerald.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: ﴿أو﴾ is for doubt (shakk), in its basic sense, meaning that if it happened that a human being came to know its matter, it would be so swift that he would doubt whether it was like the glance of the eye or nearer. Abu Hayyan also criticized this in al-Bahr, saying that doubt is far-fetched, because this is a report from Allah, exalted is He, about the matter of the Hour, and doubt is impossible for Him, glorified is He. That is, it must be in relation to someone other than the speaker, and to adopt this is far-fetched. What confirms that this is his intent is that he justified its remoteness by impossibility. So his objection is not one that should cause wonder, as some have imagined. Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿أو﴾ is for indefiniteness (ibham), and it was criticized that there is no benefit in leaving the matter of its speed indefinite; the benefit lies in leaving the time of its arrival indefinite. It was answered that what is meant is that it is indefinite to the one who witnesses its speed, whether it is like the glance of the eye or less, so reflect. What is transmitted from Ibn Jurayj is that it means "bal" (rather), and many follow this. What is meant is the depiction of the speed of its arrival and its being close, in the form of exaggeration. Such exaggeration is abundant in verse, and among it is the saying of the poet:

Lightning said to him, and the winds said to him, all together, and they are what they are:
"Will you run with us?" He said, "If you become energetic, you will make both of you laugh at yourselves."
Indeed the returning of the glance has outpaced it, reaching the goal ahead; so who are you two?

It has also been said that the meaning is: and the matter of establishing the Hour, whose knowledge is exclusive to Him, glorified is He, which is the causing of the living to die and the raising of the dead, from the first and the last, and the altering of the forms of all existence, has been denied by those who deny it, and they have deemed it among what does not fall within the realm of possibility, in speed of occurrence and ease of accomplishment, except like the glance of the eye, or it is nearer, according to what has passed of the sayings regarding ﴿أو﴾. ﴿Indeed Allah is over all things capable﴾, and among all things is that He brings it in the quickest possible way; so He is capable of that. And according to the second view, one says: among that is the matter of its establishment, and He, glorified is He, is capable of it. So the clause is in the position of a justification. In al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari's commentary), it is said: on the assumption that the unseen is general and encompasses all that is hidden in the heavens and the earth, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the matter of the Hour﴾ is as if derived from the first and is like a preface to it; that is, the knowledge of every unseen thing, the Hour and other than it, is exclusive to Him, so He is the One who brings it, by knowledge and power. For this reason He followed it with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed Allah﴾, etc. As for when the unseen is intended to be the Hour, it is clear. End of quote. It is not hidden what the situation is according to the view that the unseen refers to what is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Allah has knowledge of the Hour and sends down the rain﴾ [Luqman: 34], etc. And according to the last view regarding the unseen, the mention of "the Hour" is the placing of the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, to strengthen the meaning of the clause.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 78:

﴿And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah made for you mates from yourselves﴾ [al-Nahl: 72].

[Page 200]

It is included with it in the string of proofs of tawhid (divine unity). From the words of the scholar al-Tibi it is understood that He, glorified is He, followed His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is competent over all things﴾ with His saying, majestic and exalted is He, ﴿And Allah brought you forth﴾ and so on, conjoined by the particle wa (and), signifying that His capabilities have no end, and what is mentioned is only a part of them. The coordination is with His saying, glorified is He: (Indeed Allah) and so on. What the soul finds agreeable is the first view.

Al-ummahat (the mothers) is pronounced with a damma on the hamza and also with a fatha on the hamza. It is the plural of umm (mother), and the ha' in it is an added letter (ha' al-ziyadah). Its addition is frequent, and it occurs without it too, and the meaning in both cases is one. It was said: the form with the added letter is for humans, and the form without it is for animals. The pattern of the singular is fuʿl, because of their saying al-umumah (motherhood). It came with the hā' as in the saying of Qusayy ibn Kilab, may the mercy of God be upon both of them:

Ummahti Khindif wa-Ilyas abi
("My mothers are Khindif, and Ilyas is my father.")

This is rare, and rarer still is the addition of the hā' in the verb, as is said in aharaqa (to spill). There is a discussion on this; return to the Sihah (Sihah al-Jawhari) and other works.

Hamzah recited with a kasra on the hamza and the mim here, and in al-Zumar, al-Najm and al-Rum; al-Kisa'i with a kasra on the mim in these. Al-A'mash recited with the deletion of the hamza and a kasra on the mim; Ibn Abi Layla with its deletion and a fatha on the mim. Abu Hatim said: the deletion of the hamza is inferior, but the reading of Ibn Abi Layla is more correct. And it was so according to al-Bahr, because the kasra on the mim is only for assimilating it to the vowel of the hamza; so when the hamza is deleted, the assimilation ceases. This differs from the reading of Ibn Abi Layla, for he kept the mim on its own vowel.

﴿You do not know anything﴾: it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). (Shay'an) is in the accusative either as a verbal noun (masdar) or as the object of (ta'lamun), and the negation is directed at it. Al-ʿilm (knowledge) here means ma'rifah (recognition), i.e., you were not knowing anything at all of the right of the Benefactor or otherwise. It was said: anything of your benefits. It was said: of what He decreed upon you of happiness or misery. It was said: of the covenant He took from you in the loins of your fathers. The apparent meaning is generality, and there is no reason to restrict it. On the authority of Wahb: the child is born stupefied for seven days, not perceiving comfort or pain.

Some have claimed that the soul is not free, at the beginning of its natural disposition (fitrah), from immediate knowledge (al-ʿilm al-hudūrī), which is its knowledge of itself, since the immaterial does not become absent from its own essence at all. The Shaykh (Ibn Sina) said in some of his glosses, when establishing the immateriality of the soul: "You are never unaware of your essence at all, in any state, even in sleep or intoxication. If it were permitted that one be unaware of his essence in some states, so that between him and inanimate matter there is no difference in this state, then this proof would not profit against him." Bahmanyar said in al-Tahsil, in the section on intellect and the intelligible: "Then the human soul is aware of its own essence, so its existence must be intellectual, so the very existence of it is the very apprehension of it, and for this reason it is never absent from its essence." Its like is in al-Shifa'. You know that the non-vacuity is based on hidden premises, such as the immateriality of the soul, which the naturalists (al-tabi'iyyun) all denied, and that every immaterial thing is a world, and the proof is not complete on this. Also, what is reported, that the soul's knowledge of its essence is identical with its essence, does not preclude that for the essence to be knowledge of itself a condition is required; so as long as that condition is not realized, the essence is not knowledge of itself, just as for the overflowing principle (al-mabda' al-fayyad) to be a treasury of the intelligibles of Zayd, for example, is a condition, which if realized is realized, and otherwise not. This is confirmed by the fact that the soul's knowledge of its attributes is also, according to them, the very attributes themselves, and yet it is permissible to be unaware of an attribute at some times, as is not hidden.

Also, if we say: the reality of the essence is not absent from it, and we say: that is knowledge of it, it follows that the reality of the immaterial soul would be known to everyone, and it is clear that this is not so. Moreover, the verifier al-Tusi has rejected their saying: "You never become unaware of your essence." He said: the one under anaesthesia may be unaware of his essence at the time of anaesthesia, and like it are many psychological illnesses. Among the wonders is that some of the eminent scholars mentioned that the intended meaning of its being empty at the beginning of its natural disposition is its emptiness at the time of its attachment to the body, and he said: this does not preclude

[Page 201]

what the Shaykh said, that the infant attaches to the breast at the moment of birth by an innate inspiration, because the state of attachment is prior to that. This was after he mentioned that the emptiness at the beginning of the natural disposition only becomes apparent to those with intuition (dhawi al-hads) by observing the state of the infant and the experiences of its conditions. The wonder of it is evident; understand this and do not be heedless.

Interpreting knowledge as recognition (ma'rifah) is what many have adopted. In Amali al-ʿIzz: it is not permissible that it be left on its original sense and that (shay'an) be a verbal noun, meaning "you do not know knowledge," for two reasons. The first is that it entails the deletion of both objects, which is contrary to the original rule. The second is that if it were left on its original sense, people would know the subject that is one of the two objects before coming out of the wombs, and that is impossible, since knowledge of one who has not been born is impossible. The explanation of this is that when we say: "I knew Zayd to be residing," it must be that knowledge of Zayd precedes this knowledge, and this knowledge relates only to his residing. Likewise, when you say: "I did not know Zayd to be residing," what was not known is the residing of Zayd, while he himself is known, and this is established from the usage. So wherever knowledge is affirmed or negated, the first must be known, and so it is necessary to take knowledge to mean recognition. Thus it is clear from this that it is not right to leave knowledge on its own sense, and (shay'an) is its first object while the second object is deleted.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿And He made for you hearing, sight and hearts﴾ may be a fresh independent sentence, and it may be coordinated with the sentence which is the predicate (khabar) and the wa does not require sequence. The reason for delaying it is that hearing and the like, the instruments of perception, are only counted when they perceive and apprehend, and that is after coming forth. And (ja'ala) if it is transitive to one object, by being in the sense of (khalaqa, created), then (lakum, for you) is connected to it; and if it is transitive to two, by being in the sense of (sayyara, made), then it is its second object. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the objects is for what has passed more than once.

The meaning: He made these things for you as instruments by which you obtain knowledge and recognition, by your senses perceiving the particulars of things and by your hearts apprehending them, and by your being alert to what lies between them of agreements and differences through repeated sensation; thus there arise for you self-evident knowledge (ʿulum badihiyyah) by which you are enabled, through reflection on them, to acquire acquired knowledge (ʿulum kasbiyyah). This is the summary of what the Imam (al-Razi) mentioned in this place, and the basis of what many of the philosophers (hukama') adopted: that the soul at the beginning of its affair is empty of knowledge; then when it employs the outer senses, it perceives through the estimative faculty (al-quwwah al-wahmiyyah) particular matters with partial agreements and differences among them, and so it becomes prepared for the overflowing principle to pour upon it the universal agreements. They assert four stages for the soul: the stage of the material intellect (al-ʿaql al-hayulani); the stage of intellect in habit (al-ʿaql bi-l-malakah); the stage of intellect in actuality (al-ʿaql bi-l-fiʿl); and the stage of the acquired intellect (al-ʿaql al-mustafad). They claim that the soul does not perceive the material particular, and on this point they have a long discourse and a broad inquiry.

The People of the Sunnah say: the soul perceives the universal and the particular absolutely, by using the senses and without them, as is detailed in its place. The verification of this matter, with what is for it and what is against it, requires extensive elaboration, and it has been set out. The help is sought from the Living, the Self-Subsisting, majestic is His majesty and general His bounty, against the events that cause the disruption of the affairs of the elite and the common folk, which have confused my mind and come between me and the verification of that. I ask God, glorified is He, to bestow upon us what gladdens the heart, and to facilitate for us what will help in attaining the aim.

In sum, what is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, regarding this verse, is that he said: "He, glorified is He, intends that He made these for you so that you hear the admonitions of God, the Exalted, and see what God, the Exalted, has bestowed upon you of bringing you forth from the wombs of your mothers until you became men, and comprehend His greatness, glorified is He." It was also said: the meaning is: He made for you hearing so that you hear by it the texts of the Book and the Sunnah, which are auditory proofs, so that you may infer by them what sets right your religious affairs; and sight so that you see by it the wonders of His creation, the marvels of His created things, glorified is He, so that you infer by them His unity, majestic and exalted is He; and hearts so that you may understand by them the meanings of the things which He, glorified is He, made as signs for you. Hearing and sight, according to these two sayings, are in their apparent sense, and we have not seen anyone who permitted removing them from that.

It is permissible that by them be meant the outer senses according to the first view. (Al-af'idah, hearts) is the plural of fu'ad, which is the core of the heart, and it stands to the heart as the heart stands to the chest. This plural, according to what is in the Kashshaf, is of the paucity plurals (jumu' al-qillah) which function as the plurals of abundance, when no other forms are heard, as shusu' came as the plural of shis' only. So it took that course. Al-Zajjaj said: fu'ad was not pluralized in the form of the greatest number; it may be said af'idah and fi'dan, as they say aghribah and ghirban as plurals of ghurab. In al-Tafsir al-Kabir: perhaps fu'ad was pluralized in the paucity pattern to indicate that hearing and sight are many, while the heart is few, because it was created only for true recognitions and certain knowledge, and most of creation does not have that; rather they are occupied with bestial acts and beastly attributes, so their heart is as if it were no heart, and for this reason the paucity plural was used for it. End. But this is refuted by al-absar (sights), which is also a paucity plural. In al-Bahr, after quoting it, he said: it is a delirious saying, and were it not for the eminence of its author, we would not have recorded it in books. What should be said about this is what al-Zamakhshari said of what he mentioned earlier, except that his saying "shusu' is the only plural of shis'" is not correct; rather ashsa' came in it, a paucity plural of the paucity pattern. End. So memorize this and do not be heedless.

Some have claimed that the heart perceives only what is not bounded by such things as where, how, how much, and other things, and that for each perceived thing there is a perceiving faculty suited to it that cannot perceive it by anything else, as with the outer sensibles such as sounds, colours, tastes and the like, and the outer senses of hearing, sight, taste, and so on. And this, as you see, is (questionable).

The singular of hearing (al-sam') is used in consideration that it is originally a verbal noun. It was also said: sight is in the plural and hearing in the singular only to indicate that the objects of hearing are one kind, while the objects of sight are more than that. Its being placed first is because it is the channel for receiving revelation, or because its perception is earlier than that of sight. It was also said: because its objects are fewer than those of sight. The disagreement about which of them is better is famous and has passed. Its being placed before the hearts, which refers to the intellect, is because the outer precedes the inner, or because both have a role in perceiving it to some extent; indeed they are its servants, and servants walk before masters. Many of the sunan (recommended practices) are commanded to be placed before the obligatory acts of worship. Or because the objects of the two are a very small portion relative to the objects of the intellect; how could it not be so, when its objects are hardly countable? Even if it is said that the intellect has a limit at which it ends, as sight has a limit likewise, and some have taken as evidence the mention of what points to it alone, without adding what points to the other inner faculties, to negate the five inner senses which the philosophers established, with some turbidity, and the detailed discussion is in its place.

﴿So that you may give thanks﴾: so that you may know what He, glorified is He, has bestowed upon you, time after time, and thus give thanks to Him. It was said: the meaning is that He made that so that you thank God, exalted is He, by using what was mentioned for that for which it was created.

Page 203

﴿Have they not seen﴾. Ḥamzah, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ṭalḥah, al-Aʿmash and Ibn Hurmuz read ﴿Have you not seen﴾ with the second-person ta' (تاء فوقية). This is address to the general public, and the intended audience is all of creation, those addressed earlier in His words ﴿And Allah brought you forth from the wombs of your mothers﴾. It is not that the addressee is those mentioned in His words ﴿and they worship besides Allah﴾, with a shift in the mode of address (iltifat, الالتفات: a change in grammatical person within a passage). This is because the second person suits the rhetorical question of denial (al-istifham al-inkari). For this reason the majority reading (qirāʾat al-jumhūr, قراءة الجمهور: the standard recitation) uses the third-person ya' of absence, in view of the absence of ﴿they worship﴾, and they did not regard that as iltifat. In that case the denial is based on their being included in the general public. The seeing is visual: that is, have they not looked ﴿at the birds﴾, the plural of ṭā'ir, like rakb and rākib, and it can also apply to the singular, though that is not intended. It is also said in the plural ṭuyūr and aṭyār. ﴿Subjected﴾: made subservient to flying. This indicates that their flight is not by the demand of their nature.

﴿in the air of the sky﴾: in the air distant from the earth. The lawh (the expanse) and the sukkāk (the upper atmosphere) are further away than it. It is also said that al-jaw is the distance between the sky and the earth, and al-jaw is a dialectal variant of it. Its attribution to the sky is because it lies on the side of the sky from the viewpoint of the observer, and to demonstrate the perfection of power. From al-Suddi, al-jaw is interpreted as al-jawf (the hollow, interior space), and on this reading "the sky" is interpreted as the direction of height. Birds may fly in this direction until they disappear from sight, and no one knows the limit of their height in flight except Allah the Exalted. From Kaʿb: birds do not rise higher than twelve miles.

﴿None holds them up﴾ in the air from falling, ﴿except Allah﴾, Mighty and Majestic, by His vast power, for the weight of their bodies and the thinness of the air require their fall. There is no tie above them and no support beneath them. The clause is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, حال: a clause describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) from the implicit pronoun in ﴿subjected﴾, or from ﴿the birds﴾, or it is a new independent clause (mustaʾnafa, مستأنفة). ﴿Indeed in that﴾, referring to what has been mentioned of their subjection in the air and their being held up in it. It is also said that what is indicated is what this verse and the one before it contain, ﴿are signs﴾ indicating the perfection of His power, exalted is His majesty, ﴿for a people who believe﴾: that is, it is incumbent on them to believe. This is specified for them because they are the ones who benefit from it.

The Imam (al-Imam) confined the referent to what is in this verse and said: "This is evidence of the perfection of Allah's power and His wisdom, glory be to Him. He, exalted is His majesty, created the bird with a nature by which flight is possible for it. He gave it a wing which it extends at one time and folds at another, like the swimmer's action in water. He created the air with a nature by which flight is possible. He created it with a fine nature by which it is easy to cleave and pass through. Without that, flight would not be possible." End of quotation.

Likewise Mawla Abu al-Suʿud said: "Indeed in that which has been mentioned, the subjection of birds to flight, by creating them with a nature by which they can do so, by giving them light wings and similarly light tails, and making their bodies so light that when they spread their wings and tails, their weight cannot prevent them from cleaving the thin air beneath them and cleaving the air before them, since they do not meet it with a large mass, are clear signs." He mentioned that their subjection is by what He created for them of wings and supporting means.

Abu Ḥayyān followed this with his words: "What we say is that it was possible for the bird to fly even if no wing had been created for it, and that it was possible for it to cleave a dense object, by the power of Allah the Exalted. We do not say that were it not for the wing, the fineness of the air and the instruments, flight would not have been possible." End of quotation. I do not think anyone denies the inherent possibility of flight without a wing, for example, but it is not far-fetched to deny it without the fineness of the air; whenever the dense is cleaved, the air is fine. So understand.

The verse has been cited as evidence that the servant is the creator of his own actions. The judge (al-Qadi) interpreted it otherwise, and that is an assertion contrary to the apparent meaning without any evidence.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 80:

﴿And Allah has made for you﴾ is conjoined to what came before. The fronting of *lakum* ("for you") before what follows serves to arouse interest (*tashwīq*) and to indicate from the outset that this making is for your benefit. His saying, ﴿from your houses﴾, specifies that indefinite made thing in general terms and reinforces the interest already aroused. The genitive (*iḍāfa*) here is one of familiarity (*li-l-ʿahd*), meaning: from your familiar houses, which you build of stone, clay, and wood. ﴿A place of rest (sakanan)﴾: *sakan* is a noun of the pattern *faʿal* in the sense of *mafʿūl* (object of the verb), like *naqaḍa* (broken, in the sense of what is broken). Al-Farrāʾ recited:

When winter came and I had not made a place of rest,
Woe to me, from digging the holes of the (dwellings of) the cold!

It is not a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), as Ibn ʿAṭiyya held. It means a place in which you rest during your stay. It is also permissible that the meaning is: you find rest in it without moving from its place, i.e., He made some of your houses such that you find rest in them and are at peace with them.

﴿And He made for you from the hides of the cattle houses﴾: that is, other houses, different from your familiar houses, namely the tents made of leather (*adam*). The apparent view is that the houses made of hair, wool, and fur are not included in these houses. Ibn Sallām and others said they are included, because insofar as they stand upon their hides, it is true to say that they are made of their hides. It has been objected that *min* (from) in the first case is partitive (*tabʿīḍiyya*), while if the houses made of hair and the like are intended, it is initial (*ibtidāʾiyya*, indicating origin). If that is generalized, it would entail using a homonym (*mushtarak*) in both its meanings. It was answered that the one who holds this view perhaps considers such usage permissible, and among those who said so is al-Bayḍāwī, who was a Shafiʿi. It was also said: "hides" is a metonymy (*majāz*) for the whole.

﴿You find them light﴾: that is, you find them light and easy to handle. The *sīn* here is not for requesting, but for finding, as in *aḥmadtuhu* (I found him praiseworthy, i.e., *wajadtuhu maḥmūdan*). ﴿On the day of your departure﴾: at the time of your moving on, in dismantling and carrying. ﴿And on the day of your residence﴾: at the time of your alighting and settling during your travels, as it happens in pitching and erecting. It is also permissible that the meaning is: you find them light at times of travel and at times of settlement. Ibn al-Munīr preferred the first, saying: "This is the interpretation, because the favour in their lightness while travelling is more complete and stronger, since the resident does not concern himself with their matter." In *al-Kashshāf* he said: "This is true." Some of the learned said: "The second ought to be preferred, for generality, since both states of travel are included in 'the day of your departure', where it is intended as the opposite of residence. Lightness is also a blessing for the resident, for he pitches them, and sometimes moves them from one place to a nearby place for a reason that calls for it. So it is better that the verse not be free of allusion to this." End of quotation. It is not hidden that the inclusion is clear if by *ẓaʿn* (departure) is meant the opposite of residence, but if it is meant the opposite of alighting, as you have heard, it is not clear.

Indeed, it is permissible to intend that. Al-Ḥaramayn (Ibn Kathīr and Nāfiʿ) and Abū ʿAmr read *ẓaʿanikum* with a fatḥa on the ʿayn. The rest of the seven read it with a sukūn on it. These are two dialects, and the fatḥa, according to *al-Maʿālim*, is more eloquent (*ajzal*). It was said: the original is the fatḥa, and the sukūn is a lightening because of a guttural letter, as in *al-shaʿr* and *al-shiʿar* (hair).

﴿And from their wool, their fur, and their hair﴾ is conjoined to His saying ﴿from the hides﴾, and the pronoun refers to the cattle by way of categorization: that is, and He made for you from the wool of sheep, the fur of camels, and the hair of goats. ﴿Furnishings (athāthan)﴾: that is, household goods, such as carpets and other things, as al-Mufaddal said. Al-Farrāʾ said: "It has no singular from its own form, just as *matāʿ* (goods) has none. If you pluralize it, you say *aʾaththah* for the few and *uthuth* for the many." Abū Zayd said: its singular is *athāthah*, and its root is, as al-Khalīl said, from their saying: *athatha* (the plant or the hair) and it is *athīth* when it has grown abundant. Imru' al-Qays said:

And a branch that adorns the back, black, jet-dark,
Abundant, like the cluster of the palm tree laden with dates.

Its accusative case is because it is conjoined to *buyūtan* (houses), the object of *jaʿala* (made). In that case it is an instance of conjoining a prepositional phrase that is fronted with an accusative noun upon the same pattern, as in *ḍarabtu fī al-dāri Zaydan wa fī al-ḥujrati ʿAmran* (I struck Zayd in the house and ʿAmr in the room). This is permissible and not objectionable, contrary to what was claimed in *al-Īḍāḥ*. It is also permissible that it be accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*), in which case it is conjoining merely a prepositional phrase upon a similar one, meaning: and He made for you from the hides of cattle houses, and from their wool, fur, and hair while they are furnishings. Al-Samīn criticized this, saying: "The meaning is not this, and this is apparent."

﴿And goods (matāʿan)﴾: that is, something you enjoy and benefit from in trade and livelihood, as al-Mufaddal said. From Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, *matāʿ* means adornment. Al-Khalīl said: *athāth* and *matāʿ* are one and the same, and the conjunction is for placing the difference in wording in the position of difference in meaning, as in His saying: *wa-alfā qawlahā kadhiban wa-maynā* (and he found her saying false and deceitful). The first is preferable. ﴿For a time (ilā ḥīn)﴾: until the end of your needs from it. From Muqātil: until its wearing out and its perishing. From Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both: until death. The discussion of the ordering of the objects is like what was said before, more than once.

[Page 205]

﴿And Allah has made for you, from what He has created,﴾ [things that cast] shade, without any making by you, ﴿shades﴾: things under which you seek shade, from clouds, trees, mountains, and other things. This is what the apparent sense requires. It is related from Qatadah, from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), and from Mujahid that it is restricted to clouds. It is also related from al-Zajjaj and Qatadah, likewise, that it is restricted to trees. It is related from Ibn Qutaybah that it is restricted to trees and mountains. Probably all of these are by way of illustration (tamthil). It is related from Ibn al-Sa'ib that the intended meaning is the shadows of houses, and that is as you see. He, glory be to Him, specified what He mentioned because those lands were predominantly hot. ﴿And He has made for you, from the mountains, refuges (aknan)﴾, places where you take shelter in caves and the like. The singular is kinn, and its root meaning is a covering, from akannahu and kannahu, meaning he covered it. Its plural is aknan and akinnah.

﴿And He has made for you garments (sarabil)﴾: the plural of sirbal, which is anything worn, that is, He has made for you clothing of cotton, linen, wool, and other materials. ﴿That protect you from the heat﴾. He specified it by mention, as al-Mubarrad said, relying on the mention of one of the two opposites over the other, namely cold. Cold was not specified by mention because protection from heat is more important to them, as has passed just before.

Some of them said: "From the head." He specified heat by mention because protecting from it is more important. The claim of greater importance has been challenged by saying that mention of protection from cold earlier, in His saying ﴿for you therein is warmth (dif')﴾, refutes it. Then it was said: This is the reason for restricting to heat here, since the opposite was mentioned there earlier.

It was objected: We do not concede that affirming warmth there refutes the claim of importance. Rather, the difference of the two styles indicates this importance. al-Zajjaj said: "Heat was specified by mention because what protects from heat protects from cold." al-Zamakhshari mentioned this after mentioning importance, and in al-Kashshaf he said: "This is the (better) aspect." The specification of heat by mention is for what he presented in the first aspect, meaning importance. As for what is said, that the first (shade) has priority because of His saying ﴿of what He created, shades﴾, it is nothing, because He, exalted is He, followed it with His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿from the mountains, refuges﴾. How could it be, when it is in the context of comprehensiveness? End. The speaker of that view is Ibn al-Munayyir. It has also been objected to his saying that what protects from heat protects from cold, that this is contrary to what is known, for what is known is that protection from heat is thin and light shirts, while protection from cold is the opposite. If a person wore in each of the two seasons, summer and winter, the other's clothing, he would be counted among the dull-witted. So reflect.

﴿And garments (sarabil)﴾ of coats of mail and armor ﴿that protect you from your violence (ba's)﴾, that is, the violence that reaches some of you from others in wars, from striking and thrusting. Some of them said: The root meaning of ba's is severity, and it is intended here to mean war, and the speech is with an omitted modifier, that is, harm of your violence. According to the first (view), there is no need for that. This has been preferred for that reason. ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like that completion (of favor) in the past, ﴿He completes His favor upon you﴾ in the future. From here it was said:

As Allah did good in the past, so He does good in what remains.

Or: like this complete completion, He completes His favor upon you. The singular "favor" (ni'mah) is either because what is meant by it is the verbal noun, or to show that this, in relation to the majesty of the Divine Presence, is a small thing. Ibn 'Abbas read "tatimmu" with an open ta', and "ni'matuhu" in the nominative, as the subject, with the attribution of completion to it by way of extension (ittisa'). It is also related from him, may Allah be pleased with him, "ni'amuhu" in the plural form. ﴿So that you may submit (tuslimun)﴾, that is, the intention that you look at the favors He has bestowed upon you, so that you know the right of their Benefactor, so that you believe in Him alone, and abandon what you used to associate with Him. This is on the basis that Islam is in its well-known meaning, namely the companion of faith. It may also be in its linguistic meaning, which is surrender and submission, that is, so that you surrender to Him, glory be to Him, and submit to His command, exalted and majestic is He. In either case, it is placed in the position of its cause, as has been indicated, or it is used as a metonymy for it.

[Page 206]

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) read "tuslamun" with an open ta' and lam, from salamah (safety), that is: you give thanks and so you are safe from punishment, or you look into them and so you are safe from polytheism. It was said: you are safe from wounds by wearing those garments. There is no harm in interpreting it as safety from calamities in general, so that it includes the calamity of heat and cold. The reading of the majority is closer in meaning to the second interpretation.

Moreover, in some reports it is related that a Bedouin heard His saying, ﴿And Allah has made for you, from your houses, a dwelling﴾, up to the end of the two verses. He said at every favor: "O Allah, yes." When he heard His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿so that you may submit﴾, he said: "O Allah, this is enough (fa-la)." So it was revealed.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 82:

﴿Fa-in tawallaw﴾ is a past-tense verb in the manner of iltifat (the shift from address to third-person reference), and directing the speech to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is a consolation to him, peace be upon him. That is, if they persist in turning away and refusing to accept what was conveyed to them of the clear proofs. ﴿Fa-innama 'alayka al-balagh al-mubin﴾ means: so it should not harm you, because your duty is only the clear conveyance, or the evident conveyance, and you have fulfilled it in a way that cannot be improved upon. This is from the category of placing the cause in the position of the effect (wad' al-sabab mawdi' al-musabbab).

Ibn 'Atiyya said: the implied meaning is, if they turn away, you are not capable of creating faith in their hearts; so your duty is only the conveyance, not the creation of faith.
