It is also permissible that (tawallaw) be a present-tense verb (mudari') in which one of its two taa's has been elided, its original form being (tatawallaw), so there is no iltifat. But it has been objected that the connection of the conditional clause with its response does not then become apparent except with effort, and therefore some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) did not adopt this view.

In the use of the form of the verbal pattern (tafil) there is an indication, as has been said, that the original disposition (al-fitrah al-ula) calls one to turn towards Allah, the Exalted, and turning away does not occur except with a kind of effort and deliberate treatment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 83:

﴿They recognize the blessing of Allah﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) explaining that the turning away of the polytheists and their aversion from Islam is not because they have no knowledge at all of the blessing of Allah, Glorified is He, for they do recognize that it is from Allah, Exalted is He. ﴿Then they deny it﴾ through their deeds, in that they did not single out its Bestower for worship. Thus it is as though they had not worshipped Him, Glorified is He, at all, and this is ingratitude (kufran) which is placed in the position of denial.

Ibn Jarir and others related from Mujahid that he said: their denial of it is their saying, "We inherited it from our fathers." He, and others also, related from Awn ibn Abd Allah that he said: their denial of it is that a man says, "Had it not been for so-and-so, I would have been afflicted with such-and-such, and had it not been for so-and-so, I would not have obtained such-and-such." In another wording, denying it is attributing it to secondary causes. It was also said: their saying is that it comes by the intercession of their gods with Allah, Exalted is He. The author of al-Ghaniyan related: they recognize it in hardship, then deny it in ease. It was also said: they recognize it with their hearts, then deny it with their tongues.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from al-Suddi that he said: the blessing here is Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Tabari preferred this view, meaning: they recognize, by the miracles, that he (peace be upon him) is a Prophet, then they deny that and reject him out of obstinacy. In the wording of Ibn Abi Hatim, he said this concerning the report of Abu Jahl and al-Akhnas, when al-Akhnas asked Abu Jahl about Muhammad (ﷺ), and he said: "He is a Prophet."

The meaning of "then" (thumma) is the remoteness of denial after recognition, because the right of one who recognizes a blessing is to acknowledge it and to render its due, not to deny it. The attribution of recognition, and of the denial that follows from it, to the pronoun of the polytheists in an unrestricted manner is an instance of attributing the state of some to all. For some of them are not like this, as is apparent from His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿and most of them are the disbelievers﴾, that is, those who deny in their hearts, not those who acknowledge what has been mentioned. The judgment against them as disbelievers in an unrestricted sense, which indicates completeness in quantity, does not contradict the completeness of the first group in quality; so it has been said. It is also permissible that the attribution mentioned earlier is on its apparent sense, and the meaning is that most of them are the persistent ones who remain steadfast in their disbelief until the day they meet Him. The expression "most" is then due to His knowledge, Exalted is He, that among them are some who will believe. It was also said: the meaning is that most of them are those who deny out of obstinacy. The expression "most" is either because some of them did not know the truth due to deficiency of intellect and failure to be guided to it, or because they did not reflect on the proofs in a way that leads to the goal, or because the proof was not established against them, since they had not reached the age of accountability due to youth or the like. Or it is because it is put in the place of the whole. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 84:

﴿And [mention] the Day when We raise up from every nation a witness﴾, a group of people, ﴿a witness﴾ who testifies for them regarding faith and obedience, and against them regarding disbelief and disobedience. What is meant by it, as Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from Qatadah, is the prophet of that nation. ﴿Then the disbelievers will not be given permission﴾, meaning to make excuses, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿This is a Day when they will not speak, nor will they be given permission so that they may make excuse﴾. The apparent meaning is that they seek permission for that, and it is not granted to them. It is also possible that they neither seek permission nor is it granted, since they have no proof to be mentioned and no excuse to be offered. Abu Muslim said: the meaning is that their speech will not be heard after the testimony of the witnesses, nor will it be paid attention to, as in the verse of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

"In a gathering where the shaykh permits him to speak, and a narration like that of one who is pointed to."

It was also said: they will not be permitted to return to the abode of the world. The first view is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-'Aliyah. The particle ﴿thumma﴾ (then) is used to indicate that their being tested by not being given permission, which indicates total despair, and that being said to them, "Be gone into it, and do not speak to Me" (23:108), is more severe than their being tested by the testimony of the prophets, peace be upon them; so it is for graded sequence (al-tarakhi al-rutbi). ﴿Nor will they be asked to make amends﴾, meaning it will not be demanded of them that they remove the displeasure (ʿatab) of their Lord, that is, His anger, through repentance and righteous deeds, since the Hereafter is the abode of recompense, not the abode of action, and returning to the world is something that will not happen. As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "i.e., it will not be said to them: 'Please your Lord'," it is an explanation by way of a necessary consequence. It was also said: the meaning is that their pleasure will not be sought from them, by showing kindness to them, from "istaʿtabahu" like "aʿtabahu," when he gave him ʿutba, which is contentment. In any case, what is meant is the continuation of the negation, not the negation of continuation. The accusative of the adverbial phrase, according to al-Hawfi and others, is governed by an omitted verb whose estimate is "mention," and some estimated it as "warn them," in which case it is a direct object. It was also said that it is accusative as an adverb of time governed by an omitted element, i.e., "on the Day We raise up [a witness], there will befall them what will befall them." Al-Tabari said it is conjoined to an omitted adverb whose governing element is "they will deny it," i.e., "then they will deny it today, and on the Day We raise up from every nation a witness, so he testifies against them and refutes them," and this is not correct. These possibilities also apply to His, exalted is He, statement:

When those who did wrong see the punishment: that is, the punishment they deserve for their wrongdoing, which is the punishment of Hell. By "those who did wrong" is meant those who disbelieved. The apparent expression would have been the pronoun, but the explicit noun was used in its place to censure them for what is mentioned in the relative clause. Attaching the seeing to the punishment is for emphasis. It has also been said that the intended meaning is Hell itself, used figuratively. Its pronoun in His words, ﴿it will not be lightened for them﴾, is meant in its literal sense, by way of istikhdam (a rhetorical device in which one word is used in one sense and its pronoun in another), but this is not the right view.

As for this clause, it has been said that it is a new independent sentence. It has also been said that it is the response clause of "idha" (the conditional particle "when"), with an implied element, so that the meaning is: "then it will not be lightened for them," because the present-tense verb, whether affirmative or negative, when it is the response clause of "idha," is not joined with the particle "fa" (then). Abu Hayyan favoured this view. He reported from al-Hawfi that he held that this clause is the response clause and that it governs "idha." Then he said: "We have already explained that what precedes the response particle "fa" other than "amma" does not govern what comes before it, and we have shown that the element governing "idha" is the verb that follows it, like the rest of the conditional particles, although this is not the view of the majority." Al-Khafaji criticised the view that this is the response clause, on the grounds that it requires the implied element you have heard, and that this, besides being contrary to the original rule, conflicts with the purpose, which is the difference between the two clauses in the composition: namely His words, ﴿it will not be lightened for them﴾, and His words, glorified is He, ﴿nor will they be reprieved﴾, meaning they will not be given respite. The point is that the absence of lightening occurs after the seeing of the punishment, and therefore no nominal sentence was used for it, unlike the absence of respite, which is established for them in that state. [End of quotation.]

In the words of al-Zamakhshari, as quoted in al-Kashf (the commentary on al-Zamakhshari's al-Kashshaf), there is an indication that the omitted governing element of "idha" is "baghatahum" (it overtook them suddenly), and that this is the response clause. He said, after explaining the reason for the accusative case of "the Day": "Likewise, when they see the punishment, it overtakes them suddenly and weighs heavily upon them, so it will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved," like His words, ﴿Rather, it will come upon them suddenly and confound them﴾, and the verse. In this there is also an indication that the absence of lightening and of reprieve shows that it is heavy and sudden, as is stated in the other verse, where it is said that it comes suddenly and confounds, which is the heaviness and something more. It is ordered upon this: ﴿so they will not be able to avert it, nor will they be reprieved﴾. Such a "fa" is, in his view, eloquent (fasih). So understand this.

In al-Tafsir al-Kabir (the Great Commentary of Fakhr al-Din al-Razi), the theologians (mutakallimun) said: The punishment must be pure, free from any admixture of benefit, and this is what is meant by His words, ﴿so it will not be lightened for them﴾. It must also be everlasting, and this is what is meant by His words, glorified is He, ﴿nor will they be reprieved﴾. But there is consideration in this.

[Page 208]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 86:**

﴿When those who associated partners [with God] see their partners﴾, those whom they used to claim were partners with God, may He be exalted, and whom they worshipped alongside Him, may He be mighty and majestic. What is meant by them is everyone they took as a partner to Him, may He be majestic and exalted: an idol, a statue, a devil, a human being, or a king. Their being attributed to the pronoun of the polytheists is because of this taking. It has also been said that what is meant by them is their false objects of worship, as was mentioned earlier. The attribution to them is because they assigned to them a share of their wealth and livestock. Some scholars restricted it to idols, but it is likely that the generalization is more appropriate. Al-Hasan (al-Basri) said: "Their partners are the devils, who shared with them in wealth and children." It has also been said: they shared with them in disbelief, meaning they disbelieved like their disbelief. It has also been said: they shared with them in the consequences of that, since they led them to it. ﴿They will say﴾, meaning with their tongues. It has also been said: God, exalted is He, sealed their mouths and made their limbs speak, and so they say about them: ﴿Our Lord, these are our partners whom we used to call upon besides You﴾, meaning we used to worship and obey them. Perhaps they said this hoping that the punishment would be divided among them.

It has been objected that this does not fit interpreting the partners as idols. The answer is that they will be brought into a state in which they can comprehend their punishment, so there is no harm in that, whether the partners are interpreted as idols alone or as what includes them and others. Abu Muslim said: their purpose in this is to shift the blame onto the partners, supposing that this would save them from the punishment of God, or would reduce their punishment somewhat.

Al-Qadi criticized this, saying: it is far-fetched, because the disbelievers will know with necessary knowledge in the Hereafter that the punishment will descend upon them, and that there is no help, no ransom, and no intercession. He raised something similar against what we have mentioned, on the basis that they will also know necessarily that no one will bear any part of their punishment.

It was answered: even granting that they acquire this necessary knowledge at that time, they may be so dazed that they become heedless of it, and so they say what they say, hoping for what was mentioned. This is similar to their saying: "Our Lord, lighten the punishment from us for a day" [cf. Qur'an 41:... as the commentator cites], ﴿O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us﴾, ﴿Our Lord, bring us out, and we will do righteous deeds﴾, and other such statements, which some of them consider necessarily impossible to occur. It has also been said: these people, although they know that what they hope for and aspire to will not happen to them at all, do not remain heedless of that, because their souls overpower them by the demand of their nature, due to the severity of what they are in, and we seek refuge in God, exalted is He, until their hopes become attached to the impossible. It has also been said: they said this as an acknowledgment that they had been mistaken in their worship. This is criticized as not fitting His saying, exalted is He: "besides You" (min dunika). There is room for reflection on this.

Yes, the saying of God, exalted is He: ﴿Then they will throw to them the word: "Indeed you are liars"﴾, meaning their partners, is more fitting with the first point. Their denial of what they said is clearly for defense and for escaping the danger of its content. The apparent meaning is that the denial refers to the claim that they used to worship them or obey them besides God, exalted is He. Their intended meaning, as it has been said, is: "You did not truly worship us; you only worshipped things that you imagined with your corrupt minds, and you thought that we were those things." But far, far is it! There is no common ground between us and them, and no beneficial connection. It has also been said: they denied them even though they had been worshipping them, because the idols were not pleased with their worship of them. So their worship was as if it was not worship of them, just as the angels, peace be upon them, said: «Rather, they used to worship the jinn» (Qur'an 34:41), meaning that the jinn were the ones who were pleased with their worship, not we. The devils, although they were pleased with their worship of them, did not compel or force them, as Iblis said: ﴿I had no authority over you except that I called you, and you responded to me﴾ (Qur'an 14:22). So it is as if they said: "You did not truly worship us; you only worshipped your own desires." It has also been said: it is possible that the devils were lying in their report of the falsehood of those who worshipped them, just as Iblis, may the curse of God be upon him, lied in his saying: ﴿Indeed, I disown what you associated [with God] before﴾ (Qur'an 14:22). It is also permitted that the denial refers to their being partners with God, not to their having been worshipped, and that their intention is to declare God, exalted is He, free of having a partner in that situation. Some scholars restricted this to the interpretation in which the partners are meant as devils, so understand this. The apparent meaning is that the speaker of this is all of the partners. Interpreting the partners as including idols does not prevent this, since there is no improbability in God making them speak, He who made everything speak. It is also permitted, under the generalization, that the speaker is some of them, namely those among them who can reason. The apparent wording would have been: "They said to them, 'Indeed you are liars,'" but the noble wording was changed to indicate that they said this to them openly, in a way that it could be perceived and distinguished from others. It also contains an indication of their eagerness to deny them. This is supported by their emphasizing the statement with the particle of emphasis (inna) and the nominal sentence, which indicates their denial with the strongest emphasis. This phrase is in the position of an appositive (badal) for "the word," as al-Imam said: they threw to them, "Indeed you are liars."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 87 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And they will offer submission﴾ to God on that day. That is, those who associated partners (with God). It has also been said that they and their partners together are meant, but most commentators take the first view. ﴿Submission (al-salam)﴾ means yielding and submitting to His judgment, the Mighty, the Overpowering, after their refusal and arrogance in this world. So on that day they have no stratagem and no means of defence. Ya'qub, on the authority of Abu 'Amr, recited «(al-salm)» with a sukun on the lam. Mujahid recited (al-sulum) with a damma on the sin and the lam. ﴿And what they used to fabricate will be lost to them﴾, meaning it will perish and be void: the claim that God has partners and that these partners will help them and intercede for them, once they have seen what they have seen.

* * *

This, and among the esoteric allusions (ishara) in the verses: ﴿Then when He removes the harm from you, behold, a group of you associate others with their Lord﴾, by attributing that (blessing) to other than Him, glhorified be He, and by seeing it as coming from others. ﴿So that they may be ungrateful for what We have given them﴾ of blessing, by being heedless of its Giver. ﴿Enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know﴾ the consequence of that. Or: ﴿you will soon know﴾ through the manifestation of Divine Oneness (tawhid) that nothing other than Him, exalted is He, has any real effect on anything. ﴿And they assign to what they do not know﴾, so they believe about it whatever ignorance they believe, and that is the right (path) ﴿a share of what We have provided for them﴾, so they say: "It gave me such-and-such; had it not given me, it would have been such-and-such." ﴿And indeed, in the livestock there is a lesson for you. We give you to drink from what is in their bellies, between excrement and blood, pure milk, pleasant to the drinkers﴾. The allusion here, according to what is in the secrets of the Qur'an, is to what the spirits drink, which is obtained in pure intellects between the soul and the heart, from the clear water of the sea of contemplation (mushahada). There are the stations of reflection of those who reflect. The allusion in God's words: ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and the grapes you take intoxicant and good provision﴾ is, according to what is also said about it, to what the spirits and the inner secrets take from the fruits of the palm trees of the hearts and the grapes of the intellects: the wine of love and intimacy that carries them to the courtyard of holiness:

*Had they sprinkled some of it on the dust of a dead man's grave, the spirit would have returned to him and the body would have revived.*

﴿And your Lord revealed to the bee﴾. It has been said: that is, the bee of the spirits. ﴿Take for yourselves houses in the mountains﴾, that is, the mountains of the lights of the Essence, ﴿and in the trees﴾, that is, in the trees of the lights of the Attributes, ﴿and in what they build﴾, the lights of the trellises of the Acts. ﴿Then eat of all the fruits﴾, that is, of the fruits of those attribute-trees, of the light of the splendour of the Essential Lights, and of the blossoms of the Lights of Acts. ﴿Then follow the ways of your Lord﴾, which are the deserts of His holiness and the wildernesses of His majesty, exalted be His glory, ﴿made smooth﴾, submissive to what they have been commanded. ﴿From their bellies comes a drink﴾, which is the drink of the knowledge of Him, exalted is He, through the eternity of His majesty, the might of His permanence, and the holiness of His Essence, glorified be He, ﴿varying in its colours﴾
*Page 210*
according to the variety of fruits. ﴿In it is healing for people﴾: for every one sick with love, every one stricken by intimacy, and every one bitten by longing. It has also been said that the allusion in the bee is to those who are at the beginnings of the spiritual path (suluk), from among the people of preparedness (isti'dad). From here the Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, said about our master Ibn al-Farid, may his secret be sanctified, when he was asked about him: "A bee humming around the sacred enclosure." God first commanded them to take as dwelling places the doctrines of faith, which are like mountains in firmness and steadiness, and the legally prescribed acts of worship, which are like trees in their branching, and the praiseworthy dealings, which are like trellises in their elevation. Then they should follow His ways and His paths that lead to Him, exalted be His glory: through the refinement of the inner self, watchfulness, reflection, and the like, humbled, submissive, and not self-admiring. In this there is an allusion that the spiritual path is only valid after correcting the doctrines and knowing the legal rulings, so that the wayfarer acts with insight. Otherwise he is like one who rides a blind beast and gropes like a blind camel. Whenever he travels in that manner, he attains the goal, the springs of wisdom gush forth from his heart, and what his heart pours out becomes like honey, a healing from the ailments of desires and the diseases of the soul, especially the disease of sloth and indolence in worship, which is the phlegmatic disease.

Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: When the bee followed the command and followed the paths of its Lord as it was commanded, its saliva was made a healing for people. Likewise, when the believer follows the command, guards the secret, and turns to his Lord, mighty and majestic, his vision, his speech, and his company become a healing for creation. Whoever looks at him takes a lesson, whoever hears his words is admonished, and whoever sits with him is made happy. End quote.

In the verse there is also an allusion that God may deposit a precious thing in a lowly person. He, glorified be He, deposited in the bee, which is among the most lowly and weakest of creatures, honey, which is among the most delicious and sweetest of foods. So one should not be bound by outward forms nor veiled by appearances. In a hadith: "Many a dusty, disheveled person with two tattered garments, if he swears by God, God will fulfil his oath."

From the leader of the believers, 'Ali, may God honour his face: "Do not look at who said it, but look at what was said." ﴿And God has favoured some of you over others in provision﴾. It has been said: the allusion here is to the differences in the provisions of the wayfarers. The provision of some is acts of obedience, of others stations, of others states, of others unveilings, of others witnessings, of others knowledge, of others love, of others unity, and so on. They mention that the provision of bodies is servitude, the provision of spirits is seeing the lights of Lordship, the provision of intellects is thought, the provision of hearts is remembrance, and the provision of secrets is the realities of the hidden sciences unveiled to them in the sessions of nearness and the witnessing of the unseen. ﴿So do not strike similitudes for God﴾, because He, exalted be He, is holier than fancies, allusions, and expressions, and He is far beyond the grasp of creation, for creation only grasps creation. For this reason 'Ali, may God honour his face, said: "Instruments only define themselves, and tools only point to their likes. No one knows God except God, mighty and majestic." The prohibition is given a reason in God's words: ﴿Indeed God knows, and you do not know﴾.

﴿God struck an example: a slave owned, who has no power over anything﴾, a lover of other than God. There is no doubt that the lover is a captive in the hand of the beloved, unable to do anything, because he is bound by the chains of love. ﴿And one whom We have provided with good provision from Us﴾, so We made him a lover of Ours, turned with his heart toward Us, stripped of whatever is other than Us, and We gave him knowledge from Our presence. ﴿He spends from it secretly﴾, and that is of the inner blessings, ﴿and openly﴾, and that is of the outward blessings. ﴿And God struck an example: two men, one of them mute﴾, with no preparedness for speech, and he is like the polytheist, ﴿who has no power over anything﴾, because of his inability and the weakness of his strength due to the inherent deficiency of his preparedness. ﴿And he is a burden on his master﴾, because of his natural incapacity to obtain any need. ﴿Wherever he directs him, he brings no good﴾, because of his lack of preparedness and his innate wickedness, so only evil, which is nonexistence, suits him. ﴿Are they equal, he and one who commands justice﴾, who is the monotheist, standing by God, annihilated from other than Him. Justice, it has been said, is the shade of Unity in the world of multiplicity. ﴿And he is on a straight path﴾, the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy, upon which are His elect, from among the people of permanence after annihilation, stretched over the fire of nature. For the people of Reality they pass over it like a flashing lightning.

﴿And to God belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾: the knowledge of the levels of the unseen, or what is hidden of their reality, or what is concealed in them of the matter of the Great Resurrection. ﴿And the matter of the Hour﴾, that is, the Great Resurrection, in relation to temporal affairs, ﴿is but as a glance of the eye or nearer﴾. This is based on an analogy; otherwise it has been said that the matter of the Hour is not temporal, and what is like that is perceived by whoever perceives it not in time. ﴿Indeed God is over all things competent﴾, and among that is the matter of the Hour. ﴿And God brought you out from the wombs of your mothers, knowing nothing﴾, the verse. He said in the Secrets of the Qur'an: He, glorified be He, informs that He brought them out from the bellies of destinies, the wombs of nonexistence, and the loins of will, in the state of ignorance, knowing nothing of the rulings of Lordship, the matters of servitude, or the attributes of eternity. So He clothed them with hearing from the light of His hearing, covered them with sight from the light of His sight, and deposited in their hearts the knowledge of His unseen, so that perhaps they would be thankful. End quote. This clearly indicates that the "hearts" (af'ida) here means the hearts.

One of those we have met among the ascetics mentioned in his book al-Fawa'id and its commentary that the senses of man are the chest, meaning the imagination and the universal soul, which is the locus of scientific forms, universal or particular. So it is the locus of knowledge, which is opposed to ignorance. The heart is the locus of meanings and certainty concerning judgmental relations, opposed to doubt and suspicion. The fu'ad (inner core) is the locus of divine knowledges, stripped of all forms, relations, conditions, directions, times, and it is opposed to denial. It is the highest of the senses. And the light of God, exalted be He, is the one indicated by the words of the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him: "Beware the insight of the believer, for he sees by the light of God, exalted be He."

It is existence, because it is the highest aspect of man, I mean his face toward his Lord. Through it he knows God, exalted be He. It stands in man as the king stands in the city, and the heart stands as the vizier to him. End quote. He also has another discussion about the mother and likewise about the father, different from what was mentioned: the father is applied to matter and the mother to form. He claimed that the saying of the truthful one, may God be pleased with him: "God created the believers from His light and dyed them in His mercy, so the believer is the brother of the believer, by his father and his mother: his father is the light and his mother is mercy," is an allusion to that. He also held that what the earlier philosophers and sages agreed upon, that the father is the form and the mother is the matter, and that when form marries matter there comes forth from them a thing, is a supposition on their part that resurrection and creation within the womb of matter are far from proper analogy, and so on to the end of what he said. So take heed. And beware of deviating from the straight path.

﴿Have they not seen the birds subjected in the midst of the sky?﴾ In this there is an allusion to the subjugation of the birds of the spiritual and psychic faculties: thought, the intellect (theoretical and practical), and even imagination and fancy, in the space of the world of spirits. ﴿None holds them up﴾ without attachment to matter, without reliance on a heavy body, ﴿except God﴾, mighty and majestic. ﴿And God has made for you shades from what He created﴾. These are what one seeks shade from the heat of the fire of need: water is a shade for the thirsty, food is a shade for the hungry, and everything that meets a person's need is a shade for him. In a report: "The sultan is the shadow of God on earth; every oppressed person takes refuge in him." It has also been said: the shades are the saints, whom the aspirants take shade under from the intense heat of separation, and to whom they take refuge from the tyranny of oppression. The words of God, ﴿And He made for you from the mountains shelters﴾, may be interpreted in a similar way, for how alike the saints are to mountains. ﴿And He made for you garments that protect you from the heat﴾. In this there is an allusion to the garments of the spirit of intimacy given to the knowers, so that they do not burn in the fires of holiness. And He pointed, by the words of His majesty, ﴿and garments that protect you from your violence﴾, to the knowledge and love with which He favoured them, to repel by that the plots of devils and souls. ﴿Thus He completes His blessing upon you that perhaps you will submit﴾, that is, that you will yield to His command, glorified be He, in servitude, and humble yourselves before the might of Lordship. Ibn 'Ata' said: the completion of the blessing is tranquillity in the Benefactor. Hamdun said: its completion in this world is knowledge, and in the Hereafter, vision. Abu Muhammad al-Hariri said: its completion is the heart's freedom from hidden polytheism and the soundness of

*Page 212*

and the self from showing off and seeking reputation. ﴿They recognize the blessing of Allah﴾, and it is the guidance of the Prophet, or his existence, by the strength of the innate disposition (fitrah). ﴿Then they deny it﴾ out of their obstinacy and the dominance of their souls' qualities. ﴿And most of them are disbelievers﴾, because their innate natures bear witness to its reality. ﴿And [mention] the Day when We raise up from every nation a witness, then permission will not be given to those who disbelieved﴾ to make excuses for their failure to respond to His call, since they have no excuse, ﴿nor will they be asked to make amends﴾, because the word has already taken effect against them according to the requirement of their predisposition. We ask Allah the Exalted for pardon and well-being. ﴿And they will offer submission to Allah that Day﴾. It has been said: this refers to the second station, when the veils of their dark souls weaken and their dense coverings grow thin. As for the first station, when the forms of vices are strong and the soul is fierce in its devilish obstinacy, they do not submit, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On the Day when Allah will raise them all up, and they will swear to Him as they swear to you﴾. And it has been said: some of them submit and some of them swear. So understand, and Allah the Exalted knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 88:

﴿Those who disbelieve﴾ within themselves, ﴿and bar﴾ others ﴿from the way of Allah﴾, by preventing those who wish to embrace Islam from it, and by compelling those whom they have made light-minded to disbelieve. Thus, barring from the way (al-sadd 'an al-sabil) is more general than preventing from it at the outset and in continuation (al-man' 'anhu ibtida'an wa baqa'an). So it is said. The apparent meaning is the first. The apparent meaning is that the relative pronoun (al-mawsul, "those who") is the subject (mubtada'), and His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We shall increase them in punishment upon punishment﴾ is its predicate (khabar).

Ibn 'Atiyya permitted that the relative pronoun be a substitute (badal) for the subject of (yaftaruna, "they fabricate"), and that ﴿We shall increase them﴾ be a new independent clause (isti'naf). Some permitted that the first be in the accusative on the basis of censure (nasban 'ala al-dhamm), or in the nominative on that basis, in which case the verb is necessarily elided together with the subject, and ﴿We shall increase them﴾ remains in its state. This increase is either in intensity or in another kind of punishment, and the second is what is transmitted. Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib related from al-Bara' that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about that and said: "Scorpions like tall palm trees, which will sting them in Hell." Al-Hakim related something similar and authenticated it, as did al-Bayhaqi and others, from Ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi that he said: When the people of the Fire become distressed by its heat, they seek refuge in a shallow pool in the Fire. When they reach it, scorpions will meet them, like dark mules, and vipers, like Bactrian camels, and they will strike them. That is the increase. From Ibn 'Abbas: it is rivers of molten brass flowing from beneath the Throne, with which they are punished. From al-Zajjaj: they will go out from the heat of the Fire to the zamharir (intense cold), and out of the intensity of its cold they will rush back to the Fire.

﴿for what they used to corrupt﴾ is connected to (zidnahum, "We increased them"), meaning: We increase them in punishment upon the punishment which they deserve for their disbelief, because of their persistence in corruption, which is barring from the way. It is also permitted to explain it as that which is more general than disbelief and barring, and the meaning is: We increase them in punishment upon their punishment which they deserve merely for disbelief and barring, because of their persistence in these two ugly matters. The reason for this is that persisting in disobedience for two days, for example, is uglier than persisting in it for one day, and persisting for three days is uglier than persisting for two days, and so on. From here they said: persisting in a minor sin becomes a major sin. It has also been said: the people of Hell deserve from the punishment a particular degree, which is what they experience at their first entry into it, and the increase beyond it is only to preserve it, for had it not increased they would have grown accustomed to it and their souls would have been content with it, like one who places his hand in hot water, for he finds at the first moment of placing it what he does not find after an hour has passed. And it is, as you see, far-fetched.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 89 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And on the Day We raise up in every nation a witness against them﴾ — and it is, as has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, their prophet who was sent to them in the world. The meaning of his being ﴿from among themselves﴾ is that he is one of them, and that is so that the proof against them may be more decisive. Lot, peace be upon him, is not an objection to this, for when he took a wife among them and dwelt with them, he was counted among them as well. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: It is permissible that Allah the Exalted should raise up witnesses from among the righteous alongside the prophets, peace be upon them. Some of the Companions, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them, have said: "If you see someone committing a sin, forbid him; if he obeys you, well and good, and otherwise you will be a witness against him on the Day of Resurrection." Al-Imam (al-Razi) mentioned two opinions regarding the verse: the first is that every prophet is a witness over his people, as has preceded; the second is that every generation and assembly that comes into being in the world must have among them someone who is a witness over them, and that person must not be liable to error, otherwise he would need another, and so on, which would entail an infinite regress. The existence of such a witness in the age of the Prophet ﷺ is evident, but after him there must be in every age groups of people by whose word the proof is established, and they stand in the place of the infallible witness. Then he said: "This necessarily means that the consensus of the Community is a proof." To the view that there must be in every age someone whose word is a proof for the people of his age, al-Jubba'i and most of the Mu'tazilah went. Al-Tabarsi said in Majma' al-Bayan: "Their position agrees with the position of our companions, meaning the Shi'ah, although it differs from it regarding who that proof is." You know that the argument from the verse for this claim is weak, and the detailed discussion of that belongs in its proper place.

Al-Asamm said: The intended meaning of "witness" is parts of the human being, for Allah the Exalted makes ten parts of him speak: the two ears, the two eyes, the two feet, the two hands, the skin and the tongue, and they testify against him, because He, glorified is He, said regarding the witness: "from among themselves."

Al-Qadi and others objected to this, saying that his being a witness over the nation requires that he be other than them. Also, His saying, "in every nation," refuses this, since it is not valid to describe individual limbs as being of the nation. Also, the contrasting of that with His saying, glorified is He: "And We bring you as a witness against these," removes what has been mentioned, as is not hidden. The intended meaning of "these" is his nation, peace and blessings be upon him, according to most of the exegetes, but it has not been deemed far-fetched that the intended meaning may include those present at the time of the revelation and others until the Day of Resurrection, for the deeds of his nation, upon him be blessings and peace, are presented to him after his death.

It has been related from him, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, that he said: "My life is good for you: you speak and it is spoken to you; and my death is good for you: your deeds are presented to me, so whatever good I see I praise Allah for it, and whatever evil I see I seek forgiveness of Allah the Exalted for you."

Indeed it has come that the deeds of a servant are presented to his relatives among the dead. Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated from Abu Hurayrah that "the Prophet ﷺ said: 'Do not disgrace your dead by the evil deeds of your actions, for they are presented to your protectors among the people of the graves.'"

Ahmad narrated from Anas, traced to the Prophet: "Indeed your deeds are presented to your relatives and your kin among the dead; if it is good they rejoice, and if it is otherwise they say: 'O Allah, do not let them die until You guide them as You guided us.'" Abu Dawud narrated it from the hadith of Jabir with the addition: "And inspire them to act in obedience to You."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated from Abu al-Darda', that he said: "Your deeds are presented to your dead, and they are gladdened or saddened." Abu al-Darda' used to say about this: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from my maternal uncle 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah disliking me when I meet him," saying this in his prostration. The Prophet ﷺ is to his community in the position of a father, rather more so. I have not come across the presentation of the deeds of earlier nations to their prophets after death, and I have not seen anyone who addressed this, neither negating nor affirming it. If it is said that they are presented, then the matter of testimony is beyond doubt concerning a prophet who was not sent to his community after they were left without another prophet; and if it is said that they are not presented, the matter of testimony requires investigation into the existence of something that yields the knowledge which validates it, or commitment to the view that the witness is not the prophet alone, as you have heard previously. Furthermore, the hadith of presentation to our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is problematic in light of the hadith "Some people will surely be driven away from the Basin," the full report; al-Manawi mentioned this and did not answer it, and I have answered it in some of my notes, so reflect.

It has been said: the intended meaning of "these" is the witnesses of the nations, who are the prophets, peace be upon them, because of his knowledge, peace and blessings be upon him, of their creeds and his comprehensive encompassing of their rules; not the community, because his being a witness over his community has been known from what preceded. So the verse is directed toward his witnessing, peace and blessings be upon him, over the prophets, may he be blessed, and thus it is free of repetition. It was refuted by saying that the intended meaning of his witnessing, peace and blessings be upon them, over his community is his purifying and vouching for them after they bear witness to the conveyance of the prophets, peace be upon them, according to what they know from their Book, and this was not known from what passed, so that it would be a repetition, and this is what occurs in the hadith. Many have mentioned it in the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: "Thus We have made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over mankind and the Messenger may be a witness over you." The preposition "over" (ʿalā) is not harmful in it, and if it were harmful, the harm would be shared. Indeed, it was not understood from what precedes the testimony of this nation over the conveyance of the prophets, peace be upon them, so that the testimony would be clearly for purification, as in the verse of al-Baqarah; and perhaps the matter in that is easy.

In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim it is said that His saying, exalted is He: "And on the Day We raise up," is a repetition of what preceded for the purpose of reinforcing the threat, and the intended meaning of "these" is the nations and their witnesses. The choice of the word "coming" over "raising" is for complete care for his affair, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, and the use of the past form is to indicate the certainty of occurrence. End of quotation. It was criticized by saying that taking "these" to mean what has been mentioned is contrary to the apparent sense, and it was permitted that the choice of "coming" over "raising" is to signal the difference between the two testimonies, based on the premise that his testimony, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, over his community is for purification, whereas the testimony of the rest of the prophets, peace be upon them, over their nations is not of this kind.

The adverbial phrase is governed by an omitted element, as has passed, and what is meant by it is the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾, the complete one in bookhood, deserving that the generic noun be restricted to it. This, according to what is in al-Bahr, is a resumed statement and not included with what precedes it, due to the difference in the two times.

Several have permitted it to be a circumstantial clause with "qad" implied. Some eminent scholars mentioned that His saying, exalted is He: "And We have brought you" and so on, if it is an independent statement not conjoined to His saying, glorified is He: "raise up" and "witness," is a presumed circumstantial clause, so there is no difficulty in its being circumstantial; and if it is conjoined to it, the expression in the past tense is as is known in such cases, so the content of the circumstantial clause is preceded by a great deal, and thus the interpretation they mentioned to correct the past form being circumstantial here does not hold; so there is discussion regarding its validity as a circumstantial clause, unless it is based on the time not applying to Him, glorified and exalted is He. It was criticized by saying that this is nothing, for His saying, glorified is He: "an explanation of everything" includes creeds and rules by a prior inclusion, and that continues until the resurrection and what follows it; and there is no need for what has been said, that the meaning is "in a state that We sent down to you," and that state is established for Him, glorified and exalted is He, forever. End of quotation. In this there is scrutiny.

Some have claimed that the clause is a circumstantial clause of the subject pronoun in the verb governing the adverbial phrase, i.e., "fearing that day while We had sent down to you the Book," and this, as you see, is not right; the safer view is the resumption. "Tibyan" is a verbal noun indicating intensity, according to what Tha'lab narrated from the Kufans and al-Mubarrad from the Basrans. Salamah al-Anbari said in the commentary on the Maqamat: every verbal noun that comes from the Arabs on the pattern taf'al is with a fatha on the ta', except two words, and they are tibyan and tilqa'. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is a noun and not a verbal noun, and this pattern is also rare in nouns. From Ibn Malik, he said in Nazm al-Fara'id: it came on the pattern tif'al with a kasra, and it is not a verbal noun: rajul tiklam, tilqam, til'ab, timsah (for the liar), tidrab (for the she-camel close to the stallion's mating), timrad (for a dovecote), tilfaf (for two folded garments), tijfaf (for what covers a horse), tihwa' (for a past portion of the night), tinbal (for the short base person), ti'shar and tibrak (for two places). Ibn Ja'wan added timthal and tifaq (for the agreement of the crescent). Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas in the commentary on the Mu'allaqat limited himself to fewer than that, saying: in the speech of the Arabs there are only four nouns on tif'al, and a fifth that is disputed: they say tibyan, and they say for a woman's necklace tiqsar, ti'shar, and tibrak; and the fifth is timsah, and timsah is more common and more eloquent. End of quotation. The known view is that "tibyanan" is a verbal noun and not a noun, though it is said to be the view of most grammarians. Al-Zajjaj permitted the fatha in it outside the Qur'an. The intended meaning of "everything," according to what a group went to, is what relates to matters of religion, that is, a eloquent explanation of everything that relates to that, and among its components are the conditions of the nations with their prophets, peace be upon them, and likewise what this verse informed of, the raising up of witnesses and his raising up, peace be upon him. Thus the connection of the verse with what precedes is evident. The evidence for the assumption of the qualifying description specifying the thing is that the sending of the prophets, peace be upon them, is only for clarifying the religion, and therefore the question about the crescents was answered as it was answered, and he, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, said: "You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your worldly life." The Book's being an explanation for that is in regard to the fact that it contains explicit statement regarding some matters and a referral of others to the Sunnah, in that he was ordered to follow the Prophet ﷺ; and it has been said regarding it: "Nor does he speak from desire," and an incitement to consensus in His saying, glorified is He: "and follows other than the way of the believers," the verse, for it is, according to what has been related from al-Shafi'i and a group, the evidence for consensus. The Prophet, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, was pleased for his community to follow his companions when he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Upon you is my Sunnah and the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs after me; hold fast to it with the molars."

They strove, analogized, and trod the paths of ijtihad, so the Sunnah, consensus and analogy were grounded in the explanation of the Book.

Some said: "kull" is for multiplication and magnification, as in His saying: "destroying everything by the command of its Lord," since the comprehensiveness and generality refuse what is in al-Tibyan of hyperbole in explanation, and that some matters of religion are particularized, which the context does not require. The second was refuted by what you have just heard, and the first by saying that the hyperbole is in terms of quantity, not quality, as was said regarding His saying: "And your Lord is not unjust to the servants," that it is from your saying: "So-and-so is unjust to his servant" and "a great oppressor to his servants," and from it His saying, glorified is He: "And the wrongdoers have no helpers." Some of them said: each of the two statements has a direction; the preponderant for the first is keeping each on its literal meaning in general. It was criticized by saying that what preponderates the second is keeping "thing" on its generality and its freedom from the restriction, which is contrary to the original, and from metaphor according to the view of "nam." Most exegetes went to considering the particularization, and that was narrated from Mujahid.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 89 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Jalal al-Mahalli said, in response to those who did not permit specifying the Sunnah by the Book: "What indicates permissibility is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an exposition of everything﴾, even though some of its generality has been specified by things other than the Qur'an. The explanation of its being an exposition of everything that pertains to the religion in terms of what has preceded is what the words of more than one of the great scholars (al-ajillah) require. It is reported from al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, that he once said in Makkah: 'Ask me about whatever you wish, and I will inform you of it from the Book of Allah, the Exalted.' He was asked: 'What do you say about a muhrim who kills a wasp?' He said: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾.' And Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah narrated to us from 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr, from Ribi' ibn Hirash, from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, from the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, that he said: ''Follow the two after me, Abu Bakr and 'Umar.''"

"And Sufyan narrated to us from Mis'ar ibn Kidam, from Qays ibn Muslim, from Tariq ibn Shihab, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he ordered the killing of a muhrim's wasp." Al-Bukhari reported from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: ''Allah, the Exalted, has cursed the women who tattoo and those who have themselves tattooed, those who pluck facial hair and those who file their teeth for beauty, who alter the creation of Allah, the Exalted.'' A woman said to him about this, and he said: "Why should I not curse one whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ cursed, and who is in the Book of Allah, the Exalted?" She said to him: "I have read what is between the two covers and I did not find in it what you say." He said: "If you had read it, you would have found it. Did you not read: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾?" She said: "Yes." He said: "Indeed, he, peace be upon him, has forbidden it."

Some scholars held to what the apparent meaning of the verse requires, without asserting specification, nor that "kull" (every) means "much," and said: "There is no matter of religion or worldly affairs except that it can be extracted from the Qur'an, and He has explained in it every thing with eloquent explanation." They took into account the differing levels of people in understanding, so something may be an eloquent explanation for one person and not for another, and may even be an explanation for one person and not for another, let alone whether the explanation is eloquent or not. This is only due to the differences in the faculties of insight, and the parallel of this is the differing levels of sensory perception due to differences in the faculties of sight.

It was also said: the meaning of its being an exposition is that it is so in itself, and this does not require the existence of an explainer for it, let alone all people sharing in realizing this attribute in relation to them, by understanding the state of each thing in it in the most complete manner. The parallel of this is the sun, which is luminous in its own essence even if there is no one illuminated or looking at it. This consideration is made unnecessary by the consideration that the hyperbole is in terms of quantity, not quality.

The apparent view is supported by the fact that al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, and others have extracted from it countless worldly events. I have seen a literal table attributed to the Shaykh, written on it that from it one may know the events of the people of the gathering (al-mahshar), and another written on it that from it one may know the events of the people of Paradise, and another written on it that from it one may know the events of the people of Hell, and all of this, as they claim, is extracted from the Noble Book. Similar is the comprehensive "Jafr" attributed to the Commander of the Faithful 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, for they said: it encompasses whatever Allah wills of worldly events, and it too is extracted from the Mighty Qur'an.

Al-Jalal al-Suyuti quoted from al-Mursi that he said: "The Qur'an gathered the knowledge of the first and the last, such that none truly encompasses it in knowledge except the One who spoke it, then the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, apart from what He, glorified is He, has reserved for Himself. Then most of that was inherited from him by the leading Companions and their notables, such as the Four Caliphs and such as Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, to the extent that the first (Abu Bakr) said: 'If the tether of a camel were lost to me, I would find it in the Book of Allah, the Exalted.' Then the Successors (al-tabi'un) inherited from them in excellence. Then aspirations fell short, resolves weakened, the people of knowledge diminished and grew too weak to bear what the Companions and Successors bore of its sciences and all its branches, so they divided its sciences, and each group took up one of its branches." It was also said: "The age is never without one who knows all of that, and he is the Muhammadan heir, and he is called the Ghawth (Helper), the Qutb al-Aqtab (Pole of the Poles), the most complete manifestation, the manifestation of the Greatest Name, and so on."

This is refuted against these speakers by the hadith of pollination and his, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, saying: ''You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your worldly life.''

It is answered that it is possible that this was said by him, peace and blessings be upon him, before the revelation of what is known from it, peace and blessings be upon him, at the time of the pollination. It is also possible that it was said after the revelation, and that he, peace and blessings be upon him, said this before returning to it and reflecting on it; had he returned and reflected, he would have known more than they knew. Thus, the statement about their knowledge of their worldly affairs came because their knowledge of that did not need returning and reflection, whereas his knowledge, peace and blessings be upon him, needed that. This is like his saying, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him: ''Had I known at the start what I learned at the end, I would not have brought the sacrificial animals.'' Yet bringing the sacrificial animals is among the religious matters, and they said that the Mighty Qur'an is an exposition of them. This would refute them were it not for this answer, so reflect. The discussion is, moreover, not free of contention and dispute.

Some of them said: matters are either religious or worldly. Worldly matters are not a concern of the Lawgiver, since he was not sent for them. Religious matters are either fundamental or derivative, and concern for the derivative without concern for the fundamental is not enough, for what is primarily sought in the sending of the prophets, peace be upon them, is monotheism and what resembles it. Indeed, what is sought from the creation of servants is knowledge of Him, the Exalted, as His saying, glorified is He, testifies: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me﴾, on the basis of interpreting worship broadly as knowledge, and His saying, the Exalted, in the well-known sacred hadith that is common on the tongues and which is deemed sound by way of the Sufis: ''I was a hidden treasure, so I loved to be known, so I created creation that I might be known.''

The Mighty Qur'an has undertaken to explain the fundamental religious matters in the most complete manner, so let the intended meaning of "everything" be that. This does not need the interpretation that the explanation requires in the case of taking "everything" to mean all matters of religion absolutely, by our saying: it is so in that it contains explicit statement regarding some and refers others to the Sunnah, and so on. Some later scholars chose that "everything" is on its apparent meaning, but that the intended exposition is an exposition in summary, and that there is nothing except that its state has been explained in the Book in summary, and it suffices for this to explain some of its states, with hyperbole in terms of quantity not quality, as you have known previously. Were "exposition" taken to encompass both summary and detail, while considering the one being explained and considering distribution, it would also be permissible; so reflect.

The accusative of "tibyanan" is as a circumstantial (hal), as Abu Hayyan said.

It is permitted that it be an object of purpose: that We sent down the Book for the sake of exposition, ﴿and as guidance and mercy﴾ for all, by the context of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We did not send you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾. The deprivation of the disbelievers is due to their own negligence, ﴿and as good tidings for the Muslims﴾ specifically. It is also permitted to apply all of these to them, since they are the ones who benefit from it, or because guidance is the guidance of indication that leads, and mercy is complete mercy.

God indeed commands justice (al-'adl) and excellence (al-ihsan). Here, "in what He has sent down to you as an explanation of everything." The use of the present-tense form in this verb and in what follows serves to indicate renewal and continuity. ﴿Justice﴾ means observing the middle course between the two extremes of excess (ifrat) and deficiency (tafrit). It is the head of all virtues, and it encompasses the angelic rational faculty's virtue, which is wisdom (hikma), a mean between shrewdness (jahbadha) and dullness (balada); the bestial appetitive faculty's virtue, which is chastity ('iffa), a mean between licentiousness (khala'a) and rigidity (jumud); and the beastly irascible faculty's virtue, which is courage (shaja'a), a mean between recklessness (tahawwur) and cowardice (jubn).

Among the doctrinal wisdoms is tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), a mean between ta'til (denial of divine attributes) and nafy al-sana'i' (denial of the Creator's works), as the Dahriyya (materialists who deny a creator) say, and tashrik (associating partners with God), as the Thanawiyya (Zoroastrian-influenced dualists) and the Wathaniyya (idolaters) say. On this Ibn 'Abbas limited his interpretation of justice, as transmitted from him by al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, and by Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others. Some added to it the doctrine of kasb (acquisition of action by the servant), a mean between pure jabr (compulsion) and qadar (predestination).

Among the practical wisdoms is worship through performing obligatory duties, a mean between falsehood and abandoning action on the claim that there is no benefit in it, since the wretched and the blessed are already determined from eternity, as some heretics (malahida) held; and asceticism (tarahhub) through abandoning permissible things, imitating the monks (ruhban).

Among the ethical wisdoms is generosity (jud), a mean between miserliness (bukhl) and squandering (tabdhir).

It is reported from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna that justice is the equality of the inner and outer conduct in action.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that he said: 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz summoned me and said to me: "Describe justice for me." I said: "Bakh! You have asked about a weighty matter. Be a father to the young among the people, a son to their elders, a brother to those of your own age, and likewise to the women. Punish people in proportion to their sins and in proportion to their bodies, and do not strike with a single lash out of your anger, lest you be among the transgressors."' Perhaps the choice of this answer was because it was most suited to the situation of the questioner; otherwise, what preceded in its explanation is better.

﴿And excellence﴾ means excellence in actions and worship, that is, performing them in the proper manner. This may be according to the manner (kayfiyya), as indicated by what al-Bukhari transmitted of the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Excellence is that you worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, He sees you." Or it may be according to quantity (kammiyya), such as voluntary supererogatory acts that compensate for shortcomings in obligatory duties. It is also permissible that excellence here means excellence with the preposition ila (to), not excellence used transitively by itself; for one says ahsanahu and ahsana ilayhi, meaning excellence toward people and bestowing favour upon them.

For Ibn al-Najjar in his history transmitted through al-'Ukli from his father, who said: 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God honour his face, passed by a group of people who were talking, and he said: "What are you about?" They said: "We are discussing manliness (muru'a)." He said: "Has God, Mighty and Majestic, not sufficed you with that in His Book, when He says: ﴿Indeed God commands justice and excellence﴾? So justice is fairness, and excellence is bestowing favour. Nothing remains beyond this."

The highest level of excellence on this interpretation is excellence toward one who wrongs you, and our Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to do this.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Sha'bi that he said: 'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon him, said: "Excellence is only that you do good to one who has wronged you; it is not excellence to do good to one who has done good to you."' And Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, after interpreting justice as tawhid, interpreted excellence as performing the obligatory duties; and in this there is the consideration of ihsan as transitive by itself.

[p. 218]

It was also said: justice is that one is fair and accepts fairness, while excellence is that one is fair but does not demand fairness. It was also said: justice is in deeds, and excellence is in words.

﴿And giving to the near of kin﴾ means giving relatives their due of kinship and kindness. This is included under justice or excellence, but it is mentioned explicitly out of concern for its importance. The apparent meaning of "the near of kin" is that it embraces all relatives, whether on the mother's side or the father's side. This is the meaning of dhawu al-arham (blood relatives) whose maintenance the Lawgiver (al-Shari') urged, peace be upon him, according to the more correct view. It was also said that dhawu al-arham are relatives on the mother's side. Al-Tabarsi mentions that what is related from Abu Ja'far is that the near of kin here refers to the Prophet's (ﷺ) own kin, who are meant in God's saying: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of war booty, a fifth of it is for God and for the Messenger and for the near of kin﴾ [8:41].

﴿And He forbids indecency﴾: excess in pursuing the appetitive faculty, such as fornication for example. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, interpreted indecency (fahsha') as this. Perhaps this is an illustration rather than a restriction. ﴿Wrongdoing (al-munkar)﴾ is what is condemned in the one who practises it, of excess in displaying the irascible faculty. It was also related from Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil that it means polytheism (shirk). From Ibn al-Sa'ib that it means whatever God has threatened with the Fire. From Ibn 'Uyayna that it means the contradiction of inner conduct to outer conduct. It was also said: what does not entail a legal penalty (hadd) in this world, but entails punishment in the Hereafter.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it is what reason (al-'uqul) rejects. Ibn al-Munir criticised him, saying: this is a hint toward Mu'tazilism (i'tizal). Had he said: "al-munkar is what the Lawgiver has rejected," he would have been right, but he does not abandon the innovation of the Mu'tazila regarding good and evil being known by reason. In al-Kashf, after his statement "what reason rejects," it says: that is, after reducing it to the principles of the Law, rejection by reason is necessary, and the disagreement is only about its source. The point is that what can be interpreted according to both positions should not be contested over; this is like an allusion to Ibn al-Munir.

Abu Hayyan judged that al-munkar is more general than fahsha', saying: because it includes sins and vices. And upon... first, the matter is not so; it will come, God willing.

﴿And wrongful transgression (al-baghy)﴾: seeking elevation, domination over people, and tyranny over them. It is one of the effects of the satanic illusory faculty (al-quwwa al-wahmiyya al-shaytaniyya), which results from the vices of the two faculties mentioned, the appetitive and the irascible. The original meaning of baghy is seeking, then it became specific to seeking to overstep through injustice and aggression. For this reason it was interpreted as it was. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with both of them, interpreted it in this way. The specification of each of the three prohibited items in the coordinated list to one of the three faculties is something that many scholars have held.

It has been objected that this has no proof. Some said: al-munkar is more general than the three, in the sense that it refers to what the Law rejects and condemns, whether words or deeds, whether its ugliness and corruption is great or not, and whether it affects others or not. Fahsha' refers to what is greatly ugly of that, and from this it is said of one whose stinginess is greatly ugly that he is "fahish" (indecent). Al-Raghib interpreted the poet's verse accordingly:

I see death shunning the noble and choosing
the most precious wealth of the stingy, over-strict miser.

Baghy is tyranny through injustice and aggression. So in the verse there is the coordination of the general with the specific and of the specific with the general. It was also said: the meaning of fahsha' is the opposite of justice, and it is explained as what goes out of the paths of moderation toward excess. And al-munkar is what is opposite to what has excellence in it, and it is explained as what is done in a manner other than the proper one, rather in a way that is rejected and considered ugly. And baghy is what is opposite to giving to the near of kin, and it is explained as what was explained earlier.

[p. 219]

Thus in the verse the command is contrasted with the prohibition, and each of the things commanded is paired with each of the things forbidden. The command and the prohibition are combined, although commanding something is a prohibition of its opposite and prohibiting something is a command of its opposite, for greater emphasis and concern.

Imam al-Razi has extended discussion on this point and mentioned that the apparent meaning of the verse requires difference between the three things commanded, and also requires difference between the three things forbidden. He began explaining the difference between the first. Then he said: The conclusion is that justice is an expression for the required measure of good things, and excellence is an expression for the increase in acts of obedience in terms of quantity, manner, motives and deterrents, and in terms of absorption in witnessing the station of servanthood and lordship. Its interpretation includes reverence for God's command and compassion for His creation, may He be glorified. It is evident that compassion for creation has many kinds, the noblest and greatest of which is maintaining ties of kinship. Therefore, He, glorified, singled it out for mention. Then he began explaining the difference between the last and said: The detailed account of this is that He, exalted, placed in the human soul four faculties: the appetitive beastly faculty, the irascible beastly faculty, the satanic illusory faculty, and the angelic rational faculty. This last one does not need the human being to refine it, because it is of the essence of the angels, peace be upon them, and the results of the holy, supreme spirits. What needs refining are the three before it. Since the first, I mean the appetitive faculty, seeks only to obtain appetitive pleasures, and this kind is specifically named fuhsh (indecency; you see that He, exalted, named fornication fahisha), He indicated its refinement by His saying, glorified: ﴿And He forbids indecency﴾, meaning the prevention of obtaining appetitive pleasures outside the permission of the Law. Since the second, I mean the irascible beastly faculty, always strives to bring evil, harm and injury to the rest of people, He, glorified, indicated its refinement by His prohibition of al-munkar, since there is no doubt that people reject that state. So al-munkar is an expression for the excess occurring in the effects of the irascible faculty. Since the third, I mean the satanic illusory faculty, always strives for domination over people, for self-exaltation and for displaying leadership and precedence, He, glorified, indicated its refinement by prohibiting baghy, since it has no meaning except overstepping and exalting oneself over people. Then he said: Among the wonders in this matter is that the wise men said: the lowliest of these three faculties is the appetitive, the middle is the irascible, and the highest is the illusory. God, exalted, observed this order, so He, glorified, began with mentioning fahsha', which is the result of the appetitive faculty, then al-munkar, which is the result of the irascible faculty, then baghy, which is the result of the illusory faculty. End of quotation. What was transmitted earlier from more than one scholar is derived from this. Let one consider whether the proof of specification is established by what he has established, so that the earlier objection is dispelled or not. Then, the apparent meaning according to this is that the coordination of baghy with what precedes it is like the coordination of ﴿giving to the near of kin﴾ with what precedes it.

In sum, this verse, as al-Bukhari transmitted in al-Adab al-Mufrad, and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, is the most comprehensive verse for good and evil. Al-Bayhaqi transmitted similar from al-Hasan. Al-Baghawardi and Abu Nu'aym in Ma'rifat al-Sahaba transmitted from 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr, who said: "The report of the departure of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) reached Aktham ibn Sayfi, so he wished to go to him, but he went to his people. Two men were delegated, and they came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: 'We are the messengers of Aktham, who asks you: who are you, and what have you brought?' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'I am Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah and His Messenger.' Then he recited to them this verse: ﴿Indeed God commands﴾ etc. They said: 'Repeat this saying to us.' He repeated it to them, peace be upon him, until they memorised it. Then they came to Aktham and informed him. When he heard the verse, he said: 'I see that he commands noble character and forbids its blameworthy opposites. So be at the head in this matter, and do not be followers (adhnab) in it.'"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 90 (part 2 of 2):

This verse also, as al-Imam Ahmad, al-Tabarani and al-Bukhari in al-Adab narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, was the cause of the firm establishment of faith in the heart of 'Uthman ibn Maz'un and of his love for the Prophet (ﷺ). Because of what it contains, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz established it (as a practice) when the caliphate came to him, in place of what the Banu Umayyah, may Allah's anger be upon them, used to do: at the end of their sermons they would make it a practice to revile 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and curse everyone who hated him or reviled him. That was among his greatest virtues, may Allah be pleased with him.

More than one scholar said: Had the Qur'an contained nothing but this noble verse, it would have sufficed as an explanation of everything and as guidance. Perhaps its placement after His saying, ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾, is to draw attention to this, for when one considers that it has gathered what it has gathered, together with its brevity, the eyes of insight awaken and are moved to reflect upon what is other than it.

Ahmad narrated from 'Uthman ibn Abi al-'As, who said: "I was sitting with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when his gaze became fixed, and he said: 'Jibril (peace be upon him) came to me and commanded me to place this verse in this position: Indeed Allah commands...' etc."

It has been cited as evidence that the form of the root a-m-r (command) encompasses both the obligatory and the recommended, and that its underlying meaning is the common element; the verification of this is in the books of usul al-fiqh.

﴿He admonishes you﴾, i.e., He reminds you, with what He commands and forbids, in the best manner of reminding, glorified is He. It is either a new (independent) statement, or a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in the two verbs. ﴿So that you may remember﴾: seeking that you may be admonished by it and take heed.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 91:

﴿And fulfil the covenant of God﴾. Qatada and Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning the alliances of the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic period) in matters of enjoining good or forbidding evil. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, on the authority of Mazida ibn Jabir, that it was revealed concerning the pledge of allegiance to the Prophet (ﷺ), whereby whoever embraced Islam pledged allegiance upon Islam. Its apparent meaning is that it concerns the pledge of allegiance upon Islam in general, so the intended sense of "the covenant of God" is that pledge, as more than one scholar has stated explicitly. It has been objected that the apparent meaning is that it is general to every binding pact, which is what the statement of Maymun ibn Mihran implies, and that the occasion of revelation is not one of the specifying factors; therefore they said: "The consideration is for the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion." It has been answered that the indicator of specification is His statement, exalted is He, earlier in the passage: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾ and so on, but this is open to scrutiny. Al-Asamm said: the intended meaning is jihad and what is obligated in wealth of right, and this does not suit His statement: ﴿when you have made a covenant﴾. It was also said that the intended meaning is the vow (nadhr), and it was said: the oath (yamin). The Imam criticised this by saying that in that case His statement would be—

﴿And do not break the oaths after their confirmation﴾. This is a repetition, because fulfilling the covenant and prohibiting its breaking are close in meaning, since the command to do an act necessarily entails the prohibition of abandoning it. If "covenant" is taken in its general sense, such that the oath falls within it, then this is of the category of singling out some individual instances by mention for the sake of giving them special attention. Some of those who interpreted the covenant as the pledge of allegiance to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took the oaths to mean what occurred at that pledge, while some permitted taking them in the general sense of all oaths.

In the Sa'dian marginal notes (al-Hawashi al-Sa'diyya) it is stated that the apparent meaning is that the intended "oaths" are the things sworn upon, as in his (ﷺ) statement, peace be upon him:

"Whoever swears to an oath and then sees something other than it to be better, let him do what is better and make expiation for his oath." Because if the intended meaning were the mention of the name of God, exalted is He, it would be the very emphasis and not the thing emphasised, and so there would be no place for the mention of the conjunction, as has been established in the science of meanings (al-Ma'ani). It has been rejected: the intended meaning is the contract, not the object sworn upon, because breaking pertains to the contract, and this does not contradict His statement: ﴿after their confirmation﴾, because the intended meaning is that the contract is confirmed by mention of God, exalted is He, and not by mention of anything else, as the common ignorant folk do. Thus the meaning is that this prohibition is for the reason mentioned, not concerning breaking an oath by other than God, exalted is He.

Al-Wahidi said: His statement, glorified is He, ﴿after their confirmation﴾ is to exclude the vain oath (lagh al-yamin), such as "No, by God" and "Yes, by God", on the basis that the meaning is "after their confirmation by resolve and binding", and the vain oath is not of this kind. Then, if the oath is taken in its general sense, it is—as the Imam said—general, and it has been specified by the preceding hadith, which indicates that whenever there is benefit in breaking an oath, it is permissible to break it.
