It has been critically examined: there is room for reflection in this, because if the prohibition were not still in force, the expiation that covers the sin would not be needed. It has been answered: the obligation of expiation is by way of deterrence, since the basic principle of oaths is that they are binding, even if forbidden, so it does not contradict the necessity of its consequence. It has also been allowed to say that this is for the act of swearing by God, exalted is He, in an inappropriate context, so let it be considered. [Page 221] "Confirmation" (al-tawkid) means strengthening (al-tawthiq); and from it comes "ukkida" (it was confirmed), with the wāw converted into a hamza, according to what al-Zajjaj and others among the grammarians held. Others held that "wakkada" and "akkada" are two original dialects, because the usages of the root are equal, so it is not appropriate to say that the wāw is a substitute for the hamza, as in al-Durr al-Masun; and this is what Abu Hayyan chose.

﴿And you have made God your surety over you﴾. That is, a witness and a watcher, for the surety (kafil) takes into account the condition of the one for whom he stands surety and watches over him. The use of "kafil" in this sense is either of the category of metaphor (isti'ara) or of the unrestricted metonymy (al-majaz al-mursal), with the relation being necessity.

The apparent view is that their "making" (God a surety) is also a metaphor, because when they did that while God, exalted is He, was aware of them, it is as if they made Him a witness. This was said by al-Khafaji. Then he said: If "surety" were kept in its literal sense and taken as an analogy for their not escaping His punishment, and that He would hand them over to it just as a surety hands over the one he has stood surety for, as it is said: "Whoever wrongs has set up a surety for his wrong", as an alert that it is impossible for him to escape punishment, as al-Raghib mentioned, that would be a very eloquent meaning, so reflect upon it. The apparent view is that the sentence is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of ﴿you break﴾; it has also been allowed that it is a circumstantial clause from the subject of the verbal noun, though it is elided. His statement, glorified is He:

﴿Indeed, God knows what you do﴾, that is, of breaking, so He will requite you for it. It is in the position of a reason (ta'lil) for the preceding prohibition. Al-Khafaji said: it is like an explanation of what came before it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 92:

﴿And do not be[come]﴾ in what you do of breaking [your oaths] ﴿like her who unravelled her yarn﴾. Ghazlaha (her yarn) is a verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, i.e. maghzulaha (what was spun). The verb from it is ghazala, yaghzilu, with the vowel of the zay being kasra. Naqḍ (unravelling) is the opposite of ibram (twisting firmly), and in the case of a physical object it means separating its parts from one another. The phrase ﴿after its strength﴾ is connected to naqaḍat as an adverbial complement of time (ẓarf) to it, not as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥal); and min here is a superfluous (zā'idah) particle, which is regularly used in such constructions. The meaning is: like the woman who unravelled her yarn after having twisted and firmly tightened it.

﴿Ankathan﴾ (into shreds) is the plural of nikth, with the nun kasra, and refers to that which is untwisted after being spun. Its accusative case is said by some to be a circumstantial qualifier (ḥal) emphasising ﴿ghazlaha﴾. Others say it is a second object of naqaḍa, since the verb implies the meaning of ja'ala (made). Al-Zajjaj permitted that the accusative is a verbal noun (maṣdar), because naqaḍat carries the sense of nakathat (broke), so it corresponds in meaning to its governing verb.

Al-Kashshaf says: making it an object by way of tadmin (implication of a different verb) is preferable to making it a circumstantial qualifier or a verbal noun. Bringing it in the plural form amounts to hyperbole, and likewise the omission of the qualified noun, so as to indicate the foolish, senseless woman and the like. In al-Kashshaf there is also something pointing to the consideration of tadmin, where he says: that is, do not be like the woman who unwound her spun yarn after having made it firm, thus turning it into shreds. In his phrase "unwound" (anḥat), according to al-Qutb, there is an indication that naqaḍat is a metaphor for "intended to unravel," on the pattern of His words, exalted is He: ﴿when you stand up to prayer﴾. It is mentioned that it was interpreted this way in order to combine intention and action, to indicate her foolishness and her deserving blame for this. For if her unravelling had been without intention, she would not deserve that. Also, a simile is the better the more detailed it is. The problems with considering tadmin and this metaphor are not hidden, and perhaps for this reason it was said that the consideration is of intention, since what is understood from an deliberate action is the voluntary sense. In al-Kashshaf, that meaning emerged from His words, exalted is He: ﴿after strength﴾, for unravelling what has been firmly twisted happens only after a strong effort and a complete intention. The relative pronoun does not refer to a specific woman, but rather to anyone who has this description. So in the verse the condition of the one who breaks is compared with the condition of the breaker in his most despicable state, as a warning against it, and that this is not the act of sensible people, and whoever does it is counted among the foolish women. It has also been said: the intended one is a known woman among those addressed, who used to spin, and when she had twisted her yarn she would unravel it. She was called the "foolish woman of Mecca." Ibn al-Anbari said: her name was Rabṭa bint 'Amr al-Mirya, known as al-Ḥafra'. Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said: she was a woman of Quraysh named Rabṭa bint Sa'd al-Taymi, who made a spindle about a cubit long, a whorl like a finger, and a very large spindle-whorl suited to her size. She and her female neighbours would spin from morning until noon, then she would order them and they would unravel what they had spun.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Bakr ibn Hafs, who said: Sa'ida al-Asadiyya was insane, gathering hair and fibre, and this verse was revealed: ﴿And do not be like her who unravelled her yarn.﴾

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Ata': "She complained of her madness to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him to pray for her to be restored to health. He, peace be upon him, said to her: 'If you wish, I will pray and Allah will heal you; and if you wish, you may be patient and seek reward, and you will have Paradise.' So she chose patience and Paradise."

'Ata' mentioned that Ibn 'Abbas showed it to him. From Mujahid: this was the practice of the women of Najd, one of whom would unravel her yarn and then tease it out and spin it again with wool. Qatada, may Allah have mercy on him, held that it was not specified.

﴿Taking your oaths as means of deceit among yourselves﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥal) either from the pronoun in (do not be) or from the prepositional phrase that occupies the position of the predicate.

It is permitted that the predicate of "do not be" and ﴿like her who unravelled﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. Al-Imam said: the clause is a fresh sentence in the form of a denying interrogative: "Do you take your oaths...?" The dakhal (deceit) originally means what enters a thing without being part of it, then it was used as a metaphor for corruption and hidden enmity, like dagal (hidden treachery). Qatada explained it as treachery and betrayal. Its accusative is as a second object, and it has been said it is an accusative of cause. The purpose of the clause being in circumstantial position is to indicate the aspect of comparison: that is, "do not be those compared to a woman of such a character, taking your oaths as a means of treachery and corruption among you."

﴿That one community may be more numerous than another community﴾, i.e. that a group be greater in number and richer in wealth ﴿than another community﴾, i.e. than another group. The meaning is: do not betray a people because of their being many or few, but keep your oaths with them. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from Mujahid that he said: They used to make alliances with allies, and when they found others more numerous and mightier, they would break their alliance and ally themselves with those who were mightier. So they were forbidden from this: do not betray a group because another group is more numerous and mightier. Rather, you must fulfil and observe your oaths, even if the one you bound yourselves to is few and the other is many.

In "takūna" it is permitted that it be complete or incomplete, and in "hiya" that it be the subject and a pronominal support (imād). "Arbā" may be either nominative or accusative. You know that the Basrians do not permit "hiya" to be a support for the indefinite "umma."

Some of the Shi'a claimed that this verse was distorted, and its original reading was: "that there be imams who are purer than your imams." By my life, they have strayed from the right path.

﴿Indeed Allah tests you by it﴾: the pronominal suffix in "bihi" refers either to the verbal noun formed from "an takūna," or to the verbal noun understood from "arbā," which is ar-rabw in the sense of increase. The statement of Ibn Jubayr, Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil, "by abundance," their intended meaning is this, and they were content with explaining the resulting sense. Ibn al-Anbari supposed that they meant the pronoun refers to abundance itself, but since its feminine gender is not real, the masculine is valid. This, as you see, is weak. It was also said that it refers to "arbā" because it is interpreted as "the more." It was also said it refers to the command to fulfil, which is implied by His words, exalted is He: ﴿and fulfil﴾, etc. There is no need to make it understood from the prohibition against treachery in covenant. Some preferred the first, because it is quicker to come to mind, i.e. He treats you as one who is tested by that state, to see whether you hold fast to the cord of fulfilment with the covenant of Allah, exalted is He, and the pledge of His Messenger (ﷺ), or whether you are deceived by the numerical strength and might of Quraysh and the weakness and small number of the believers according to outward appearance.

﴿And He will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection that about which you used to differ﴾, so He will recompense you for your deeds with reward and punishment.

[Page 223]

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 16, verse 93:

﴿Had God willed, He would have made you﴾, O people, ﴿one community﴾, agreed upon Islam. ﴿But﴾ He does not will that, out of regard for wisdom. Rather, ﴿He leads astray whom He wills﴾, and His leading astray means that He creates misguidance in him, in accordance with how He directs his following choice to his readiness for it. ﴿And He guides whom He wills﴾, His guidance being in accordance with how He directs his following choice to his readiness for attaining it. ﴿And you will surely be questioned﴾, all of you, on the Day of Resurrection, a questioning of reckoning and recompense, not a questioning of inquiry and understanding, ﴿about what you used to do﴾, that is, what you persisted in doing in the world, through your capacity that has effect by God's leave, the verse being clear that God's will for the Islam of all creation did not occur. He, glorified is He, willed from them separation and discord, so there was faith and disbelief, affirmation and denial, and the matter occurred as He willed, exalted is He and high.

The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school) deny that misguidance occurs by His will, and they claim that He, glorified is He, willed from all of them only faith, and what He willed did not occur, may His majesty be exalted. Al-Zamakhshari answered regarding the verse that the meaning is: had He willed in the manner of compulsion and coercion, He would have made you one Muslim community, for He is capable of that. But wisdom required that He lead astray and abandon whom He wills, from among those whom He knows, glorified is He, choose disbelief and insist upon it, and guide whom He wills by showing kindness to those whom He knows choose faith. The conclusion is that He, exalted is He, founded the matter upon choice and upon what merits kindness or abandonment, reward or punishment, and He did not point to compulsion, by which nothing is merited. Had the servants been forced toward guidance and misguidance, He would not have attributed to them an act about which they are questioned, by His saying: ﴿and you will surely be questioned about what you used to do﴾. Al-Askari has similar words. I have mentioned to you more than once that the true doctrine, as clarified by the later scholar al-Kurani, who wrote several treatises on it, is that the servant has an effective capacity by God's leave. It is not that he has no capacity whatsoever, as the Jabriyyah (a determinist school) say, nor that he has a concomitant capacity that is non-effective, as is well known among the Ash'ariyyah (followers of al-Ash'ari), nor that he has an effective capacity even without God's leave, as the Mu'tazilah say. Rather, he has a choice given after seeking his readiness, which is established in God's knowledge. So in this doctrine the servant has choice, and the servant is "compelled" in it in the sense that it must be his, because his eternal readiness, which is not created, has sought it from the Absolute Bestower and the Wise who places things in their proper places. Reward and punishment are consequent upon the readiness for good and evil established in reality itself, and good and evil indicate that readiness, in the manner that an effect indicates its cause and an end indicates its purpose. ﴿God did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves﴾, and ﴿whoever finds good, let him praise God, and whoever finds other than that, let him blame no one but himself.﴾

Ibn al-Munir said: Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni people) are far removed from compulsion, because they affirm for the servant capacity, choice, and acts, and yet they profess the oneness of God in its true sense. They make His capacity, glorified is He, the one that originates and has effect, and the servant's capacity merely concomitant. By this, the voluntary is distinguished from the coerced, and the proof of God against His servants is established. End of quote. This is the well-known doctrine of the Ash'ariyyah, and it is as you see. The full discussion of this station, and what it contains of refutation and affirmation, will come, God willing, later.

[p. 224]

﴿And do not take your oaths as a means of deception among yourselves﴾. They said: this is an explicit prohibition against taking oaths as a means of deception (*dakhal*), after the earlier prohibition implied by the restriction. This is because the taking mentioned earlier served as a qualifier of what was forbidden, so it was implicitly forbidden too, as emphasis and an intensification of the ugliness of what is forbidden, and as a preparation for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿lest a foot slip﴾ from the path of truth ﴿after it had been firmly planted﴾ upon it and established in it through faith. Others said: what preceded was a prohibition against entering into oaths and breaking covenants, whether few or many, while what is here is a prohibition against the deception (*dakhal*) of oaths by which one intends to seize rights. It is as if it were said: do not take your oaths as a means of deception among yourselves, so that by them you may reach the cutting off of the rights of the Muslims.

Abu Hayyan said: the prohibition is not repeated, for what preceded is a report that they had taken their oaths as a means of deception, motivated by a specific matter, namely that one community be more numerous than another. The prohibition that comes afterwards is a directive (*insha'i*) prohibition against taking oaths as deception in general, so it includes all forms: swearing in pledges, cutting off financial rights, and other things. It was answered that the qualifier of what is forbidden is not a pure report, and there is no generality in the second, because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿lest a foot slip﴾ etc., is an allusion to the earlier cause in summary. Moreover, it may be said that the specific is also mentioned within the general, so there is no escape from repetition either. Even if what he mentioned is granted, consider it carefully.

The verb ﴿tazillu﴾ (slip) is in the subjunctive, with an implied *an* after the prohibition, to explain what follows from it and what it requires. In *al-Bahr* it is said: this is a metaphor for falling into a great matter, because when a foot slips a person passes from a state of good to a state of evil. The singularity and indefiniteness of ﴿qadam﴾ (foot), as al-Zamakhshari said, indicates that the slipping of a single foot, whatever foot it was, whether high or low, is a great danger; how much more so when there are many feet.

Abu Hayyan said: the plural is sometimes considered in terms of the collective as a whole, and sometimes each individual is considered. In the first case the predication takes into account the plurality of the group, and in the second the predication corresponds to the plural form, often so that what is predicated is pluralized, and to each individual so that it is singular, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and she prepared for them a couch﴾, where *muttaka'* (couch) is singular because each one of them was considered. Had it been intended to mean the plurality, or the many in the second manner, it would have been pluralized. On this basis, His poet's saying should be understood:

"For I have found the lean ones, their goods perish and vanish, so take from my provision."

That is, every lean one; this is why the pronoun is singular in *yamutu* (perishes) and *yafna* (vanishes). Since the meaning here is that none of you should take, it came as ﴿a foot slips﴾, in observance of this meaning. Then He, glorified is He, said ﴿and you taste evil﴾, in observance of the collective, or of the plural form in the frequent manner. If we say that the predication is to each individual, then the verse addresses the prohibition against taking oaths as a means of deception both with respect to the group and with respect to each individual, and this is indicated by the singular ﴿qadam﴾ and the plural pronoun in ﴿wa-tadhuqu﴾ (and you taste).

It was objected that what al-Zamakhshari mentioned is a secret subtle point, whereas this is a justification for the singular from the standpoint of Arabic grammar, so it does not contradict the aforementioned subtle point. The meaning of evil (*su'*) is worldly punishment: killing, captivity, plunder, expulsion, and other things that cause harm. The metaphor in ﴿taste﴾ is not hidden. ﴿Because you averted﴾: because of your turning away and aversion, or the averting and preventing of others ﴿from the way of Allah﴾, which includes fulfilling covenants and oaths. For whoever breaks the pledge and apostatizes makes that a precedent for others, whom those after him follow in it, from among the people of wretchedness and those who turn away from the truth; thus he becomes one who averts from the way.

Some have taken this as evidence that the verse concerns those who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and that is, as you see, [a weak view]. ﴿And for you﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿is a great punishment﴾, whose greatness none knows except Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 95:

﴿And do not sell the covenant of Allah for a small price.﴾ By it, according to many, is meant the pledge (bay'ah) of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ upon faith, and "purchasing" (ishtira') is a metaphor for "exchanging" (istibdal), because of the words of the Exalted: ﴿a small price﴾, for the price is that which is bought with. That is, do not take, in exchange for His covenant, a meagre bit of worldly gain. Al-Zamakhshari said: There was a group among those who had embraced Islam in Makkah whom Satan adorned with anxiety at what they saw of the dominance of Quraysh, their oppression of the Muslims, and their harm to them, and with what the Quraysh promised them if they returned to disbelief: that they should break what they had pledged to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. So Allah strengthened them by this verse and forbade them to exchange that for the worldly goods the Quraysh had promised them. Ibn 'Atiyah said: This is a prohibition of bribery and of taking wealth in return for abandoning what the taker is obligated to do, or for doing what he is obligated to refrain from. Thus the meaning of "the covenant of Allah" encompasses what preceded and other things, and its goodness is not hidden. ﴿Indeed, what is with Allah﴾, that is, what He has granted and stored up for you in this world and the Hereafter, ﴿is better for you﴾ than that small price, ﴿if you knew﴾. That is, if you are among the people of knowledge and discernment. Here the verb is treated as intransitive. It has also been said that it is transitive, with its object omitted, namely the excess between the two exchanges; but the first (reading) is more eloquent and needs no estimation. And in the use of ﴿in﴾ (as the conditional particle) there is what is not hidden. The sentence serves as a justification for the prohibition in the manner of affirmation, just as the saying of the Exalted:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 96:

﴿What is with you﴾ etc. is a justification for the superiority (of what is with God) by way of resumption (istinaf); that is, what you enjoy of the bounties of this world is not (lasting), rather this world and all that is in it ﴿will vanish﴾, that is, will come to an end and perish, even if its number is great and its duration long. It is said: نَفِدَ (nafida) with a kasra on the ʿayn, yanfadu with a fatha, nafadan and nufudan, when it departs and is exhausted. As for نَفَذَ (nafadha) with the dhal dotted, it has a fatha on the ʿayn and its present tense is yanfudhu with a damma. ﴿And what is with God﴾ of the treasures of His mercy, worldly and otherworldly, ﴿is lasting﴾, having no end. As for the otherworldly, it is evident; as for the worldly, since it is connected to the otherworldly and follows from it, it is included in the string of the lasting good deeds (al-baqiyat al-salihat). Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Jubayr that what is meant by ﴿what is with God﴾ in both places is the otherworldly reward, and some of the imams chose this view. The use of the noun form rather than the present tense indicates permanence, which is not hidden. This is refuted by the verse against Jahm ibn Safwan, who claimed that the bliss of Paradise is cut off.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will surely reward﴾ with the nun of majesty, which is the reading of ʿAsim and Ibn Kathir, by way of iltifat (shift) from the third person to the first person, is a repetition of the promise derived from His saying, glorified is He: ﴿What is with God is better for you﴾, in the manner of an emphatic oath, for the sake of intensifying the urging to remain steadfast in the covenant. The rest of the seven readers read it with the ya', so there is no iltifat.

The departure from what the apparent situation requires, namely to say "and We will surely reward you" (with nun or ya') "your reward for the best of what you used to do," is for the sake of drawing attention to their deeds and indicating that these are the cause of the reward; that is, "by God, We will surely reward those who endured" in the covenant or in the harm of the polytheists and the hardships of Islam, of which fulfilling covenants is part, even if those who break them are promised what they were promised. ﴿Their reward﴾ is the object of (la-najziyannahum), that is, We will surely give them their particular reward in return for their patience ﴿according to the best of what they used to do﴾, which is patience, for it is among the inward deeds. The statement is elliptical, meaning: We will surely reward them with the recompense of their patience. Patience was the best of deeds because all the obligations depend on it, so it is their head, as Abu Hayyan said. In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim: the best was attributed to what is mentioned only to indicate the perfection of its goodness, as in His saying: ﴿and the best reward of the Hereafter﴾, not to restrict the reward to the best of it excluding the good; for that does not occur to anyone's mind, especially after His saying: "their reward." Thus the idafa is for encouragement.

It is also permitted that the meaning be: We will surely reward them according to the best of their individual deeds; that is, We will give them, in return for the lowest of their deeds, what We give in return for the highest of them of the great reward, not that We give the reward according to their varying individual deeds in degrees of goodness, by rewarding the good among them with good and the best with the best. In this there is what is not hidden of a beautiful promise, by forgiving whatever of partial distress may befall them in the midst of patience, and by including it under beautiful patience. It is also permitted that "best" be an adjective of an omitted reward, and the idafa be in the sense of the comparative: that is, We will reward them with a reward better than their deeds, and its being better is due to its being multiplied. It was also said: what is meant by "the best" is that whose performance is preferred over its omission, such as obligatory and recommended acts; or that whose omission is also preferred, such as prohibited and disliked acts; and "good" is what whose performance is not preferred nor its omission, and for this one is not rewarded. It was objected in Irshad that this does not fit the context of urging them to remain steadfast in the good specific deeds they are upon and encouraging them to attain their fruits, but rather it touches on removing some of their deeds from the scope of reward, which is like restricting the wide mercy in a context of widening its sanctuary. It was also said: what is meant by "the best" is the supererogatory act, and it was best because it is not made obligatory but a person performs it by choice, not compelled. And if you know that reward is given for the supererogatory act which is best, you know that reward is given for the obligatory act which is good. It is not hidden that it is not good at all.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 97:

﴿Whoever does righteousness﴾ means: a righteous deed, of any kind whatsoever. This, as it has been said, is the beginning of an exhortation to all believers to every righteous deed, after the encouragement of a group of them to persist in a particular righteous deed that they were already doing, in order to repel the notion that the great reward belongs only to them and to their deed. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿whether male or female﴾ is a repulsion of the notion that ﴿whoever﴾ (man) is restricted to males, because of what is immediately understood from the apparent wording of "man," since it is masculine and its pronoun refers back to it, even though it includes both sexes by its linguistic convention according to the more correct view. This is supported by what al-Tirmidhi narrated, the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever drags his garment out of arrogance, Allah, exalted is He, will not look at him," and the saying of Umm Salama: "Then how should women do with their hems?" (the hadith continues).

Umm Salama, may Allah be pleased with her, understood that women are included in "whoever," and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) confirmed her in that. Also, they (the scholars) agreed that if someone said, "Whoever enters my house is free," and female slaves entered it, they would be freed. Some also derive this from this verse, since if it did not include females by its wording, it would not be correct to specify it by both sexes. In al-Kashshaf it is said: The apparent meaning was that it includes males, on the basis that females do not enter into most rulings and modes of address; and although inclusion by way of generalization and predominance (taghlib) is present, when explicitness was intended, so that it would be more gratifying to both groups and a clear text on the inclusion of both, it was made explicit by mentioning both sexes. End of quotation. The more correct view is that inclusion does not need predominance. The full discussion of this is in the books of usul (principles of jurisprudence).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while he is a believer﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of ﴿did﴾, and it is restricted by it, since there is no reliance on the righteous deeds of disbelievers for entitlement to reward, by consensus. It has been disputed whether lightening of punishment is consequent upon them. Some said: it is not consequent either, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when those who did wrong see the punishment, it will not be lightened for them﴾ and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make it scattered dust﴾.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: The benefit of a righteous deed in lightening punishment is not conditional on faith, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾, and the hadith about Abu Talib, that he was the least of people in punishment, owing to his love (for the Prophet) and his protection of the Prophet (ﷺ). In al-Bahr it is said that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ is specified by this verse and the like, or by "an atom's weight" is meant an atom's weight of faith, as came concerning those who come out of the Fire from among the sinning believers. Al-Kirmani said: The lightening of punishment for Abu Talib is not a reward for his deed; rather it is for the hope of others, or it is one of the distinctions of our Prophet, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him. Some said: Faith is a condition for the consequence of lightening upon righteous deeds when their validity depends on intention (niyyah), which is not valid from a disbeliever; and it is not a condition for the consequence upon them when they are not of that kind. The full discussion of this station will come, if Allah, exalted is He, wills.

The choice of the nominal sentence (al-jumlah al-ismiyyah) serves to show the obligation of the continuation of faith and its being concurrent with the righteous deed, in the consequence of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾, etc. By "a good life" is meant the life that is in Paradise, since there is life without death, wealth without poverty, health without sickness, sovereignty without ruin, and happiness without misery. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated from al-Hasan, who said: Life is not good for anyone except in Paradise. Something similar was related from Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. And by Allah, how right is the one who said:

"There is no pleasure in living while it is spoiled in its delights
by the remembrance of death and of old age."

Sharik said: It is a life that is in the barzakh, for it has come: "The grave is a garden of the gardens of Paradise, or a pit of the pits of Hellfire."

[Page 227]

Others said: It is in this world, and by it is meant a life accompanied by contentment and satisfaction with what Allah, exalted is He, has apportioned and decreed for him. Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Abi Hatim and others narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he explained it thus, and said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to supplicate: "O Allah, make me content with what You have provided me, bless me in it, and replace for me, with good, everything I have lost."

Contentment has come to be described as wealth that does not run out. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: It is a life accompanied by the sweetness of obedience. Abd al-Razzaq and others narrated from Ibn Abbas that he was asked about it and said: The good life is lawful provision. This was also related from al-Dahhak. Some explained the goodness of this life by saying that no punishment is consequent upon it, unlike life by unlawful provision, for it has come: "Any flesh that grew from sukht (unlawful gain), the Fire is more deserving of it."

He (al-Alusi) said: It is as you see. It has also been said: other than that. The most correct of the views, on the assumption that it refers to this world, is to explain it as that which is accompanied by contentment.

Al-Wahidi said: Its explanation by that is good and preferred, for in this world only the life of the content one is pleasant, whereas the greedy one is always in toil and hardship. Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: The life of the believer in this world is more pleasant than the life of the disbeliever, for several reasons:

The first: When he knows that his provision came about through the ordaining of Allah, exalted is He, and that He, glorified is He, is Benevolent and Generous, who does only what is right, he is content with everything He has decreed and decided, and he knows that his welfare lies in it. The ignorant one does not know these principles, so he is always in grief and misery.

The second: The believer always keeps in his mind the various kinds of calamities and trials, estimates their occurrence, and finds his soul content with that. So when they occur, he does not take them to be great; whereas the ignorant one is heedless of those realities, so when calamities occur, their effect on his heart is great.

The third: The believer is expanded by the light of knowledge of Allah, exalted is He. When the heart is filled with knowledge, it has no room for the sorrows caused by the circumstances of this world. The ignorant one's heart is empty of knowledge, free for sorrows from worldly calamities.

The fourth: The believer knows that the goods of physical life are base, so his joy in finding them is not great, nor his grief in losing them. The ignorant one knows no other happiness that differs from it, so his joy in finding them is great and his grief in losing them is great.

The fifth: The believer knows that the goods of this world are necessarily subject to change and quick to vanish, and that were it not for their change and reversal, they would not reach him. So when they reach him, his heart does not cling to them, nor does he embrace them with the embrace of a lover, so their passing does not grieve him. The ignorant one is the opposite. End of quotation. There is room for discussion in it.

It has been objected to the preferred explanation that some who did righteous deeds while being believers were not granted contentment, but were rather tested with covetousness. It was answered that by "believer" is meant one whose faith is complete, or it may be said: by "whoever does righteousness" is meant one all of whose deeds are righteous.

Al-Baydawi, explaining the consequence of His giving him a good life, said: If he is poor, the matter is evident; and if he is wealthy, the goodness of his life is through contentment, satisfaction with the apportionment, and expectation of the great reward in the Hereafter, that is, despite the non-fulfillment of some of his wishes and the straitness of his life. Al-Khafaji said: These matters must be present to some degree in the believer, and the last of them, that is, expectation of reward in the Hereafter, is general and encompasses every believer, so it is not objected that this is not found in everyone who does righteousness, such that the believer must be interpreted as one whose faith is complete, and so on to the end of what you have heard. It was rebutted: contentment is satisfaction with the apportionment, as in al-Qamus and others, and expectation of the great reward does not exist without that; and how would reward be obtained along with non-fulfillment of wishes and straitness of life together with complaint and lack of satisfaction? His words are apparent in the realization of this expectation even if there is no contentment and satisfaction, and this hardly happens from a knowing believer, so interpretation is necessary.

Some also examined it on the ground that the perfection of faith does not occur without satisfaction, and likewise that all deeds being righteous does not exist without it, because deeds include inward and outward ones, and satisfaction is of the first kind. The meaning of ﴿We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾

[Page 228]

is: We will surely give him that by which his life becomes good. Then the meaning of the verse is interpreted, on the assumption that contentment and satisfaction are meant, as: whoever is satisfied with the apportionment and does such-and-such while being a believer; or whoever does righteousness while being satisfied with the apportionment, characterized by such-and-such, of what contains the perfection of faith: then We will surely give him satisfaction with the apportionment, by which his life becomes good; and it includes: whoever is satisfied with the apportionment, then We will surely give him satisfaction with the apportionment by which his life becomes good. And this, as you see, and in it is what is not hidden. Yes, the explanation of the good life as what is in Paradise is free from this talk and debate, and by it is meant that which is safe from the notion of death and old age, the sweet pain, and sickness. Then His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ is an indication of the averting of harms; and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and We will surely reward them with the best of what they used to do﴾ is an indication of the bringing of benefits. And because the first is more important, it is placed first, so let it be pondered. It seems that what is meant by "and We will surely reward them" etc. is in the manner in which the patient are treated; so there is in the verse no trace of repetition, as al-Tabarsi claimed. The plural in the pronouns referring back to the relative pronoun is for regard of the sense, just as the singular earlier is for regard of the wording. The preference for this in reverse order is based on the view that the enlivening is a good life in this world and the reward recompense in the Hereafter, because the occurrence of recompense in the manner of collectivity suits the collective, and the occurrence of what is in the relative clause and what follows from it in the manner of separation and succession suits the individual. It was also said, on the basis that this is in the Hereafter: the plural and singular are for what preceded; and likewise the preference for the reverse order in what is other than the pronoun of "We will surely cause him to live," but regarding the pronoun of it, the reason is that enlivening into a good life, in the sense of what is safe from what has preceded, is one matter that all share, in which the people of Paradise do not differ; so they are as one thing in it. And since the recompense is not like that, and the people of Paradise differ in it, the plural pronoun is used with it. So ponder all of this. It is narrated from Nafi' that he read "and surely He will reward them" with ya', as a shift from first person to third person.

Abu Hayyan said: It should be that this is on the assumption of a second oath, not coordinated with ﴿So We will surely cause him to live﴾, so it is a coordination of an oath-clause with a similar oath-clause, both of them elided; and it is not a coordination of a response with a similar response, because the attributions differ, and the shift from the second to the speaker's report about himself is a report of the absent, and that is not permitted. On this basis it is not permitted to say: "Zayd said, 'I will surely strike Hind' or 'He will surely deny her'," meaning "let Zayd surely deny her." But if you make it on the assumption of a second oath, it is permitted, i.e., "and Zayd said, 'He will surely deny her'," because in this construction there is a report of meaning and a report of wording. From the second is ﴿and they will surely swear, "We intended nothing but good"﴾, and from the first ﴿They swear by Allah that they said nothing﴾; and if the wording were quoted, it would be said, "We did not say," End of quotation. The verse has been cited as evidence that faith is distinct from righteous deeds, as the distinction of a condition from what is conditioned.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 98:

هَذا وإذْ قَدِ انْتَهى الأمْرُ إلى مَدارِ الجَزاءِ وهو صَلاحُ العَمَلِ وحُسْنِهِ رُتِّبَ عَلَيْهِ بِالفاءِ الإرْشادُ إلى ما بِهِ يَحْسُنُ العَمَلُ الصّالِحُ، ويَخْلُصُ عَنْ شَوْبِ الفَسادِ فَقِيلَ: ﴿فَإذا قَرَأْتَ القُرْآنَ فاسْتَعِذْ بِاللَّهِ﴾ أيْ إذا أرَدْتَ قِراءَةَ القُرْآنِ فاسْألْهُ عَزَّ جارُهُ أنْ يُعِيذَكَ ﴿مِنَ﴾ وساوِسِ ﴿الشَّيْطانِ الرَّجِيمِ﴾ كَيْلا يُوَسْوِسَكَ في القِراءَةِ فالقِراءَةُ مَجازٌ مُرْسَلٌ عَنْ إرادَتِها إطْلاقًا لِاسْمِ المُسَبِّبِ عَلى السَّبَبِ، وكَيْفِيَّةُ الِاسْتِعاذَةِ عِنْدَ الجُمْهُورِ مِنَ القُرّاءِ وغَيْرِهِمْ أعُوذُ بِاللَّهِ مِنَ الشَّيْطانِ الرَّجِيمِ لِتَظافُرِ الرِّواياتِ عَلى أنَّهُ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ كانَ يَسْتَعِيذُ كَذَلِكَ.

[Then] al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi narrated: "That Ibn Mas'ud recited in his presence (ﷺ), and he said: 'I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Shaytan.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'O son of Umm Abd, say: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. Thus did Jibril recite it to me from the Pen, from the Preserved Tablet.'"

Yes, Abu Dawud and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, in the context of the slander (al-ifk), she said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sat up, uncovered his face, and said: 'I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Shaytan. Indeed, those who brought the slander...'" — the verse. And both of them narrated from Sa'id that he said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rose at night and began the prayer, he would say: 'Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You, blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You.' Then he would say: 'I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing...'" etc.

صفحة 229
Accordingly, those who sought refuge in this manner acted upon it. In al-Hidayah it is preferred that one say: "Astaʿidhu billah" so as to conform to the Qur'an (lit. "I seek refuge in Allah") and to be closer to "A'udhu billahi min al-shaytan al-rajim," etc. The preferred view is what you heard first, because the word "isti'dh" (seek refuge) is a request for refuge, and his saying "A'udhu" is a compliant act matching its requirement. Closeness of wording is disregarded, and the majority's position is sufficient in its preference, since it is what was transmitted in the reports. Some of our companions said: The one seeking refuge should not add "the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing," because it is praise, and what follows the seeking of refuge is the place of recitation, not the place of praise. The response to this is that, even after granting the two previously mentioned reports, this is not sound, since in that there is no bringing of praise after the seeking of refuge, but rather bringing it within it, as is not hidden. The command to it is for recommendation (nadb) according to them.

Abd al-Razzaq narrated in al-Musannaf, and Ibn al-Mundhir from Ata', and it is reported from al-Thawri, that it is obligatory for every recitation, whether in prayer or otherwise, due to this verse. They took the command in it to mean obligation, considering that it is literally (haqiqah) for that. The inability of its serving to repel the whispering in recitation is not a diverting factor from it; rather, the legislating of obligation remains valid with it. It is answered that this contradicts the consensus. It is unlikely that they would invent a statement contrary to it after knowing that this is not permissible. So Allah knows best the diverting factor according to the position of the majority. It may be said: it is his (ﷺ) teaching the Bedouin the prayer without mentioning it (the seeking of refuge).

It may be answered that his teaching him it is by teaching him what is among its specifics, and it is not among its obligations, but rather among the obligations of recitation. Or that its being said at the time of recitation was apparent and well known, so it was dispensed with mentioning it. And in it: this does not hold according to what you will hear shortly, God willing, from the statement of Abu Yusuf, may Allah have mercy on him. Al-Khafaji said: taking the command to mean recommendation is because of what is narrated of the Prophet (ﷺ) leaving it, and if this is established, it is sufficient as a diverting factor. The position of Ibn Sirin and al-Nakha'i, and it is one of the two statements of al-Shafi'i, is that it is legislated in the recitation in every rak'ah, because the command is conditional upon a condition, so it is repeated with its repetition, as in His saying: ﴿وإنْ كُنْتُمْ جُنُبًا فاطَّهَّرُوا﴾ [And if you are in a state of major impurity, then purify yourselves]. Also, since it is legislated in the first rak'ah, it is legislated in the other rak'ahs by analogy, for the shared cause. The position of Abu Hanifah—and it is the other statement of al-Shafi'i—is that it is legislated only in the first, because the recitation of the whole prayer is like one recitation. It was said: according to Imam Abu Hanifah, it is for the prayer, and therefore it is not repeated. What is mentioned in al-Hidayah and others is that according to the Imam and Muhammad, it is for the recitation, not the praise, so that the one who joins late (masbuq) recites it, but not the one who follows an imam (muqtadi). Abu Yusuf said: it is for the praise. In al-Khulasah it is stated that this is the most correct. The fruit of the disagreement appears in three issues mentioned therein. What the author of al-Qil mentioned, we have not found in the books of our companions. Malik does not regard seeking refuge in an obligatory prayer, but regards it in other prayers, such as the night prayers of Ramadan. What is transmitted from him outside prayer, as you heard from some of his followers, and from Abu Hurayrah, Ibn Sirin, Dawud, and Hamzah among the reciters, is that seeking refuge after recitation is in accordance with the apparent meaning of the verse.

For the majority is what the imams of recitation narrated with a chain (musnad) from Nafi', from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say before recitation: "A'udhu billahi min al-shaytan al-rajim." Al-Kashshaf said: the hadith shows that the preceding of it is the Sunnah, so the causal connection of recitation to it remains, and the fa' in (fa-isti'dh) indicates the causal connection, so the intention (of the act) must be supposed for it to be valid. Also, completing the act does not suit seeking refuge from an enemy; rather, what suits it is beginning it and being in its midst. So it must be supposed that both (recitation and seeking refuge) are caused by one single cause, not merely an incidental association, which the fa' negates. To this indicated the author of al-Miftah with his statement: "by the indication of the fa' and the widely transmitted Sunnah," end of quote.

From this it is known that what is said—that the fa' has no indication for what was mentioned, and that their consensus on the validity of this figurative usage shows that the preventing indication against the literal meaning is not a condition in it—is nothing. Likewise, the claim of a distinction between this verse and His saying: ﴿إذا قُمْتُمْ إلى الصَّلاةِ فاغْسِلُوا﴾ [When you rise to prayer, wash...], etc., that there is a clear proof for the figurative usage there, so the apparent meaning is abandoned for it, unlike our case. The apparent meaning is that by "the Shaytan" is meant Iblis and his helpers. It was said: it is general to every rebellious transgressor among jinn and mankind. Directing the address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and specifying the recitation of the Qur'an among good deeds for seeking refuge when intending it, is to alert that it is for others besides him (ﷺ), and in all other good deeds it is more important. For he (ﷺ), when commanded to do it at the recitation of the Qur'an, to which falsehood does not come from before it or from behind it, then what is the assumption about one other than him (ﷺ) regarding other deeds besides recitation?

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 16, verse 99:**

﴿Indeed, He﴾: the pronoun refers to the matter (al-sha'n) or to Satan. ﴿has no authority﴾: no power of domination or control ﴿over those who believe and upon their Lord they rely﴾: that is, they turn to Him, exalted is He, and not to anyone else. They entrust their affairs to Him and take refuge in Him. The meaning, then, is the negation of domination after seeking refuge, so the sentence serves as a justification for the command to seek refuge, or as a justification for its implied response, meaning: "that He may protect you and the like."

Some have said: the meaning is the negation of such domination absolutely. Abu Hayyan said: "This is what the apparent sense of the reports requires." It was objected: if he has no domination, why were they commanded to seek refuge from him? It was answered: the meaning is the negation of great domination. Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Sufyan al-Thawri that he said regarding the verse: "He has no authority to lead them into a sin that will not be forgiven for them, and [the verse concerns] seeking refuge from lesser matters. They do not obey his commands or accept his whisperings except in matters they consider trivial, and that only occasionally and through heedlessness. So they were commanded to seek refuge from him for greater care in preserving them." Al-Baydawi also took this view, then said: "He mentioned the authority after the command to seek refuge, lest it be supposed that he has any authority."

In al-Kashf [by al-Zamakhshari], it is stated that this sentence functions as an explanation of the seeking of refuge that was commanded, and that mere empty words are not sufficient for it, without resorting to God, exalted is He. Resorting is only through faith first and reliance (tawakkul, trust in God) second. In any case, the reason for omitting the conjunction is clear. The choice of the past tense in the first relative clause indicates affirmation, just as the choice of the future-form in the second indicates continuous renewal. And the mention of the attribute of Lordship (rububiyyah) serves to emphasize the negation of authority over the believers who rely upon Him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 100:

﴿Indeed, his authority is only over those who take him as a patron﴾, i.e., who make him a ruler over themselves, so they love him, obey him, and respond to his call. Thus, what is meant by "authority" (sultan) is domination (tasallut) and rule (wilayah) through invitation, which results in responding to it, not what encompasses that and also domination by compulsion and coercion. For in making taking-as-patron the relative clause (silah) of "innama" there is a clear negation of the intention of compulsory domination, since one who is compelled is far removed from this meaning. This has also been negated of the disbelievers in His, the Exalted's, saying, reporting about the accursed one: ﴿And I had no authority over you except that I invited you, and you responded to me﴾, ﴿and those who are, because of him,﴾ i.e., because of Satan and his misleading them, ﴿associators﴾ with Allah, the Exalted. It was said: i.e., by their associating Satan (with Allah), they are associators of Allah, the Exalted. It is also permitted that the pronoun refers to the Lord, exalted is His station, and the "ba'" is for transitivity (ta'diyah). This has been narrated from Mujahid, but the first view is preferred because of the unity of the pronouns in it, along with its immediate understanding. In Irshad al-Aql al-Salim there is something that indicates preference for the last view. It is also mentioned there that restricting the authority of the accursed to those mentioned, right after negating it from the believers who rely upon Him, is evidence that there is no intermediary in reality between reliance upon Allah, the Exalted, and taking Satan as a patron, though there is an intermediary in concept; and that whoever does not rely upon Him, the Exalted, is included in the thread of those who take Satan as a patron without realizing it, since the explanation is completed by it. So there is exaggeration in urging reliance and warning against its opposite.

The choice of the verbal, future-oriented nominal clause in the first relative clause, for what has passed just now, and the nominal clause in the second, to indicate permanence, and the repetition of the relative pronoun, to guard against the assumption that the second relative clause is circumstantial, implying that non-associators among Satan's allies do not fall under his authority.

The first is placed before the second, which corresponds to the first relative clause in what preceded, to observe the comparison between them and what corresponds to them of reliance upon Allah, the Exalted. Had the previous order been observed, each of the two parallel phrases would have been separated from what corresponds to it, etc. Since each of faith and patronage is the source of what follows it, the one is placed before it. The fronting of the prepositional phrase is to observe the rhyme (fawasil).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 101:

﴿And when We substitute a verse in place of another verse﴾ — that is, when We send down a verse of the Qur'an in place of a verse of it, and make it a replacement for it by abrogating it (naskh) with it. The apparent meaning, according to what is in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit of Abu Hayyan), is that what is intended is the abrogation of both the wording and the meaning. It is also permissible that what is intended is the abrogation of the meaning while the wording remains. ﴿And Allah knows best what He sends down﴾ of benefits. So each of the abrogating and the abrogated is sent down as the wisdom and the public interest require, for every time has its own requirement, different from the requirement of another time. How many a benefit turns into a harm at another time, because of the change of the circumstances that call for it. We see the skilled physician who may order the patient to take a certain draught and then, after that, forbid him from it and order him to take its opposite. The sacred laws (shara'i') are nothing but benefits for the servants and remedies for their spiritual ailments, so they differ according to the difference of these in times. Glory be to the All-Wise, the All-Knowing. The clause is either parenthetical (mu'tarida), to rebuke the disbelievers and to alert to the corruption of their opinion; and in the shift to the third person (ghayba) together with the attribution to the Exalted Name is what is not hidden of the cultivation of awe and the realization of the meaning of parenthesis. Or it is a circumstantial clause (haliyya), as Abu al-Baqa' and others said.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read «yunazzilu» from the causative (al-inzal). ﴿They say﴾ — that is, the disbelievers, ignorant of the wisdom of abrogation: ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ (muftari), one who invents speech against Allah the Exalted, commanding a thing and then it appears to you so you forbid it. They have exaggerated — may Allah the Exalted fight them — in attributing fabrication to the presence of the Truthful, the one whose truthfulness is affirmed, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, in that they directed the address to him, upon him be prayer and peace, and used the nominal sentence with the emphasis of innama. The relating of this saying of theirs here is to indicate that they are disbelievers arising from the prods of Satan, and that he is their protector. In al-Kashf: the reason for mentioning it after the command to seek refuge (isti'adha) at the time of recitation is that it is a great door of it, by which he tempts the deficient ones, whispering to them about badaa' (change of mind), contradiction, and other things. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾ — that is, they know nothing at all, or they do not know that in the mentioned substitution there are far-reaching wisdoms. The attribution of this judgment to most of them is because among them are those who do know this, but deny it out of obstinacy. The verse is evidence for the abrogation of the Qur'an by the Qur'an, and it is silent regarding the negation of its abrogation by other than that, which is detailed in the books of the principles of jurisprudence.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 102:

﴿Say: "The Holy Spirit has brought it down"﴾. That is, the Qur'an, which is indicated by the verse. Al-Tabrisi said: that is, the abrogating (nasikh) revelation, which is indicated by what precedes it. ﴿The Holy Spirit﴾ means Gabriel, peace be upon him. He was called this because he descends with holiness (al-qudus) from God Most High, that is, with what purifies souls: the Qur'an, wisdom, and divine overflow. It is also said that he was so named because of his purity from human defilements. According to some, the construction is one of specification (lil-ikhtisas), as in ﴿Lord of Might﴾. Some verifiers (muhaqqiqun) took it to be the addition of a qualified noun to its attribute, by making the holiness itself intensive, as in "bad news" (khabar su') and "a truthful man" (rajul sidq), as preferred by al-Radi. Similar to this are "Hatim of generosity" (Hatim al-Jud) and "Sahban of eloquence" (Sahban al-Fasahah). Sahib al-Kashshaf dissented, choosing that it is for specification. What is in the form of tafil (intensive verbal form), if it is held that it denotes gradualness (tadrij), is not hidden in its suitability to the requirement of the context, since it indicates that He sent it down in stages according to the interests (masalih). ﴿From your Lord﴾: in the addition of the Lord to his pronoun (ﷺ) there is an indication of establishing the effusion of the effects of lordship upon him, upon him be blessings and peace, which is not present in its addition to the first-person ya' (my), which signals pure instruction, as in Irshad al-Aql al-Salim. It seems that He gave attention to this implication, and so He did not say "from your Lord" [addressing them]. Also, omitting address to them lowers their rank, as is evident. ("Min") here is for the beginning of the limit (li-ibtida' al-ghayah), metaphorically. ﴿With truth﴾: that is, accompanied by the wisdom that requires it, such that it never separates from it, whether abrogating or abrogated. ﴿To strengthen those who believe﴾: that is, in faith in what must be believed in, due to the decisive proofs and clear evidences it contains,
Page 232
or in faith that His speech is true. For when they hear the abrogating revelation and reflect upon what it contains of consideration of interests, their beliefs become firm and their hearts are at rest. Some interpreted the verse in this way, saying: "to show their steadfastness." This was objected to on the grounds that there is no need for it, since strengthening after abrogation did not exist before it. However, if one considers faith in general, it is valid. It was also read as ﴿li-yuthabbita﴾ (from the verb form af'ala).

﴿And as guidance and good tidings for the Muslims﴾: this is coordinated with the grammatical position (mahall) of ﴿li-yuthabbita﴾, according to al-Zamakhshari and those who followed him. It is like the saying "I visited you to speak with you, and out of honor for you," meaning: for steadfastness, guidance, and glad tidings. It was objected that if the whole is considered the act of the one who sent it down, by way of metaphorical attribution, there is no clear reason for mentioning the lam (the particle of purpose) with some and omitting it with others. Likewise if the act of God Most High is considered, as it truly is. And if the act is considered for some as the act of the one who sent it down, so that the subject of the verbal noun and the subject of the verb it is given as cause are the same (hence the lam is omitted for it), while the other part is the act of God Most High so that the subject differs (hence the lam is used), there is also no clear reason for this specification, and the beauty of the composition is lost by it.

Al-Khafaji said: The omission of the lam in the coordinated element while it is present in the element it is coordinated with, despite the existence of the condition for omission in both, may be explained as follows: the verbal noun formed with "an" (al-masdar al-maslub) is definite, as is established in Arabic grammar, whereas the explicit object of purpose (al-maf'ul lahu al-sarih), even though it is not obligatorily indefinite, as is attributed to al-Riyashi, its opposite is rare, such as the line: "And I forgive the faults of the noble, saving them (for later)." So he distinguished between them for variety (tafannun) and in conformity with the more eloquent usage in both. The point in this is that steadfastness is an incidental matter occurring after the one who is made steadfast has come into being, so the form of occurrence (al-huduth) was chosen for it along with mention of the agent, to indicate that it is an act of God Most High exclusive to Him. By contrast, guidance and good tidings occur through an intermediary. It is also said that the existence of the condition is permissible, not obligatory, and the choice is preferred, along with the benefit of showing that both constructions are permitted. In this there is the point that, upon close examination, it does not stand as a valid reason. Abu Hayyan objected here with what was stated earlier in discussing the words of God Most High: ﴿that you may make clear to them that about which they differ, and as guidance and mercy﴾. He mentioned that it is not impossible that the coordination be with the verbal noun formed with "an," since it is in the genitive, so that ﴿guidance and good tidings﴾ would both be in the genitive. Abu al-Baqa permitted that both be in the nominative, on the basis that they are predicates of an omitted subject, that is, "and it is guidance and good tidings," the clause being in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (nazzalahu).

The intended meaning of "the Muslims" is those who believe. The shift away from their pronoun is to praise them by both designations. Some interpreted Islam according to its lexical meaning, saying that this serves, after describing them with faith, to add [the sense of submission]. Apparently ﴿for the Muslims﴾ is a qualifier of guidance and good tidings. I have not seen anyone address the possibility that it qualifies only the good tidings, as was addressed in the verse ﴿guidance and mercy and good tidings for the Muslims﴾, as I have heard there.

In this verse, according to what they say, there is an allusion (ta'rid) to the occurrence of the opposites of the mentioned matters for those other than the mentioned ones among the disbelievers, since God Most High's words ﴿Say: "The Holy Spirit has brought it down"﴾ are a reply to their saying ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾. Thus ﴿Say: "The Holy Spirit has brought it down"﴾ suffices for the reply, and the additional elements are for the sake of the allusion. Al-Tibi said: ﴿The Holy Spirit has brought it down﴾ is a substitute for "God has brought it down," and in it there is an added vividness in the reply. The words of God Most High ﴿with truth﴾ were added to draw attention to the rebuttal of the criticism in the most subtle manner. Then He denounced their ugly deeds by His words ﴿that He may strengthen﴾ etc., alluding to the fact that they are unsteady, astray, reproached, warned of disgrace, punishment, and curse in this world and the Hereafter, and that their punishment is the reverse of this, so as to increase their rage and fury. In the passage there is something close to the wise (hakim) style. End. So reflect.

[Page 233]

﴿And We certainly know that they say﴾ something other than the monstrous saying that was reported from them. ﴿"It is only a human being who teaches him"﴾, meaning he teaches the Prophet (ﷺ) the Qur'an. This is what the apparent sense of the words of Qatadah, Mujahid and others requires. It was preferred that the pronoun refer to the Qur'an, so that it agrees with the pronoun in (He sent it down), meaning: they say, "It is only a human being who teaches the Qur'an to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him." ﴿A human being﴾ is stated categorically, although it is evident that the Holy Spirit (ruh al-qudus) sent it down to him, peace and blessings be upon him. The emphasis of the sentence (with the particle inna) serves to confirm what it implies of threat. The form of the present tense (yaqulun, "they say") indicates the continuity of the knowledge in accordance with the renewed continuity of its object, for they are continually uttering that great calumny. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit of Abu Hayyan) it is said that the meaning is in the past tense, so the intended sense is "he taught us," and by "this human being" they meant a certain person. It was said: Jabr, the Roman, slave of Amir ibn al-Hadrami, who had read the Torah and the Gospel. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to sit with him when the people of Makkah harmed him, and they then said what they said.

This is also reported from al-Suddi. It was said: he was a freed slave of Huwaytib ibn Abd al-Uzza, whose name was ʿAʾish or Yaʿish, who used to read the books, and he had embraced Islam and his Islam was sound. This was stated by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. It was also said: Abu Fakihah, a freed slave of a woman in Makkah. It was said his name was Yasar, and that he was a Jew. This was stated by Muqatil and Ibn Jubayr, except that Ibn Jubayr did not say he was a Jew.

Adam ibn Abi Iyas, al-Bayhaqi and a group narrated from Abdullah ibn Muslim al-Hadrami, who said: "We had two Christian slaves from the people of Ayn al-Tamr, one called Yasar and the other Jabr. They used to make swords in Makkah, and they used to read the Gospel. The Prophet (ﷺ) would sometimes pass by them while they were reading, and he would stop and listen. The polytheists said, 'He is only learning from them.'" In some of the reports it is said that one of them was told, "You are teaching Muhammad (ﷺ)," and he replied, "No, rather he is teaching me."

From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, it is reported that he said: "In Makkah there was a non-Arab Roman boy belonging to some of the Quraysh, called Balʿam, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to teach him Islam. The Quraysh said, 'This one teaches Muhammad (ﷺ) from the side of the foreigners.'"

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Dahhak that it was Salman al-Farisi, may Allah be pleased with him. This is weakened on the grounds that the verse is Makkan, whereas Salman embraced Islam in Madinah, and because its being a report of an unseen matter does not suit the context (al-siyaq, the flow of the surrounding verses). The report that he embraced Islam in Makkah, and that Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, bought him and freed him there, is said to be weak and not to be relied upon, just as the possibility that this verse is Madinan is not to be relied upon.

Someone I trust informed me about one of the Christians who said to him, "Your Prophet (ﷺ) used to frequent, in the cave of Hira', two men, a Christian and a Jew, who taught him." I have not found this from any of the polytheists. It is a pure lie with no origin and utter slander with no basis. The names of those whom they claimed were teaching him, peace and blessings be upon him, were not explicitly stated, although the claim was included within the evidence of their falsehood. This indicates that the basis of their error is not attributing to him (ﷺ) learning from a specific person, but from a human being, whoever he may be, together with the fact that he, peace and blessings be upon him, was the source of the knowledge of the earlier and later generations.

﴿"The tongue of the one they refer to is foreign"﴾. The word "tongue" (lisan) is a well-known metaphor for speech. Al-ilhad (deviation, "inclining") means to incline, as in one says: lahada and alhada, when one deviates from the straight course. From it comes lahd al-qabr (the niche of the grave), because it is a hole inclined from its middle. The one who is mulhid (a heretic) is so called because he inclines his doctrine away from all religions. The aʿjami (foreign, non-Arabic) is one whose speech is not clear. Abu al-Fath al-Mawsili said: the root ʿ-j-m in the speech of the Arabs signifies obscurity, concealment, and the opposite of clarity and explanation. From it come their sayings: a man is aʿjam and a woman is ʿajma, when they do not speak clearly. ʿAjam al-zabib (the raisin was "ʿajam") was so named because it is hidden and concealed. The beast is called al-ʿajma because it does not make clear what is in its soul. They named the two prayers of Dhuhr and ʿAsr al-ʿujmawayn, because the recitation in them is silent. As for their saying, aʿjamtu al-kitab (I made the book non-Arabic, i.e. I removed its obscurity), its meaning is "I removed its obscurity," just as ashkaytu Zaydan means "I removed Zayd's complaint." The aʿjami and the aʿjam are the one who has a foreign quality in his speech, whether he is of non-Arab origin or of Arab origin. Among such is Ziyad al-Aʿjam, who was an Arab but had a dialectal impediment in his speech. Likewise Habib al-Aʿjami, the student of al-Hasan al-Basri. May Allah sanctify their secrets, as I have seen in some of the histories.

The word "alladhi" (the one) is, according to the view that there were several persons to whom they attributed the teaching, meant as a generic category. The object of (yulhidun, "they refer") is omitted, meaning: the speech of the one to whom they incline their saying away from uprightness, i.e., they attribute the teaching to him, is not clear and its meaning is not evident.

The apparent sense of the words of Ibn Atiyyah is that "tongue" is in its literal meaning, namely the well-known organ. Al-Hasan read "al-lisan alladhi" with the definite article on lisan and the description with alladhi.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abdullah ibn Talhah, al-Sulami and al-Aʿmash read "yalhadun" with a fatha on the ya and the ha, from lahada. Alhada and lahada are two eloquent and well-known dialects.

﴿"And this"﴾, the noble Qur'an, ﴿"is a clear Arabic tongue"﴾, possessing clarity and eloquence, as is indicated by its description as mubin (clear) after its description as ʿarabi (Arabic). According to Ibn Atiyyah, the speech contains an omitted element (muḍaf, a possessed term), meaning: the recitation of a tongue, or the utterance of a tongue. According to al-Zamakhshari, the two clauses are resumptive sentences (mustaʾnafatan, new independent sentences) for refuting their accusation. Abu Hayyan permitted that they be two circumstantial clauses (hal, adverbial clauses) of the subject of (yaqulun, "they say"). Then he said: "This is more forceful as a rebuke," meaning: they say this while the fact that they know the foreignness of this human being and the Arabic character of this Qur'an should have prevented them from such a saying, as when you say, "Do you insult so-and-so when he has done good to you?" Al-Zamakhshari went to the view of resumption because the coming of a nominal sentence as a circumstantial clause without a waw is, in his opinion, rare, and this is a weaker view that he followed from al-Farra', since its coming in this way in the speech of the Arabs is more than can be counted.

The statement of refutation, as al-Allamah al-Baydawi said, admits two aspects. The first: what they hear from that human being is a foreign speech which neither he nor you understand, whereas the Qur'an is Arabic, which you understand with minimal reflection. How then could what he received from him be it? The second: suppose he learned the meaning from him by listening to his speech, yet he did not receive the wording from him, because that is foreign and this is Arabic. The Qur'an, just as it is miraculous in respect of its meaning, is also miraculous in respect of its wording. Moreover, the many sciences found in the Qur'an cannot be learned except by constant association with a teacher who excels in those sciences for a long period. How then could he have learned all of that from a lowly slave who heard from him some transmitted matters in foreign words, the meanings of which he perhaps did not know? The sum of this is the denial that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, learned from him, together with its chain of transmission, and then granting that he learned the meaning, since his wording differs from the wording of that person, which is self-evident. This suffices as proof for him in that what he brought is the inimitable wording. This can be established in a similar manner against the other earlier views concerning the human being.

Al-Kirmani said: the meaning is, "You are the most eloquent, most articulate and most capable of speech among people, in prose and in verse, and you have been unable, and all the Arabs have been unable, to produce its like. So how can you attribute it to a foreign, stammering person? And it is as you see." In general, clinging in the course of attacking to such feeble fables is strong evidence of their complete incapacity. They have endeavored to join day and night, and to make equal the Pleiades and the sun:

*So leave them to claim that morning is night;*
*Will those who look be blinded to the light?*

[Page 234]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 104:

﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of Allah﴾ i.e., do not affirm that they are from Him, the Exalted; rather they say about them what they say, calling them at one time "fabrication" and at another "tales of the ancients" taught by humans. It has also been said: the intended meaning of "the signs" is the miracles that indicate the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Qur'anic verses are included in them by primary inclusion. The first (view), as has been said, is more fitting to the context.

﴿Allah will not guide them﴾ It has been said: i.e., to Paradise; rather He drives them to the Fire, as His saying indicates: ﴿and for them there is a painful punishment﴾.

Some of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) said: the meaning is that He does not guide them to what would save them of the truth, because He knows of the badness of their readiness (istiʿdad). In al-Bahr it is said: i.e., He does not create faith in their hearts. This is a general statement with a specific exception, for some people who disbelieved in the signs of Allah the Exalted were guided. Al-Jalabi said: the meaning is that the cause of their not believing is that He, the Exalted, does not guide them, because of His sealing upon their hearts; or He, glorified is He, does not guide them as a requital for their not believing that those signs are from Him, the Exalted. Al-Askari said: it is possible that the meaning is that if they do not believe in these signs, they will not be guided; and the intended meaning of "Allah will not guide them" is that they will not be guided. For it is only said "Allah the Exalted guided so-and-so" absolutely when he himself becomes guided; but as for one who does not accept guidance, it is said of him: "Allah the Exalted guided him, but he was not guided," as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾. It has also been said: the meaning is that those who do not direct their choice toward belief in the signs of Allah the Exalted, He, glorified is He, does not create it in their hearts. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: what is understood from the existing wording is that those whom Allah the Exalted does not guide do not believe in His signs; but He placed the first and the last out of order (qadama wa-akhkhara) to complete the picture, to denounce their condition and to censure their error, as in His saying: ﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾. What al-Jalabi mentioned first achieves the effect of this reordering, but most of it is not free from unease (daghdaghah).

Al-Qadi said: the strongest of what has been said regarding the verse is what was mentioned first, and that its being an interpretation suited to the Mu'tazilah in accordance with their principles is open to question. Whatever the case, the intended meaning of the verse is the threat and warning to those disbelievers for what they are upon of disbelief in the signs of Allah the Exalted, and attributing to His Messenger (ﷺ) fabrication and being taught by humans, after removing their doubt and refuting their accusation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 105:

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah fabricate lies﴾ is a preparation for their being the fabricators, and it turns the charge back upon them, after He had established, by a demonstrative proof, the innocence of His Messenger (ﷺ) from the taint of fabrication. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is those who are the liars﴾ is an allusion to the Quraysh who said: "You are only a fabricator." It is an explicit statement following an allusion, so that it serves as a brand upon them. This style is more eloquent than saying, "You, O company of Quraysh, are fabricators," as regards what is alluded to. And establishing the proof that they are such, and that those whom they accuse of it cannot be attached to its hem (nashab minhu), i.e., the fabrication of lies is fitting only for one who does not believe, because he does not expect punishment for it, and the Quraysh are such; so they are the liars. Or it is an allusion to ﴿those who do not believe﴾, so that the speech continues in a single course. The meaning is that the true liar is this liar, as they established in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is those who are the successful﴾. The article (al-) is for the genus, and it is a testimony against them to perfection in fabrication. Thus lying, in reality, is restricted to lying about the signs of Allah, exalted is He, and it is stated without restriction to indicate that there is no lie beyond it, so that it serves as a proof of the perfection of fabrication. Or lying is unrestricted in this respect, in the sense that they are those for whom lying is a habit, and therefore they dared to deny the signs of Allah, exalted is He, as an indication that such conduct proceeds only from one who is accustomed to lying in speech. This meaning is confirmed by the expression in the nominal sentence, and for this reason it is coordinated with the verbal sentence.
