There is in this a fine antithesis (qalb hasan) and an allusion to the fact that the Quraysh, since lying was their custom, began to deny the signs of Allah, exalted is He, and those who brought them. Then they were not content with this until they attributed to fabrication the one whom they had testified to as trustworthy and truthful.

The place of the beauty lies in the indication to the prior states of the Prophet (ﷺ) and of the Quraysh. Or lying is restricted in this respect also by what they attributed to him, upon him be prayer and peace, of fabrication. "Those who do not believe," on this intended meaning, refers to the Quraysh, by way of placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun. The choice of the present tense over the past tense indicates the continuity of their non-belief and its renewal following the revelation of each verse, and the bringing of it to mind. This aspect is less preferred in comparison with the preceding ones. Al-Zamakhshari, the author of the Kashshaf, mentioned these aspects, and the scholar al-Mawla al-Mudaqqiq has clarified them in his Kashf. The restriction in the rest of them is not real, and there is no istidrak (corrective exception) in the verse, especially on the first of them; and it is of the speech that is equitable in some of its aspects. Its connection with His saying, glorified is He, reporting them: ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ is because, as you have heard, it is a response to that, and the insertion of what was inserted is for what is not hidden of its close connection to the first response.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 106 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Whoever disbelieves in God﴾, that is, by uttering the word of disbelief, ﴿after his belief﴾ in Him, exalted is He. Apparently, this is the beginning of a new statement explaining the state of those who disbelieve in the signs of God after having believed in them, following the explanation of the state of those who do not believe in them at all. (Man) is a relative pronoun whose position is nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted, as indicated by the following ﴿upon them is wrath﴾, and the omission of the like of this is common in speech. It is also permitted for it to be nominative or accusative by way of a detached phrase (qat') for the purpose of censure, meaning: they, or I censure whoever disbelieves. Detachment is used for censure and praise, although it is customary in the case of an attribute (na't). (Man) is not described by it, but there is no obstacle to considering it in other positions, such as apposition (badal), and Sibawayh explicitly stated this. Indeed, Abu Hayyan said: the accusative for censure is remote. Al-Hawfi and al-Zamakhshari permitted it to be an apposition to ﴿those who do not believe in the signs of God﴾, and the saying of the Exalted, ﴿and those are the liars﴾, is a parenthetical clause between them. Abu Hayyan and others objected to this, saying that it implies that only those who disbelieve after their belief would fabricate lies, whereas the reality indicates that the one who fabricates lies is the one who does not believe at all, and they are the majority of fabricators. Also, the apposition is the intended element, and the verse was revealed to refute the Quraysh, who were original disbelievers.
Al-Tibi justified this by taking the saying of the Exalted, ﴿after his belief﴾, to mean after his being firmly established in it, like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought misguidance in exchange for guidance﴾. He mentioned that this includes a reinforcement of the path of gradual progression (istidraj) and a regret for them over what they missed of affirmation and what they committed by attributing to him, upon him blessings and peace, the fabrication. In it, as in the Kashf, is that the saying of the Glorified, ﴿except one who is forced﴾, does not support this, and interpreting being firmly established in it as something more general than being firmly established in its origination and its continuation is not without problems.
The Muddaqiq said: the better interpretation is to make the meaning: whoever finds disbelief among them, a change to apostasy as well, and that whoever finds this trait among them is not far from fabrication; and this is made a pretext to rebuke them for what they used to do with the believers of mutilation, and to incorporate within it the concession of uttering the word of disbelief by the tongue under compulsion, and the difference between the one who holds to the resolute course and the one who holds to the concession. There is no concealment of problems in this either, and that it is not suitable for the occasion of revelation.
Al-Khafaji said: You may say: the closer view is that the statement remains on its apparent meaning without strain, and that this is a denial of them in the most eloquent manner, as one says to one who says: "The sun is not rising on a day when it is clear," "This is not a lie," because a lie occurs in what intellects may accept. This applies on the assumption that the intended meaning of ﴿God does not guide them﴾ is that He does not guide them to the truth. So when God did not guide them to truth and sincerity, and sealed their senses, they descended to the station of one who does not know it, so that his tongue would assist him in uttering it, and the ugliness of their denial is greater than to be called a lie; one lies only when one deliberately does so and speaks it once. Thus the first verse is an explicit refutation of the Quraysh, and the other is an indication in the most eloquent manner. End of quote. By my life, this is the extreme of strain. Similar to this is the apposition from (ulaika) and the apposition from (al-kadhibun), and al-Zamakhshari also permitted both, and al-Hawfi also permitted the latter, while al-Zajjaj permitted nothing other than these.
Many have permitted that (man) be a conditional particle, nominative in position as the subject, and al-Bahr favoured this, with the response omitted, as indicated by the following, as you have heard in the first view. The discussion about the predicate of a conditional (man) is well known. The apparent practice of al-Zamakhshari is to prefer apposition, which I regard as strange from him. In the Kashf, that (man) being conditional and a subject is a view of apparent soundness, except that what led the Jar Allah to prefer (man) being an apposition is seeking harmony among the parts of the noble composition, not that it should begin a statement of a ruling; and there is no concealment of the weakness of this excuse. The apparent view is that the exception of ﴿one who is forced﴾, that is, to utter disbelief under a threat he fears for his own self or one of his limbs, is a contiguous exception (istithna' muttasil) from disbelief, because disbelief is uttering what indicates it, whether it agrees with belief or not.
Al-Raghib said: It is said "so-and-so disbelieved" when he holds disbelief, and it is said when he manifests disbelief even if he does not believe it. Thus this excepted item enters into the mentioned item excepted from. It is said: it is an exception from the predicate, the omitted response; and it is said: it is a fronted exception from the saying of the Exalted ﴿then upon them is wrath﴾, and it is not that; the intended meaning is to exclude him from the ruling of wrath and punishment or censure. The saying of the Glorified ﴿while his heart is at rest with faith﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the excepted item, and the governing element, as in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, is the disbelief that occurs under compulsion, not compulsion itself, because the coinciding of the heart's tranquillity with faith does not benefit under compulsion; what is beneficial is its coinciding with the disbelief that occurs by it, meaning: except one who disbelieves under compulsion, or except one who is forced and so disbelieves while his heart is at rest with faith, his conviction having not changed. The original meaning of tranquillity (i'tmi'nan) is calm after agitation, and what is meant here is calm and steadfastness upon what he was upon after the agitation of compulsion. The governing element was not stated explicitly, as a hint that it is not disbelief in reality.
Verse 106 has been cited as evidence that faith is affirmation by the heart, and that confession by the tongue is not a pillar of it, as has been said. It has been objected that whoever made it a pillar did not intend that it is a real pillar that never falls at all, but rather that it indicates the reality which is affirmation, since that cannot be perceived directly, so its falling away in cases such as compulsion or incapacity does no harm. So reflect.
﴿But whoever opens his breast to disbelief﴾, that is, believes in it and is content with it in his soul. (And breast) in the sense of his breast, since humans are unable to open the breast of another. Its accusative, as al-Imam said, is that it is an object (maf'ul bihi) of "opened"; and some permitted that it is an accusative of specification (tamyiz). (Man) is either conditional or relative. But if it is made conditional, Abu Hayyan said, a subject must be supposed before it, because "lakin" is not followed by conditional sentences, and the supposition here is "but they are the one who opens to disbelief a breast", meaning: among them. And like it is his saying: "But whenever the people seek my support, I support them", meaning: "but I, whenever the people seek my support, etc." It was objected that this supposition is not necessary. The saying of the Exalted ﴿then upon them is wrath﴾ is the response of the condition on the assumption that (man) is conditional, and it is a predicate of it on both assumptions, and on the assumption of relativity, and so too on the assumption of conditionality in one opinion; the disagreement is well known. Some made it a predicate for this (man) and for the first (man), for the unity of meaning, since what is meant by "whoever disbelieves" is the category that opens its breast to disbelief. Abu Hayyan criticized it: here there are two conditional sentences separated by the particle of contrast, so each one needs a response of its own; so the supposition of omission is more suitable in the craft of grammar.
They have weakened the view of Abu al-Hasan in his claim that the saying of the Exalted ﴿then peace be upon you from the companions of the right﴾ and the saying of the Glorified ﴿then rest and sweet basil﴾ is the response of "amma"; and because this and that are two conditional particles, one following the other. By this, in my view, it is remote to make it a predicate of both on the assumption of relativity. The contrast is from the compulsion, as has been said, and it has been justified that the saying of the Exalted ﴿except one who is forced﴾ gives the impression that the forced person in general is excepted from what came before, and the saying of the Glorified ﴿while his heart is at rest with faith﴾ does not remove that impression, so contrast was needed to remove it; and in this there is clear discussion. It has been said that the intended meaning is mere emphasis, as in such a case: "If Zayd had come, I would have honoured you, but he did not come." You know what is in this, so reflect deeply.
The tanwin of ﴿wrath﴾ is for magnification, meaning a great wrath, whose essence no one can comprehend, coming ﴿from God﴾, majestic is His majesty, ﴿and for them is a great punishment﴾, because of the greatness of their crime; so they are recompensed in kind with their deeds. In the choice of the noble Name there is some inculcation of awe and a strengthening of the magnification of the punishment. The plural in the two pronouns in the genitive is in regard to the sense, just as the singular in the hidden pronoun in the relative clause is in regard to the wording.
It is narrated that the Quraysh compelled Ammar and his parents Yasir and Sumayya to apostasy, but they refused. So they tied Sumayya between two camels, and a spear was brought against her, and they said: "You only embraced Islam for the sake of men." So they killed her and killed Yasir, and they were the first two martyrs in Islam. As for Ammar, he gave them with his tongue what they had compelled him to say. It was said: "O Messenger of God, Ammar has disbelieved." The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "No indeed! Ammar is filled with faith from his head to his feet, and faith has mixed with his flesh and blood." Ammar came to the Messenger of God, upon him blessings and peace, weeping, and the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, began wiping his eyes and said: "What is wrong with you? If they return, then return to them with what you said." In another narration, they seized him and did not leave him until he reviled the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, and mentioned their gods with good. Then they left him. When he came to the Messenger of God, upon him blessings and peace, he said: "What is behind you?" He said: "Evil. I was not left until I had insulted you and mentioned their gods with good." He said: "How do you find your heart?" He said: "At rest with faith." He, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "If they return, then return." So this verse was revealed.
It seems that the command to return in the first narration is for permission, according to what al-Nasafi said, that it is its lowest level; and likewise the command in the second narration, if it is taken as restricted by what was restricted in the first narration. But if it is taken as restricted by the tranquillity of the heart, as in al-Hidaya, meaning: return to placing it before your eyes and remain firm upon it, then the command is for obligation. The verse is evidence for the permissibility of uttering the word of disbelief under compulsion, even though it is better to avoid that, to honour the religion, even if death is certain, as Yasir and Sumayya did; and this is not casting oneself into destruction, but is like being killed in a raid, as they have explicitly stated.
Ibn Abi Shaybah related from al-Hasan, and 'Abd al-Razzaq in his Tafsir from Ma'mar, that Musaylima seized two men. He said to one of them: "What do you say about Muhammad?" He said: "The Messenger of God." He said: "What do you say about me?" He said: "You too." So he released him, and said to the other: "What do you say about Muhammad?" He said: "The Messenger of God." He said: "What do you say about me?" He said: "I am deaf." He repeated it to him three times, and he repeated the same in his answer, so he killed him. The news of the two reached the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, and he said: "As for the first, he took the concession of God, the Exalted. As for the second, he proclaimed the truth, so good tidings to him."
In the Ahkam of al-Jassas: it is obligatory upon one compelled to disbelief to make it occur to his mind that he does not intend it; if that does not occur to his mind, he has disbelieved.

In the commentary *Sharh al-Minhaj* by Ibn Hajar, it is stated that there is no apostasy (*ridda*) for one who is compelled to disbelieve when his heart is at peace with faith, in accordance with the verse. Likewise, if his heart is stripped of both [faith and disbelief], then in what appears preferable, the ruling is the same, because of their general statement that the one under compulsion is not obliged to use *tawriya* (equivocation, saying something true in a sense that differs from what the listener understands). So understand this.

The judge (*al-Qadi*) said: It is obligatory for the one under compulsion to expose himself to being killed, and it is not permissible for him to utter the words of disbelief, because that is a lie, and lying is ugly in its own essence. It is therefore ugly in every circumstance. If it were permissible for it to depart from ugliness for the sake of preserving some interests, it would not be impossible for God, glorified is He, to commit lying for their sake. In that case, there would remain no certainty regarding His promise and His threat, because of the possibility that He, glorified is He, committed a lie for the sake of an interest that only He knows. Its refutation is evident.

This disagreement applies when the one under compulsion is confined to either committing a lie or exposing himself to destruction. Otherwise, whenever he is able to use something like *ta'rid* (allusion), or to phrase his speech as a denying interrogative (*istifham inkari*), it is not obligatory upon him to expose himself to harm; this is agreed upon (*ijma'*).

The permission to utter the words of disbelief under compulsion has been used as evidence for the permissibility of all other sins under compulsion according to him as well. In this there is room for discussion. The Imam mentioned that among sins there are some whose commission is obligatory under compulsion, such as drinking wine, eating carrion, and eating the flesh of swine, because preserving the self from perishing is obligatory. So whenever eating becomes the only way, and there is no harm to an animal nor any humiliation of the right of God, the Most High, it is obligatory, on the basis of His saying, the Most High: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾. Among them are things that are forbidden, such as killing a sacred human being or cutting off one of his limbs. Regarding whether retaliation (*qisas*) is obligatory upon the one under compulsion, there are two opinions of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him.

He also mentioned that among actions there are some that do not admit compulsion, and he gave the example of fornication (*zina*), because compulsion produces intense fear, and this prevents the erection of the member. Therefore, when fornication occurs in fact, we know that it took place by choice and not by way of compulsion. The full discussion of this matter is to be sought in its proper place.

**﴿That﴾** is a reference to disbelief after faith, or to the threat contained in His saying, ﴿upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a great punishment﴾, or to the wrath and punishment mentioned. ﴿Because they﴾, that is, because those who expounded their breasts to disbelief ﴿preferred the worldly life﴾, that is, they chose it and gave it precedence. And since preferring (istihbab) includes the meaning of choosing over (ithar), it was said ﴿over the Hereafter﴾, so it was construed with ʿalā (over). According to al-Bahr, the intended meaning is that they acted as those who prefer it would act; otherwise they did not believe in the Hereafter.

﴿And that Allah does not guide﴾ to faith and to what necessitates steadfastness upon it. It was also said: to Paradise. al-Imam (al-Razi) rejected this. Some interpreters explained the guidance negated here as the guidance of compulsion, that is, He does not guide with the guidance of coercion and compulsion, and this is attributed to the Mu'tazilah. ﴿The disbelieving people﴾, that is, in His all-encompassing knowledge; so Allah, exalted is He, does not protect them from deviation and from what leads to it of wrath and punishment. And had it not been for one of the two matters, either their preferring the worldly life over the Hereafter or Allah's not guiding them, [that they preferred the Hereafter over the world] or [that Allah guided them], it would not have been so; but both of these do not occur, because that contradicts what is in His knowledge of things as they are in reality. Some said: but the second contradicts wisdom, and the first is something that does not fall under occurrence; and to this points His saying, glorified is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 108:

﴿Those﴾, i.e., those described by what was mentioned, ﴿whose hearts, hearing and sight Allah has sealed﴾, so they are not opened to perceive the truth and to acquire what leads to it. Abu Hayyan (Abu Hayyan al-Andalusi) inclined to hold that this refers to what they deserved of wrath and punishment, and said: the words of His, exalted is He, ﴿they preferred﴾ refer to acquisition (kasb), while ﴿and that Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ refers to origination (ikhtira'). Thus the verse combines both matters, and that is the creed of the People of the Sunnah, so understand. The discussion of sealing (tab', i.e., divine sealing of the heart) has already been presented. ﴿And those are the heedless﴾, i.e., the perfect in heedlessness, for there is no heedlessness greater than heedlessness of reflecting on consequences and considering what is beneficial. It is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: heedless of what is intended for them in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 109:

﴿Without doubt, they are in the Hereafter the ones who are the losers.﴾ Because they wasted the capital of their wealth, which is their lifespans, and spent it on what leads to nothing but the everlasting punishment. And for God Most High is the one who said:

When your capital is your life, then guard it carefully from spending in other than what is obligatory.

In another verse occurs ﴿al-akhsarun (the greatest losers)﴾. This is due to what the context requires, as is not hidden to the one who considers it; or because the rhyming endings (fawasil) here rely on the alif, like al-kafirin and al-ghafilin, so it was expressed with it to observe that. And this is an easy matter. The discussion of "la jarama" (without doubt) has preceded, so recall it, for what is in the covenant is not of antiquity.

[p. 240]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 110:

﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated﴾ to the abode of Islam, and they were ʿAmmar and his like, meaning: for them, with guardianship and support, not against them, as the apparent sense of their earlier actions might suggest. So the prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa-al-majrur) is in the position of the predicate of inna. It has also been permitted that its predicate is omitted, since the predicate of the second inna indicates it, and the prepositional phrase is related to that omitted predicate. Abu al-Baqa' said: the predicate is the one that follows, and the second inna with its noun is a repetition for emphasis and does not require a predicate in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis). The prepositional phrase is related to one of the two nominative nouns by way of operation (al-a'mal). It has also been said that it is related to an omitted element by way of explanation, as if it were said: "I mean, for those," that is, forgiveness. This is not worthwhile. It has been said that there is no predicate for inna here, because the predicate of the second one suffices for it. This is not good, as is not hidden. (And "thumma") is for indicating the great distance between the rank of their state in this condition and the rank of their state that is conveyed by the exception from merely departing from the judgment of anger and punishment, not from the rank of the state of the disbelievers. ﴿After they had been tried﴾, meaning: they were punished for apostasy. The root of fitan is putting gold into fire so that its quality may appear from its inferiority; then the word was used figuratively for affliction and the torment of a person.

Ibn ʿAmir read "fatanu" in the active voice, and its subject, according to more than one scholar, is the polytheists. That is, they tortured the believers, like al-Hadrami, who forced his freedman to apostasy until he apostatized, then they both became Muslim and emigrated. Or they fell into trial, for fatana comes both transitively and intransitively, and fitna is used for what occurs under torment.

Abu Hayyan said: The apparent meaning is that the pronoun refers to those who emigrated, and the meaning is: they tried themselves by what they gave the polytheists of speech, as ʿAmmar did, or because they were patient upon Islam and were tortured on account of that, they became as if they had tortured themselves. ﴿Then they struggled﴾ against the disbelievers ﴿and were patient﴾ upon the hardships of struggle, or upon what befell them of hardships in general. ﴿Indeed your Lord, after these﴾, that is, the aforementioned matters of trial, emigration, ﻿struggle, and patience, ﴿is surely*﴾ — and this is an explicit statement of what the construction of the judgment upon the relative clause implied by way of the causality of the relative clause.

It has also been permitted that the pronoun refers to the trial understood from the preceding verb, and that what is mentioned is an explanation that this does not disrupt the judgment. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: it may refer to repentance, and the discourse gives it, even though it has not been mentioned explicitly. ﴿Surely Forgiving﴾ of what they did before, ﴿Merciful﴾, who bestows favor upon them in recompense for what they did afterward. In the mention of the title of lordship in both places there is an indication of the reason for the judgment. As for the addition of "Lord" to his pronoun (peace be upon him), along with the manifest effect upon the aforementioned group, it is a demonstration of the complete kindness toward him (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him), in that the bestowal of the effects of lordship upon them, of forgiveness and mercy, is through him (peace be upon him), and because they are his followers.

That the verse concerns ʿAmmar and his like (may Allah be pleased with them) is among what more than one scholar has mentioned. Ibn Ishaq explicitly stated that it was revealed concerning him, and concerning ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿa, al-Walid ibn Abi Rabiʿa, and al-Walid ibn al-Walid. Ibn ʿAtiyya criticized this, saying that mentioning ʿAmmar in this is not sound, for he is of a higher rank than these, and these are among those whose breast was expanded to disbelief. Allah the Exalted opened for them the door of repentance at the end of the verse. He mentioned that the verse is Medinan and that he knows of no disagreement about this. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) that it was revealed, so the Muslims wrote with it to those who had embraced Islam in Mecca: "Indeed Allah the Exalted has made for you a way out." So they went out, and the polytheists caught up with them and fought them, until whoever was saved was saved and whoever was killed was killed. Ibn Mardawayh recorded this. In another report, they went out, pursued them, and fought them, and then it was revealed. Ibn al-Mundhir and others recorded this from Qatada. Thus the meaning of struggle is their fighting against those who followed them.

Ibn Jarir recorded from al-Hasan and ʿIkrima that it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Sarh, who used to write for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Then Satan made him slip, so he joined the disbelievers. The Prophet (peace be upon him) ordered that he be killed on the day of the Conquest of Mecca, but ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan (may Allah be pleased with him) interceded for him, and the Prophet (ﷺ) granted him protection. The meaning is that it was revealed concerning him and concerning those like him, as is explicitly stated in some reports. On this basis, they interpreted "they were tried" as their being tempted by Satan, who made them slip, until they apostatized by their own choice. What Ibn ʿAtiyya mentioned about those he named alongside ʿAmmar is not accepted. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Qatada that ʿAyyash (may Allah be pleased with him) was the maternal half-brother of Abu Jahl, and that he (Abu Jahl) used to beat him with a whip and his mount with a whip, so that he would apostatize from Islam. In the Tafsir of al-Khazin, it is said that ʿAyyash, who was a brother of Abu Jahl through nursing, and it was said: through the mother; and Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl ibn ʿAmr, Salama ibn Hisham, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and ʿAbd Allah ibn Salama al-Thaqafi. The polytheists tried them and tortured them, so they gave them some of what they wanted in order to be safe from their evil. Then after that they emigrated and struggled, and the verse was revealed concerning them. And Allah the Exalted knows best the reality of the matter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 111:

﴿On the Day when every soul comes pleading for itself﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarfiyyah), governing ﴿Merciful﴾. It was also said that it is in the accusative as an object of an implied verb, udhkur ("remember"). The first view is preferred because of the connection of the discourse (irtibat al-nazm) to it and because it stands in contrast to God's words ﴿In the Hereafter, they are the losers﴾. Restricting mercy to that day is not a problem, because mercy on other days is established all the more so. The day here is the Day of Resurrection. ﴿Pleading for itself﴾ means defending itself and striving for its own deliverance through excuses, and it does not concern itself with the affairs of others, such as child, parent, or relative.

Ahmad related in al-Zuhd, and a group related from Ka'b, who said: "I was with Umar ibn al-Khattab, and he said: 'Frighten us, O Ka'b.' I said: 'O Commander of the Believers, is there not among you the Book of God and the wisdom of His Messenger (ﷺ)?' He said: 'Yes, but frighten us.' I said: 'O Commander of the Believers, if you were to arrive on the Day of Resurrection with the deeds of seventy prophets, you would consider your deed (too small) in comparison with what you see.' He said: 'Add more.' I said: 'O Commander of the Believers, Hell will exhale an exhalation on the Day of Resurrection, and no angel brought near, nor any sent prophet, will remain but that he will fall to his knees, kneeling, until even Abraham, His intimate friend, will kneel and say: "My Lord, myself, myself! I ask You today for nothing but myself."' Umar lowered his head for a while. I said: 'O Commander of the Believers, do you not find this in the Book of God?' He said: 'How?' I said: 'The saying of God in this verse: ﴿On the Day when every soul comes﴾, etc.' Some considered this statement to be the 'pleading' (judal), but Ibn Atiyya did not accept it. The truth is that it contains nothing but an indication of not caring about the affairs of others, which is part of what the verse indicates.

It is related from Ibn Abbas that this pleading is between the spirit and the body. The body says: "Through you my tongue spoke, my eye saw, and my foot walked; without you I would have been a log thrown down." The spirit says: "You earned and you disobeyed; not I. You were the carrier and I was the carried." Then God says: "I will strike for you both a parable: a blind man who carried a paralytic to an orchard, and they both ate of its fruits; so the punishment is upon you both." The apparent meaning is that this report from this scholar (al-habr) is not authentic, for he is far too exalted to take the pleading in the verse to mean what was mentioned.

The pronoun in ﴿its own﴾ (nafsiha) refers to the first "soul" (nafs). So it is as if it were said: "pleading for the soul of the soul." Its outward form suggests the annexation (idafah) of a thing to itself, and this was justified by saying that the first nafs is the essence and the whole (al-jumlah), that is, the person with all his parts, as in your saying "a noble soul" (nafs karimah) and "a blessed soul" (nafs mubarakah). The second, "its own" (ʿaynuha), that is, the one which functions as an emphasis and indicates the reality and identity of the thing according to context. The difference between them is that the parts are considered in the first but not in the second. The original is the second, but because there is no difference in reality between the essence and its owner, it was used in the sense of "owner," and then the essence was annexed to it. Thus the pattern of ﴿every soul﴾ is like your saying "every person does such-and-such," as in al-Kashshaf. In al-Fara'id it is said that difference between the annexed and the annexing is a condition, since annexation (nisbah) is impossible without two related parties. Therefore they said: it is impossible to annex a thing to itself. However, difference before the annexation is sufficient, and it is realized here, because what is meant by "soul" in general does not necessarily mean "your soul," while your soul necessarily means "soul" in general. So when something that is not necessarily your soul was annexed to your soul, the annexation was valid, even though the two become identical after the annexation. For this reason one may say "the very thing" (ʿayn al-shayʾ), "its whole" (kulluh), and "its self" (nafsuh), unlike "the lion, the lion" (asad al-layth) and "prevention of the prohibition" (habs al-manʿ) and similar expressions.

Ibn Atiyya said: the first nafs is the well-known one, and the second is the body. Al-Askari said: a human being is called nafs. The Arabs say: "No one came to me except one nafs," meaning one person. In reality, nafs does not come, because it is the thing by which a person lives. So reflect. In the nafs there is something in some of what they have said. The apparent meaning is that the famous question and answer concerning "every man and his land" (kull rajul wa daytuh) apply here too, so consider this carefully.

In al-Bahr: the reason why it did not say "pleading for her" (tujadiluha ʿanha) instead of ﴿pleading for its own﴾ is that when a verb is not of the category of ẓanna and faqada (verbs of the heart requiring two objects) and cannot transitively take an apparent object, whether its subject is a noun or a pronoun, it cannot be connected to its attached pronoun. So one does not say "Hind struck her" or "Hind, she struck her." Rather, one says "Hind struck herself" (ḍarabat nafsaha) and "Hind struck herself." The feminine form of ﴿comes﴾ (taʾtī), with ﴿every﴾ (kull) as its subject, though kull is masculine, is in observance of the meaning. The same applies to what follows. Upon this is the saying of the poet:

Every abundant-flowing eye poured upon it,
So they left every garden like a dirham.

﴿And every soul will be paid in full﴾, that is, it will be given in full and complete, ﴿for what it did﴾, that is, the recompense of its deed, or what it did, if good then good, and if evil then evil, by way of applying the name of the cause to the effect, indicating the complete connection between the recompenses and the deeds. The explicit noun here in place of a pronoun serves to increase the affirmation, and to indicate that the time of the pleading and the time of the full payment differ, even though both occur on one day.

﴿And they will not be wronged﴾, by an increase in punishment, or by punishment without sin. It was also said: by a reduction in their rewards. This was objected to on the grounds that this is already known from what precedes. It was answered that the one who said it may have meant by the recompense of what they did the punishment, and if the more general meaning is intended, then this is a repetition for emphasis. The reason for the plural pronoun is clear.

﴿And Allah sets forth an example: a town﴾, that is, the people of a town. This is either by using the word "town" to mean its inhabitants, or by supposing an omitted noun (mudaf). Its case-ending is accusative as the first object (maf'ul awwal) of "daraba" (sets forth), on the basis of its being construed (tadmin) with the sense of "made" (al-ja'l). It was postponed so that the second object would not separate the described noun from its description and what follows from it. Placing it after everything would damage the harmony and interlocking of the parts of this sublime composition. Also, delaying what should properly come first creates in the soul a longing for its arrival, especially when the preceding part contains what calls for it, as here. So when it arrives, it becomes firmly fixed to a greater degree.

It is related from al-Zajjaj that the accusative is in apposition (badaliyyah, substitution). In his view the original is "Allah sets forth an example: the likeness of a town," so the noun was omitted and the noun in the genitive took its place. The "town" intended is either a real town among the towns of earlier peoples, or a hypothetical one, and the existence of the thing compared to is not necessary. Abu Hayyan did not permit this, because of the place of...

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 113:

﴿And there had certainly come to them a messenger from among them﴾, and you know that it does not preclude [this interpretation].

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid that it refers to Mecca. This is also reported from Ibn Zayd, Qatadah and 'Atiyyah. Ibn Abi Hatim and others related from Sulaym ibn 'Umar, who said: "I accompanied Hafsah, the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), as she was leaving Mecca for Medina. I was informed that 'Uthman had been killed, so I turned back. She said: 'Turn back with me. By Him in whose hand my soul is, it is indeed the town of which Allah the Exalted spoke,' and she recited what is in the verse." Perhaps she meant that it is [a] similitude of it. The narration about the [Prophet's] companions can be understood in this way. The meaning is that Allah the Exalted made it an example for the people of Mecca, or for every people upon whom Allah the Exalted bestowed blessings, but the blessings made them insolent, so they did what they did, and were requited with what they were requited. The people of Mecca are included in this in a primary way. Perhaps this is the preferred view. ﴿It was secure﴾: it is said, it was in a state of security, with nothing coming upon it that would necessitate fear, as happens to some towns through raids by the people of evil and attempts to strike them. ﴿Tranquil﴾: calm and settled, with nothing occurring that would necessitate disturbance, as happens in some towns through strife among their inhabitants and some of them attacking others. For such a town is rarely safe from a wicked raider. And far, far is it that you would see two people who are friends in it:

"A man fears his father and his son, and his brother and neighbour betray him therein."

It is said that it is understood from the words of some of them that tranquility is a consequence and a necessary result of security, insofar as fear necessitates disturbance and contradicts tranquility. In al-Bahr it is said that it is an increase in security. ﴿Its provision comes to it﴾: its sustenance, ﴿abundantly﴾: plentifully, ﴿from every place﴾: from all its directions. The style of this description has been changed from what preceded to what you see, because the coming of provision is renewed, whereas its being secure and tranquil is constant and continuous. The Imam [al-Razi] mentioned that the verse contains three blessings, which their saying gathers:

"Three things with no end: security, health and sufficiency."

So ﴿secure﴾ is an indication of security, [﴿tranquil﴾] of health, and [﴿its provision comes to it﴾, etc.] of sufficiency. The cause of tranquility is taken to be the suitability of the town's air to the temperaments of its people, but this requires reflection. ﴿So it denied the favours of Allah﴾: plural of ni'mah (favour), like shiddah and ashudd, with the feminine ending omitted, because the regular plural pattern is fi'l to af'ul, not fi'lah. Al-Fadil al-Yamani said it is a collective noun for ni'mah. Qutrub said it is the plural of nu'm, with the nun vowelled with a damma, like bu's and ab'us, and that ni'am in his view means na'im (bounty). This is taken to be the meaning of their saying: "This is a day of food and bounty." According to others, it means ni'mah. The intended favours are what the verse previously included, and perhaps it is in effect many favours, indeed it is so. The use of the plural of paucity indicates that denial of a few favours necessitated this punishment, so what do you think of denying many favours? ﴿So Allah made it taste the garment of hunger and fear﴾: he likened the effect of hunger and fear and the overwhelming harm they cause to a garment, by the common feature of encompassing and enveloping. So the name of a garment is borrowed for it, and the verb "made taste" (idhaqah), borrowed for "afflicting," is applied to it. "Made taste" was chosen to indicate the intensity of the effect, which would be lost if "afflicting" were used. They explained the relationship: what is perceived from the effect of harm is likened to what is perceived from the taste of a bitter, unpleasant thing, by way of borrowing a sensible term for an intellectual notion, because sensory perceptions are attached to intellectual ones. The same applies to the first. Because the usage of "making taste" for this is widespread and it is frequently used in speech, it became like a literal usage. For this reason, its application to the garment was made an abstraction (tajrid), since abstraction is appropriate or valid only with a true meaning or with what is attached to it of common metaphor. So there is no difference between "made it taste it" and "afflicted it with it." The reason he did not say "clothed them" is that he preferred tarshih (the metaphor-supporting term) so as not to lose what "making taste" conveys of effect, perception and the taste of hunger, due to the indication of comprehensiveness in the garment. The author of al-Miftah took the garment to refer to the discoloration and shabbiness of appearance that necessarily accompany hunger and fear, and the metaphor in that case is of a sensible for a sensible. What was mentioned first is preferable, since it does not diminish the position of "making taste," and "affliction" would have a more eloquent position.

It is related from the [Ash'ari] companions that the word "garment" in their view is takhyil (imaginative metaphor). This was explained by likening hunger and fear, in their effect, to a person with a garment who intends the effect and exaggerates it, so he creates for it a form like a garment and applies its name to it. It was objected that this does not suit the eloquence of the Mighty Qur'an, because if hunger is likened to a fully capable agent who intends what he undertakes, it would be fitting for a form to be imagined for it that is an instrument of effect, not the form of a garment, which has no part in the effect. It was replied that the author of al-Miftah holds that takhyili is used for a fanciful matter that the speaker imagined to be similar to its real meaning. So if the garment is takhyili, it could be that the intended meaning is something that encloses hunger as a garment does, like drought, and encloses fear, like an enemy's encirclement. Therefore there is no basis for his saying that the form of a garment is among what has no part in the effect. The claim that with an agent only the mention of an instrument of effect is appropriate has not been stated by any of the scholars, and it cannot be maintained in every metaphor. Do you not see that if you say: "The distance of the poem, it kept folding it until it arrived at his door," likening praise to a traveller to whom distance is attributed imaginatively, and what follows is tarshih, it is a fine metaphor, and its indicator is not an instrument for that agent, but a matter among its necessary attributes. Many such examples occur in the speech of eloquent writers. End.

You know that this, despite what it contains, does not distinguish, according to sound takhyil, the view attributed to the companions from what was mentioned first, nor does it equate it with it. The well-known view is that in ﴿libas﴾ (garment) there are two metaphors, a tasrihiyyah (explicit) and a makniyyah (implicit). This was explained by likening what covers the person in hunger and fear, as harm's effect, in respect of enveloping, to a garment, so the name of a garment is borrowed for it, and in respect of aversion, to a bitter, unpleasant taste. So it is an explicit metaphor considered from the first aspect, and an implicit one from the second, and "making taste" is takhyil. There is a well-known discussion on this among students. It was also permitted that the garment of ﴿hunger﴾ is like the cloak of water, i.e., Allah made them taste the hunger which, in its encompassing, is like a garment. The first, too, is preferable. A similar example is the verse of Kuthayyir:

"He overwhelmed the cloak when he smiled laughing, and the necks of wealth were shackled by his laughter."

For he borrowed "cloak" for the good deed, because it protects the honour of its owner as a cloak protects what is put upon it, and he attributed "overwhelming" to it, which in describing a good deed is a metaphor that functions as literal usage; its true meaning comes from "ghamrah," which is the bulk and abundance of water.

Mentioning hunger, which arises from the loss of provision, before fear, which follows from the cessation of security mentioned earlier before the coming of provision, is either because it is more suitable for "making taste," or to observe the parallelism between that and the coming of provision.

In the Mushaf of Ubayy it reads: "the garment of fear and hunger," with fear placed first. Likewise 'Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] read it, except that he did not mention "garment." Abu Hayyan counted this as an exegesis rather than a reading. Al-'Abbas reported from Abu 'Amr that he read "wal-khawfa" (and fear) in the accusative, as a conjunction to "libas" (garment). Al-Zamakhshari took it as the omission of a modifier with the modified placed in its position, meaning "and the garment of fear."

Sahib al-Lawami said: it is permissible that its accusative is by a suppressed verb, and that in contrast to what preceded with hunger and fear only, there is something that indicates counting security and tranquility as one thing; otherwise the apparent form would have been ﴿Allah made them taste the garment of hunger and fear and disturbance﴾. ﴿For what they were doing﴾: before this, or in the sense of continuity, which is the denial mentioned. "Ma" is a relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning "that they were doing." It was also permitted that "ma" is a verbal-noun particle, and the construction in both cases is causal. The two pronouns are said to refer to "the people" supplied as a modifier of "the town," after the preceding pronouns had returned to the word itself. It was also said they refer to the town, meaning by it its people.

In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim it says: the attribution of what was mentioned to the people of the town is for confirming the matter after the attribution of denial to it and the application of the tasting to it, intending exaggeration. In the form of the verb "do" (sun'ah) is an indication that denial of a favour is a firmly established practice for them and an established custom. ﴿And there had certainly come to them﴾: part of the parable, and the pronoun in it refers to the one to whom the two preceding pronouns returned. This was mentioned to show that what they did, namely denial of Allah the Exalted, was not merely opposition by them to the dictate of reason, but was also opposition to Allah's proof over creation. That is: there had certainly come to the people of that town ﴿a messenger from among them﴾, i.e., of their kind, whom they know by his origin and lineage. So he informed them of the obligation to thank for the blessing, and warned them of the bad consequence of what they were upon. ﴿So they denied him﴾: in his mission, or in what he informed them of among what was mentioned. The fa' is explanatory (fasihah), and not mentioning what it expresses indicates the surprise of their denial without hesitation. ﴿So the punishment seized them﴾: the uprooting punishment that eradicated them, after what they had tasted of it, as you have heard. ﴿While they were wrongdoers﴾: i.e., in a state of being entangled in wrongdoing, which is denial and disbelief, not desisting from it despite the preliminary deterrents they had tasted. This indicates their persistence in disbelief and obstinacy and their exceeding every customary limit in that.

The ordering of the punishment's seizure upon the denial of the messenger follows the way of Allah the Exalted, as indicated by His saying: ﴿And We were not punishers until We sent a messenger﴾. With this the parable is completed. For the state of the people of Mecca, whether the parable was struck for them specifically or for them and all who follow their path, is more similar to the state of the people of that town than a crow is to a crow. For they were in a secure sanctuary, while people were snatched away around them, and no trace of fear ever passed through their minds, and no disturbance ever disturbed their hearts, and the fruits of everything were brought to them. And a messenger had certainly come to them from among them, and what a messenger! One is bewildered in grasping the exaltedness of the rank of intellects, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, as long as the south wind and the north wind alternate. So warn them and caution them. But they denied the favours of Allah the Exalted and denied him, upon him be blessings and peace. So Allah the Exalted made them taste the garment of hunger and fear, when it struck them through his supplication, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace: "O Allah, tighten Your hold on Mudar, and make it upon them years like the years of Joseph."

What befell them was a severe drought and an unsurpassable crisis. They were compelled to eat carrion, dead dogs and burnt bones, and al-'Ahlaz, which is a food made in years of famine from blood and wool. One of them would look at the sky and see something like smoke from hunger. The earth had become constricted for them despite its vastness, by the expeditions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since they used to raid their livestock, caravans and convoys. Then on the day of Badr He seized them with the punishment that He seized them with. This is what Shaykh al-Islam chose, and he said: it is what the situation requires and what the arrangement demands. As for what most exegetes agreed upon, that the pronoun in His saying ﴿And there had certainly come to them﴾ refers to the people of Mecca, and that the speech is a transition to mention their state explicitly after mentioning their parable, and that the messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ), and the punishment is what befell them of drought and the battle of Badr, it is far from verification. How so?

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾ is a consequence drawn from the preceding parable, and a deterrent for them from what would lead to a similar end. The meaning is: since the condition of those who disbelieved in the blessings of Allah, Exalted is He, denied His Messenger, and what befell them because of that, in both the lesser and the greater respects, has become clear to you, then desist from what you are engaged in, namely ingratitude for the blessings and denial of the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, lest there befall you what befell them. Recognise the true worth of Allah's blessings, Exalted is He, and obey the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, in his commands and prohibitions. ﴿So eat of the provision of Allah, Exalted is He, as lawful and good﴾, and abandon what you fabricate of prohibiting the baheera (a she-camel released for idols) and the like. ﴿And give thanks for the blessing of Allah﴾, recognise its due and do not requite it with disbelief.

The "fa" (so) in meaning is attached to the command to give thanks. Its attachment to the command to eat is because eating is a means (dhari'ah) to giving thanks. It is as if it were said: "Then give thanks for the blessing of Allah after eating it, as lawful and good." Within this is embedded (idmaj) the prohibition against claiming that such things are forbidden. There is no doubt that this can only be conceived at the time when the total destruction (al-'adhab al-musta'sil) was still expected and its beginnings had been laid down. As for after it had occurred, who would then be warned, and who would then be commanded to eat and give thanks? The saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿Then the punishment seized them while they were wrongdoers﴾, if taken as a report of that before it occurred, is rejected by the engagement in their reform through command and prohibition; though the expression in the past tense does not reject it, since its use for the future that is certain to occur is a common figurative usage (majaz).

As for directing the address of the command to eat to the believers, although what follows of address of prohibition is directed to the disbelievers, as al-Wahidi did, he said: "So eat, O believers, of what Allah has provided for you of the spoils of war, that which is not unbecoming to the status of the revelation." End of quote. It has been criticised: once the punishment has been explained as the total destruction that uproots the root, how can it be intended to refer to what happened at Badr, when those who remained of them outnumbered those who were lost? Even if such a thing is sufficient for the uprooting, then the one warned and the one commanded would be those who remained of them. What he (al-Wahidi) mentioned from al-Wahidi about directing the address of the command to eat to the believers, al-Imam (al-Razi) related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Then he transmitted from al-Kalbi what implies that the address is to the people of Makkah, where he said: "The leaders of Makkah spoke to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, when they were in hardship, and said: 'You have fought the men, so what is the matter with the children and women?' The supply of food had been cut off from them by the command of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him. So he permitted transporting it to them, and food was carried to them. Then Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾, etc." Then he said: "The view is what Ibn 'Abbas said, and what supports it is the saying of Allah, Exalted is He, after it: ﴿He has only forbidden you carrion﴾, etc., meaning: since you have believed and abandoned disbelief, eat the lawful and good, which is the spoils, and leave the foul things, which are carrion and blood." End of quote.

In the Tafsir of al-Khazin, the view that the address is to the believers of Madinah is the correct one, for the correct view is that the verse is Madinan, as Muqatil and some of the exegetes said. The "town" (qaryah) is Makkah, which Allah struck as a parable for the people of Madinah, warning and cautioning them lest they do the like of what they did, so that there befall them what befell them of hunger and fear. What confirms the correctness of this is that the fear mentioned in the verse was from the expeditions (bu'uth) and raiding parties (sara.ya) which the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, used to send, according to the saying of all the exegetes, because the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, was not commanded to fight while he was in Makkah, but was commanded to it while in Madinah. So the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, used to send expeditions toward Makkah, frightening them thereby while he was in Madinah. The intended meaning of the punishment is what befell them of hunger and fear, and this is preferable to taking it to mean the killing on the Day of Badr. The apparent meaning is that the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: ﴿And there had certainly come to them﴾, etc., according to him, as it is according to the majority, is a transition from the parable about them to the explicit statement of their condition that is included within it, and it is not part of its completion, for, according to what has been said, it is contrary to what comes first to the understanding. Yes, the address of the prohibition afterwards being to the believers is extremely far-fetched, and making it for the disbelievers [p. 246] while making the preceding address of command to the believers is also far-fetched, but less so than that. Abu Hayyan claimed that the apparent meaning is that the address of prohibition is, like the address of command, to all those who are legally responsible. He related that the address of prohibition is to them from al-'Askari, and that it is to the disbelievers from al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyyah and the majority. Perhaps the preferable view is what Shaykh al-Islam mentioned, except that restricting the punishment to the total destruction, and the claim that the condition of the people of Makkah is exactly like the condition of the people of that town, feather for feather, without any difference between them even in a single distinct trait, is not free from difficulty, insofar as the people of Makkah were not uprooted. So reflect on this, and may Allah, Exalted is He, take charge of your guidance. ﴿If it is Him you worship﴾: obey, or, if your claim is true that by worshipping the idols you intend the worship of Him, glorified is He. Whoever said that the address is to the believers left this on its apparent meaning, i.e., if you single Him, Exalted is He, out for worship, and the speech is issued in the manner of stirring up and inciting.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 115:

﴿Indeed, He has forbidden you only the carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked.﴾ This is a reason (ta'lil) for the permissibility of what He commanded them to eat of what He had provided for them. The restriction (hasr) here is relative (idafi), according to what many have said: that is, He has forbidden the eating of these things only, rather than what you claim of the bahira, the sa'iba and the like. Thus it does not conflict with the prohibition of things not mentioned, such as beasts of prey and domestic donkeys. It was also said: the restriction is on its apparent meaning, and beasts of prey and the like were not forbidden before, but were forbidden afterwards; the restriction is only with regard to the past.

Al-Imam said: Indeed, the Exalted restricted the prohibited things to these four in this surah, and in Surat al-An'am by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Say: I do not find in what has been revealed to me anything forbidden to an eater who eats it, except that it be carrion﴾, and so on. Both are Meccan. He also restricted them to these four in al-Baqarah, and likewise in al-Ma'idah, for He, the Exalted, said therein: ﴿Lawful for you are the beasts of cattle, except what is recited to you﴾, so He permitted all of them except what is recited to them. They agreed that what is meant by "what is recited" is His saying, the Exalted, in that surah: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than Allah has been invoked﴾. What He mentioned of the strangled (al-munkhaniqah), the beaten to death (al-mawqudhah), the fallen (al-mutaraddiyah), the gored (al-nati-hah), and what a beast of prey has eaten, falls under carrion; and what is slaughtered on the altars (nusub) falls under "that over which other than Allah has been invoked." Thus it is established that these four surahs indicate the restriction of the prohibited things to these four. Surat al-Nahl and al-An'am are Meccan, and Surat al-Baqarah and al-Ma'idah are Medinan, and al-Ma'idah is among the last to be revealed at Medina. Whoever denies the restriction of prohibition to the four, except what consensus and decisive proofs have specified, is in danger of being blamed, for these surahs show that restricting the prohibited things to these was established and valid from the beginning of Mecca to its end and from the beginning of Medina to its end; and repeating the explanation silences excuses and removes doubts. Ah. So reflect and do not be heedless.

﴿But whoever is forced﴾, that is, whom the necessity of hunger compels to consume something of that, ﴿neither desiring [it] nor transgressing﴾, against another person in necessity, ﴿nor exceeding﴾, going beyond the measure of necessity and of staving off hunger. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, that is, He, glorified is He, will not hold him accountable for that; so its cause is put in place of it. And to magnify the matter of forgiveness and mercy, the noble Name is used. Shaykh al-Islam sanctified it, and thought that the verse ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [was intended], so he explained the secret of mentioning the attribute of lordship (rububiyyah) and its being attributed to his pronoun ﷺ. Glory be to Him who does not forget.

The verse has been cited as evidence that the disbeliever is obligated to the subsidiary rulings (al-furu').

[Page 247]

Then He, exalted is He, emphasized what is understood from the restriction (ḥaṣr) by forbidding declaring things lawful or unlawful according to whims. So He, mighty is His saying, said: ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely⁠—⁠﴾ and so on. This construction does not conflict with the coordination (ʿaṭf), as is not hidden. The lām is attached to the verb "say," like it in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of God, "They are dead"⁠﴾ and your saying: "Do not say of nabidh (a date-based drink) that it is lawful." Its meaning is exclusivity (ikhtiṣāṣ). The "mā" is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah), and its returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: do not say concerning that which your tongues describe, of the beasts, as lawful or unlawful, in your saying: ﴿What is in the wombs of these livestock is exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives⁠﴾, without that attribute resulting from observation and reflection, let alone from its being based on revelation or on analogy (qiyās) founded upon it, but merely from a saying with the tongue.

[Page 248]

(al-kadhib, "the lie") is in the accusative as a direct object of "taqūlū" (you say). His saying, glorified is He: "This is lawful and this is unlawful" is a substitution (badal) of it, a substitution of the whole (badal kull). It has been said that it is in the accusative by an implied verb, "I mean" (aʿnī). It has also been said that (al-kadhib) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), and "this" is the content of the saying. It is permitted that it be a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimāl). It is also permitted that (al-kadhib) be the content of the stated saying, and that another verb be implied after the attribute, with the lām remaining in its place, meaning: do not say the lie for what your tongues describe, so that you say "This is lawful and this is unlawful." The sentence then explains and clarifies His saying: ﴿what your tongues describe⁠﴾, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So repent to your Creator and kill yourselves⁠﴾. It is also permitted that the saying not be implied, according to the Kufan school, and that its speaker be supposed, so that the supposed element is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of the tongues. It is also permitted that the lām be causal (lil-taʿlīl) and that mā be a verbal noun, with (al-kadhib) as the object of "describe," and "this is lawful..." etc. being the content of the saying, meaning: do not say "this is lawful and this is unlawful" for the sake of your tongues describing the lie. This is the view of al-Kisāʾī and al-Zajjāj. Its essence is: do not declare lawful or unlawful merely because your tongues describe the lie, depict it, and verify its reality, as if their tongues, being the source of lying and the spring of falsehood, were a person who knows its essence and encompasses its reality, describing it to people and making it known with the clearest description and the most evident definition. Similar to this occurs in the speech of Arabs and non-Arabs. You say: "She has a face that describes beauty," "a mouth that describes the wine," and "an eye that describes magic." The verse of al-Maʿarrī has preceded. The verse has been exaggerated in that their saying is made a lie, then the tongue that utters that statement is made its source, depicting it in the very form it has. This is from the class of metaphor by allegory (istiʿārah bil-kināyah). Some have made it from the class of figurative attribution (isnād majāzī), like "his day is fasting." As if their tongues, being described by lying, became as if they were its essence and its source by which it is known, to the point that it seems to describe it and make it known, as in his saying:

"Your right hand has become, from generosity, depicted;
no, rather, your right hand is where generosity was shaped."

al-Ḥasan, Ibn Yaʿmar, Ṭalḥah, al-Aʿraj, Ibn Abī Isḥāq, Ibn ʿUbayd, and Nuʿaym ibn Maysarah read "al-kadhibi" with a genitive (jarr). It is explained as being a substitution of mā together with what follows it, and more than one scholar made it an attribute (ṣifah) of the verbal-noun mā together with its relative clause.

Abū Ḥayyān objected to this: a verbal noun formed from mā, an, or kay together with the verb is definite like a pronoun, and it is not permissible to describe it with an adjective. So one does not say "It pleased me that you come quickly" as one says "Your quick coming pleased me." Not every implied element has the status of what is pronounced, and it follows only the usage of the Arabs.

Muʿādh, Ibn Abī ʿAblah, and some people of Syria read "al-kudhubu" with a ḍammah on all three letters, as an attribute of the tongues. It is the plural of kadhūb, like ṣabūr and ṣubur. The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: or it is the plural of kidhāb, with a kasrah on the kāf and a light dhāl, a verbal noun like qitāl, described with it for emphasis (mubālaghah), and the plural pattern fuʿul like kitāb and kutub; or it is the plural of kādhib, like shārif and shurf. Maslamah ibn Muḥārib read, as Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said, or Yaʿqūb as the author of al-Lawāmiḥ said, and he attributed the reading of Muʿādh and those with him to Maslamah: "al-kudhuba" with two ḍammahs and a fatḥah (accusative). It is explained in several ways. The first: that it is accusative by way of reproach and blame (shatm wa dhamm), and it is a detached attribute (naʿt maqṭūʿ) of the tongues. The second: it is a direct object of "taṣif" (describe) or of "taqūlū" (you say), and what is meant is the false words. The third: it is an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq) of "taṣif," derived from its meaning, on the basis that it is the plural of kidhāb, the verbal noun. "This is lawful..." etc. is parsed as above, and there is no difficulty in its being a substitution, since it is a word (kalim) in terms of its constituent parts and an apparent statement (kalām).

﴿So that you may fabricate against God the lie⁠﴾: the lām is the lām of consequence and outcome (lām al-ʿāqibah wal-ṣayrūrah), and it is also causal, because what came from them was not for the sake of fabricating against God, exalted is He, but for other purposes, and that consequence followed from it, as mentioned. This is the view of al-Zamakhsharī and a group. Some of them said: it is permissible that it be causal, and it is not far-fetched that they intended that, as they said: ﴿We found our fathers upon it, and God commanded us with it⁠﴾. In al-Baḥr it is said that this is the apparent meaning, and it is not an emphasis of the previous causal sense, on the supposition that the lām is causal and mā is a verbal noun, because this includes a warning about those against whom they fabricated the lie, whereas the earlier statement does not; rather, this states the lie absolutely. So in this there is an indication that, because they had trained themselves in lying, they became bold in lying against God, exalted is He, and so they attributed to Him what they had declared lawful and unlawful.

al-Wāḥidī said: "So that you may fabricate" is a substitution for "what your tongues describe..." etc., because their describing the lie is a fabrication against God, exalted is He. According to al-Baḥr also, this holds on the supposition that mā is a verbal noun, because if it is made a relative pronoun, the lām cannot be causal, so that what conveys causation may be substituted for it. It has been said: there is no obstacle to causation on the supposition of mā being relative, so when causation is intended, substitution is permissible. The meaning of the verse, as al-ʿAskarī stated explicitly, is: do not name as lawful or unlawful what has not come to you from God and His Messenger (ﷺ) regarding its permissibility or its prohibition, lest you be liars against God, exalted is He, because the basis of lawfulness and unlawfulness is nothing but His judgment, glorified is He. Hence Abū Naḍrah said: "I have always feared issuing legal opinions since I heard the verse of al-Naḥl, until this day of mine."

Ibn al-ʿArabī said: Mālik and a group disliked that the mufti say "this is lawful and this is unlawful" in matters of ijtihād (independent reasoning). Rather, that is said only regarding what God, exalted is He, has stated explicitly. In matters of ijtihād one says: "I dislike such and such," and similar expressions, for that is further from anything that might suggest fabricating against God, glorified is He.

﴿Indeed, those who fabricate against God the lie⁠﴾ in any matter of affairs ﴿will not succeed⁠﴾, meaning they will not attain what is sought. ﴿A brief enjoyment⁠﴾, meaning: the benefit they intended by that fabrication is a small benefit, cut off soon. Thus "matāʿ" is the predicate of an omitted subject, and "qalīl" is its attribute. The sentence is an explanatory resumption (istiʾnāf bayānī), as if, when they were denied success in attaining what they sought, it was said: How is that, when some benefit has been obtained for them through fabrication? So it was said: That is a brief enjoyment, of no account. Ultimately the matter returns to this: the intended meaning is the negation of attaining a goal that is of any worth, and to the fact that

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 117:

﴿Mata'un﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'). Abu al-Baqa' went this way, though he said: "That is, their survival is a little enjoyment (mata'un qalil), and the like." Al-Hawfi said: "﴿A little enjoyment (mata'un qalil)﴾ is a subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar)." In this there is the objection that an indefinite noun (nakira) may not be used as a subject without a justifying qualifier (musawwigh), and interpreting it as "their enjoyment" (mata'uhum) and the like is far-fetched. ﴿And for them﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿is a painful punishment (adhab alim)﴾, whose reality (kunh) cannot be comprehended.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 118:

﴿And to those who were Jews﴾, specifically and not others of the earlier peoples, ﴿We forbade what We have related to you before﴾, i.e., before the revelation of this verse, and that is in His saying, exalted is He, in Surat al-An'am: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws﴾ (6:146), the verse [in full].

The apparent meaning is that (min qabl, "before") is connected to (qasasna, "We have related"), but it has been permitted to connect it to (harramna, "We forbade"), and the omitted genitive complement is what has already passed, also.

It is possible that (min qabl) be understood as the forbidding of what was forbidden to your community (ummatika), and this is better according to what has been said. It has also been permitted that the speech be of the type of tanazu' (the grammatical dispute over a shared element between two verbs). This is a confirmation of what preceded regarding the restriction of the prohibited things to what was detailed, by nullifying what contradicts it from the slander of the Jews and their denial of that. For they used to say: "We are not the first to whom it was forbidden; rather, it was forbidden to Noah and Abraham and those after them, until the matter reached us." ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ by that prohibition, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾, in that they did what they were punished for by it, according to what His saying, exalted is He, reproached them with: ﴿For the wrongdoing of those who were Jews, We forbade them good things that had been made lawful for them﴾ (4:160), the verse [in full]. In this there is an indication of the difference between them and others regarding prohibition, and that just as it may be for harm, it may also be for punishment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 119:

Page 249

﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who did evil﴾: this is what harms its doer, whether disbelief or disobedience, and it includes slandering Allah, exalted is He. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that it means shirk (associating partners with Allah), but the general sense is preferable. ﴿In ignorance﴾: i.e., on account of it, in the sense that ignorance (jahala) is the cause that drives them to the deed, like the jahili zeal (al-ghayra al-jahiliyya, the pre-Islamic sense of honour) that drives to killing and other things. Ignorance has also been explained as the matter that is not befitting. Ibn 'Atiyya said: here it means overstepping the bounds and recklessness, not the opposite of knowledge. From this is what came in the report: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from acting ignorantly or being treated ignorantly by others," and the words of the poet:

Let none of us act ignorantly toward us, lest we act with more ignorance than the ignorant.

Yes, this ignorance, which means the opposite of knowledge, is very often accompanied by [the deed]. Some have explained it this way and made the "ba'" (ba') denote accompaniment, with the prepositional phrase in the position of a circumstantial clause, meaning: "associated with ignorance, not knowing Allah, exalted is He, nor His punishment, or not reflecting on the consequences, because desire overcame them." ﴿Then they repented after that﴾: i.e., after they had done what they did. The explicit mention of it, although "then" (thumma) indicates it, is for emphasis and intensification. ﴿And reformed﴾: i.e., they reformed their deeds, or entered into righteousness. Some have explained reform as steadfastness in repentance. ﴿Indeed your Lord, after it﴾: i.e., after the repentance, as more than one has said. Perhaps reform is included within repentance and completes it. Abu Hayyan said: the pronoun refers to the verbal nouns (masadir) understood from the preceding verbs, i.e., after the doing of evil, the repentance, and the reform. It was also said that it refers to ignorance, and it was said that it refers to evil in the sense of disobedience, but this is not the right view. ﴿Surely He is Forgiving﴾ of that evil, ﴿Merciful﴾, who keeps steadfast in His obedience, exalted is He, in act and in abstention. The repetition of "indeed your Lord" is for emphasizing the promise and showing full care in its fulfilment. The mention of the attribute of lordship together with its addition to his pronoun, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, while the effect is manifest in those who repent, is to hint that the bestowal of the effects of lordship, namely forgiveness and mercy, upon them is through his mediation (ﷺ) and their being among his followers, as passed shortly before. The restriction to ignorance: it has been said that it is to state the reality, because everyone who does evil does it only out of ignorance.

Al-'Askari said: the meaning is not that He, exalted is He, forgives those who do evil in ignorance and does not forgive those who do it without ignorance. Rather, the intended meaning is that all who repent are on this path. He specified those who do evil in ignorance only because most who commit sins commit them with little thought about the outcome, or when desire overcomes them, or in the ignorance of youth. So He mentioned the majority, according to the Arab custom in such matters, and by the general rules, a restriction carries no implied contrary meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 120:

﴿Indeed, Abraham was an ummah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: That is, he possessed such goodness as was possessed by an ummah, which is a large community. Its application to him, peace be upon him, is because he combined perfections that are hardly found except scattered among a numerous people:

"It is not far-fetched for Allah to gather the world into one man."

He, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, was the leader of the monotheists (muwahhidun) and the exemplar of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun), who established the proofs of monotheism, raised its banners, lowered the banners of polytheism (shirk), and with conclusive arguments struck its heads. Mujahid said: He, peace be upon him, was called an ummah because he stood alone in faith for a certain period of time. In Sahih al-Bukhari, it is related that he, peace be upon him, said to Sarah: "There is no believer on the earth today other than me and you." It is mentioned in al-Qamus that among the meanings of ummah is one who is upon the truth while opposing all other religions. The apparent meaning is that it is a metaphor, by treating him as if he were the whole of that age, because the disbelievers are as though they were non-existent. It has also been said: ummah here is on the pattern fu'lah in the sense of maf'ul, like ruhlah in the sense of "that to which one travels," and nukhbah in the sense of "the one chosen from its people," if it is aimed at or followed; that is, he was one who was followed or who was taken as a model, for people used to seek him out for benefit and to follow his conduct.

Ibn al-Anbari said: This is like the saying of the Arabs: "So-and-so is a mercy, a scholar, and a great genealogist," where by the feminine form they intend the extreme of the attribute described. The mention of him, peace be upon him, immediately after the refutation of the doctrines of the polytheists, including their shirk, their slander against prophethood, and their prohibition of what Allah has made lawful, is to indicate that the correctness of the religion of Islam and the falsehood of shirk and its branches are a matter established beyond doubt. This also contains a rebuttal of the Quraysh, who claim that they are upon his religion. It has also been said: when He, may He be exalted, clarified the condition of the polytheists and mentioned the Jews, He placed the way of Abraham, peace be upon him, between them, to show the difference between his condition and the condition of the polytheists and the condition of the Jews. ﴿Devoutly obedient to Allah﴾: obedient to Him, glorified is He, standing upright in His command, may He be exalted. ﴿Upright (hanif)﴾: inclining away from every false religion toward the true religion, never departing from it.

﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾: in any matter of their religion, in both its fundamentals and its branches. This was stated explicitly despite its being evident. It has been said: it is a rebuttal of the disbelievers of Quraysh in their saying: "We are upon the religion of our father Abraham." It has also been said: it is for that reason and also as a rebuttal of the polytheist Jews in their saying: ﴿Uzair is the son of Allah﴾, in their fabrication and their claim that he, peace be upon him, was upon what they were upon.
