This is like His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Abraham was neither a Jew nor a Christian, but he was a hanif, a Muslim, and he was not of the polytheists﴾, since by it the matter of mentioning the prohibition and the Sabbath, both before and after, is coherent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 121:

﴿Grateful for His favours﴾ is a third attribute of "ummah" (community), and the prepositional phrase is related to "shakiran" (grateful), as is apparent. The plural form used is that of paucity (jam' al-qillah), and it is said that this is to indicate that he, peace be upon him, does not fall short in giving thanks for a small favour, so how much more for a great one; and to make clear that he, peace be upon him, was contrary to what they were upon of ingratitude for the blessings of God, Exalted is He, as alluded to by the coining of the parable. It is also said that the plural of paucity here is used metaphorically for the plural of multitude, but there is no need for this.

It is related in some reports that he, peace be upon him, would not take his midday meal except with a guest. One day he did not find a guest, so he delayed his meal. Then behold, there was a group of angels, peace be upon them, in the form of humans, so he invited them to the food. They imagined that he had leprosy, so he said: "Now your eating with me is obligatory, in thanks to God, Exalted is He, that He has spared me from what He has afflicted you with."

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that the prepositional phrase be related to the words of God, Exalted is He, ﴿He chose him﴾, though this is contrary to what is apparent. Some have made the object of this a deleted element, meaning: He chose him and selected him for prophethood. The origin of ijtiba' (choosing) is gathering in the manner of selection, and it is applied to God, Exalted is He, singling out a servant with a divine overflow from which various kinds of blessings accrue to him without any effort on his part; and this is for the prophets, peace be upon them, and those close to them. ﴿And guided him to a straight path﴾ leading to Him, Exalted is He, which is the religion of Islam. The result of this guidance is not—as in Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim—merely his own being guided, peace be upon him, but along with guiding the creation as well and calling them to it, by the aid of the indication of the ijtiba'.

Some permitted that (to a straight path) be related to both "ijtabahu" and "hadahu" by way of tanazu' (the grammatical dispute over a shared complement), and the clause is either a circumstantial clause (hal) with qad implied, according to the well-known view, or a second predicate of inna. Abu al-Baqa' also permitted that it be a new independent sentence (isti'naf).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 122:

﴿And We gave him in this world a good reputation﴾. That is, He made him beloved to the people, to the extent that all the adherents of the religions befriend him and praise him, peace be upon him, just as he asked when he said: ﴿And grant me a tongue of truthfulness among later generations﴾. This is also narrated from Qatadah and others. And from al-Hasan: the good (ḥasanah) is prophethood. It was also said: righteous children in old age. It was said: wealth which he spends in the ways of goodness and piety. It was also said: a long life in ease and obedience. So "ḥasanah" in the first view means a good conduct (sīrah ḥasanah), and according to what follows it means a gift or a good blessing; so it is said. It is also permissible for all of these to mean a good gift (ʿaṭiyyah ḥasanah). The shift to the first person (in ﴿We gave﴾) is to show complete care for his affair and to magnify his station, peace be upon him. ﴿And indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾: he is counted among them, being with them in the lofty ranks of Paradise, just as he asked when he said: (And join me with the righteous). By "the righteous" he meant the prophets, peace be upon them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 123:

﴿Then We revealed to you, "Follow the creed (millah) of Ibrahim, a man of pure faith."﴾ It is, according to what is related from Qatadah, Islam, which was expressed a little earlier as "the straight path." In another report from him, it is the whole of his sacred law (shari'ah), except what the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to abandon. In al-Khazin's tafsir this is reported from the scholars of the principles (ahl al-usul). And from Ibn Amr ibn al-'As, it is the rites of the Hajj.

Al-Imam said: Some people said: The Prophet ﷺ was upon the creed and the sacred law of Ibrahim, and he had no law unique to himself. Rather, he was sent, upon him be blessings and peace, to revive the sacred law of Ibrahim, on the basis of this verse. They therefore understood the creed (millah) to mean the sacred law in both its fundamental principles and its subsidiary rulings. This is a weak opinion. What is meant by ﴿the creed of Ibrahim﴾ is tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness) and the negation of shirk (associating partners with God), which is understood from His words, ﴿and he was not of the polytheists﴾. If it is said: The Prophet ﷺ only negated shirk and affirmed tawhid on the basis of decisive proofs, so this does not count as following, and therefore the creed must be taken to mean the laws in which following is valid. We say: It is possible that what is meant is the command to follow him in the manner of calling to tawhid, namely calling to it by way of gentleness and ease, and presenting proofs again and again in many kinds, as is the customary method of the Qur'an. End of quotation.

Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying: It is not necessary, because the belief which the rational proofs require does not preclude that it be revealed, so that rational and transmitted evidence may reinforce belief in it. Do you not see His words, ﴿Say: It is only revealed to me that your God is one God﴾, how the revelation included what rational proof necessitates? So there is no impossibility that the Prophet ﷺ be commanded to follow the creed of Ibrahim, upon him be peace, in negating shirk and affirming tawhid, even if that was already established for him, upon him be blessings and peace, by rational proof, so that the rational and the transmitted proofs reinforce one another in this sublime matter. Another objection is that the apparent sense is to take the creed as the manner of calling, and there is no doubt that this is not included in its meaning. For the creed is what God has prescribed for His servants through the tongues of the prophets, peace be upon them, from amlaltu al-kitab (I dictated the book), when one dictates it. It is the very religion (din), but considered in terms of obedience to it. Its verification is that the divine ordinance, whenever it is attributed to the one who conveys it from God, is called a creed (millah), and whenever it is attributed to the one who establishes it, it is called a religion (din). Al-Raghib said: The difference between them is that millah is only attributed to the Prophet ﷺ to whom it is ascribed, and it is hardly ever found attributed to God, nor to individual members of the Prophet's community, peace be upon him. It is used only for the totality of the laws, not for their individual parts. Din is not like this. Most exegetes hold that what is meant here is the fundamental principles of the laws. What is related from Qatadah at first may be understood in this sense, and there is no harm in what is related from him secondly.

As for the argument of some Shafi'is for the obligation of circumcision and of whatever was part of the sacred law of Ibrahim, upon him be peace, and for which no abrogating text has come, it is built upon this, as is not hidden. As for what is related from Ibn Amr ibn al-'As, al-Bahr mentions it. But what Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, and a group of others transmitted from him is that he said: "Jibril, peace be upon him, led Ibrahim in the Dhuhr and 'Asr prayers at 'Arafat. Then he stood until the sun set, then he set off with him. Then he led him in the Maghrib and 'Isha' prayers at Jam', then he led him in the Fajr prayer as quickly as any of the Muslims pray. Then he stood with him until, when it was as slow as any of the Muslims pray, he set off with him. Then he threw the pebbles at the jamrah, then he slaughtered and shaved, then he poured him out toward the House and circumambulated with him. Then God, exalted, said to His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Then We revealed to you, 'Follow the creed of Ibrahim.'﴾" It may be that what was mentioned first is derived from this.

You know that it is not an explicit text on this, and I do not think anyone agrees to restrict his creed, upon him be peace, to the rites of the Hajj.

Page 252

(Wa-an) is either explanatory or verbal (masdariyyah), and the discussion of its connection to the imperative has passed. (Thumma) has been said to indicate temporal sequence (al-tarakhi al-zamani), since it is evident that the days of the Prophet ﷺ came long after the days of Ibrahim, upon him be peace. But the scholars have chosen that it indicates sequence in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because that is more eloquent and more fitting to the context.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Indeed, in this ﴿thumma﴾ there is an indication that the most noble of the honours bestowed upon the Friend of God, peace be upon him, and the most sublime of the blessings he was given, is that the Messenger of God ﷺ follows his creed, and it is an exaltation of the station of our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and a glorification of his place. As for the first, it is from the indication of ﴿thumma﴾ that this bestowed matter differs from the rest of the ranks and distinctions that were granted to him, peace be upon him. As for the second, it is because the Friend, despite the greatness of his standing with God, the Exalted, the highest of his ranks is that He revealed to the Beloved to follow his creed. In the phrase ﴿We revealed﴾ followed by the command to follow the creed, and not the command to follow Ibrahim, peace be upon him, there is something which indicates, as in al-Kashshaf, that the Prophet ﷺ is not a follower of him, but rather he is independent in taking from the same source from which Ibrahim, peace be upon him, took. ﴿Hanifan﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to Ibrahim, the genitive-attached noun, because the noun attached (mudaf) to what follows it, due to the strength of its connection, takes the position of a part of it, and so it is counted as belonging to the type of "I saw the face of Hind, standing."

Ibn 'Atiyyah transmitted from Makki the impermissibility of its being a circumstantial clause referring to it, giving as the reason that it is a genitive-attached noun. He critiqued this by saying: That is not as he said, because the circumstantial clause may be governed by prepositions when they govern the one it refers to, as in "I passed by Zayd standing." There is a discussion in both statements that is not hidden.

Abu Hayyan prohibited the occurrence of a circumstantial clause referring to the genitive-attached noun in this type of construction as well, and claimed that the permission in it is something Ibn Malik alone held. He insisted that ﴿hanifan﴾ is a circumstantial clause referring to ﴿millah﴾, because it has the meaning of ﴿din﴾, or to the pronoun in ﴿ittabi'﴾. This is not correct. Ibn Malik did not hold this alone; rather, al-Akhfash preceded him to it, and a group followed him. ﴿And he was not of the polytheists﴾. Rather, he was the exemplar of the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqin). This is a repetition of what came before, for the sake of added emphasis and confirmation of his purity, upon him be peace, from what they held in belief and practice.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 124:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the Sabbath was only prescribed﴾ means: indeed, what was enjoined was the glorification of it, devoting oneself to worship, and abstaining from hunting in it. This is a confirmation of that absolute negation and a clarification of it, by refuting what might be imagined as detracting from its universality. For the Jews used to claim that the Sabbath was among the rites of Islam (islam, here meaning submission to God in the general sense) and that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, used to observe it. That is to say: the Sabbath is not among the laws of Ibrahim and the rites of his religion, peace be upon him, which he was commanded to follow, so that there would be some connection in general between him and some of the polytheists. Rather, it was legislated for the Children of Israel after a long period of time. The verb being cast in the passive voice follows the patterns of majesty and indicates that there is no need to mention the agent explicitly, because attributing it to another is impossible.

Abu Haywa read "ju'ila" in the active voice. It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash that they read "Innama anzalna al-sabt" (Indeed, We sent down the Sabbath). According to Abu Hayyan, this is an interpretation of meaning and not a recitation, since it contradicts the consensus of the written Qur'an (sawad al-mushaf). The widely transmitted report from them is that they recited, like the community, "Innama juʻila al-sabtu ʻala alladhina ikhtalafu fihi" (the Sabbath was only prescribed for those who differed concerning it), meaning: over their Prophet, when he commanded them to observe Friday, and they chose Saturday. They were the Jews.

Al-Shafi'i in al-Umm, and al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) in their Sahihs, narrated from Abu Hurayra who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "We are the last (in the world) but the first on the Day of Resurrection, though they were given the Book before us and we were given it after them. Then this is their day which was made obligatory upon them, meaning Friday, but they differed concerning it, so Allah the Exalted guided us to it. People are thus following us in it: the Jews tomorrow and the Christians the day after tomorrow."

It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: Musa, peace be upon him, commanded the Jews to observe Friday and said: "Devote yourselves to Allah, the Exalted, one day in every seven days, which is the day of Friday, and do not perform any of your work on it." But they refused to accept this and said: "We want only the day on which Allah, the Exalted, finished creation, which is Saturday." So it was imposed upon them and the command concerning it was made strict. Then 'Isa, peace be upon him, came with Friday, and the Christians said: "We do not want their festival to come after our festival," so they adopted Sunday. It seems they chose it because it is the beginning of creation.

This Imam (al-Razi) chose this and took "fi" to mean causality, i.e., they differed against their Prophet on account of that day. Al-Khafaji said: the meaning of "ikhtalafu fihi" is that all of them opposed their Prophet, so it is a disagreement between them and their Prophet. The apparent sense of the reports requires that Friday was first designated for them. Qadi 'Iyad said: The apparent meaning is that the glorification of Friday was enjoined upon them without specification, and it was left to their own judgment, so their rabbis differed about specifying it, and Allah the Exalted did not guide them to it. He then enjoined it upon this community with specification, and they achieved its virtue. Had it been explicitly stipulated, it would not be correct to say "they differed"; rather it would be said "they opposed."

Imam al-Nawawi said: It is possible that they were commanded explicitly and it was stated, and they differed concerning it: whether its specification was binding or whether they might substitute it, so they substituted it and erred in substituting it.

Al-Wahidi said: The matter of this disagreement has been problematic for many exegetes, to the extent that some of them said: the meaning of their disagreement over the Sabbath is that some of them said it is the greatest of days in sanctity because Allah the Exalted finished creating things on it, while others said the greatest of them in sanctity is Sunday because Allah, glory be to Him, began creation on it. This is an error, because the Jews were not two factions over the Sabbath; rather, the Christians chose Sunday after them by a period of time.

It has also been said: the intended meaning is that they differed among themselves concerning its status. One group preferred it over Friday and was not content with Friday, while another group preferred Friday over it and inclined to it, based on the report that Musa, peace be upon him, brought them Friday, but most of them refused except the Sabbath, and a small group among them accepted it. So Allah the Exalted permitted them the Sabbath and tested them by forbidding hunting in it. Those who were content with Friday obeyed the command of Allah, the Exalted, and did not hunt, but their descendants did not patiently refrain from hunting, so Allah the Exalted transformed them into apes, while those obedient ones were spared.

The first interpretation is the interpretation of the chief of the exegetes, the interpreter of the Qur'an and the scholar of the community, related through sound chains from the best of prophets and the most knowledgeable of creation regarding the intent of the Lord of the worlds, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace. ﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them﴾, i.e., between those who differed, ﴿on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ﴾, i.e., He will judge between them by recompensing them for their disagreement with their Prophet and their opposition to him in this matter; or He will separate the two groups among them from the enmity and disagreement, and will recompense each group according to what it deserves of reward and punishment. In this, according to this view, there is an allusion that what occurred in this world, the transformation of one of the two groups and the deliverance of the other, is, in comparison with what will occur in the Hereafter, a thing of no account. He expressed the imposition by the word "ju'ila" (was prescribed) connected with the preposition "ʻala" (upon) to indicate that it includes stringency and testing leading to punishment. He referred to the Jews by the relative pronoun with "ikhtalafu" (differed) to indicate the reason for that.

It has also been said: the meaning is that Allah appointed as the consequence of abandoning the glorification of the Sabbath, which is the transformation, to be upon those who differed concerning it, i.e., who permitted hunting in it at times and forbade it at other times, and it was incumbent upon them to agree on its prohibition as Allah the Exalted commanded. This is related from Qatada. The judgment among them was interpreted as recompense for their differing actions, by permitting at times and forbidding at other times.

The reason for mentioning this here is that it is intended as a warning and threat to the polytheists of what is in opposing the prophets, peace be upon them, of ruin, as the town that disbelieved in the blessings of Allah, the Exalted, was mentioned as an example for this. It has been objected that inserting this between the narration of the command of the Prophet, Allah bless him and grant him peace, to follow the religion of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and his command, Allah bless him and grant him peace, to call to it, is like separating a tree from its bark. It was answered that there is in it an urging to answer the call contained in the preceding discourse and commanded in the following discourse, so the intermediate matter has a relation to both extremes, which removes it from being a separation like that between a tree and its bark, and this is, as you see, far-fetched.

It has also been objected that the word "bayнahum" (between them) requires that the judgment means separating the disagreement between the two groups, not recompense for their differing actions by permitting at times and forbidding at other times. This also refutes interpreting it as judgment by recompense for their differing, all of them, against their Prophet and opposing him in what was brought to them. It has been interpreted thus according to the interpretation transmitted from the interpreter of the Qur'an, and some interpreted it according to what was interpreted in the interpretation transmitted from Qatada, which is refuted by the same objection, along with the saying that it implies the two differences are the same in meaning, while the apparent view is that they are one. Some answered the objection by denying that "bayнahum" requires what was mentioned earlier, so consider this carefully.

Interpreting "the Sabbath" as the specific day is the apparent meaning to which most have gone. It has also been permitted that it is a verbal noun from "sabbatat al-Yahud" when the Jews glorified their Sabbath. It has been said: according to this, it is also possible that there is in the verse a double meaning (istikhdam).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 125 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Invite﴾, that is, whoever you have been sent to among the community, all of them. The object is omitted to indicate generality. It is also permissible that the meaning is "perform the invitation," treating the verb as intransitive, aiming at the act of invitation itself, to indicate that the generality of the invitation needs no specification, and that the intended matter is the command to carry it out in a particular manner. It has been objected that this does not suit the context, just as it does not suit His saying, ﴿and argue with them﴾.

﴿to the way of your Lord﴾: to Islam, which is expressed at times as "the straight path" and at other times as "the religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him)." In the mention of the title of Lordship together with the attribution to the pronoun of the Prophet (ﷺ), there is what is not hidden.

﴿with wisdom﴾: with a firmly constructed statement, which is a decisive argument that removes doubts. Close to this is what is in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), that it is the correct speech that proceeds from the soul in the most beautiful position. ﴿and good admonition﴾: which are persuasive addresses and beneficial lessons, by which they know that you are advising them. ﴿And argue with them﴾: debate with their obstinate opponents ﴿in the way that is best﴾: by the best of the methods of debate and disputation, from gentleness and softness, choosing the easier aspect, and employing well-known premises, to calm their contention and extinguish their flame, as the Friend (Khalil, Ibrahim) (peace be upon him) did. It has been said that the people of rational sciences (ahl al-ma'qul) derived from the verse that what is considered in invitation, among the five arts (al-sina'at al-khams), is only demonstration (burhan), rhetoric (khitabah) and dialectic (jadal), since the verse limited itself to what points to them. The methods of his invitation (peace be upon him) varied according to the varying ranks of people. Among them are the elite, who are people of luminous souls, strong in readiness to grasp meanings, strongly drawn to lofty principles, inclined to attain certainty in its various degrees, and these invite by wisdom in the earlier sense.

Among them are the common people, who are people of turbid souls, weak in readiness, very accustomed to sensible things, strongly attached to customs and habits, and unable to reach the level of demonstration, but they have no obstinacy, and these invite by good admonition in the sense previously mentioned.

Among them are those who are obstinate and dispute with falsehood in order to refute the truth with it, because of what has overcome them of blind imitation of their forefathers and what has become firmly rooted in them of false beliefs, so that admonitions and lessons do not benefit them. Rather, it is necessary to bridle them with the best methods of argument, so that their stubbornness may soften and their obstinacy may leave. These are the ones whom he (ﷺ) was commanded to argue with "in the way that is best." Sophistry (mughalatah) and poetry (shi'r) were not counted, because the benefit of sophistry is to mislead the opponent, whereas avoiding misleading him is what is required, and the station of the Messenger (peace be upon him) negates that he should be misled, and exalts him above being misled. As for poetry, although it is beneficial to the elite and the common people, since people in matters of advancing and withdrawing are more obedient to imagination than to assent, its foundation is falsehood. For this reason it is said: "The most eloquent poetry is the most false." So it is not befitting for the truthful one who is believed, as His saying, ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it befitting for him﴾, testifies. It is not said: poetry, which is one of the arts, is a syllogism composed of imaginative premises, while the poetry whose foundation is falsehood, which is metrical and rhymed speech, is that whose teaching He negated from him (ﷺ). This is because it has been said: the reprehensibility of poetry is not due to it being metrical and rhymed speech, but due to its containing false imaginings. Thus they are of one kind. Some of the later scholars mentioned this.

Many have held that the verse indicates the differing ranks of those invited, but he (the one just mentioned) disagreed in some of what preceded. In al-Kashshaf, after mentioning that the speech of al-Zamakhshari indicates that he (peace be upon him) should combine the three in invitation, so that the speech in itself is well-composed, producing what it is connected to of the purpose, and yet is intended as advice to the one addressed by it, and the speaker is of good character in that, a teacher, a sincere advisor, kind and gentle, the text is: "The best, according to what the researchers (al-muhaqqiqun) have held, is that it is a generalization of the invitation according to the ranks of those invited in understanding and readiness. Whoever invites with the tongue of wisdom, so that certainty of direct vision or demonstrative certainty is gained, these are the foremost. Whoever invites with good admonition, which is wisdom-based persuasion and not well-known addresses, is a group below these. Whoever invites with good argument are the general population of Muslims and also the disbelievers. End quote."

I do not see what requires denying that the intended meaning of "good admonition" is well-known addresses, and that their being composed of premises that are presumed or accepted from a person held in belief is what is required. It is not befitting for the Prophet (may God's blessings and peace be upon him) to use presumptive matters or to take the words of others, and invitation with such would necessitate that. What is in this is not hidden, so reflect on it.

Al-Ihsa'i, the leader of the pure sect in our time, called the Kashfiyya, mentioned in his book Sharh al-Fawa'id what in summary is: those invited among the responsible persons are three kinds, and likewise the proofs to which the verse points. If they are among the wise intellectuals and the noble scholars, their invitation to the truth that God desires from them is through knowledge by the proof of wisdom, which is the tasting, direct-vision proof, from which necessarily arises necessary knowledge of what is proven, because it is a kind of direct witnessing. Like our saying in refuting one who claims that the realities of things were latent in His Essence, in a more noble manner, and then He poured them forth: it is necessary that the Essence, glorified be He, before the outpouring, has a state different from what follows it, whether the change is in the Essence itself or in what is in the Essence. If the change occurs in the Essence, its originatedness necessarily follows. If it occurs in what is in the Essence, that is, the latent realities of things, then the Essence must be a locus for the changing and varying, and from that its originatedness follows.

And like our saying in proving that He, glorified be He, is more manifest than everything: every effect resembles a influencing attribute, and that it subsists by its act, subsisting by emanation, like rays with luminous bodies and speech with the speaker. Thus things are the manifestation of the Necessary Existent through them to them, because He, glorified be He, does not manifest by His Essence, otherwise His two states would differ. And nothing is more manifest than the Manifest in its manifestation, because the Manifest is more manifest than its manifestation, although the attainment of knowledge of Him is only possible through its manifestation. Like standing: the one standing is more manifest in standing than standing itself, and the one sitting is more manifest in sitting than sitting itself. Although knowledge of the two is only attainable through standing and sitting, you say: "O Standing One" and "O Sitting One," and the meaning for you is the one standing and the one sitting, not standing and sitting, because by His manifestation to you through that, He is hidden from your witnessing, and if you turn to it, the standing one and the sitting one are veiled from you. This is the instrument for knowing the true realities, like unity (tawhid) and what is joined to it. Its support is the heart (fu'ad), which is the light of God, Exalted, indicated by his (ﷺ) saying: "Beware the insight (firasa) of the believer, for he sees by the light of God, Exalted."

Transmission from the Book and the Sunnah, whose condition on which the opening of the door of light depends is three things. The first: that you be just toward your Lord and accept from Him, glorified be He, His word, and not follow the desire of your soul. The second: that you stop at your explanation, your clarifying and your making clear, based on His saying, Exalted: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — about all those one will be questioned﴾. The third: that you look at those states, meaning the explanation and what follows it, with the eye of God, Exalted, which is the eye that is the attribute of His own Self for you, meaning your existence from the standpoint of being an effect and a light, not with your eye which is you, from the standpoint that you are you. For with this eye you know only the originated, needy, perishing things.

If they are among the scholars with minds and the masters of hearts, their invitation to the truth that God, glorified be He, desires from them is of true certainty in their beliefs, by the proof of good admonition, which is the rational certain proof from which certainty in faith in Him and in what He commanded them to believe arises. It is the instrument for the knowledge of the path, the refinement of character, the knowledge of certainty and piety. Although these sciences may be gained from other than it, without attending to it one cannot reach the certainty and tranquility which is the root of the science of character. Its support is the heart and transmission, and the condition of its validity and benefit is that your intellect be characterized by it, by your binding yourself to what it binds you and not wronging it. It is like His saying, Exalted: ﴿Say: "Have you considered, if it is from God and you disbelieve in it, who is more astray than one in extreme dissension?"﴾ and His saying, Exalted: ﴿Say: "Have you considered, if it is from God and you disbelieve in it, and a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like and believed, while you were arrogant? Indeed, God does not guide the wrongdoing people."﴾ And other than these, of what is countless in number.

If they are among the scholars who are people of conventional forms, like the theologians (mutakallimun) and their counterparts, their invitation to the truth that God, glorified be He, desires from them is of conventional certainty, according to the requirement of their deficient nature, by the proof of argument in the way that is best. This is the decisive scientific proof from which knowledge of the matters mentioned arises. It is the instrument for the knowledge of the law (shari'ah), and its support is knowledge and transmission. Its condition is that the opponent be just, by presenting it in the manner established in the science of logic (ilm al-mizan). The scholars have mentioned it in their books of principles (usul) and of branches (furu'). Indeed, one hardly hears from them other than this proof, and it is the locus of debates and objections. As for the first two proofs, there is in them neither debate nor objection. If an objector objects to them, he objects to them with other than them. End quote. Its meaning is as you see, and I mentioned it so that you know the state of the subordinate from the state of the leader. I have seen the shaykhs of this group speaking in a way that is like the thorns of porcupines, while they reckon it to be like the plumes of peacocks.

It is also permissible that by wisdom and good admonition is meant the Glorious Qur'an, for it combines both matters. So it is as if it were said: invite by the Qur'an, which is wisdom and good admonition. Other things have been said. Among them is that wisdom is prophethood, and this is not of wisdom. Some have explained "good argument" as turning away from their harm, and claimed that the verse is abrogated (mansukha) by the verse of the sword. The majority hold that it is muhkam (decisive, not abrogated), and that the meaning of the verse is what preceded.

Because wisdom is the highest and most noble of proofs, and those invited by it are the perfected seekers of divine knowledge and true sciences, and they are few, it was mentioned first. Because argument is the lowest of proofs, since its purpose is nothing but to bind the opponent and silence him, and it is used only with the deficient who are dominated by contention and quarrelsomeness and are not in the position of attaining those sciences, it was mentioned last. Because good admonition is below demonstration and above argument, and those invited by it are the intermediate who have not reached the perfection of the verifying sages, nor are they in the deficiency of those contentious troublemakers, it stood between the two matters. It seems that He did not say: "invite to the way with wisdom, admonition, and the best argument," because argument is not of the category of invitation. Rather, its intent is another purpose different from it, namely binding and silencing, as the Imam (al-Razi) said, so understand.

﴿Indeed your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way﴾, which He commanded you to invite the creation to, and who turned away from accepting it.

﴿He knows best who is guided﴾ (wa-Huwa a'lamu bil-muhtadin), which gives the reason for the two matters mentioned earlier. It is as if it were said: "Follow the method mentioned in the call (da'wah) and debate (munazarah), and nothing else is incumbent upon you. As for the attainment of guidance and misguidance, and the recompense for each, these belong to God, glorified is He, and to no other, for He knows best who will remain in error and who will be guided. He will then recompense each of them with what they deserve." This is what has been said. It has been objected that the verse's indication of recompense is accepted, but that the attainment of guidance and misguidance not being in the power of anyone other than God is not indicated by the verse at all. It has been answered that when the knowledge of guidance and misguidance is restricted to Him, exalted is He, it is known that no one else possesses knowledge of them, and so how could anyone else possess their attainment? Therefore the claim that the verse does not indicate this is not sound. It has also been said: the meaning is, "Follow the method mentioned in the call and debate, for He, exalted is He, knows best the state of one who does not refrain from error because of his poor choice, and the state of one whose affair will end in guidance because of the good in him. So what He has prescribed for you in the call is what wisdom requires, for it is sufficient for guiding those who are guided and for removing the excuse of those who go astray."

[Page 257]

It has also been said: the meaning is, "Your duty is only to convey the message, so do not press them insistently if they refuse after conveying it once or twice, for example. Your Lord knows them best. Whoever has good in him, brief counsel suffices him, and whoever has no good in him, stratagems fail with him." The mention of those who go astray first is because the discourse concerns them. The expression of misguidance in the verbal form (fi'l), which indicates occurrence (huduth), is because it is a change of God's fitrah (natural disposition), upon which He created people, and a turning away from the call, and this is an accidental matter. This is unlike guidance, which is a term for steadfastness upon the fitrah and continuing in accordance with what the call requires. For this reason it is expressed in the nominal form (ism), which indicates permanence.

As for the clause ﴿He knows best who is guided﴾, it has been said that it is coordinated (ʿatf) with the clause ﴿Indeed your Lord﴾ etc., or with the predicate of inna. The repetition of ﴿He knows best﴾ is for emphasis and to signal the difference in the states of the two groups and their outcomes in punishment and reward. The pronoun Huwa in the first clause is a separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl) for specification, as is evident in the words of some, or for reinforcement, as has been said. Nor is it hidden what delicacy there is in the mention of the title of Lordship (rubūbiyyah) together with its attribution to his pronoun (ﷺ).

[Page 258]

"And if you punish" means: if you intend to punish, "then punish with the like of what you were punished with," meaning the like of what was done to you. He expressed it as punishment ('iqāb) by way of naming the cause by the name of its effect, as in "as you judge, so you will be judged" (kamā tadīnu tudānu), through the figure of mushākalah (congruity of expression). Al-Khafājī said: In common usage, 'iqāb means any punishment, even when it is the initial act. In the original language, however, it means requital for a previous punishment. If the second is considered, then it is mushākalah; if the first is considered, then there is no mushākalah. On both considerations, the form mufā'alah (the morphological pattern denoting mutual action) does not imply reciprocity.

The verse was revealed concerning the mutilation of Hamzah, may Allah be pleased with him, on the day of Uhud. It is authentically reported from Abū Hurayrah that "the Prophet (ﷺ) stood over Hamzah on the day he was martyred, and he looked at a sight that he had never looked at anything more painful to his heart than it. He looked at him after he had been mutilated, and said: 'May the mercy of Allah be upon you, for you were, as far as I know, one who joined the ties of kinship and one who did much good. Had it not been for grief over you, it would have pleased me to leave you until Allah raises you from the beasts of prey. By Allah, I will mutilate seventy of them in your place.' Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, descended while the Prophet (ﷺ) was standing at the final verses of Surat al-Nahl, 'And if you punish...' to the end. Thereupon the Prophet (ﷺ) made expiation for his oath, restrained himself from what he had intended, and endured patiently." Accordingly, the surah on this account is Medinan.

Al-Nahhās held that it is Meccan and not concerning the mutilation of Hamzah, may Allah be pleased with him. Some scholars preferred this view because of the consequence that follows from the other view, namely a lack of connection (irtibāṭ), which the Speech of the Lord of Might, exalted is His majesty, is far above. For that incident has no relation to what precedes it. As for the view that it is Meccan, the connection is that when the Glorified commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to call to the religion and explained its method, He indicated to him, peace be upon him, and to those who follow him, the need to observe justice with those who oppose them, and equivalence. For the call (to Islam) can hardly be free of this. How could it be otherwise, since it necessitates turning faces away from the worshipped directions and placing necks into a collar not known before, decreeing upon them the corruption of what they do and what they abandon, and the falsehood of a religion their forefathers of old continued upon, while their stratagems have failed them, their pretexts have been exhausted, the paths of argument and debate have been closed to them, and the doors of discussion and dialogue have been shut before them. Their breaths have become strained in their chests, and they have fallen into utter bewilderment, striking hands and feet together, finding nothing but spear-points as a mount, and choosing red death over the religion of Islam as a creed.

Most exegetes went to the first view, and it is recorded in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī. Indeed, al-Qurṭubī said: It is among the things on which the exegetes are unanimous. What was mentioned about the consequence of a lack of connection is not valid, for drawing attention to that incident serves to indicate that the call (to Islam) is never free of such things, and that disputation leads to fighting. When it occurs, the fitting response is what has been mentioned. Thus, in terms of the ultimate outcome, there is no difference in connection between the verse being Meccan or Medinan. The particularity of the occasion of revelation does not negate the generality of the meaning. Therefore, what is relied upon is not departing from what the majority has said.

Ibn Sīrīn recited: "And if you retaliate, then retaliate" with the letters qāf (ق) both doubled, meaning: and if you pursue with victory, then pursue with the like of what was done to you without exceeding it. The verse has been cited as evidence that the one seeking retaliation (qiṣāṣ) may do to the offender the like of what he did, in kind and in measure, and this is something on which there is no disagreement. As for the unity of the instrument, that one is killed with the stone with which he killed, and with the sword with which he killed, for example, some imams have held this. The position of Abū Ḥanīfah, may Allah be pleased with him, is that there is no retaliation (qawad) except by the sword. The reason for this, even though the verse apparently indicates otherwise, is that killing by stone or the like cannot be equated in its degree of severity and weakness, so equivalence was considered in the act of killing and the taking of life, and the basis for this is the sword, as al-Rāzī mentioned in his Aḥkām.

Some have mentioned that this verse was subject to disagreement. Al-Shāfi'ī took its apparent meaning, while the Ḥanafīs replied that the equivalence is in number, so that one is killed for one, because it was revealed in response to the words of the Prophet (ﷺ), "I will mutilate seventy of them," when Hamzah was killed and mutilated, as you have heard. Thus there is no evidence in it. Al-Wāḥidī said: It is abrogated (mansūkhah, i.e., by naskh) like other verses about mutilation. There is discussion of this in the commentaries on al-Hidāyah.

In restricting the command by His words, "And if you punish," there is an encouragement to pardon, by way of allusion, in view of what the conditional "in" (in) implies of not being certain that what follows it will occur. It is as if it were said: "Do not punish, even if you punish..." like the statement of a physician to a patient who asked him about eating fruit: "If you eat fruit, then eat the pear." This was stated explicitly in the more emphatic form, so He said: "But if you endure patiently," meaning: refrain from retaliating in kind, "it is indeed better," that is, your patience is better, "for the patient," in the manner of "Be just; that is nearer to righteousness." It is better than victory through retaliation "for the patient," that is, for you. Yet He turned from this to what is in the sublime wording, praising them and commending them for patience. In this there is guidance that if you are patient, then this is your known character, so do not abandon it in this matter. Or it is a description of them with an attribute that comes to them when they refrain from retaliation, as in the saying "whoever kills a slain man," which is the apparent sense of the wording. In this there is an intense encouragement to patience. It is permissible for the pronoun to refer to the general notion of patience implied by the verb, and the intended meaning of "the patient" is their category, so these (the Prophet and those who follow him) enter into it in the first and foremost manner.

Then God, exalted is He, explicitly commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to do what others were only encouraged to do by allusion, namely to be patient. This is because he, peace and blessings be upon him, was the most worthy of all people of the steadfast resolves of affairs (ʿazaʾim al-umur), owing to his greater knowledge of God's affairs, may He be glorified, and his greater trust in Him, exalted is He. So He said: ﴿And be patient﴾ over what befell you from them of various kinds of pain and harm, and what you witnessed of their total aversion from the truth after the call. ﴿And your patience is not except through God﴾ is an exceptive construction with no stated object (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of things, meaning: your patience is not accompanied or joined by anything except the remembrance of God, exalted is He, total absorption in watching over His affairs, and devotion to Him, may He be glorified, with the full concentration of resolve. In this there is consolation (tasliyah) for the Prophet (ﷺ), an easing of the hardships of patience for him, and an honouring of him beyond which there is no greater honour. Or it means: not except through His will, which is founded on profound wisdoms leading to praiseworthy outcomes. Thus the consolation lies in the fact that it comprises sublime ends. This is what Shaykh al-Islam said.

Others have said: that is, not except through His grace and His assistance. Thus the consolation lies in the facilitation and making easy of patience. This is perhaps more evident than what preceded.

﴿And do not grieve over them﴾, that is, over the disbelievers and their disbelief in you and their not following you, similar to His saying ﴿So do not grieve over the disbelieving people﴾. It has also been said: over the believers and what was done to them of mutilation on the day of Uhud. ﴿And do not be in distress﴾ is read with a fatha on the dad, while Ibn Kathir read it with a kasra; this is also reported from Nafi', but it is not sound according to what Abu Hayyan said about him. They are two dialects, like al-qawl and al-qil. That is, (Page 259) do not be in narrowness of breast and constriction. In this there is a metaphor that is not hidden, and there is no need to resort to a reversal (qalb) of the form. Abu ʿUbaydah said: al-dayq with a fatha is a lightened form of diq (narrow), like hayyin and hayyin; that is, do not be in a narrow matter. This was refuted by Abu ʿAli, as recorded in al-Bahr, on the ground that the adjective is not specific to the qualified noun, so it is impermissible to claim an elision; that is why one may say "I passed by a writer" (katib) but not "a one who eats" (akil) is barred. This was countered with a denial, because when the adjective is general and a general qualified noun is supposed, there is no obstacle to it. ﴿Of what they plot﴾, that is, of their plotting against you in the future. The first, as stated in Irshad al-ʿAql al-Salim, is a prohibition against grieving over something desirable from them that has already passed, and the second is a prohibition against grieving over a feared harm from them that is yet to come. In this there is that the prohibition against both, although their absence is among the necessary consequences of the patience commanded, is for the sake of added emphasis and showing full care for the matter of consolation. Otherwise, would anything desirable occur to the mind of one who has turned to God, exalted is He, with his whole being, detached from everything other than Him, may He be glorified, from preoccupations, so that He would forbid grief over its loss? It has also been said: "yamkurun" means "makaru" (they plotted), and the present tense is used only to bring the past scene vividly before the mind. The first prohibition concerns grief over their wretched state in themselves, through their being characterised by disbelief and aversion from the call; the second concerns grief over their wretched conduct towards him (ﷺ), through their harming him by mutilating his beloved ones and the like. The purpose of both prohibitions is purely consolation, not the binding force of a prohibition. And know that the apparent meaning is to keep the present tense in its literal sense, so reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 16, verse 128 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who are mindful of Him⁠﴾. This is a reason (ta'lil) for what preceded of commands and prohibitions. By "being with" (al-ma'iyya) is meant the constant guardianship (wilaya) that no anxiety, grief, constriction of the breast, or anything that the particle (ma'a, "with") implies of following the God-fearing is able to come between its possessor and. The reason is that they are the ones who actually practise taqwa (God-consciousness), and what is meant by it here is its highest level, namely, freedom from everything that occupies the innermost heart (sirr) away from the Truth, glorified is He, and wholly devoting oneself to Him, exalted is He. This is because that is what brings about His guardianship, mighty and majestic is He, which is coupled with the good tidings of ﴿Surely the friends of Allah, no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve⁠﴾. The meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, is the guardian of those who have wholly devoted themselves to Him, glorified is He, and have kept themselves free from everything that would occupy their inner hearts away from Him, mighty and majestic is He. So nothing of what is desired or feared comes to their minds, let alone grief over it, whether over its loss or its occurrence. This is the meaning by which patience, which is commanded, is achieved according to the first of the previously mentioned possibilities. Thereby the connection is established and the reasoning is complete. Otherwise, mere guarding against sins would not be the basis for any of the resolute acts (al-'aza'im) whose abandonment is permitted, so how much more so for the patience referred to and its companions. Its basis is only the meaning mentioned. It is as though it were said: "Indeed, Allah is with those who are patient." The noble wording was preferred over that in order to emphasise exhortation to patience, by alerting to the fact that it is among the characteristics of the most excellent sublime attributes and their attendants. Likewise, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and those who are doers of good⁠﴾ is for indicating that it belongs to the category of ihsan (excellence) in which competitors vie. What indicates this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And be patient, for Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good⁠﴾. And He, glorified is He, has alerted that each of patience and taqwa is of the kind of ihsan by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, whoever is mindful and patient, then indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the doers of good⁠﴾. The reality of ihsan is performing actions in the fitting manner. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained it as: "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, He sees you." The repetition of the relative pronoun (alladhina) is to signal that each of the two clauses is sufficient for His guardianship, glorified is He, without one of them being a completion of the other. The first is stated in verbal form to indicate occurrence (huduth), while the second is stated in nominal form to indicate that its content is a firmly established disposition in them. Taqwa is placed before ihsan because takhliya (emptying) precedes tahliya (adorning). The two relative clauses refer either to the category of the God-fearing and the doers of good, in which case the prayers and peace of God be upon him enter into their company by a primary entry, namely he (ﷺ) and his followers, may Allah be pleased with them; and this description of them is used as praise and commendation of them with the two beautiful qualities. In it there is an allusion that his (ﷺ) conduct entails that the community follow him, like the saying of one who said to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, at the time of condolence:

"Be patient, and you will be patient through your example,
for the patience of the subjects follows the patience of the head."

He said: All of that is in guiding the sound intellect. And, regarding the sentence being in the position of a reason for what preceded, al-'Allama al-Tibi went this way, saying: When He, exalted is He, commanded His beloved to be patient with the harm of the opponents and forbade him from grieving over their obstinacy and refusal of the Truth, and over what befalls him of their deception and cunning, He gave the reason for that by His saying, glorified is He: "Indeed Allah..." etc., meaning: do not care about them and their cunning, for Allah, exalted is He, is your guardian, your beloved, your helper, and the one who abandons them and humiliates them. He generalised the ruling as guidance to follow his example, the prayers and peace of God be upon him. In it there is an implicit reference against the opponents and their being forsaken, as He stated explicitly in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because Allah is the protector of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no protector⁠﴾. He mentioned that the second clause being nominal, and the construction of "doers of good" upon "they" (hum) in the manner of emphasis on taqwa, indicates the continuity and firm establishment of ihsan. This necessarily entails the continuity of taqwa, because ihsan is only complete if one does not return to what one was upon of wrongdoing. To this is the allusion in what is reported: "Part of the goodness of a person's Islam is his leaving what does not concern him."

What has been mentioned about interpreting taqwa as its highest level is not definitive, and what he mentioned in its explanation is not free from scrutiny, as is not hidden from the reflective. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and others have reported from al-Hasan that he said regarding the verse: "Be mindful of Allah regarding what He has forbidden them, and do good regarding what He has obligated upon them." The speech of some of them implies that the sentence is in the position of a reason for the command to requite with the like, when he said: The meaning is that Allah, by aid, mercy and grace, is with those who feared the punishment of Allah, exalted is He, and were apprehensive of it, so they show compassion to His creation after excess in punishment. He interpreted ihsan as leaving off wrongdoing, as it is said: "Leaving off wrongdoing is ihsan and a summary." What is in this of remoteness is not hidden. These verses include teaching good manners in calling (to Allah), abandoning transgression, and the command to be patient with what is disliked, together with good tidings for the God-fearing doers of good. Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and others have reported from Harim ibn Hayyan that he was told at the time of his death: "Make a bequest." He said: "A bequest is only from wealth, and I have no wealth. But I bequeath to you the final verses of Surat al-Nahl, this."

* * *

From the door of allusive interpretation (ishara) in the verses: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation of all things⁠﴾, meaning, of what has been and what will be, by which is distinguished between the one upholding the truth and the one in falsehood, the truthful and the liar, the follower and the innovator. It has also been said: "All things" is the Prophet (ﷺ), just as it has been said that he, the prayers and peace of God be upon him, is the Imam in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And all things We have enumerated in a clear Imam⁠﴾. ﴿Indeed, Allah commands justice, excellence, and giving to kindred, and forbids immorality, wrongdoing and oppression. He admonishes you that you may remember⁠﴾. Al-Sayyadi said: Justice is seeing the grace from Him, exalted is He, both of old and in the present. Excellence is steadfastness with the condition of fulfilment unto eternity. It has also been said: Justice is that the servant does not see himself as slackening in obedience to his Master while not looking for a return. Giving to kindred is excellence towards relatives in recognition, love and religion, so that one serves them with sincerity and compassion and pays their rights to them. Immorality is making light of the Sharia, and wrongdoing is persistence in sin in whatever manner it may be. Oppression is wronging the servants. It has also been said: Immorality is attributing things to other than Him, exalted is He, in ownership and origination. ﴿And fulfil the covenant of Allah⁠﴾, which was taken from you in the world of spirits, by remaining upon its ruling, which is turning away from other than Him and being stripped of attachments and hindrances in turning towards Him, exalted is He, ﴿when you pledge⁠﴾, that is, when you remember it through the illumination of the light of the Prophet (ﷺ) upon you and his reminding you of it. Al-Nasrabadhi said: Covenants vary. The covenant of the common people is adherence to outward appearances; the covenant of the elite is guarding the inner secrets; the covenant of the elite of the elite is being emptied of all for the One to whom all belongs. ﴿What is with you⁠﴾ of attributes is exhausted because of the place of origination. ﴿And what is with Allah is lasting⁠﴾ because of the place of eternity. So the true servant is he who is annihilated from his own attributes and remains through what is with Allah, exalted is He, as is found in Asrar al-Qur'an. ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female⁠﴾, that is, an action that brings him to his perfection which his capacity requires. ﴿While he is a believer⁠﴾, one who holds the Truth with firm conviction. ﴿We will surely cause him to live a good life⁠﴾, that is, a true life after which there is no death, by being stripped of bodily matter, joining the thread of the holy lights, and delighting in the perfections of the attributes and in the witnessing of the manifestations of the acts and attributes. ﴿And We will surely reward them their reward⁠﴾ from the gardens of the attributes and the acts ﴿according to the best of what they used to do⁠﴾, since their deed corresponds to their attributes which are the sources of their acts, and their reward corresponds to the attributes of Allah, exalted is He, which are the sources of His acts. So consider how much difference there is between them in beauty. It is also said: The good life is that which is with the beloved, and from here it has been said:

"Every life that passes without being with a beauty has no salt for that life."

﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they were tested, then struggled and were patient, indeed your Lord after that is Forgiving, Merciful⁠﴾. Sahl said: It refers to those who turned back in the path of their journey, then returned. That is: indeed your Lord is for those who forsook the companions of evil after the temptation had appeared to them from them in their company, then struggled against their own selves to keep company with the people of goodness, then were patient with them in that, and did not return to what they were upon in the temptation, while a concealer of what proceeded from them is the Bestower upon them with various kinds of bounty. It has also been said: Indeed your Lord is for those who emigrated, that is, who distanced themselves from the abode of the self by abandoning the familiar and the desired, after they had been tested by them by the nature of human creation, then struggled for Allah, exalted is He, through spiritual exercises and traversing His path, glorified is He, by ascending through the stations and stripping away attachments, and were patient regarding what the self loves and what it dislikes, by steadfastness in the journey. Indeed your Lord is Forgiving, who covers the veils of the carnal attributes, Merciful in bestowing perfection and holy attributes. (Allah sets forth an example) for the receptive soul which is fit to receive the overflow of the heart, which is steadfast in the path of acquiring virtues, safe from fear of losing them, tranquil through belief in them. ﴿Its provision comes to it abundantly⁠﴾ of knowledge, virtues and lights, ﴿from every place⁠﴾, from all the directions of the bodily channels such as the senses, limbs and faculties, and from the direction of the heart. ﴿But it denied the favours of Allah⁠﴾, it manifested through its attributes arrogance and self-admiration with its adornment, and looked at its own essence with its splendour and radiance. So it veiled itself with its dark attributes from those lights, and inclined to the lowly matters, and the flow of the heart to it was cut off, and the meanings coming to it through the channels of sense turned into dark forms of the sensible objects to which it had been drawn. ﴿So Allah made it taste the garment of hunger⁠﴾ through the cutting off of the supply of meanings, virtues and lights from the heart, and fear of the loss of its acquisitions from the desires and familiar things, ﴿because of what they used to do⁠﴾, of denying the favours of Allah, exalted is He. ﴿And there had certainly come to them a messenger from among them⁠﴾, that is, from their own kind, and this is the rational faculty. ﴿But they denied him⁠﴾ regarding what was presented to them of intelligible meanings and true opinions. ﴿So the punishment seized them⁠﴾, that is, the punishment of deprivation and veiling. ﴿While they were wrongdoers⁠﴾, in the state of their wronging and their elevating themselves above the path of virtue and their diminishing the rights of their companion. ﴿Indeed Abraham was a community⁠﴾, by the gathering in him of what is scattered in others of perfect attributes. Likewise every prophet. For this reason it came in the report, as has been said: "If I were weighed against my community, I would outweigh them." ﴿Devoutly obedient to Allah⁠﴾, obedient to Him, glorified is He, in the most perfect manner. ﴿Upright⁠﴾, inclining away from everything other than Him, exalted is He. ﴿And he was not of those who associate⁠﴾, by ascribing anything to other than Him, glorified is He. ﴿Grateful for His favours⁠﴾, using them in the manner that is fitting. ﴿He chose him⁠﴾, selected him without the intermediary of work, because he was of those for whom the good had preceded, so their unveilings preceded their journeying. ﴿And guided him⁠﴾ after the unveiling ﴿to a straight path⁠﴾, which is the station of guidance and calling, by which they reach the station of distinction after unification. ﴿And We gave him in this world good⁠﴾, which is the good remembrance, the great kingdom and prophethood. ﴿And indeed in the Hereafter⁠﴾, it has been said, that is, in the world of spirits, ﴿he is surely among the righteous⁠﴾, those firmly established in the station of uprightness. It has also been said, that is, on the Day of Resurrection, he is among the righteous fit to sit on the carpet of nearness and witnessing without a veil. This is to remove the misconception that what he was given in this world diminishes his station in the afterlife, just as it is said that the station of the well-known saint is less than that of the saint who is in the corners of obscurity. To this is the allusion in the saying of people: "Fame is a calamity." And it has been explicitly stated

Concerning this, al-Sha'rani, in one of his books, [said regarding] ﴿The Sabbath was only ordained for those who differed concerning it﴾, and they are the Jews. They chose it because it is the day on which the days of creation were completed, so it was, in their assumption, most suitable for abandoning worldly occupations. And according to what the Greatest Shaykh (al-Shaykh al-Akbar, Ibn al-'Arabi), may his secret be sanctified, said in al-Futuhat, it is the Day of Eternity (yawm al-abad) which has no end: its night is in Hell and its day is in Paradise. The Christians chose Sunday because it is the first day on which Allah, exalted is He, attended to the creation of creatures, so it was, in their assumption, more fitting to devote oneself to the worship of Allah, exalted is He, and to thanking Him, glorified is He. But Allah, exalted is He, has guided [us] to what is greater than that, namely Friday, the day on which Allah, exalted is He, completed creation, and in which the wisdom of imitating the creation of man appears, the man who was created in the form of the Most Merciful. So it is more fitting that a person devote himself on it to worship and thanksgiving than those two days. Glory be to Him who created and guided.

﴿And if you punish, then punish with the like of that with which you were punished. But if you are patient, it is indeed better for the patient﴾, because in that there is subduing of the self, which necessitates its ascent to the highest stations.

﴿And be patient, and your patience is not except by Allah﴾. It has been said: patience has divisions: patience for Allah, the Exalted; patience in Allah, the Exalted; patience with Allah, the Exalted; patience from Allah, the Exalted; and patience by Allah, the Exalted. Patience by Allah, the Exalted, is among the necessary qualities of faith and the first of the degrees of Islam; it is restraining the self from anxiety upon the loss of something desired or the occurrence of something disliked. It is among the virtuous character traits bestowed by Allah's grace upon the people of His religion and obedience, which entail a great reward. Patience in Allah, the Exalted, is steadfastness in following the path of truth, settling the self to strive by choice, abandoning what is familiar and pleasurable, bearing afflictions, and strength of resolve in turning toward the source of perfections; it is among the stations of the wayfarers, which Allah, the Exalted, grants to whomever He wills among the people of the path. Patience with Allah, the Exalted, belongs to the people of presence and unveiling, upon being stripped of the garments of actions and attributes, and being exposed to the manifestations of beauty and majesty, and the successive arrival of the states of intimacy and awe; it is, by presence of the heart for whoever has a heart, and guarding against heedlessness and absence at the variations of states by the appearance of the self; and it is far harder on the self than striking the head, though it is very delicious. Patience from Allah, the Exalted, belongs to the people of direct vision and witnessing, from the lovers who yearn, who turn through the stages of manifestation and concealment, who are stripped of the human nature and clothed in the light of divinity, such that no heart or attribute remains for them; whenever a light from the flashes of the lights of beauty appears to them, they burn and perish, and whenever a veil is set up for them and their existence is returned, out of longing and exaltation, they taste of the pain of yearning and the burning of separation, by which their patience is spent and their death is realized. Patience by Allah, the Exalted, belongs to the people of establishment (al-tamkin) in the station of steadfastness, whom Allah, the Exalted, has annihilated entirely, leaving nothing of the remainder of selfhood and duality upon them; then He bestowed upon them an existence from His own essence, so that they stand by Him and act by His attributes. This is among the characteristics of Allah, the Exalted, in which no one has a share. For this reason, after Allah, glorified is He, commanded it to His Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, He made clear to him, upon him be blessings and peace: "Indeed you do not undertake it except through Me, and you cannot bear it except by My strength." Then He, glorified is He, said to His Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: ﴿And do not grieve over them﴾, for all is from Me; ﴿and do not be in distress over what they plot﴾, because your breast is expanded through Me; ﴿Indeed, Allah is with those who fear Him﴾, who have left their remnants and passed away in Him, glorified is He; ﴿and those who are doers of good﴾, by witnessing the unity within multiplicity. These are the ones whom distinction does not veil from union, nor union from distinction, and who are capable of attending to both the Truth and creation.

Al-Tibi mentioned that taqwa in the verse is in the position of repentance for the knower, and ihsan is in the position of journeying and wayfaring through the states and stations until one reaches the effacement of traces and arrival at the chamber of intimacy. This is what there is; and Allah, glorified is He, is the Guide to the straight path. So we ask Him, majestic is His station, to guide us to Himself, to grant us success in beneficial knowledge from Him, to open for us the treasures of secrets, and to protect us from the evil of the wicked, by the sanctity of the Great Qur'an and the Noble Messenger, upon him be the best of blessings and the most complete of peace.
